0044afd3-0f41-5241-b9c1-a6db304da182.name: Dish.
0044afd3-0f41-5241-b9c1-a6db304da182.description: A dish with a slightly foliated rim. The decoration, executed in underglaze painting, extends all the way to the edge of the bowl. It features a floral spray which includes blue tulips growing on turquoise stems and greyish-purple, carnation-like blossoms growing at the ends of spiky green stems. The flowers appear to be distributed at random, but in fact the composition is quite orderly: the large blue tulips alternate around the rim of the dish with groupings in which one smaller tulip (characterised by a fork-like turquoise 'frame') is sandwiched between two purple blossoms. The only place in which this rhythm is interrupted is at the upper right, where a lonely cloud-band takes the place of the expected tulip. The long stems of all these flowers are balanced out in the middle of the bowl by judiciously placed blossoms. This type of composition represents a transitional period in Iznik ceramic decoration, when a taste for elaborate compositions with long serrated leaves and large rosettes was giving way to a more free and naturalistic idiom.
0044afd3-0f41-5241-b9c1-a6db304da182.short_description: A dish with a slightly foliated rim, decorated with a spray of blue tulips and greyish-purple blossoms. The composition represents a transitional period in Iznik ceramic decoration, when a taste for elaborate compositions was giving way to a more free and naturalistic idiom.
0044afd3-0f41-5241-b9c1-a6db304da182.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
0044afd3-0f41-5241-b9c1-a6db304da182.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, Istanbul/London, 1989, p.142 and fig. 369.
0044afd3-0f41-5241-b9c1-a6db304da182.author: Barry Wood

005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.name: Group of four tiles.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.description: A group of four stone-paste ceramic tiles painted in blue, emerald-green and red underglaze with large split-palmettes and lotus blossoms. The four tiles together create a symmetrical formation of leaves and flowers that would have been part of a larger group covering the interior of a building. Split-palmettes form a geometric structure surrounded by softer swirling flowers and small green leaves. The brilliant flame-red was created from iron-slip made from the iron-rich bole found in Armenia. Introduced to the ceramics industry in Iznik in about AH 956 / AD 1550, the iron-slip was applied thickly to prevent it from running under the glaze. New forms of decoration appear with this striking red underglaze; alongside the so-called *saz* leaf found in tiles and vessels from the previous decades, are more realistic plant forms such as hyacinths, carnations and tulips, as well as large lotus blossoms.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.short_description: These tiles feature the distinctive *saz* leaf next to flowers such as hyacinths, carnations, tulips and lotus blossoms. The bright red glaze on these tiles was a colour introduced to the Iznik ceramic industry in about AH 956 / AD 1550 and became popular for both vessels and tiles.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.type: Stone paste blue, red and turquoise painting
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.dates: Second half of hegira 10th / AD 16th century.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.method_for_datation: A number of buildings from the second half of the 10th / 16th century feature tiles with similar designs painted with the same distinctive flame-red colour; for example, the Mosque of Rustam Pasha of 969 (1559) in Istanbul, or the mihrab and sultan's lodge in the Selimiye Mosque of 976–82 (1569–75) in Edirne.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.method_for_provenance: It is not known where this particular group of tiles originated, but they were certainly produced in Iznik for a building in the Ottoman domain. In the second half of the 10th / 16th century, the major output of Iznik kilns was tiles rather than vessels. A number of documents record frequent missives from the imperial court in Istanbul pressing the potters of Iznik to concentrate on the tiles needed for imperial architectural projects.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.obtention: Part of the Godman Bequest of 1983.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.bibliography:
Atasoy. N., and Raby, J., Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey, London, 1989.  
  
Carswell, J., Iznik Pottery, London, 1998, pp.74–89.  
  
Porter, V., Islamic Tiles, London, 1995, pp.104–9, fig. 97.
005b3121-9261-5bac-a10d-c020d7f52f78.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Geometric decoration; floral decoration; hyacinths; tilework
materials: Stone-paste ceramic with blue, emerald-green and red painting under the glaze.

008afac0-e38b-550a-a0d2-9a4b088b3083.name: Bowl with inscription
008afac0-e38b-550a-a0d2-9a4b088b3083.short_description: A ceramic bowl covered with a white slip and transparent glaze. The sole decoration on a white background is an Arabic inscription in black and a stylized flower in the centre. The inscription is benedictory in the *kufic* script: “Blessings and joy to the owner”. The bowl belongs to a type of pottery typical of the Samanid workshops in eastern Iran. The characteristic inscriptions usually include proverbs or wishes, and the reader is invited to rotate the object to read them.

0124cd97-dd77-5681-bbcc-85d4dc5ef20b.name: Teapot
0124cd97-dd77-5681-bbcc-85d4dc5ef20b.short_description: This hand-painted teapot from Afghanistan is made of Russian Gardner porcelain, a factory that produced goods in vibrant colours with European-style floral patterns for the market of Central Asia in the mid-18th century. The metal repairs were done by professional porcelain restorers that are typical of Afghanistan. Total recycling; nothing is thrown away, and everything is repaired.
0124cd97-dd77-5681-bbcc-85d4dc5ef20b.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
0124cd97-dd77-5681-bbcc-85d4dc5ef20b.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.
0124cd97-dd77-5681-bbcc-85d4dc5ef20b.obtention: Collected 1969 by Dr. Alfred Janata, curator at the Museum für Völkerkunde, during his fieldwork in Afghanistan.
0124cd97-dd77-5681-bbcc-85d4dc5ef20b.bibliography: Steinmann, Axel, *Afghanistan, exhibition catalogue*, Vienna: Museum für Völkerkunde, 2003: 132.

01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.name: Rectangular tile.
01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.description: A stone-paste (fritware) rectangular tile that would originally have formed part of a border surrounding a large tile panel. It is composed of an interlacing arabesque design in white with red detailing. The entirety is outlined in black, with accents on the inside curves of the arabesques and on the red detailing also rendered in black. The entire composition is set against a vivid turquoise background.
01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.short_description: Tiles of this decorative style are associated with the extensive tile production of Iznik in Turkey from the AH late 10th–early 11th centuries / AD mid-16th–17th centuries. Originally this tile would have formed part of a border surrounding a large tile panel.
01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.dates: Hegira, late 10th century / AD late 16th century.
01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.method_for_datation: This tile has been dated on the basis of stylistic comparison with related Iznik pieces attributed to the late 10th / late 16th century.
01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.method_for_provenance: Tiles of this decorative style are associated with the period of almost exclusive production of tiles in preference to other ceramic wares in the Iznik workshops from the late 10th–early 11th century / late 16th–early 17th centuries.
01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.bibliography: Carswell, J., *Iznik Pottery*, London, 1998 (for general reference).
01f5cb79-72ae-5641-9e6b-2cdc4bbb24ac.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware), blue, black and turquoise underglaze, with bole-red slip, over which a clear glaze.

021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.name: Jar
021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.description:
This container for transporting and storing date molasses was made from the stomach lining of an animal, such as a sheep or goat.  
Made from raw leather, this jar has been waterproofed with several layers of natural resin. It has a large stained wooden stopper. The rim of the opening is made of gypsum and three layers of leather to ensure a truly waterproof seal. This use of animal leather demonstrates the commitment of populations living on seasonal pastures in the desert and involved in the production and trade of date syrup.  
  
In Qatar, it's known as a *dabba*.
021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.obtention: Object has been in the National Museum's permanent collection since 1975.
021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.author: Tania Abdulmonem Al Majid

023e92fe-fb35-54cf-a11d-cb41fb889495.name: Dish with hyacinths
023e92fe-fb35-54cf-a11d-cb41fb889495.short_description: Dish painted with hyacinths, rosettes, and stems springing from a common root. The palette is characteristic of the so-called Damascus ware with manganese-purple, sage-green, cobalt blue and turquoise colours. These are characteristic of the work produces around 1555-1570 and may be attributed to the circle of the ‘Master of the Hyacinths’. The Iznik potters depicted recognisable flowers from among the local flora, no longer limiting themselves to the traditional stylised floral arabesques.
023e92fe-fb35-54cf-a11d-cb41fb889495.type: Ottoman ceramic, fritware with polychrome underglaze decoration
materials: Frit ware with polychrome underglaze decoration

02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.name: Pair of candlesticks.
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.description: A pair of ceramic candlesticks of identical shape, with blue-and-white underglaze. Candlesticks of this shape were not usually produced in ceramic; the form derives from metalwork, of a type produced for the Italian market. The sloping sides of one of the candlesticks are painted with oval-shaped medallions interspersed with floral motifs, while the second candlestick has an undulating leafy scroll around the sides of the body. Both have floral scrolls around the base, a blue-and-white striped candle-holder, with a further row of flowers around the top. The distinctive 'tadpole' leaf featured here is a common feature of blue-and-white ceramics of this period. The origins of early Iznik blue-and-white ceramics can be traced to Chinese porcelain. These candlesticks were produced during the reign of Sultan Suleyman (AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66) when there was a considerable expansion of the ceramics industry in Iznik.
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.short_description: The design of these Iznik ceramic candlesticks is influenced by Chinese blue-and-white porcelain. This pair was produced in the early years of Süleyman the Magnificent’s reign, when the Iznik ceramic industry expanded considerably.
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.type: Stone paste blue and turquoise painting
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.method_for_datation: The date of this type of blue-and-white ceramic is established by a dated cut-down bottle in the British Museum dated 935 (1529). There are also tiles in the tomb of Mustafa Pasha (d. 934–5 / 1528–9) at Gebze, east of Istanbul depicting similar floral types and leaves.
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the main centre of manufacture for ceramics of this style, and produced by this technique, in Ottoman Turkey.
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by John Henderson in 1878.
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.bibliography: Carswell, J., *Iznik Pottery*, London, 1998, pp.51–2, plate 28.
02bdeffc-6e44-572b-83b7-207f18622c2d.author: Emily Shovelton

0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.name: Ceramic tile with a picture of the Ka‘ba.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.description:
Blue, green and red pigments have been used on a white background. A border with a chain-motif, drawn in black on a blue background, frames the single-piece tile. This is enriched by a second border made up of blue palmettes which ends at the top of the tile in a *mihrab* shape. The *mihrab*'s two corners are decorated with interlacing *rumi* (split-palmette) motifs on a dark-blue background. In the middle of the *mihrab*, also on a dark-blue ground, is a symmetrical pediment motif decorated with arabesques, at the bottom of which is an inscription in three rows of black *naskhi* script. The inscription contains *sura* 3, verses 96–7 of the Qur'an: 'Lo! the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind was that at Becca \[Mecca\] a blessed place, a guidance to the peoples; Wherein are plain memorials (of Allah's guidance); the place where Abraham stood up to pray; and whosoever entereth it is safe.' Below this text, the Masjid al-Haram is depicted within a rectangle drawn in green and blue. The Ka'ba is shown in the middle of the Masjid al-Haram, recognisable by its porticoed courtyard. The various buildings, gates, sacred spots (*maqams*), and water-wells located within the porticoes are represented and identified with their names.  
  
Introducing the holy cities of Islam (Mecca and Medina) and the sacred sites therein with books, and reinforcing this introduction with pictures, is seen from the early period of Islam. Detailed pictures of these holy places were put in pilgrimage certificates, which were made especially in the Ayyubid period, and which have an important place in the Museum's collection. These documents begin with the banner of the caliph of the time and show painted images of Mount Arafat, Muzdalifa, the Sacred Enclosure (al-Haram al-Sharif), Medina, and even Jerusalem. Similar pictures of the holy places were made for pilgrimage certificates in Ottoman art. Beginning at the end of the 10th / 16th century images of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca are also found depicted on tiles in certain mosques.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.short_description: This tile panel is assumed to have been produced at Iznik for the Mosque of Neslişah Sultan in Edirnekapı, Istanbul. The purpose of tile panels depicting the Ka'ba was to feel its presence, the most sacred shrine of Islam, during prayer at the mosque.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.initial_owner: Sultan Neslişah (d. 987 / 1579; granddaughter of Sultan Bayezid II).
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.dates: Hegira last quarter of the 10th century / AD 16th century.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.method_for_datation: The panel was originally embedded in the wall of the Neslişah Sultan Mosque built in the late 16th century. Since such panels are not found in every mosque, and the quality of the work suggests that it was made for a structure built by an important person, it is plausible to think it was specially made for the aforementioned mosque.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.method_for_provenance: The materials, techniques and colours used are typical of an Iznik-produced tile.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.obtention: The tile was transferred to the Museum in 1914 from the mosque of Neslişah Sultan, the grandchild of Sultan Bayezid II, in the Edirnekapı section of Istanbul.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.bibliography: Ölçer, N. *et al, Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, p. 282.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.author: Cihat Soyhan
materials: Iznik tile of white clay, with a painting of the Ka‘ba in underglaze.

03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.name: Pilgrim flask
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.short_description: The basic form of the canteen, which is still in use today, may be traced to Roman times; it has changed little over the centuries. While medieval Islamic canteens are sometimes referred to as pilgrim flasks, most seem to have played a more quotidian role as water vessels. There are large numbers of such unglazed canteens, mainly ranging in date from Hegira 6th–8th centuries / AD 12th–14th centuries and attributable to Iran, Syria, and Anatolia. A few canteens are glazed as well, such as this example; all have applied handles, which would allow for suspension.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.dates: Hegira mid-6th century / AD mid-12th century
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.method_for_datation: The carved relief decoration, a central rosette surrounded by a leafy scroll on one face and a rabbit circumscribed by the same leafy scroll on the other, is related to similar designs on ceramic wares from Syria, which are generally dated to the 12th century.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.method_for_provenance: The canteen’s carved relief decoration is related to similar designs on ceramic wares from Syria.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.obtention: Collection of Maan Z. Madina (1926-2013), New York, until 2002 (sold to); LACMA, The Madina Collection of Islamic Art, gift of Camilla Chandler Frost.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.bibliography:
Komaroff, Linda, *Lo Terrenal y lo divino: Arte islámico siglos VII al XIX Colección del Museo de Arte del Condado de Los Angeles*, Santiago, Chile: Centro Cultural La Moneda, 2015: 133, 136.  
Komaroff, Linda, *Beauty and Identity: Islamic Art from the Los Angeles County Museum of Art*, Los Angeles: Los Angeles County Museum of Art, 2016: 102.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.author: LACMA Staff
keywords: Pilgrim flasks; vessels; ceramic; Zangids; pilgrimage
materials: Fritware, carved and glazed, with applied neck and handle

03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.name: Kütahya ceramics.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.description:
Inv. no. 4083, a cup, is decorated with green and yellow radial designs with flowers in them.  
  
Inv. no. 4092, a cup, is decorated with a stylised tulip within a circle and a band around the rim. On the exterior a flower grows from a red and dark-green base. Inv. no. 4151, a rosewater sprinkler, has a pear-shaped body divided by yellow bands into sections with stylised arabesques and flowers.  
  
Inv. no. 4215, a plate, is decorated in purple, green and blue with a painting of a woman in local dress between two bouquets of flowers. Inv. no. 4216 is a canteen decorated with floral motifs in yellow, red, green and blue. Inv. no. 4231 is another canteen, the back and front of the round body decorated with raised circles. The front has a rosette surrounded by chain motifs. The other sides bear stylised flower and leaf motifs.  
  
After the cessation of tile and ceramic production at Iznik, the ceramic workshops at Kütahya came to the fore. The most common products of these workshops are fine and delicate cups, bowls, ewers with lids, rosewater sprinklers, candlesticks, incense burners, small goblets, and canteens. They are made of hard white clay and have painted underglaze decorations of flowers, leaves, ivy, teardrops, birds, fish, and people in local dress. In the last years of the AH 12th / AD 18th century and the first years of the AH 13th / AD 19th century the quality of these wares is seen to decline. Forms are simplified and become rough; lilac and red disappear, and dark colours, including purple, dominate the decoration. During this period stylised leaves, lines, speckles, and zigzags appear, all painted with brushstrokes.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.short_description: Kütahya replaced Iznik as an Ottoman ceramic and tile production centre in the AH 12th–13th / AD 18th–19th centuries. Like Iznik ceramics, Kütahya ceramics were also an important merchandise exported worldwide via land or sea.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.dimensions: 4083: height 7 cm, diameter 8 cm; 4092: height 4.2 cm, diameter 7.3 cm; 4151: height 16.5 cm, diameter 5.6 cm; 4215: diameter 15 cm; 4216: diameter 18 cm; 4231: diameter 16 cm.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.method_for_datation: The style, designs and colours point to a date in the 12th–13th / 18th–19th centuries.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.method_for_provenance: The designs and colours indicate production in Kütahya. Today Kütahya is still one of  Turkey's major centres of glazed-ceramic production.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.obtention: All of the objects were recovered from a shipwreck in the Sea of Marmara and were purchased by the Museum in 1985.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.bibliography: ölçer, N. *et al, Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, pp.332–3.
03e3d46a-3509-564e-8a0c-ed2a1920de29.author: Cihat Soyhan
materials: hard white clay with underglaze painting.

0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.name: Dish.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.description:
When the kilns of Manises and Paterna were in their heyday, the fashion of the time moved towards plant themes, betraying a gradual departure from Hispano-Muslim tradition. Certain designs remained very simple and schematic, such as the dotted flowers used to decorate the bases of the pieces in the 'Hail Mary' series, so called because of their inscriptions about the Virgin Mary in German Gothic characters. The most common type, to which this dish belongs, consists of groups of between three and six large dots, circumscribed by a thin line, inscribed in irregular circular spaces formed by slender, enveloping stems. They are surrounded by tiny dots and occasionally, as in this case, there is a central circle with a cross also finished in dots. For this reasons, this type has been called the 'dotted series'.  
The dish, turned on a potter's wheel, has a broad flat brim, a concave bottom and an umbo. It is covered in a creamy white tin glaze, upon which the decoration has been applied by means of successive oxidising and reducing firings. The bird is rendered in cobalt-blue with golden dots.  
Although Valencian ceramicists produced different sized dishes, there is a predominance of smaller ones. Along with large examples, such as this one, there are other smaller ones with deer, gazelles, parrots, *fleurs-de-lys* and crowned initials.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.short_description: This dish was produced during the peak of technical creativity of the Manises potteries, at a time when Mudéjar ceramics in Valencia began to move away from the Hispano-Muslim decorative tradition and to incorporate new motifs, such as this realistic long-legged bird.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.dimensions: Height 4.5 cm, diameter 33.5 cm, diameter of base 11 cm.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.method_for_datation: From its style and the extensive documentation held in Valencian archives and published by a range of different authors, including Martínez Caviró (see bibliography). The coats of arms are very important references.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.method_for_provenance: From its characteristics described above, it is unquestionable that the piece originated in Valencia. Manises was the most important centre of production, lending its name to an entire style of ceramics. Recent excavations in Paterna have revealed the existence of other similar workshops, although the pieces found so far, produced using the same technique, are of inferior quality.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from Vicente Juan y Amat on 27 June 1872.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.bibliography:
Camps Cazorla, E., *Catálogo Sumario del Museo Arqueológico Nacional. Cerámica Española (Nuevas Instalaciones)*, Madrid, 1936, p.32, plate IV.  
Franco Mata, á., Balmaseda Muncharaz, L., Arias Sánchez, I. and Papí Rodes, C., “La Documentación de las Cerámicas Valencianas Medievales en el Museo Arqueológico Nacional”, in *La Cerámica de Paterna. Reflejos del Mediterráneo*, Exhibition catalogue, Valencia, 2002, pp.106–18.  
Martínez Caviró, B., *Cerámica Hispanomusulmana*, Madrid, 1991, p.152, fig. 148.
0420c3d3-1445-51f2-9539-5a794d209ebf.author: Ángela Franco
keywords: Dish; clay; kaolin; firing; glazed; gold highlights; Mudéjar; Manises; Valencia
materials: Clay, kaolin; firing, glazing, golden highlights.

043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.name: Dish.
043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.description:
A circular stone-paste (fritware) dish with a shallow well, an everted rim and a circular foot. The well shows a frontally disposed female figure, reserved in white and outlined in black, against a green background. She wears a short-sleeved, kaftan-like coat (*üçetek*) that is belted with a green sash and worn over a long dress. The coat has a tulip-shaped bottom edge that opens at the front and slit at each side. She wears a cape-like garment rendered in white with blue spots around her shoulders and a tall head-cover formed from a folded scarf, and decorated with tulips and leaves in red and blue. On her feet she wears red socks and flat shoes. Her left arm is raised while in her right, she holds a tall, slender ewer with a red teardrop-shaped centre. The woman is surrounded on both sides by four sprays of flowers, comprising two prunus blossoms, a tulip, a carnation and a rose-like plant. All grow from four leafy tufts below. The rim shows a debased wave border. The underside of the dish is decorated with six small green, leaf motifs with black outlines, set at regular intervals.  
Plates such as this mark the last phase of Iznik production starting in the early AH 11th / AD 17th century. The woman on this plate has been compared to similar figures occurring as album paintings prepared for Sultan Ahmed I and to single-figure paintings produced contemporaneously for Europeans in the bazaars of Istanbul.
043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.short_description: Plates like this one mark the last phase of Iznik production starting in the early AH 11th / AD 17th century. The lady on this plate resembles figures from album paintings prepared for Sultan Ahmed I and single-figure paintings produced for Europeans in the bazaars of Istanbul at the time.
043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.dates: Hegira, early 11th century / AD early 17th century.
043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.method_for_datation: This plate belongs to a well-known sub-group of Iznik ceramics with individual male or female figures forming the main design, generally attributed to the early 11th / early 17th century.
043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.method_for_provenance: Stylistically related pieces are known to have been produced in Iznik during the early 11th / early 17th century.
043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.obtention: Purchased from Jan Struther Antiques, Edinburgh, in 1973.

043212e6-dcaa-5260-93ad-6764b61c5752.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware), green, blue, red and black underglaze, over which a clear glaze.

0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.name: Table.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.description:
A low table made of wood inlaid with cloud-bands and simple arabesque compositions in ebony and mother-of-pearl; set into the top is an underglaze painted ceramic tile with a centralised design featuring flowers on an arabesque framework, surrounded by a border with cloud-bands on a turquoise background. The table has 12 sides, to match the 12 sides of the ceramic top, but it is constructed with spandrel-like joins between the legs so that it stands on six legs.  
  
This table is a rare example of furniture from the Ottoman imperial court, as well as a most unusual use of Iznik tilework. The beautiful, bright colours of the tile make a striking contrast to the subdued tones of the inlaid wood. It seems unlikely that such a fine piece of furniture would have been intended for everyday use; more likely, it was used as part of the elaborate ceremonials which defined Ottoman court protocol and impressed foreign ambassadors.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.short_description: A table made of wood inlaid with ivory and mother-of-pearl, with a 12-sided Iznik tile serving as the top. A rare example of furniture from the Ottoman court, this splendid table may have been used in the elaborate ceremonials which defined court protocol and impressed visiting ambassadors.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.type: Woodwork, mother of pearl, painted, glazed ceramic
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.method_for_datation: The technique, materials and style of the woodwork are similar to those found on the throne of Sultan Süleyman in the Topkapı Palace Museum in Istanbul. The tile, too, is similar to those found in Sultan Süleyman's mosque (completed in 963 / 1557), though its size and distinct shape mean it must have been made specifically as a table-top.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period; Istanbul, as home to the imperial ateliers, may be where the wood was inlaid and the final product assembled.

Mitter, P. and Clunas, C., "The Empire of Things: The Engagement with the Orient", A Grand Design: The Art of the Victoria and Albert Museum (eds. M. Baker and B. Richardson), London, 1997, p.255.  
  
Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.103.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.author: Barry Wood
materials: Wood, mother-of-pearl, painted and glazed ceramic.

045254ba-cb4b-504a-ab29-8546af52208c.name: Albarello
045254ba-cb4b-504a-ab29-8546af52208c.short_description:
This elegant albarello, a pharmacy jar with concave sides, has a form that was developed in Iran and Syria and became popular in Europe via Spanish-Moorish majolica.  
It is unusually large and was made up of two parts that were joined in the center of the body. The decoration was derived from the Persian Sultanabad style, which spread in the 14th century to Syria and Egypt.
keywords: Albarello; Persian style; Fritware; medicine; medical plant
materials: Fritware painted in blue and black under the glaze

04925050-34fb-5313-ba81-db73b9a96789.name: Bowl with a lion attacking a fox
04925050-34fb-5313-ba81-db73b9a96789.short_description: It is now thought that stonepaste wares and lustre painting reached Syria from Fatimid Egypt almost simultaneously, in the late 11th or early 12th century, most probably through migrant craftsmen who later in the 12th century moved eastwards to Iran. They evidently established themselves in north-east Syria on the Euphrates (notably at Raqqa), but some pieces, including this example, have been associated with the site of Tell Minis, south of Aleppo and are consequently known as ‘Tell Minis wares’. The decorative repertory, generally in a monochrome chocolate lustre, is much influenced by the work of the Fatimid Egyptian lustre-painters on pottery and glass. The treatment of the decoration on this bowl, a lion attacking a fox on a ground of floral scrolls, is similar in style to the work of the Fatimid-Egyptian lustre painter, Sa‘d, who worked on both pottery and glass in Fustat (Old Cairo) in the early years of the 12th century.
04925050-34fb-5313-ba81-db73b9a96789.type: Bowl; stonepaste ware, lustre paint; ‘Tell Minis’ ware
04925050-34fb-5313-ba81-db73b9a96789.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
04925050-34fb-5313-ba81-db73b9a96789.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on stylistic and technical grounds.

keywords: bowl; stone-paste; lustre; Ayyubid; ‘Tell Minis’ ware; lion
materials: Stonepaste ware, with lustre-painted decoration over a colourless transparent glaze (‘Tell Minis’ ware)

04a11491-a326-52d7-ac85-c37a115eacb8.name: Bowl with birds
04a11491-a326-52d7-ac85-c37a115eacb8.short_description: The silhouettes of the four stylised birds, separated by vegetal motifs of Chinese inspiration, are outlined with rice-grain perforations largely considered a typically Chinese feature, but actually originating in medieval Persian pottery. Covered with a clear glaze, the perforations enhance the airy quality of the bird-decorated register, while the fish and the undulating aquatic plants on the bottom reveal a scene with paradisiacal connotations in Islamic art. The underglaze painting in two shades of blue, the elegant drawing and fine ceramic paste suggest that the bowl dates back to the seventeenth century. The blue-and-white decoration of Chinese influence adopted by the Safavid potters continued to enjoy a great popularity in Iran until the end of the nineteenth century.

05677772-fb33-5d00-af7f-9cb213149293.name: Bottle with depictions of dance and music
05677772-fb33-5d00-af7f-9cb213149293.short_description: This moulded bottle belongs to a group of like examples produced during the seventeenth century in Isfahan, Iran. One side of the bottle depicts a woman playing a tambourine; the other a seated prince watching a woman dance. These scenes of courtly leisure are common to a wide variety of Safavid (1501–1722) arts, including textiles, doors, tilework, and life-size wall paintings in palaces.

05945c6c-5991-53ff-b891-6b20f4a3899a.name: Tile panel
05945c6c-5991-53ff-b891-6b20f4a3899a.short_description: This panel consists of 185 tiles and 3 half tiles, each with embossed tulip, hyacinth, saz leaf, and cloudband motifs that form a large-scale repeating arabesque pattern. Indigo, turquoise, green, and red glazes are on a white background.

05f8401e-7094-5321-82a6-63bc32507180.name: Oil lamp.
05f8401e-7094-5321-82a6-63bc32507180.description: A ceramic, roughly triangular lamp that has four nozzles and a large handle, which has a highly debased animal's head at the end. Within its two inner channels are decorative lines in relief; a single line of *kufic* inscription is seen on each outer channel, which reads: 'Astura wa ibin Astan' ('Astoura and son of Astan'). The lamp is moulded, hard-baked buff ware with a metallic blackish brown slip that has been blackened by smoke. Such a lamp would have been used to in a domestic context.
05f8401e-7094-5321-82a6-63bc32507180.short_description: Ceramic lamp with four nozzles and a large handle, which has a debased animal’s head at the end. The body carries a *kufic* inscription that reads: Astura wa ibn Astan (Astoura and son of Astan). Such a lamp would have been used in a domestic context.

061b77bb-faee-50ba-9c83-99e488d5500a.name: Dish
061b77bb-faee-50ba-9c83-99e488d5500a.description: Large, white plate densely covered with vivid floral decoration consisting of tulips, roses and hyacinth on curved stems in addition to other flowers and leaves. Rim decorated with simplified plant motifs. On the back side of the rim five green and three blue spots.
061b77bb-faee-50ba-9c83-99e488d5500a.initial_owner: Muzeum Techniczno-Przemysłowe w Krakowie / Industrial Museum in Kraków

061b77bb-faee-50ba-9c83-99e488d5500a.method_for_provenance: Material, technique and design are characteristic for İznik, which was a centre of quality ceramic production in this period

065ee648-ada2-516d-a7cd-4adf36e94026.name: *Habb* water jar
065ee648-ada2-516d-a7cd-4adf36e94026.description: This large water jar (*habb*) combines a utilitarian function with ostentatious decoration. It occupied a place of honour in the domestic space. Water was drawn from it with a jug or pitcher as needed for daily living. The surface is adorned with stylised female figures that reflect the persistence, through millennia and civilisations, of the mother goddess.

06703762-5053-5671-b110-5b6f3f755b04.name: Wellhead
06703762-5053-5671-b110-5b6f3f755b04.description:
Ceramic wellheads of this type are distinctive for southern Spain throughout the entire period when the region was under Muslim dominance (AH 2nd to 9th / AD 8th-15th century). This wellhead, however, comes from the AH 4th - 6th / AD 10th-12th century, and holds a monumental decoration in two bands. The wider, lower band features a procession of graceful, long-eared gazelles alternating with birds set in roundels. Above it is a beautifully conceived Kufi inscription, which is illegible.  
  
The whitish decoration, which was originally green, provides an elegant contrast to the earthenware’s red ground and, like the size of the wellhead, bears witness to the virtuosity of the ceramist.
materials: Earthenware painted in green and a manganese-colored glaze

070af261-62bc-5eb0-a1c5-2ab9fe21bf39.name: Plate with a picture of a youth
070af261-62bc-5eb0-a1c5-2ab9fe21bf39.short_description:
Made during the Safavid period, this blue-and-white bowl depicts a young man surrounded by grape vines and a floral pattern. The figure wears a turban (*mandil*) and holds a drinking bowl and a vessel in his hands.  
The design is influenced by a new type of Chinese porcelain, consisting of cobalt blue painting on a white surface, which reached the Middle East in the 14 century. The production of these Chinese-influenced objects continued well into the eighteenth century. As with this dish, the objects can bear close resemblance to Chinese originals. As a typical Persian depiction, however, the motif of this specific bowl reflects local painting styles and is found in Iranian miniature painting from the 16th to the 18th century. Based on its style, it can be assumed that this bowl belongs to the so-called Kubachi ware group. The name refers to a small town in Dagestan in the Caucasus region where a corpus of glazed pottery was found without any reference to their origin or provenance. As a result of petrographic examinations, some of those objects can now be located to Samarkand and Nishapur.
070af261-62bc-5eb0-a1c5-2ab9fe21bf39.method_for_datation: The bowl has features specific to the Safavid period.
070af261-62bc-5eb0-a1c5-2ab9fe21bf39.obtention: Purchased in 1956 with funds from the Campe's Art Historical Foundation.

073cada1-b5a8-5fa6-bce4-4879f04d6814.name: Iznik jug
073cada1-b5a8-5fa6-bce4-4879f04d6814.short_description: An Iznik jug with one handle decorated with tulips and stems carrying small blue flowers. It was bought by Alexander Benaki in 1919 by the Cairo based dealer Boghos Ispenian whose name is handwritten in ink under the base, next to an etiquette indicating that it was part of the 1925 Alexandria exhibition.

074a1fed-663f-52de-8637-7774fe3a0861.name: Dish.
074a1fed-663f-52de-8637-7774fe3a0861.description:
The polychrome underglaze painted dish with a sloping rim and a deep well presents a black-outlined figure of a woman on a white background. The woman wears a long green, belted dress, a blouse with blue sleeves, white trousers and a green hat. Her shoes and the flower that she holds in her right hand are of thick pale red. Flowers on thin curved stems fill the area around the woman. The rim shows a standardised Chinese motif of waves and rocks. On the back the dish is painted with green and blue ornaments.  
Figurative depictions on Iznik ceramics were inspired by the popular imagery of miniature costume albums, many of which were produced for sale to Europeans from the beginning of the AH 11th century / AD 17th century.
074a1fed-663f-52de-8637-7774fe3a0861.short_description: Polychrome painted dish with a deep well presenting a female figure on a white background. The area around the woman is filled with flowers. Figurative depictions on Iznik ceramics were inspired by the popular imagery of miniature costume albums.
074a1fed-663f-52de-8637-7774fe3a0861.dates: Hegira first half of the 11th century / AD first half of the 17th century.
074a1fed-663f-52de-8637-7774fe3a0861.method_for_datation: The object was dated according to its decoration. Figurative depictions occurred in great number on Iznik ceramics from the beginning of the 11th / 17th century. They were inspired by single-figure costume studies such as the Album of Sultan Ahmed I (r. 1011–25 / 1603–17) and its popular copies.
074a1fed-663f-52de-8637-7774fe3a0861.method_for_provenance: From the wave and rock pattern on the rim and from the depicted human figure, which was a popular motif of Iznik ceramics.
074a1fed-663f-52de-8637-7774fe3a0861.obtention: Bought in 1904 from the collector and art dealer I. G. Fenton, London.

076574ae-4169-58ea-8669-32621e8dc0c1.name: Two-handled pot.
076574ae-4169-58ea-8669-32621e8dc0c1.description: Two-handled long-neck pot with a foot-ring. The decoration, painted in intense red lustre on a cream-white tin glaze, consists of solid-lustre plant motifs, which was common in later Hispano-Moorish products. The dotted base of the body of the pot depicts two typical birds, known as Valencian 'pardalots', painted in a characteristic style consisting of groups of lines. 'Pardalots' and 'grotesque lions' are unusual in the decorative repertoire of this type of piece, as is the shape of the pot, the different parts of which are outlined with thick bands of solid lustre.
076574ae-4169-58ea-8669-32621e8dc0c1.short_description: This pot belongs to a large group of objects produced in Valencia that were decorated with typical motifs and styles, although the birds (known as ‘pardalots’) and grotesque lions are unusual in this type of piece, as is the shape of the pot.
076574ae-4169-58ea-8669-32621e8dc0c1.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
076574ae-4169-58ea-8669-32621e8dc0c1.method_for_provenance: The prototype for the pardalot can almost certainly be traced back to the eagle, which was often included on the base of Valencian plates in the first half of the 9th / 15th century. This style, which evolved over time to produce increasingly accentuated forms, became widespread in Valencian production in the 12th / 18th century.

07cf31a6-6851-53f9-8c13-e6ab4472665d.name: Iznik plate
07cf31a6-6851-53f9-8c13-e6ab4472665d.short_description: This Iznik plate shows a pattern of overlapping edges on a green fond and an eight-petalled white flower.
07cf31a6-6851-53f9-8c13-e6ab4472665d.method_for_datation: The distinctive texture of the underglaze indicates it was made in an Iznik workshop.

08b6e3c0-94d9-573c-a123-ddbc53534246.name: Ewer with epigraphic decoration
08b6e3c0-94d9-573c-a123-ddbc53534246.description: In Iran, during the Seljuq period, a large number of moulds were produced, typically with epigraphic expressions, though figures or foliage are also found. The potters shaped ewers that often borrowed forms developed by coppersmiths. The turquoise glaze replaces with colour the detailed decoration of carving and silver inlay found in metal pieces.

09311848-694c-5394-ba8a-5b19e1bcb2e0.name: Wall tile.
09311848-694c-5394-ba8a-5b19e1bcb2e0.description: A square tile decorated with a large, central, symmetrical lotus-rosette design that is made up of several layers of petals and leaves, and which is surrounded by two wheat-stem-shaped branches. The entire design is executed in one colour blue (without shading or black outline) on a white background. The design of this tile shows the extent to which Middle Eastern material culture was influenced by Chinese blue-and-white porcelain ceramics. The genre to which this tile belongs includes the more commonly known blue-and-white hexagonal tiles that are sometimes also found decorated in turquoise and black.
09311848-694c-5394-ba8a-5b19e1bcb2e0.short_description: The lotus-rosette design on this Damascus-ware wall tile reveals the extent to which its Chinese counterpart has influenced Islamic Art. A number of examples of this type of blue-and-white tile can still be seen on the walls of Al-Tawrizi Shrine and Mosque, built in Damascus in the AH 830s / AD 1430s.
09311848-694c-5394-ba8a-5b19e1bcb2e0.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: a number of examples of this type of blue-and-white Damascus ware can be found in European museums, furthermore a number of these tiles survive on the walls of Al-Tawrizi Shrine and Mosque in Damascus, built in the 830s / 1430s.
09311848-694c-5394-ba8a-5b19e1bcb2e0.method_for_provenance: A number of these tiles survive on the walls of Al-Tawrizi Shrine and Mosque in Damascus, built in the 830s / 1430s.
09311848-694c-5394-ba8a-5b19e1bcb2e0.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

0945f0d0-17e6-52da-8c82-4b26290bbf1b.name: Tile panel 'The Threshing of Wheat'
0945f0d0-17e6-52da-8c82-4b26290bbf1b.short_description: This tile panel depicting the treshing of wheat using animals originally covered the wall of a bakery in Lisbon. Although it reproduces a traditional technique, this tile panel exemplifies the need for modernization of stores and public buildings which took place in main cities throughout Portugal by the beginning of the 20th century.
0945f0d0-17e6-52da-8c82-4b26290bbf1b.author: DGPC

09955371-479a-5a14-b2dc-ee4a31b465c8.name: Plate made from clay
09955371-479a-5a14-b2dc-ee4a31b465c8.description: This plate forms part of the material culture of rural households in Bangladesh, where it has traditionally been used in everyday food practices.
09955371-479a-5a14-b2dc-ee4a31b465c8.author: ActionAid Bangladesh

0a232d6e-3ce2-5412-be8a-b9cb0af2bff7.name: Tile
0a232d6e-3ce2-5412-be8a-b9cb0af2bff7.short_description: Kütahya was the second most important ceramic production centre after İznik due to the rich clay deposits in the area. Although there was a decline in ceramic production at the beginning of the 19th century, in the last quarter of that same century production was revived and new designs inspired by İznik ceramics were produced.

0a3243f6-1969-529b-93a6-9d278278b70f.name: Lidded ewer
0a3243f6-1969-529b-93a6-9d278278b70f.short_description: This terracotta vessel is probably made of a special clay called terra lemnia. This clay had been credited with antitoxic powers by ancient physicians such as Dioscorides and Galen. Arab translations of classical texts on medicine introduced this to the Islamic world, leading to the production of vessels made of this material. Such drinking vessels were probably also believed to protect drinkers from being poisoned. Afraid of dying from poison, Emperor Rudolf II charged Reinholf Lubenau, the physician at the Austrian embassy to the Ottoman court, with obtaining such vessels for him.
0a3243f6-1969-529b-93a6-9d278278b70f.method_for_datation: Arthistorical and historical analysis, archival and inventory research
0a3243f6-1969-529b-93a6-9d278278b70f.method_for_provenance: Listed in the AD 1880 inventary of Ambas collection

keywords: Furnishing; terra lemnia; medicine; science; scientific manuscript; Emperor Rudolf II; Habsburg; Ottoman-Austrian relations; court life; De Materia Medica

0ae3d4ea-7c05-5061-9bda-d8c4d8859491.name: Bowl with Design of Fish
0ae3d4ea-7c05-5061-9bda-d8c4d8859491.short_description: A bowl glazed medium turquoise blue with a darker blue on the rim and on the exterior, which has six plant forms. The interior has swirling black fish under transparent turquoise glaze, with the fish in three rows and four additional ones on the bottom. The glaze is crackled. The rim and exterior at top has a yellow iridescence. The light brown biscuit is visible on the bottom and on the short foot, which are unglazed. There is a slight chip on the inside of the foot rim.
0ae3d4ea-7c05-5061-9bda-d8c4d8859491.dates: Hegira Late 5th to late 7th century / AD 12th–13th century

0b91f97f-aa76-5d14-a2ae-6751b59baea3.name: Ring-shaped flask.
0b91f97f-aa76-5d14-a2ae-6751b59baea3.description: This is a particularly fine piece of ceramic art. Thinly coated with tin-based glaze, it has no slip coating. Simple, elegant and harmonious, its beauty lies in its absence of decoration and in the finesse of its shape. From a disc-shaped base rises a hollow ring which becomes slightly broader at its upper part. A long, cylindrical neck, with two buttress–like supports, has four circles incised around the top. A handle is attached at the base of the neck.
0b91f97f-aa76-5d14-a2ae-6751b59baea3.short_description: Despite the absence of decoration, the elegant shape and the harmony and simplicity of its component parts make this piece a real work of art, with its beauty found in the sparseness of its structure. The flask has a round, flat base below a slightly inflated ring topped with a long cylindrical neck.
0b91f97f-aa76-5d14-a2ae-6751b59baea3.dates: Hegira, second half of the 3rd century / AD 9th century.
0b91f97f-aa76-5d14-a2ae-6751b59baea3.method_for_datation: Raqqada, the Aghlabid capital, was built in 263 / 876 by the Aghlabid prince Ibrahim II. Since the flask was discovered on the excavation site, this date must be a *terminus ante quem*. Moreover, the constituent shapes of the piece (base, neck …) are characteristic of the Aghlabid period, which means that we can date the piece from the 3rd / 9th century. Both its shape and decoration suggest it was a local production, from the Kairouan or Raqqada workshops.
0b91f97f-aa76-5d14-a2ae-6751b59baea3.method_for_provenance: An archaeological find among a group of other pieces of Aghlabid pottery.
0b91f97f-aa76-5d14-a2ae-6751b59baea3.obtention: The flask was among objects discovered on site during the 1960 excavations at Raqqada. It was acquired by the Great mosque at Kairouan in 1964 and transferred in 1986 to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada.

0c64afe8-ef31-5013-ab4c-0e70f49a6799.name: Traditional blue ceramic plate from Fez
0c64afe8-ef31-5013-ab4c-0e70f49a6799.description: This ceramic dish is a remarkable example of craftsmanship in Fez, a Moroccan city renowned for its pottery production since the Middle Ages. The decoration is dominated by a circular rosette in the shape of a six-petaled flower, an emblematic motif of Islamic art combining geometry and symbolism. The centre is decorated with an interlaced six-pointed star (Star of David), symbol of infinity and universal harmony. The petals, finely filled with small blue dots on an off-white background, add texture and depth. Secondary floral motifs occupy the spaces between the petals, accentuating the decorative richness of the piece. The design is framed by a thick cobalt blue border, lending the work an elegance and striking visual contrast. This technique, which combines meticulous painting under a protective glaze, testifies to the mastery of its artisans. After being painted, the dish was baked at a high temperature to fix the colours and obtain the glossy finish characteristic of Fez ceramics.
0c64afe8-ef31-5013-ab4c-0e70f49a6799.dates: Hegira mid of 13th century / beginning of the 14th century – AD end of 19th century

0d1ebd8b-952b-50c4-bf8b-872eb70782fa.name: Bowl fragment.
0d1ebd8b-952b-50c4-bf8b-872eb70782fa.description: A stone-paste (fritware) fragment from a bowl produced in Damascus and found in excavations at Fustat, Old Cairo. The fragment, the centre of a bowl, and part of one of the sides, is decorated with black line-drawings of floral sprays under a transparent pale-turquoise glaze. The centre is decorated with a palmette, while the outside of the bowl is decorated with a succession of densely placed lancet leaves. Although Fustat in the Mamluk period became known as Misr, losing its fame to the new Cairo under Mamluk rule, this bowl fragment indicates that the markets of Fustat were still attracting trade from outside Egypt throughout the Mamluk period (AH 647–922 / AD 1250–1517). Syrian potters came to work in Fustat, just as Egyptian potters migrated in search of work too. The pattern on this dish is influenced by Chinese ceramics, which were very popular in the Middle East at that time.
0d1ebd8b-952b-50c4-bf8b-872eb70782fa.short_description: This Syrian ceramic bowl was excavated in the old city of Fustat in Egypt, brought there through the strong trading links between the two sides of the Red Sea. The Chinese influence is felt through the pattern of the floral designs, which has been adapted to suit local Middle Eastern taste.
0d1ebd8b-952b-50c4-bf8b-872eb70782fa.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
0d1ebd8b-952b-50c4-bf8b-872eb70782fa.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the material composition, glaze and decoration of this fragment are typical of ceramics made in the potteries of  Syria. Several similar examples have been found in Fustat indicating that ceramics from the Middle East were brought to trade in Egypt.
0d1ebd8b-952b-50c4-bf8b-872eb70782fa.method_for_provenance: The material composition, glaze and decoration of this fragment are typical of ceramics made in the potteries of Syria. Several similar examples have been found in Fustat indicating that ceramics from the East were brought to trade in Egypt.
0d1ebd8b-952b-50c4-bf8b-872eb70782fa.provenance: Produced in Damascus, Syria; found at Fustat, Egypt.

0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.name: Strainer.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.description:
The reddish-grey earthenware fragment comes from a vessel that was provided with a slightly convex strainer. The lattice of this strainer is a geometrical design composed of circles and curved lines. The basic unit of the pattern is a circle filled with a four-sided border bent inwards to form a star with a holed circlet at the centre and four circles in the middle of the sides. The whole design is composed of three of these circles. The space between them is filled with a pointed motif flanked by two tiny holed circlets, which repeats a section of the basic pattern. An incised zigzag line bordered by two curved lines surrounds the openwork at the centre. The zigzag line is a characteristic element of Fatimid strainer designs.  
The strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of an earthenware vessel to protect the stored liquid from insects and pollution. Most strainer vessels of the Islamic period were manufactured of clay. The vessels remained unglazed in order to allow evaporation through the porous material, if it was wished to keep the stored liquid, mostly water, cool.  
Designs put together on the basis of simple geometrical shapes such as circles, lines or triangles, the repetition of these elements and their rearrangement in new patterns are a feature of Fatimid strainers. Geometrical compositions are dominant among the strainer designs of this period followed by zoomorphic and epigraphic motifs. Decorative strainers are known from excavations from the AH 2nd / AD 8th century to the AH 9th / AD 15th century, but Fatimid period was the high point of their development.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.short_description: Earthenware fragment which was integrated in a vessel as a strainer. The latticework is composed of a geometrical design of circles and curved lines. The strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the earthenware vessel to protect the stored liquid from insects and pollution.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.method_for_datation: Strainers of this pattern excavated in undisturbed strata were dated to the 5th and 6th / 11th and 12th centuries.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.method_for_provenance: Similar strainers were excavated at al-Fustat and their place of manufacture ascribed to the city. According to F. R. Martin, this strainer comes from excavations at al-Fustat.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.obtention: Purchased from the collection of the Swedish art dealer and art historian F. R. Martin in 1921.

0d8a58c2-5da1-5c7f-a4bc-5bc61e7ad347.name: Bath scraper or pumice stone
0d8a58c2-5da1-5c7f-a4bc-5bc61e7ad347.description:
This object might be related to bath scrapers or pumice stones displaying a similar conical shape and attributed to the Safavid period.  
  
This example is decorated with yellow and blue chevron motifs. Its flat side is left purposely untreated to be used as an abrasive surface that would be suitable for hammam rituals of exfoliation and purification of the skin.
0d8a58c2-5da1-5c7f-a4bc-5bc61e7ad347.author: Dounia Handis

0da353d3-8291-51cb-a468-1cc100a5bfc4.name: Vase.
0da353d3-8291-51cb-a468-1cc100a5bfc4.description: A vase with a spherical body resting on a foot-ring with a high tulip-shaped neck almost the same height as the body. The two curved handles starting at the neck rest on the upper part of the body. The clay is clear, highly fired, and the walls are very thin. Brown manganese-oxide paint covers the handles, and decorates the neck and the upper part of the body. Two different styles can be found on the neck. On the upper part, a painted strip is decorated with repeated excised motifs, in a shape of concentric half-circles. A frieze of arabesques divided by slightly curved vertical lines reminiscent of calligraphic characters seems to clumsily imitate the word 'Allah'. The same ornamental layout and design appear on the body. This type of drinking vase, or *jarrita*, with its elegant shape and a pseudo-epigraphic design that mixes the techniques of paint and excision, was widespread during the same period in the south of al-Andalus.
0da353d3-8291-51cb-a468-1cc100a5bfc4.short_description: This type of round-bellied drinking vessel (*jarrita*) with a tall tulip-shaped neck, curved handles and pseudo-epigraphic decoration crudely imitating the word 'Allah' was very common in the south of al-Andalus at this time.
0da353d3-8291-51cb-a468-1cc100a5bfc4.dimensions: Height 6.5 cm, max. diameter 11.5 cm, diameter base 4.8 cm, diameter mouth 8.2 cm.
0da353d3-8291-51cb-a468-1cc100a5bfc4.method_for_datation: Found during the excavations in the ruins of a medieval bourgeois house at the archaeological site of Lixus. The date has been confirmed by the stylistic and comparative study with reliably dated objects found in Murcia and Huelva in Spain dating from the end of the first third of 8th / 13th century.

0e9e99b6-9407-5be8-bd91-c9e2938c4e17.name: Bowl emulating Chinese stoneware
0e9e99b6-9407-5be8-bd91-c9e2938c4e17.short_description: This ceramic bowl, boldly decorated in cobalt blue against a parchment-like white slip, is one of the earliest examples to incorporate calligraphy as the main element of decoration. The Arabic word *ghibta* (happiness) is repeated on two lines in the centre and creates a balanced composition when combined with the half-circles decorating the rim. Iraqi potters of the ninth century attempted to emulate the luminous quality and hard body of Chinese whitewares by using a tin‑opacified white glaze.

0eb816fe-a6fd-5eb6-bd76-fe059b1cc12f.name: Pilgrim bottle fragment.
0eb816fe-a6fd-5eb6-bd76-fe059b1cc12f.description: An unglazed fragment from the flat side of a pilgrim bottle, with part of the depiction of an archer on horseback moulded in low relief. An idea of the original shape can be obtained from a number of pilgrim bottles that survive intact. The bottle would have been shaped like a drum with a spout attached at the top, circular in shape with two flat sides and two handles on the rounded edge. Due to their similarity with vessels brought back from the Holy Land by Western pilgrims these vessels are usually termed 'pilgrim bottles'. Unglazed pottery was used for storing water as the porous clay was especially efficient at keeping water cool, particularly important on long journeys.
0eb816fe-a6fd-5eb6-bd76-fe059b1cc12f.short_description: A fragment from an unglazed earthenware pilgrim bottle showing part of the depiction of an archer on horseback. These bottles, used for carrying water, were termed pilgrim bottles due to their similarity to vessels brought back from the Holy Land by Western pilgrims.
0eb816fe-a6fd-5eb6-bd76-fe059b1cc12f.method_for_datation: Comparable fragments have been found in excavations in Syria that can be dated to this period.
0eb816fe-a6fd-5eb6-bd76-fe059b1cc12f.method_for_provenance: There were workshops for these unglazed bottles at a number of locations in Syria. Moulds and kilns have been found in Damascus and Hama. This fragment was found at a factory site in Aleppo.
0eb816fe-a6fd-5eb6-bd76-fe059b1cc12f.obtention: Acquired by the British Museum in 1902.

0ec56979-2b66-516d-a77f-a6c3c80db240.name: Ewer with Design of Animals and Inscriptions
0ec56979-2b66-516d-a77f-a6c3c80db240.short_description:
A stoneware, brown and white Luster-painted ewer with cylindrical body that swells slightly as it rises toward the shoulder; rounded shoulder from which extends a flat handle, neck, and spout. The handle extends upwards from the shoulder and turns at a 45 degree angle to connect to the neck just below the rim. The neck is funnel-shaped with and everted rim; there is a hollow collar at the base of the neck, just above where it joins to the shoulder.  
The decoration consists of a yellow-brown Luster painting over an opaque, white glazed background and is concentrated in two zones of the ewer: the bottom section of the body and the upper section, including the neck, shoulder, handle and spout. This leaves a large, central section of opaque white glaze on the body on which a single line of inscription has been added in the yellow-brown Luster. The inscription, a quatrain in Persian, reads as follows:  
*man mihr-i tu dar miyan-i jan awardam / ba u hama khurda dar miyan awardam / akhir zi hama jahan bar awardam sar / ta 'ishq-i tu bar sar-i jahan awardam  
li-katibihi katabahu Abu Zayd bi-khattihi dar sana sittami'a*  
I brought your love to the midst of my soul / I discussed the smallest matters with it / Until I overcame the entire world / In order to bring your love to the world.  
\[This belongs\] to its writer.  
Abu Zayd wrote it in his own script in the year six hundred.  
In the lower zone is a second inscription written in reserve in large, Kufic script on a background of the yellow-brown Luster with small, delicate scrolls and spirals. This inscription mainly repeats the word *al-'izz* ("glory") along with one or two instances each of *al-dawla* ("good fortune") and al-salama ("well-being").  
The upper zone of decoration is comprised of three registers. The lowest register contains a series of plump birds with their feet on the ground and their wings in mid-flap. They are painted in Luster against a background of light scrolls. The middle register contains a chase scene moving from right to left with a cheetah, placed to the immediate left of the handle, pursuing a series of gazelles that fill the remainder of the register on either side of the spout. The cheetah is represented wearing a collar with a ring, indicating that it is a trained cheetah rather than a wild one. The animals are painted in reserve against a background of Luster with fine scrolls. The upper register of the shoulder has another *Kufic* inscription, possibly the phrase *al-'izz al-da'im* ("perpetual glory"), written in Luster and fitted tightly around the base of the neck. The neck is painted with a small-scale chain pattern. The exterior of the rim is painted in solid Luster while its interior contains *Kufic*\-style pseudo-epigraphy. Finally, the outward facing side of both the handle and the spout appear to have been painted with ascending palmette motifs.  
There are numerous hairline cracks throughout the vessel, and the spout, handle, and rim have all been partially restored. The central *Kufic* band has a notable area of blurring and streaking of the glaze.

0f40f0f0-ca7e-554c-be5f-7c891a71c669.name: Plate with Design of Arabic Inscription in *Kufic* Script
0f40f0f0-ca7e-554c-be5f-7c891a71c669.short_description: A shallow earthenware plate with inscription in dark brown slip over white slip background and a transparent glaze. The Arabic inscription in *Kufic* script serves as the main decoration; its elongated horizontal bars and ligatures form a border along the circumference of the plate while the sharply pointed vertical staffs extend towards the central depression to form a radiating design. Translated, the inscription reads "Planning before work protects you from regret! K..." There are many scratches and repaired cracks. At several spots along the edge, the white slip has chipped away, exposing the pinkish buff earthenware.

0fc12068-b2a4-51bb-a564-cc98546c289d.name: Moorish bowl.
0fc12068-b2a4-51bb-a564-cc98546c289d.description:
In a land such as Spain where sailing was of such importance it is no surprise that ships were used in the decoration of ceramics. At the centre of a bowl with a vertical rim, a sailing ship, which conforms to a type of ship known as a ‘nao’ in Spanish and a ‘nau’ in Portuguese, is depicted in front of spiralling tendrils with rosettes. Both the Spanish and the Portuguese were at the time masters of the earth’s seas.  
The ship is a single-masted type with a large, square sail. The artist has stylized the bowsprit due to lack of space; at the stern, of the two “flags”, the one aft may be a spritsail that the artist has curtailed due to lack of space. The superstructure of the rudder is decorated in Arabic letters which read "peace". The structural elements of the ship can only partially be made out on this object, with its somewhat basic and faint markings, However, knowledge of this type of ship is known from an example on a large bowl with steep, angular sides that is housed in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The decorative design of the Berlin bowl matches that of the London one. An original model nao can be seen in the Maritime Museum in Rotterdam. Under the ship on the Berlin bowl, stylised dolphins can be seen playing, occasionally intersected by the bowl’s rim. After Valencia succumbed to Christian rule in 1238, ceramic manufacturers worked under the commission of Christian patrons. The type of ship shown here demonstrates this relationship and testifies to the proximity in which Christians and Muslims lived during this time. A ship accompanied by dolphins was a known motif in the ceramics produced in Malaga towards the end of the 14th and beginning of the 15th century. The fact that only a few ceramics with this motif existed perhaps reveals that only a few commissioned this princely theme. An examination in 1983 of a fragment of the London plate conclusively confirmed that Nasrid ceramics were manufactured in Malaga. Stylistic examinations had already suggested that this was the case. These comparisons have also demonstrated the connections between the Spanish ceramics of this period and those made in Sicily and Egypt. Depictions of ships first appeared at the time of the *Reconquista* and with the emergence of Christian patrons.
0fc12068-b2a4-51bb-a564-cc98546c289d.short_description: Ships carrying trade across the Mediterranean sea appear frequently on pottery vessels made in the workshops of al-Andalus. This bowl was made in Manises near Valencia. The marks of the tripod show that such bowls were manufactured in large numbers and were traded to Mediterranean countries.

10055861-fa02-5348-9d89-bbe6682bf4ef.name: Tiles of the Buyan Kuli Khan
10055861-fa02-5348-9d89-bbe6682bf4ef.short_description:
These tile fragments are from the mausoleum of Buyan Qulï Khan in Bukhara. The turquoise glazed tile is decorated with an intricate vine pattern in white. The ornament is not painted, but cut as a relief into the clay using a complex technique.  
These tiles were a part of the decoration program of the mausoleum of Buyan Kuli Khan, who was murdered in 1358. He was the 25th successor of Genghis Khan (1155/62 / 67-1227) and ruled over the Chagatay Khanate empire. His tomb is situated in Bukhara, present-day Uzbekistan, and was covered with tiles both inside and out. The present fragment was initially installed on the outer facade. The Victoria and Albert Museum also possesses several tiles from the mausoleum.
10055861-fa02-5348-9d89-bbe6682bf4ef.method_for_datation: These tiles are from the mausoleum of King Buyan Kuli Khan. They were acquired in 1903 by Justus Brinckmann in Kabebdjan Galleries in Paris.

keywords: Architectural decor; Buyan Kuli Khan; Mausoleum

109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.name: Drum
109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.short_description: Small round drum, pointed on the bottom, covered on the top with leather, and fastened with a linen rope. It was played with a wooden stick to create special sounds of music, and it was used during the Muslim holy month of Ramadan to wake up people to eat (*suhur*) before sunrise. Some people used to volunteer to go around before dawn to wake people up during Holy Ramadan, reflecting community spirit.

1304f4ee-e28f-57f0-a08d-b92839b37afe.name: Incense burner
1304f4ee-e28f-57f0-a08d-b92839b37afe.description: Incense burners like this are usually made of clay mixed with water and kneaded until a mixture is formed that can then be shaped. The burner is then adorned with engravings, intricate drawings, and different colors. The incense burners are then fired in a kiln, after which they are ready for use. Note the handle; it makes the burner safe to carry from room to room. Incense occupies a central place in Omani life, as the passing of a fragrant burner at the end of a visit is customary in every region of the country.

13363244-5ab8-5c8e-ad7b-fd1feb510f5a.name: Dish
13363244-5ab8-5c8e-ad7b-fd1feb510f5a.short_description: Large fritware Kirman style dish with foliatae designs finely incised through the cobalt-stained slip to show the white body beneath. The lip is very finely scalloped in imitation of Chinese ware. The interior of the foot ring is covered with a transparent pale bluish-white glaze with a large roundel enclosing an artist's signature in the form of a painted 'tassel' mark.

14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.name: Lidded bowl.
14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.description:
A squat, elliptically shaped, lidded bowl of stone-paste (fritware) with a flattened domical lid topped by a gilded copper-alloy finial. A blue, red and green rosette enhances the base of the finial; the pattern on the lid itself then opens out from the base of the finial where, from leafy stems, four mythical, blue, serrated *saz* leaves with red centres sprout, moving in an anti-clockwise direction, their stems crossing. In between the *saz* leaves, there are four floral pairs, each consisting of a blue lily and a red-orange hyacinth. These also emerge from leafy stems, sinuously crossing over each other.  
The edge of the rim is decorated by a scalloped border of white on blue, a black dot in the centre of each scallop. The upper edge of the body receives a guilloche border rendered in red and green. Below, nine blue tulips with red dotted detailing flow around the bowl in a clockwise direction, giving the impression of a horizontally disposed garland, although they all rise in fact from the base. A second band below the tulips is composed of carnations, this time flowing in an anti-clockwise direction, their stems again springing from the baseline below. The well of the bowl receives a decorative roundel defined by three linear borders. It contains five flower sprays with red and blue petals. Six abstract motifs in blue fill the remaining spaces.  
The shape of this bowl recalls Iranian metal and ceramic bowls dating to the AH 7th / AD 13th century and also appears among the tableware of the Italian courts during the 15th century (as seen, for example, in an engraving by Mantegna where an attendant serves at table during a card game). In Ottoman court culture lidded bowls such as this were produced in gilt copper (*tombak*), and occurred as an integral part of the tableware used to serve food at mealtimes.
14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.short_description: In Ottoman court culture lidded bowls like this one were produced in gilt copper (*tombak*) as well as pottery and occurred as an integral part of the crockery used to serve food at mealtimes. Its style of decoration places it among other floral Iznik wares dated to the AH 10th / AD late 16th century.
14764713-cb27-5756-8029-2aade64971eb.method_for_datation: The decorative style of this lidded bowl places it among a group of floral Iznik wares dated to the 10th / late 16th century.

151fac1e-ebdf-570b-9f37-a9dcd36098e4.name: Flask: Candle holder for festival of name-giving
151fac1e-ebdf-570b-9f37-a9dcd36098e4.short_description: On the 7th day after the birth of a child, there is a candle burning naming festival in Egypt. For both boys and girls, flasks for drinking water are made of clay, and are provided with candle holders. Depending on the sex of the new-born baby, the neck of the bottle is either fashioned as a stylised female figure or ends in an implied penis. The festival is celebrated in honour of the 7 angels who stand around the new-born. On the evening of the 7th day after the birth of the child, these angels become a threat. In order to propitiate them, they are provided with a plate of food-offerings. Nearby, the clay bottle stands on a tray with beans. The beans are sprinkled with water and the candles on the flasks are lit. Each candle receives a name. The one which burns the longest is, so to speak, the "baptismal candle" of the child. The stub of the candle is then placed in a small bag, together with magical substances, and worn around the child's neck as an amulet to ward off evil.
151fac1e-ebdf-570b-9f37-a9dcd36098e4.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.

1551f405-e3e6-5970-8bcb-de56cf919879.name: Tile
1551f405-e3e6-5970-8bcb-de56cf919879.short_description: The geometric pattern of this glazed tile is made from an elaborate pattern of white lines, intersecting in knot-like patterns to form various shapes, including stars. The colours in the shapes form an alternating pattern, with bands of green and manganese brown surrounding a yellow centre.

15b3397c-76d7-510d-9b01-2bd087128afe.name: Tile panel in the shape of a tympanum.
15b3397c-76d7-510d-9b01-2bd087128afe.description:
Panel of glazed tiles decorated in blue, turquoise, green and yellow. The central composition is framed by scrolls of stylised clouds forming a serpentine band which encloses a lotus flower in a trefoil knot. Unfurling in a spiral from the central motif are slender boughs with leaves, flower buds and *hatayi*\-style motifs (garlands of flowers of Chinese inspiration). In Ottoman architecture panels of tiles were used mainly to decorate interior rooms.  
It has been claimed that this panel belongs to a set of around twelve almost identical tympana, which decorated a building commissioned to be built by Piyale Pasa, Lord of the Admiralty and protégé of Sultan Selim II. There was some doubt as to which building this might be: the mosque or the palace. The most widely held view is that the panels were removed from the Mosque of Piyale Pasa in Istanbul, probably built by the architect Sinan in AH 980–1 / AD 1573–4, since all the tympana disappeared and only the *mihrab* (prayer niche) remains.
15b3397c-76d7-510d-9b01-2bd087128afe.short_description: This tile panel belonged to the Piyale Pasa Mosque in Istanbul. The piece is dominated by plant motifs. The central composition is framed by stylised clouds forming a strip enclosing a lotus flower, from where other plant motifs are developed.
15b3397c-76d7-510d-9b01-2bd087128afe.method_for_datation: By methods of stylistic analysis and by comparison with pieces from the same period. The stylistic similarities with the tympana from the mosque of Selim II, built by Sinan in Edirne in 975–82 / 1569–75) and with the tomb of the same sovereign in Istanbul (which Sinan finished building in 981–2 / 1574–5) are undeniable. Furthermore, all the tympana which formed this set are dated to AH 980 / AD 1573, which confirms the dating of this panel.
15b3397c-76d7-510d-9b01-2bd087128afe.method_for_provenance: By expert examination. The European collections in which the tympana from this set are to be found, such as the Louvre Museum and the Museum of Decorative Arts in Paris, confirm the provenance of these panels to be the Mosque of Piyale Pasa in Istanbul.

1602f68b-990c-5682-9da4-a873d3cc650b.short_description: The pot-bellied pitcher with cockerel head, decorated with an inscription on the neck and close to the base, shows large human figures surrounded by a garden, typical of the monumental style of Kashan.

1657e49f-ee2a-5134-8524-b0acdfbf4c0c.name: Dish
1657e49f-ee2a-5134-8524-b0acdfbf4c0c.short_description: During the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, luster ceramics made in Manises, a suburb of Valencia on Spain’s eastern coast, were made for Italian, Spanish, and French patrons. Accordingly, Christian symbols, Latin inscriptions, and European blazons were standard components of Manises lusterware iconography. This exceptional dish bears the arms (two intersecting maces) of the Gondi banking family of Florence. It can be dated to the late fifteenth century.

17315f50-dba9-5ad0-a841-47bafdd7bfe6.name: Dish
17315f50-dba9-5ad0-a841-47bafdd7bfe6.short_description: The dish shows a simple, elegant decoration in manganese on an opaque white glaze.

17634e8b-75c4-531c-a525-4f57d46e78f9.name: Bowl
17634e8b-75c4-531c-a525-4f57d46e78f9.description: This bowl is a fine example of pottery from the Samanid (AD 819–1005) workshops of eastern Iran. Its design is stark and striking, featuring a single line of Arabic calligraphy that encircles the deep rim. The script, with its elegantly elongated horizontals and sharp-tipped verticals, is an early form of Arabic calligraphy known as New Style Kufic. The bowl's decoration is minimal yet visually compelling, with the inscription reading: “Knowledge is the most noble lineage and chivalry the most intricate.” The inscription’s meaning is elevated by the artistic manipulation of the letters. Through shortening, bending, and elongating, the script is transformed into abstract motifs of remarkable visual impact. The vertical flourishes interspersed among the horizontal flow create a rhythmic interplay that draws in the viewer. Likely used for serving on special occasions, the bowl’s message about the virtues of knowledge and chivalry is particularly apt.
17634e8b-75c4-531c-a525-4f57d46e78f9.bibliography: Christie's London, *Art of the Islamic and Indian World*, 2011.

17f38219-908a-521a-bc48-bdfa982ef72d.name: Small decorated glazed jar
17f38219-908a-521a-bc48-bdfa982ef72d.description:
The small size of this jug and its decoration make it a delicate piece of tableware. It has three rounded handles on the shoulder and is entirely covered with an opaque glaze on the inside and out, now stained grey. The cobalt-blue decoration has been reconstructed as an oval above two curling branches, probably a plant motif, and is repeated between each of the three handles. A bright green vertical line runs down the outside of each handle.  
  
Originally this jug would have looked bright and striking, with dark blue-and-green painted designs against a white or cream colour.
17f38219-908a-521a-bc48-bdfa982ef72d.short_description: It could have been a table vinegar pot used to contain sweet and sour sauces that were very popular in the AH 3th / AD 9th century. The painted design and technology indicate that this was manufactured either in Iraq or Iran.
