180f723a-4db3-52e6-816e-594df6310f46.name: *Zellij* panel.
180f723a-4db3-52e6-816e-594df6310f46.description:
This panel of earthenware wall-facing is square shaped. Like all *zellij* mosaics, it consists of shapes cut into the tiles and assembled. It is decorated exclusively with geometric figures, *testir*.  
The star shape obtained by dividing a circle into equal parts is the dominating form in its design. The repetitive motif that constitutes the basic element of its decoration is made up of polychrome knotwork whose dominant colours are black and turquoise blue on an ivory white base. Starting from the centre and a twelve-pointed star, black-line knotwork forms a rosette surrounded with irregular five-pointed stars by overlapping with other turquoise-blue knotwork. Combining with the second black line, it develops around this rosette to form a square whose corners are marked with eight-pointed stars. Inside the square, a yellow ochre ribbon with serrated edges circumscribes the rosette, while two black and almond green concentric octagons surround the figures in the corners of the square. This complex arrangement, strikingly harmonious both in terms of the geometric motifs and their range of colours, would have required a profound knowledge of geometric figures and their combinations. This extremely fine work is testimony to the invention and technical mastery in the art of *zellij*\-making inherited from Marinid craftsmen.
180f723a-4db3-52e6-816e-594df6310f46.short_description: This panel of wall facing, evidence of the mastery in the art of *zellij* inherited from the Marinids, consists of an arrangement of shapes cut in the tiles. It is decorated exclusively with geometric figures, with a star shape dominating the pattern.
180f723a-4db3-52e6-816e-594df6310f46.method_for_datation: The inventory register dates the house it came from to the AH 13th / AD 19th century.
180f723a-4db3-52e6-816e-594df6310f46.method_for_provenance: It was originally from a house in Fez, according to the inventory.
180f723a-4db3-52e6-816e-594df6310f46.obtention: Salvaged by the Department of Historical Monuments and deposited with museum in 1945.

18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.name: Dish.
18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.description: A dish with tall foot-ring and small flat edge. It is painted green, white, brown and blue. The bottom of the dish is decorated with small leaves. The centre is marked by a flower with four petals, inside which there is a decoration of several leaves. Four spokes radiate from this and divide the plate into four fields of similar sizes. Each of them is decorated by a large leaf, which is filled with small leaves. The flat edge is composed of concentric filaments and by a frieze decorated with leaves of different sizes.
18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.short_description: Dish from the Ilkhanid period produced in the potteries of Raghés (Sultanabad, Persia). The principal decorative motifs – in a variety of sizes and painted in green, white, brown and blue – are phytomorphic and cover the inside and rim of the dish.
18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis of the object, in relation to the decorative motifs and to the technique used in its making.
18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.method_for_provenance: The provenance of the dish was determined using the same criteria as for dating the piece.
18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.obtention: A donation from the Group of Friends of the National Museum of Ancient Art in 1920.
18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.bibliography:
Moulierac, J., *Céramiques du Monde Musulman*, Paris, 1999.  
Soustiel, J., *La Céramique Islamique*, Paris, 1985.
18f05dc3-e256-5db0-861c-eedad63d44e9.author: Paula Pelúcia Aparício
keywords: plate; glazed earthenware; Ilkhanid; plant decoration; Sultanabad; Persia; Raghés
materials: Glazed earthenware made on a wheel and painted in green, blue, brown and white.

1917f306-bbb6-5dba-b6df-5ad0d13eb882.name: Bowl
1917f306-bbb6-5dba-b6df-5ad0d13eb882.short_description: In the Abbasid era Samarra and Basra were flourishing centres offering a rich testimony of active local craftsmen. Islamic ceramists' admiration for Chinese porcelain is reflected in the production of monochrome white or cream-coloured pottery, coated with a thick opaque glaze decorated with spots of colour.
materials: Earthenware, opaque white glaze and blue spots

197c66bc-cc66-5bb1-87c4-c6327477449c.name: Box trap/Spindle traps
197c66bc-cc66-5bb1-87c4-c6327477449c.description: A rectangular trap made of fine bamboo sticks, and tied with coir rope or nylon twine. The Ghuni is constructed with specially designed involuted front and back walls that create vertical openings to guide fish inside, and it also includes an upper opening for collecting the catch. The clever device is typically used in beels, derelict waterbodies, and inundated paddy fields, especially in rural areas, for catching small-sized fish, prawns, and shrimps.
197c66bc-cc66-5bb1-87c4-c6327477449c.bibliography: Sandhya, K. M., *et al.*, “Traditional Fishing Gears, Fish Catch and Species Composition of Selected Floodplain Wetlands of Lower Gangetic Plains, West Bengal, India” in *Fishery Technology*, 56 : 2 (2019): 101–109: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/332631090\_Traditional\_Fishing\_Gears\_Fish\_Catch\_and\_Species\_Composition\_of\_Selected\_Floodplain\_Wetlands\_of\_Lower\_Gangetic\_Plains\_West\_Bengal\_India \[last accessed: 4/10/25\]
197c66bc-cc66-5bb1-87c4-c6327477449c.author: ActionAid Bangladesh

1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.name: Ewer.
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.description: A ceramic ewer with bulbous body, narrow neck flaring to an almost vertical rim, and a tall spout rising above the level of the rim. The handle is in the shape of an open-mouthed dragon. Painted in shades of blue and cobalt, the body has a scroll design with split palmettes, or arabesques. Below is a floral scroll and above the shoulder is a row of 'tadpole' leaves. Other decorative motifs are the scales painted on the handle, and the interlocking-chain design on the spout. The importance of this object lies not with the decoration, which is a clumsy rendition of early Iznik-style pottery, but in the inscription on the base. Writing in Armenian bolorgir script, the Christian craftsman gives his name – Abraham of Kütahya – and the year AH 959 (AD 1510). The presence of a date on an Iznik ceramic is unusual and therefore invaluable in establishing the date of many other blue-and-white vessels of a similar style. This ewer may have been used as a liturgical vessel.
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.short_description: An important piece. This blue-and-white ceramic ewer has an inscription on the base that includes the name of the craftsman and the date. Writing in Armenian script, the craftsman was clearly a Christian. The date enables the dating of many other vessels of similar style to be established.
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.dimensions: Height 17 cm, Diameter (at rim) 6.9 cm; (at base) 7.2 cm.
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.method_for_datation: On the base of the ewer, an inscription in seven lines of Armenian bolorgir script, gives the date 11th March 915 (1510).
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.method_for_provenance: Over the past 50 years scholars have debated whether this ewer was actually made in Kütahya or by Armenian craftsmen in Iznik. However, Carswell has shown that blue-and-white sherds were found at excavations in Kütahya. Furthermore, there are many records of pottery manufacture in this city, at least by the 11th / 17th century. Carswell also draws attention to a particularly interesting church of around 884 / 1480 in Kütahya whose inventories reveal it was made for a deacon named Abraham, described as the 'son of a potter'.
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.obtention: Part of the Godman bequest to the British Museum in 1983.
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.bibliography:
Atasoy. N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, no. 96.  
  
Carswell, J., *Iznik Pottery*, London, 1998, pp.45–6, plate 24.
1a58458a-01e5-5ba9-8601-e299f739c320.author: Emily Shovelton

1a94744a-6596-5190-8100-1548c229068b.name: Ostracon.
1a94744a-6596-5190-8100-1548c229068b.description: A triangular Ostracon that bears part of the Qur'anic sura 105 (the Elephant) written in simple *kufic* script. Unfortunately some words are missing because the sherd is incomplete. The function of this Ostracon was most probably for the study and memorisation of the sura by a student, but it is possible that it may have formed part of a vessel of some sort which would have been kept in the home to bring good luck and good fortune to its inhabitants.
1a94744a-6596-5190-8100-1548c229068b.short_description: Ostracon (inscribed pot sherd) from Petra that bears part of the Qur'anic Sura 105 (the Elephant) in *kufic* script. It was probably used by a student to study the verse, or could have been part of a vessel kept in a house to bring good fortune to its inhabitants.
1a94744a-6596-5190-8100-1548c229068b.method_for_datation: The object was dated on paleographical grounds to the early Islamic period.
1a94744a-6596-5190-8100-1548c229068b.method_for_provenance: The object was found during the course of an archaeological excavation in Petra.
1a94744a-6596-5190-8100-1548c229068b.obtention: The object was acquired during an archaeological excavation conducted by G. Horsfield in the Palace Tomb at Petra in 1936.
1a94744a-6596-5190-8100-1548c229068b.author: Aida Naghawy
keywords: Arabic inscription; kufic script; pottery; Qur’an.

1ad64436-5830-5802-954f-1fad4506d0f8.name: Bowl with horse and horseman
1ad64436-5830-5802-954f-1fad4506d0f8.short_description: Developed in Nishapur, the production of so-called "animated buff ware" was characterised by decoration obtained with liquid clays coloured with green, yellow, purple and manganese, applied on a buff-coloured surface and coated with transparent glaze. The decorations, highly influenced by Sassanid iconography, include figures of horsemen and horses, hunting scenes and fantastical animals and birds, in the midst of a richly decorated space.

1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.name: Prayer niche (*mihrab*)
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.description:
A prayer niche (*mihrab*) is located in a mosque to show every Muslim the direction of Mecca towards which they pray. The *mihrab* shown here is from the Bey Hakim Mosque, which was endowed by the physician of the Anatolian Seljuq Sultan Kılıç \[Qilich\] Arslan IV (d. AH 665 / AD 1266) and built in Konya. This prayer niche is very similar to others of the same period in its decoration in faience tiles, especially in its combination of calligraphic and decorative elements. These elements have been combined in a variety of ways, resulting in manifold decorations. Borders of differing widths featuring inscriptions and vegetal motifs create unity. Small columns with cubic capitals frame the imagined entrance to Paradise. As was always the case in this period, the lower half of the niche is embellished with geometric patterns and the niche’s upper half by a *muqarnas* (stalactite) vault also covered in geometric patterns. The vault is also framed with geometric motifs. The geometric decoration of the Berlin *mihrab* has an additional 12-star pattern. Raised eight-pointed stars can be found in both spandrel fields. The inscribed areas feature extracts from various parts of the Qur’an. Sura 29 verse 45 is cited on the forefront of the niche: ‘Proclaim what has been revealed to you in scripture and pray. Prayer protects against dishonour and temptation. And truly, to think of Allah is one’s greatest duty; and Allah knows what you do’. The aesthetic unity of the decoration was created by calligraphers and draughtsmen of ornaments in conjunction with the producers of tiles. In terms of colour palette, turquoise, dark blue, black and aubergine were selected. Craftsmen were also responsible for the cutting of the tiles, so that they could be organised into a pattern without leaving any gaps. Tile production in Konya reached its apotheosis around AH 658 / AD 1260, so that, in the AH 7th / AD 13th century, 21 mosques were decorated with faience mosaic.  
  
Click [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hxg1P6Wi4Ro&t=3s) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.short_description: Turquoise, brown and dark manganese faience mosaic was common in monumental Seljuq prayer niches. This impressive niche with Qur’anic inscriptions and arabesque and geometric patterns, once belonged to the Bey Hakim Mosque in Konya, Turkey. It was assembled from fragments and restored parts.
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.type: Mihrab, prayer niche, glazed ceramic, mosaic
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.method_for_datation: The prayer niche comes from the Bey Hakim Mosque, which was founded by the favourite physician of the Seljuq Sultan Kılıç [Qilich] Arslan IV (d. 665 / 1266), and which thus dates it to around the mid-7th / mid-13th century.
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.method_for_provenance: The fragments of this reconstructed niche in Berlin, along with other fragments housed in various cities (Paris, London, Istanbul), formed part of a prayer niche that once belonged to the Bey Hakim Mosque in Konya. Its identity has also been established through early photographs.
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.obtention: The prayer niche was reconstructed from numerous individual fragments.

*Museum für Islamische Kunst*, Catalogue, Mainz, 2001, pp.362–3.

keywords: Anatolia; prayer niche; mihrab; Rum Seljuq; Anatolian Seljuq; faience; mosque interior decoration

1bac2f91-68fb-5035-974f-d01111b23596.name: Lustre ware bowl
1bac2f91-68fb-5035-974f-d01111b23596.short_description: A conical shape bowl resting on a circular foot. Under a clear copper lustre glaze, the interior is decorated with six medallions around the sides each containing a seated figure. In the centre is a repeat of the seated figure motif. A vegetal design fills the spaces between the medallions.
1bac2f91-68fb-5035-974f-d01111b23596.dates: Late 6th-early 7th century AH / Late 12th-early 13th century AD
1bac2f91-68fb-5035-974f-d01111b23596.author: Hazelle Page

1bd4ddad-a3bc-5a69-8b22-cef129e37f47.name: Figurine
1bd4ddad-a3bc-5a69-8b22-cef129e37f47.description: Animal figurines were a short-lived phenomenon of the late 12th to 13th centuries AD in Syria and Iran. The cow or bull figure was especially popular, but in Iran it was made to function as a vessel with a filling spout in the back and an open mouth through which the liquid poured, whereas in Syria the trend was for figurines with a purely decorative function. However, as the basic form of the cow would have been moulded – suggesting that multiple versions of the same figure were made – the function of these decorative figurines remains a mystery. The present example is rendered with perfect naturalism. It can be identified as a zebu cow and calf. The mother is shown standing while her calf suckles; the hanging dewlap, small hump, swept-back horns and large cloven hooves of the breed are accurately modelled. This breed is indigenous to Syria, and would have been what people saw in the fields of the Euphrates Valley.
1bd4ddad-a3bc-5a69-8b22-cef129e37f47.bibliography:
Google Cultural Institute, *Google Art Project*, 2012.  
  
Sotheby's London, *Arts of the Islamic World, including Fine Carpets and Textiles*, 2008.
1bd4ddad-a3bc-5a69-8b22-cef129e37f47.dynasty: Ayyubid period (AH 564–end 9 th century / AD 1169–end 15 th century)
1bd4ddad-a3bc-5a69-8b22-cef129e37f47.author: Tara Desjardins
materials: Stonepaste painted under transparent turquoise glaze

1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.name: Ewer.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.description: An example of little-known AH 7th century / AD 13th-century Syrian ceramics, this bulbous-shaped ewer has an elegantly twisted handle and a small spout. The body is decorated with brown-coloured linear designs in horizontal bands. Unfortunately, the transparent glaze has deteriorated to such a degree, that it now conceals the underglaze painting. The shape of this vessel is very interesting from an artistic point of view as it is interconnected with designs in both glass and metalwork. The bulbous shape of the body and neck and the twisted handle appear in contemporary glass, while the fine lines of the decoration round the belly of the ewer remind us of contemporary metal inlay from both Iraq and Iran.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.short_description: This Raqqa lustre-decorated vessel has been inspired in its shape by both glass and metal vessels. The bulbous shape of the body and neck, and the twisted handle, appear in contemporary glass, while the fine lines of the decoration round the belly are inspired by contemporary metal inlay.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.type: Stone paste blue and turquoise painting, ceramic
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.dimensions: Height 17 cm, diameter (of rim) 4 cm; (of base) 6.5 cm; (of body) 12 cm.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: although the shape of the ewer is not as common as most other shapes in Raqqa pottery, the material composition of the body and the way it has deteriorated; the cobalt-blue colour and the glaze and lustre decoration, all belong to Raqqa ware-type ceramics of the 7th / 13th-century.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.method_for_provenance: The vessel's material composition and its deterioration is typical of Raqqa ware of the 7th / 13th century.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.bibliography:
Fehervari, G., *Ceramics of the Islamic World in the Tareq Rajab Museum*, London, 2000.  
  
Grube, E. J., *Cobalt and Lustre: The First Centuries of Islamic Pottery*, the Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, Vol. 9, London, 1994.
1bd55ea0-ed71-5324-a769-f06d5bcb1dd8.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
materials: Stone-paste with underglaze blue decoration, over which lustre glaze.

1bdcb311-686f-5698-aa9b-df0727b85070.name: Incense Burner or Lamp
1bdcb311-686f-5698-aa9b-df0727b85070.short_description:
The date palm tree (Phoenix dactylifera), an enduring symbol of Oman, is identified with the early oasis Civilisation of Magan in the 3rd millennium BC and the taming of the desert. It is one of the few tree species specifically mentioned in the Holy Qur’an, and according to Islamic tradition Maryam (Mary) gave birth to 'Iesa (Jesus) in the shade of a palm.  
  
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful:  
And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a date palm. She said, "Would that I had  
died before this, and had been forgotten and out of sight!" Then \[the infant 'Iesa (Jesus)\] cried unto her from below her, saying, "Grieve not! Your Lord has provided a water stream under you";  
And shake the trunk of date palm towards you, it will let fall fresh ripe dates upon you.  
  
Mary Chapter (Surat Maryam) (19:23-25)  
  
Highly simplified palm motifs appear as design elements on such diverse items as wooden doors, coffee pots, forefinger rings and copper spoons. The date palm is often combined with geometric or floral elements to create circular or linear patterns as a repetitive motif.
keywords: Incense Burner; Lamp; Date Palm; Floral

1c40ee85-b340-51ae-ba35-f36c089d387c.name: Water jug
1c40ee85-b340-51ae-ba35-f36c089d387c.description: The body of this terracotta jug is decorated with embossed Arabic inscriptions, and beginning from the end points of the inscriptions, there are raised dot-like ornaments about the size of a chickpea on the surface.
1c40ee85-b340-51ae-ba35-f36c089d387c.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
1c40ee85-b340-51ae-ba35-f36c089d387c.method_for_datation: Determined by the experts of the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
1c40ee85-b340-51ae-ba35-f36c089d387c.method_for_provenance: It was determined by the experts of the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
1c40ee85-b340-51ae-ba35-f36c089d387c.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

1c44d333-671b-59f9-9067-b9a5054398e1.name: Dish with moulded decoration
1c44d333-671b-59f9-9067-b9a5054398e1.short_description: The dish ranks among the finest examples of a rare group of pottery that first came to light in the excavations at Samarra and later in those at Susa. The group shares certain characteristics, such as the shallow form without articulation; low-relief decoration moulded with great precision; and the use of a fine glaze which covers the entire surface of the vessel, both inside and outside.
1c44d333-671b-59f9-9067-b9a5054398e1.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
1c44d333-671b-59f9-9067-b9a5054398e1.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on the shape of the dish and the techniques used in its production, all of which are comparable to pottery excavated in Samarra and Susa.
1c44d333-671b-59f9-9067-b9a5054398e1.bibliography:
Grube, E.J., *et al.*, *Cobalt and Lustre. The First Centuries of Islamic Pottery*, London: The Nasser D Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, volume 9, 1994: cat.15, pp.22–3.  
Rogers, J.M., *The Arts of Islam. Masterpieces from the Khalili Collection*, London: Thames & Hudson, 2010: no.24, p.48.
keywords: pottery; earthenware; green glaze; Iraq; Iraqi ceramics; moulding; Abbasid
materials: Earthenware, with moulded and incised decoration under a transparent green glaze, with patches of yellow and purple staining

1c5cb612-6069-5871-8e48-e67c020fc864.name: Tile Panel with a hunting scene
1c5cb612-6069-5871-8e48-e67c020fc864.short_description: This tile panel depicts a hunting scene. Produced during the Safavid period in Isfaha, the tile was made using a *cuerda seca* technique in which designs were outlined by an oily substance mixed with manganese, leaving a dark outline after firing. This prevented the coloured pigments from bleeding into each other. During the Timurid and Safavid periods, this technique was widely used and later introduced to Turkey. This tile panel most likely decorated a hunting palace.
1c5cb612-6069-5871-8e48-e67c020fc864.method_for_datation: The arch is from a palace near Isfahan. This scene is modelled on Persian book illumination.

1d61ec66-2c37-507e-9e98-65e166b78f82.name: ‘Escudilla de orejas’ (bowl with handles).
1d61ec66-2c37-507e-9e98-65e166b78f82.description: A cup of the ‘escudilla de orejas’ type painted with brown-red lustre on a cream background. The internal decoration includes a band with a damaged inscription in Latin characters from which the words ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1:1) and a series of stylised palmettes can be made out, all framed with solid lustre strips. On the base there is a medallion with a coat of arms decorated with a dolphin. The decoration on the outside of the piece has almost completely disappeared, but a stylised fern-leaf motif is still visible.
1d61ec66-2c37-507e-9e98-65e166b78f82.short_description: This cup is an example of Hispano-Moorish art. Probably produced in Valencia, it is made of ceramic painted with metallic lustre and decorated with an inscription in Latin characters alongside phytomorphic and zoomorphic motifs.
1d61ec66-2c37-507e-9e98-65e166b78f82.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
1d61ec66-2c37-507e-9e98-65e166b78f82.method_for_provenance: This type of cup is typical of Hispano-Moorish production and was probably produced in a Valencian workshop, although the possibility of it coming from an Aragonese workshop cannot be excluded, because of both the division of the decoration using concentric bands of solid lustre and the rendering of motifs by leaving elements uncoloured.
1d61ec66-2c37-507e-9e98-65e166b78f82.bibliography:
Ainaud De Lasarte, J., *Cèramica y Vidrio*,Ars Hispaniae, Vol. 10, Madrid, 1952.

1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.name: Bowl
1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.short_description:
The decoration on the inside of the bowl consists of six compartments delineated by two deep blue stripes. Black onion-shaped arabesque medallions dominate the white field.  
  
This bowl is one of a whole series of vessels whose aesthetics are based on the same trichord of blue, black and white. It is dominated by the so-called water-weed motif. Its popularity stems from the fact that the decoration could be painted directly onto the background with a free, unrestrained stroke of the brush. This freedom can also be seen here at the top of the medallion with its outwardly striving leaves. However, such expression is tamed by the more classical split-leaves at the bottom. This combination of free and restrained elements results in an aesthetically attractive tension.
1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.dates: Hegira  early 7th century / AD early 13th century
1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar dated objects
1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.method_for_provenance: By comparison with stylistically similar works
1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.obtention: Gift from Daeniker family in memory of Armin Daeniker
1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.bibliography: Watson, Oliver, *Ceramics From Islamic Lands*, London: Thames & Hudson, 2004: esp. 338-339.
1df0321d-307c-5a72-871d-69fcaac29119.author: Axel Langer

1e8c52f2-59ae-5930-b434-948802ee9220.name: A pilgrim’s flask.
1e8c52f2-59ae-5930-b434-948802ee9220.description:
A ceramic pilgrim's flask, sometimes called a Zamzameyyah, due to the fact that pilgrims used to fill such flasks with holy water from the famous well in Mecca called Zamzam.  
  
This type of ware is usually tan or creamy buff in color. These flasks are made of two separate moulded discs which are joined together; the neck and handles are then added. There is a guilloche decoration at the juncture to hide the join. The moulds of the discs have hollow decorations to form a pattern in relief on the surface of the flasks. Often the decoration includes an emblem or rank to indicate the status or profession of the owner, normally an official associated with the Ayyubid or Mamluk court. On this particular flask we have a lily in the middle with a sword on either side, an emblem belonging to several sultans and amirs of the time.
1e8c52f2-59ae-5930-b434-948802ee9220.short_description: A ceramic pilgrim’s flask or zamzamiyyah after the holy well of Zamzam in Mecca. Made of two moulded discs which are joined together, the design has a lily in the middle with a sword on either side, an emblem belonging to several sultans and amirs of the time.
1e8c52f2-59ae-5930-b434-948802ee9220.method_for_datation: The flask was dated by stylistic analysis and by comparing it to similar dated artifacts in other museums, such as other pilgrim's flasks displayed in Damascus National Museum.
1e8c52f2-59ae-5930-b434-948802ee9220.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this flask is unknown but it was probably produced in Syria.

البهنسي.عفيف، (تحقيق) الآثار السورية: مجموعة أبحاث أثرية و تاريخية (ماينز على الراين، 1982)، ص 285، شكل 253.

1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.name: Dish.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.description:
A lustre-painted and tin-glazed dish that is representative of this type of earthenware which was decorated by incising the outlines of the main design onto the surface of the unfired dish. The incised areas (a technique borrowed from the metalworking industry) stand out in the unusual luminescent blue of the stag, its antlers, the eight-petal flower, and the accents on some of the foliage. The brownish-gold lustre decoration of the background was added at a later stage after further firings.  
  
Manises was one of the main pottery-making towns in Valencia. It played a leading role in the manufacture of lustre-wares for export to Europe, principally to France and Italy. Manises' pottery left for export from the Valencian port of Groa where many Manises potters owned pottery warehouses and shops. These potters were a mixture of Christians and Moors (Muslims), the latter of which were not permitted to take their skills to work outside the town, testifying to the value of their special skills to the economy of Manises. By the mid-16th century (AH 956), Manises had a major monopoly on the production of lustre-wares in Valencia.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.short_description: This lustre-painted and tin-glazed dish was made in the town of Manises in Valencia. It monopolised the manufacture of this type of ceramics, which were made by Muslim potters who were remnants of its old Moorish population. Such dishes were very much sought after in both France and Italy.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.dates: Hegira late 9th–early 10th century / AD late 15th–early 16th century.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: a small number of similar dishes survive and although not precisely dated, this dish is contemporary to two other types of Spanish Islamic lustre ceramics dating from the late 9th–early10th / late 15th –early 16th centuries.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.method_for_provenance: Stylistic similarities with other types of Spanish Islamic lustre ceramics.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.bibliography: Ray, A., *Spanish Pottery 1248–1898*, with a catalogue of the collection in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 2000.
1eed41b3-c147-5628-8b7b-5a7e28136494.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
materials: Earthenware with incised relief decoration, lustre-painted and tin-glazed.

1f016872-92d0-54fb-b596-c44b25a26d1a.name: Plate
1f016872-92d0-54fb-b596-c44b25a26d1a.short_description: Kütahya was the second most important ceramic production centre after İznik due to the rich clay deposits in the area. This plate has flat rim, is slightly deep in body and has a circular bottom. It was made of white clay and coated in white on which there are patterns in cobalt blue, yellow, turquoise, purple and red covered with transparent glaze. In the middle of the plate there is an Ottoman coat-of-arms while both sides of the plate are decorated with curtains. Above the coat-of-arms, “Long Live My Sultan” is written in Turkish in Arabic letters forming a crescent and there is a *tuğra* (monogram) of Abdülhamid II (1876-1909) in the middle of the sun covering both the *tuğra* and the crescent.
1f016872-92d0-54fb-b596-c44b25a26d1a.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum

1f5adf40-300f-5b78-8290-c958c757a4db.name: Bowl
1f5adf40-300f-5b78-8290-c958c757a4db.short_description: Purchased at the 1873 World's Fair in Vienna.
1f5adf40-300f-5b78-8290-c958c757a4db.holder: MAK – Austrian Museum of Applied Arts / Contemporary Art

1fb04e5b-19da-5863-be2b-d7e7c321b743.name: Bowl.
1fb04e5b-19da-5863-be2b-d7e7c321b743.description: A large bowl on a high foot, decorated with underglaze painting. On the exterior, flowers and leaves in shades of blue and sage-green meander with relative freedom about the surface. The largest flowers feature a distinct cloud-band motif at their centre. Similar flower and leaf motifs, more regularly organised, adorn the foot, at whose base is a thin band of repeating cartouches containing four leaves each. The extraordinary size of this bowl, as well as the skill with which it is decorated, suggests production for the highest levels of the Ottoman hierarchy, although direct evidence for this is lacking.
1fb04e5b-19da-5863-be2b-d7e7c321b743.short_description: A very large footed bowl on a high foot, decorated with large leaves and flowers in blue and sage-green. The size and quality of this bowl suggests that it was made for a high-ranking Ottoman official, possibly for washing the feet during ablutions.
1fb04e5b-19da-5863-be2b-d7e7c321b743.method_for_datation: The style and details of the decoration link this bowl with a group of wares associated with the circle of an artist named Musli, who signed a mosque lamp dated 956 / 1549.
1fb04e5b-19da-5863-be2b-d7e7c321b743.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
1fb04e5b-19da-5863-be2b-d7e7c321b743.bibliography:
Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey, Istanbul/London, 1989, pp.135–8 and colour plate 356.  
  
Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.102.
1fb04e5b-19da-5863-be2b-d7e7c321b743.author: Barry Wood

1fe2bf0f-28b8-574f-bc6b-664e988fdf29.name: Pitcher
1fe2bf0f-28b8-574f-bc6b-664e988fdf29.short_description: Çanakkale was a pottery production centre between the end of 17th century and first quarter of the 20th century where pottery with interesting and original forms was produced. Mostly coarse red clay and occasionally beige-coloured paste was used. This jug with a pear-shaped body and long neck has green, brown, dark yellow, under-glazed purplish brown, dark blue and white decorations made by a brush. In front there is a single raised pattern of a flower. On either side there are painted flowers.

204250dc-0aee-5c7b-a35b-e5449a289de5.name: Dish
204250dc-0aee-5c7b-a35b-e5449a289de5.description: In the 19th century, new forms and decorative styles began to appear on dishes from Fez, which are remarkable both for the colours used and their design. This dish, decorated with two sailing boats, resembles designs seen on ceramics from Izmir in Turkey.
keywords: Applied arts; craftsmanship; Moroccan craftsmanship; ceramic; Iznik; Ottoman influence; Ottoman art

2084dfbd-b212-5edf-ac0e-b8dab11011bf.name: Tile Panel from Iznik
2084dfbd-b212-5edf-ac0e-b8dab11011bf.short_description: This door hutch contains fifty tiles and can be dated to the 1570s. It shows floral decorations such as *saz* leaves. The panel is made of fritware and decorated with polychrome painting on white slip clay under a colourless glaze. Probably it adorned the Royal Palace in Edirne.
2084dfbd-b212-5edf-ac0e-b8dab11011bf.dates: Hegira 2nd half of 10th century / AD 2nd half of 16th century
2084dfbd-b212-5edf-ac0e-b8dab11011bf.method_for_datation: The arch is probably from the Sultan's Palace of Edirne.
2084dfbd-b212-5edf-ac0e-b8dab11011bf.method_for_provenance: Ramsegger & Co. Art Dealer in Hamburg.
2084dfbd-b212-5edf-ac0e-b8dab11011bf.bibliography: Erduman-Çalış, D. and Ilgaz, N., "Furor Ceramicus: Justus Brinckmann und die Sammlung osmanischer Baukeramik aus Iznik am Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg", *EOTHEN*, 7 (2018): 75-107.
materials: Fritware; polychrome painting on white slip under a colourless glaze

21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.name: Bowl with inscription.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.description:
Round-based bowl with chamfered rim, coated with a green copper oxide glaze. In the centre of the bowl are four rows of *kufic* script written using a brown glaze (manganese oxide) with the word ‘al-Mulk’ (Sovereignty) written twice over. This expression occurs right through AH 3rd- / AD 9th-century Muslim pottery, from al-Andalus to India. The letters are drawn with split ascenders, a practice which became frequent in Ifriqiya from the second half of the AH 3rd / AD 9th century. The background colour of the lettering is yellow ochre based on antimony oxide or iron oxide and the script is surrounded by a frame of four brown rectangles.  
Green, brown and yellow ochre are the three colours typically used in Aghlabid pottery. Interestingly, these three colours have been consistently employed in Tunisian pottery through the centuries and up to the present day.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.short_description: Dish with a ring base and bevelled rim. The green, brown and yellow ochre colours used are the same as those typically found in Aghlabid ceramics, and they have remained an almost constant part of Tunisian ceramics through the centuries to the present day.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.dates: Hegira, last third of the 3rd century / AD 9th century.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.dimensions: Height 7 cm, diameter 24 cm, diameter (at base) 9 cm, thickness 1 cm.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.method_for_datation:
Raqqada, where the bowl was found, was the Aghlabid capital city, built in 263 / 876 by Prince Ibrahim II, which makes this date a *terminus ante quem*. Moreover, the bowl is characteristic in its shape, colour and decoration of that of the Aghlabid period just before the advent of the Fatimids in 296 / 909. It is therefore likely that the *terminus post quem* can be taken at the latter date.  
Unfortunately, these excavations were not carried out methodically and scientifically and no excavation record was compiled, so a more accurate dating is not possible. It is probable that the same shapes, colours and techniques were carried over to the Fatimid era.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.method_for_provenance: The discovery of this bowl on the Raqqada site, painted in the Aghlabid manner and of Ifriqiyan-style manufacture, would confirm that this was a local piece from the Raqqada potteries or from those at Kairouan, the nearest economic capital.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.obtention: This bowl was found during the Raqqada site excavations in the 1960s. At first it was kept on site, but since 1986 it has been on display at the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.bibliography:
Daoulatli, A., *Poteries et céramiques tunisiennes*, 1979, pp.32–3.  
*Tunisie: du christianisme à l'islam* (exhibition catalogue), Lattes, 2001, p.184.  
*Ifriqiya: Thirteen Centuries of Art and Architecture in Tunisia*, pp.174–5.
21203aaf-bad1-5324-9ce5-01be5dd93e89.author: Mourad Rammah

21645a7b-fc42-55ef-a2ec-27424e1c67fc.name: Tile Plate
21645a7b-fc42-55ef-a2ec-27424e1c67fc.description: The surface is covered in white clay and slip decorated in cobalt blue, coral red and green with black contours under a transparent colourless glaze. The plate’s surface is decorated with symmetrically distributed branches of tulips and red carnations with blue spots rising vertically from a single stem. Two tulips and carnations in the centre of the composition are held in place by a bracket. The composition is embellished with tulip and carnation buds, small stylised flowers, with cobalt blue Chinese-style clouds interspersed throughout the design. The use of bud and clover motifs in the decoration of plates was common during this period. A narrow border of white half-rosette flowers with red centres is framed by cobalt blue inside the rim. A double tulip and open rose motif alternate on the back.

22832cf5-d8f3-561b-aeea-71694ea3b574.name: Spouted jug
22832cf5-d8f3-561b-aeea-71694ea3b574.short_description:
The jug is covered with a transparent turquoise glaze and has two feline-shaped handles and two bullhead-shaped spouts. The designs are vertical compositions of leaf motives intercepted by curving peacock feathers.  
Two bands of inscriptions, *en reserve* on a black background read a Persian poem in the form of a *ruba\`i* (quatrain) that was a popular type of verse established by the end of the 10th century. The interior is with a group of fish.
keywords: Jug; Iran; Glaze; Persian poetry; Calligraphy motifs; Fish motifs
materials: Frit ware, underglaze painted in black

236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.name: Tile panel.
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.description:
An elongated tile panel that consists of 21 square and rectangular tiles. The design comprises a central field and a border; the central composition a tall and slender arch, the cusped apex highlighted with a fine red line. Within the arch there is a lattice of blue tiger-stripe motifs that contain individual upright and inverted *chintamani* (a design characterised by tiger-stripes and three balls) these, executed in blue and red, are surrounded by sinuous green with red detailing. The border has a continuous scroll of palmette leaves and so-called *saz* leaves that alternate with small flowers set against a deep blue background. The palmette leaves have orange or turquoise centres; those with orange centres have further detailing in turquoise, while those with turquoise centres have further detailing in orange. The heart of the *saz* leaves contain small floral stems in orange and green.  
The origin and meaning of the *chintamani* motif are still unclear, but it has been suggested that the triple dot motif may have had apotropaic associations among Turkic peoples, warding off evil by reflecting it back at the perpetrator, while the tiger-stripes seem to recall the tiger-skin worn by the Iranian superhero Rustam.
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.short_description: This tile panel is assumed to be the product of the Tekfur Saray factory near Eyüp on the Golden Horn, which was set up with the help of a group of potters from Iznik after the production centre there had declined by the end of the AH 11th century / AD 17th century.
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.dates: Hegira, late 12th century / AD mid-18th century.
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.method_for_datation: Technical and stylistic details place this tile panel within the context of Iznik 'revival wares' made at Tekfur Saray factory in Istanbul from the late 11th / late 17th century onwards.
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.method_for_provenance: The panel is said to have come from the Palace of Fuad Pasha (1815–69) in Istanbul and was probably made in the Tekfur Saray factory which was set up with the help of a group of potters from Iznik following the decline of the industry at the end of the AH 11th / AD 17th century.
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.provenance: Probably made at the Tekfur Saray factory in Istanbul, Turkey. The panel is said to have come from Istanbul and the Palace of Fuad Pasha (1815–69) who was an eminent Turkish statesman.
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.bibliography: Scarce, J., *Domestic Culture in the Middle East: An Exploration of the Household Interior*, Edinburgh, 1996, p.40 (object illustrated).
236db96b-210d-5f2b-b7a3-43f9546cfc60.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
keywords: Fuad Pasha; Eyup; Iznik-style; tilework; cintamani; floral decoration; vegetal decoration; palatial architecture

239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.name: Dish decorated with inscription.
239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.description:
This shallow *tabsil* dish is one of the few dishes from Fez decorated with a free composition that is neither radial nor with motifs arranged around the centre. The decoration is arranged in a fan around a vertical axis, unlike most earthenware dishes. The principal theme is epigraphic and architectural. The central motif, painted in blue and surrounded by a brown line, shows a mirror image of the pious formula ‘al-Mulk’, or 'power' (of God) in very stylised twisted *kufic* characters. It is framed by a poly-lobed arcature painted in blue and highlighted on the inside with a bright yellow line reminiscent of the *mihrab*. This decorative motif with religious undertones was introduced in earthenware in the AH 13th / AD late 18th century and was still in use in the early 19th century. This theme was inspired by similar designs engraved on wooden lintels from the Marinid and Sa'did eras. The arcature extends on both sides with consoles that end in fleurons, and the background is covered with floral motifs and Ottoman-style flowers.  
This type of shallow plate would normally have been used to serve *bastila* (Moroccan pie), but this example seems to have been more decorative and symbolic than practical.
239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.short_description: This type of dish was used to serve pies. The free composition of non-radiating decoration is symbolic, epigraphic and architectural. Its stylised decoration includes a mirror-image of the word ‘al-Mulk’, understood to mean 'divine power', beneath a representation of a *mihrab* arch.
239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.dimensions: Height 10 cm, base diameter 22 cm, diameter 40 cm.
239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.method_for_datation: From stylistic and comparative study. Also, the greyish, faded blue is characteristic of plates that predate the second half of the 13th / 19th century, which was a result of the quality of the cobalt oxide which remained full of impurities until 1266 / 1850. Indeed it is not until after this date, with the introduction of new industrial processes, that this type of ore could be completely cleared of its impurities and a strong blue obtained in ceramics.
239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.method_for_provenance: This type of earthenware was a speciality of Fez ceramicists from the 12th / 18th century.
239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.bibliography:
Bel, A., *Les industries de la céramique à Fès*, Algiers; Paris, 1918.  
Khatib-Boujibar, N., “La céramique émaillée”, in *Maroc, les trésors du Royaume*, catalogue, Paris, 1999.  
Loviconi A. and Belfitah D., *Regards sur la faïence de Fès*, Aix-en-Provence, 1991.  
*Andalusian Morocco: A Discovery in Living Art*, pp.128–9.
239141a6-d7e1-59fa-8b30-34134536fa01.author: Naima El Khatib-Boujibar
keywords: architectural decoration; floral decoration; epigraphic decoration
materials: Glazed earthenware, painted with cobalt oxide for the blue and limonite for the yellow.

23a0b5aa-ba65-58fa-85ce-1a8b261b0a49.name: Tympanum
23a0b5aa-ba65-58fa-85ce-1a8b261b0a49.short_description: The tympanum consists of 16 assembled tiles and comes from the palace of the grand vizier Piale Pasha (c.1515– 1578) or the mosque he founded. Both were finished in 1573 and were decorated lavishly with tile fields. A lucky knot motif of cloud bands in so-called “tomato red” dominates in front of spirals. Palace and mosque were “renovated” after the earthquake of 1890, and tile tympana sold world-wide through dealers. At least nine identical tympana are now kept in European and American museums.
23a0b5aa-ba65-58fa-85ce-1a8b261b0a49.bibliography: Noever, Peter (ed), *Global:Lab: Kunst als Botschaft. Asien und Europa 1500-1700, Exh. cat. Museum of Applied Arts Vienna*, Ostfildern: Hatje Cantz, 2009.
23a0b5aa-ba65-58fa-85ce-1a8b261b0a49.author: Mio Wakita-Elis
keywords: Tilework; Floral decoration; Iznik style; architectural decoration
materials: Quartz frit ceramic, decoration: underglaze painting in blue and so-called tomato red

23f47ae4-92dd-5aa9-bc77-16f877d33d49.name: Tile Fragments
23f47ae4-92dd-5aa9-bc77-16f877d33d49.short_description:
The ancient city of Qalhat, known as the Twin of Hormuz, was the main port of northern Oman from the 7th to 9th centuries AH / 13th to 15th centuries AD. The Great Mosque was its most famous edifice, built around 699 AH / 1300 AD by Bibi Maryam, the wife of Bahauddin Ayaz, King of Hormuz and Ruler of Qalhat. The Moroccan geographer Ibn Battuta visited Qalhat during his travels in the 8th century AH / 14th century AD and wrote a vivid description of the Great Mosque shortly after its completion:  
  
"Qalhat has fine bazaars and an exceedingly beautiful mosque, the walls of which are decorated with elaborate tile work."  
  
This fragment of a square tile features a moulded tri-lobed arch, painted in blue with a gold lustre-painted background. The lustre on this fragment has now almost completely vanished and is visible only in oblique light. It was based on a floral stem motif and was a prevalent form of decoration on the Kashan tiles manufactured for the Great Mosque.
23f47ae4-92dd-5aa9-bc77-16f877d33d49.provenance: The Great Mosque, Qalhat (Oman). Origin: Kashan, Persia (Iran)
23f47ae4-92dd-5aa9-bc77-16f877d33d49.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
keywords: Tiles; Lajvardina; lapis lazuli; Hormuz; Qalhat; Arabesque

2420606d-db2f-5da6-a8b4-ce74b2c066ae.name: Dish
2420606d-db2f-5da6-a8b4-ce74b2c066ae.short_description: Soon after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453, Iznik production grew significantly and developed a distinctive style. However, the place of honour at dining tables of discernment was held by Chinese blue and white porcelain and celadon. The response of Iznik potters was to imitate the highly admired blue and white wares of China. The earliest group of Iznik ceramics was in this colour scheme and can be divided into two groups: the first relied on the Nakkashane for designs and metalwork for shapes; the second blue and white group clearly incorporated Chinese motifs.
2420606d-db2f-5da6-a8b4-ce74b2c066ae.bibliography: Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, *The Essence of Iznik*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2011: 51-53.

24ba84ea-5d4a-55c8-b96d-2f3763e9540e.name: Hanging lamp.
24ba84ea-5d4a-55c8-b96d-2f3763e9540e.description:
A bulbous-shaped lamp made from stone-paste ceramic with flared rim; a form typical of glass mosque lamps produced during the Mamluk period. Loops attached to the side would have been used to suspend the lamp. Bands of Qur’anic inscriptions, painted in white with a blue background, surround the rim, the waist, and the base of the lamp. Between these calligraphic panels are two friezes of cloud-scrolls and arabesques, painted in blue and olive-green. A row of white tulips fills a narrow band above the central inscription. Around the base are small cartouches with inscriptions giving the name of the decorator, Musli, and the date and place of production. It is in this respect that the lamp is so important, establishing the date of Iznik pottery in this style and colour scheme.  
The austere design befits the religious setting for which this lamp was made. Between AH 936 and 946 (AD the 1530s and 40s) Süleyman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66) ordered the refurbishment of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Iznik tiles replaced the earlier mosaics on the exterior, while inside the building Iznik lamps were hung on chains. This lamp was found in the Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem in the 19th century.
24ba84ea-5d4a-55c8-b96d-2f3763e9540e.short_description: This ceramic lamp was evidently made for the refurbishment of the Dome of the Rock, ordered by Süleyman the Magnificent. Made in Ottoman Turkey in AH 956 / AD 1549, it was found in the Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem.

25cc99b8-ea3d-5a36-aad3-2fdf4e0f6ac5.short_description: Illustrates the influence of Egyptian motifs on Victorian ceramics. Part of the second wave of Egyptianisation, related to the construction of the Suez Canal.

26770047-7eca-547b-bc65-67b8abf591d5.name: Bottle
26770047-7eca-547b-bc65-67b8abf591d5.description:
In 1580 Portugal came under the rule of the Spanish Kings, giving rise to a new political situation that altered the traditional commercial relationship with both Portugal's European trading neighbours and the Far East. A deep political and economic crisis emerged and the pottery workshops of Lisbon searched for new markets. Blue Chinese porcelain, common during the Wanli period (1573–1619), was an inspiration for Portuguese faience. The wares were then exported via existing Portuguese trade routes to overseas colonies and north and north-western Europe.  
This bottle – with a flattened circular body – has a cylindrical neck and a trapezoidal foot. The neck is finished in copper. It has a lid, indicating that it would have been used as a drinking vessel. The shape, which was rare in China, is probably based on a metal model from western Asia.  
Painted in several shades of blue, the front bears the coat of arms of Philip II of Spain: a medallion with flowers sprouting out from a border of dots. On the reverse are more blooms and insects. Both sides have a blue border with dots in a darker shade, probably imitating the nails used in the metal models that inspired it.  
According to Howard and Ayers (1978), the coat of arms of King Philip II was copied from a coin. It is not clear how the piece was commissioned, however, because Spain had limited access to China via the Philippines through Formosa in the 1570s and, in around 1580 for a year, via some land granted in Pinal near Macao. Michel Beurdeley (1962) believes that Philip II had a collection of almost 3,000 Chinese porcelain objects.
26770047-7eca-547b-bc65-67b8abf591d5.short_description: A porcelain bottle with the coat of arms of King Philip II of Spain. It was inspired in both shape and decoration by a pilgrim’s flask, a precious and much coveted object of the 16th century that was used to hold drinking water when on pilgrimage.
26770047-7eca-547b-bc65-67b8abf591d5.holder: Museum and Library of the House of Braganza

2778ce78-5836-53cd-89f8-bb048bc613b1.name: Bottle with stamped design
2778ce78-5836-53cd-89f8-bb048bc613b1.description:
The overall shape of the object consists of four distinct parts: neck, handle, and upper and lower hemispheres of the body. The decoration, of great complexity, consists of patterns frequently found on jewellery, which gives the impression of a goldsmith’s work transposed to clay. Included in this profusion are roundels framing a bird downed by a hawk or passing lion, twisted columns topped with discs in the shape of flowers, fish, lotus buds, palmettes, and palm trees, circular marks…  
It is a utilitarian but decorative piece intended for pouring water in apartments or reception rooms.

27a8bc2c-716a-5b73-bc30-dce11b765646.name: Pilgrim’s flask.
27a8bc2c-716a-5b73-bc30-dce11b765646.description:
One of the specialities of Mamluk Syrian potters was the unglazed moulded pilgrim's flasks for the transportation of cool water on long journeys. These sturdy flasks became extremely popular in the AH 7th and 8th / AD 13th and 14th centuries and were certainly produced by a number of Syrian kilns. They were all made in the same manner: the globular body with its flattened sides was created from two identical moulds; the two handles on the shoulders and the short slightly tapering mouthpiece were then added separately. The moulded decoration on the body is various, including hunting scenes, mythical creatures, floral motifs, knotted designs, inscriptions and heraldic emblems which, no doubt, were meant to identify the ownership of the Mamluk officers who carried them.  
This well-preserved pilgrim's flask from the National Museum of Aleppo was uncovered during the course of recent Syrian-German excavations at Aleppo Citadel. Its decoration is highly unusual: it shows a large crescent on top of a solid triangular base, flanked by a pair of swords inscribed in a roundel. The background is covered with small impressed circles. The upper segment of the roundel is separated and decorated with foliage. Knotted bands run along the outer edges of the body.  
The unusual central composition is obviously meant to represent a Mamluk blazon, albeit the emblem depicted here is completely unknown in the canon of Mamluk heraldry. It might possibly be the result of a misunderstanding or indeed an inspired fantasy of the potter who mixed the crescent with the more popular cup symbol. It is possible that these decorations were only meant to look like heraldic emblems without actually being such. The piece has not been produced very carefully: although the same mould was used on both sides as usual, the impression on the back is seriously off centre.
27a8bc2c-716a-5b73-bc30-dce11b765646.short_description: This pilgrim's flask from the Mamluk period was found during recent excavations in the Citadel of Aleppo. Although its shape is typical, its decoration is highly unusual as the emblem is unknown in the repertory of Mamluk heraldry.
27a8bc2c-716a-5b73-bc30-dce11b765646.holder: National Museum of Aleppo, Islamic Department.

27a8bc2c-716a-5b73-bc30-dce11b765646.method_for_provenance: The flask was found during archaeological excavations in the area of Aleppo Citadel.

27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.name: *The Adoration of the Shepherds*
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.description:
This bas-relief is part of a series which includes four horizontal and four oval scenes, all are in their original frames.  
Three shepherds approach to adore the Child. The Madonna, St. Joseph and the angels, occupying the middle of the scene, point to the object of interest, Jesus. Piò moulds the tender scene to create a soft and delicate three-dimensional picture, similar to his contemporary painters.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.short_description: This sculpture is a good example of the baroque technique of Bolognese terracotta. Terracotta bas-reliefs were intended as proper paintings, framed and hanging from the walls, but lacking colours. The figures are scattered on different planes; in the foreground they are nearly three dimensional while the background figures are drawn more two dimensionally.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.holder: Museo Diocesano di Arte Sacra di San Giovanni in Persiceto
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.method_for_datation: The date is inscribed on the surface of the bas relief. The origin is described by the biographer of the artist, Zanotti.
27de28c8-df7c-5e34-b27a-6b4d7277f037.obtention: The bas-relief was originally made for the oratory of the Suffragio in San Giovanni in Persiceto. It was moved to the oratory of the Holy Sacrament and later to the church of the Madonna della Cintura. In 1948 it was moved again to the Collegiata (the main church) of San Giovanni in Persiceto. The museum of the church was opened to the public and it was exhibited there.

27f9e871-3369-55e0-b6a2-de1d5b3a2fec.name: Vase.
27f9e871-3369-55e0-b6a2-de1d5b3a2fec.description: A vase with a wide neck, bulbous body, and low flaring foot. A narrow collar around the neck, decorated with a braided rope design, divides the vase into two areas of decoration. Both are filled with floral motifs in red, green, and blue. These include carnations, tulips, and hyacinths, all of which are shown blossoming at the ends of gently undulating green stems. The use of a brilliant emerald green is characteristic of Iznik ceramics at their peak of quality, in the 1570s. Shortly thereafter, slackening patronage and other factors led the Ottoman ceramic industry to economic and aesthetic decline. This vase, then, is a splendid token of the high point of 16th-century Ottoman ceramics.
27f9e871-3369-55e0-b6a2-de1d5b3a2fec.short_description: A bulbous vase decorated with floral motifs which, rather than functioning as mere repeat units, are freely rendered and almost naturalistic. The use of brilliant red and emerald-green indicates that this vase was made at the height of the classical Iznik pottery industry.
27f9e871-3369-55e0-b6a2-de1d5b3a2fec.method_for_datation: Stylistic comparison with other Iznik wares of the 1570s.
27f9e871-3369-55e0-b6a2-de1d5b3a2fec.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
27f9e871-3369-55e0-b6a2-de1d5b3a2fec.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey, Istanbul/London, 1989, fig. 703.
27f9e871-3369-55e0-b6a2-de1d5b3a2fec.author: Barry Wood

2820e756-8db5-5af5-a547-f9d4acc23065.name: Tile panel with inscription in *thuluth* script
2820e756-8db5-5af5-a547-f9d4acc23065.short_description: From the time of the construction of the great mosque complex of Süleyman in Istanbul (Hegira 957–964 / AD 1550–1557) onward, Iznik epigraphic tiles increasingly came to grace Ottoman religious monuments. Stencils were used to transfer the designs of both epigraphic and pictorial tile compositions; however, this inscription seems not to have been conceived by one of the many professional calligraphers who flourished under the Ottomans. Rather it may be the work of a highly proficient amateur. The Arabic text, “This world is the sowing ground of the next \[world\]", appears to be an unsound *hadith*, probably a paraphrase of a verse from the Qur’an (al-Shura: 20). The inscription suggests that the panel was created for a religious context, but it does not tell us much more about its original location.
2820e756-8db5-5af5-a547-f9d4acc23065.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
2820e756-8db5-5af5-a547-f9d4acc23065.dates: Hegira second half of the 10th century / AD second half of the 16th century
2820e756-8db5-5af5-a547-f9d4acc23065.method_for_datation: Iznik tile panels of this type, underglaze-painted in red, blue and green on a white ground—a colour combination established in the Iznik potteries in the 1550s and 1560s—and decorated with a scrolling border of flowers and leaves, and a *thuluth* inscription, are roughly datable to the second half of the 16th century.
2820e756-8db5-5af5-a547-f9d4acc23065.method_for_provenance: The panel represents the classical type of Iznik ceramics, in which the palette is comprised of red, blue, green and white.
2820e756-8db5-5af5-a547-f9d4acc23065.obtention: Collection of Nasli M. Heeramaneck (1902-1971), New York, until 1973 (sold to); LACMA, The Nasli M. Heeramaneck collection, gift of Joan Palevsky.

28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.name: Coping of a well.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.description:
Cylindrical on the inside and hexagonal on the outside, this coping rests on a thick base forming a ridge and opens up with an outcurving rim, flat on the upper part and cut in eight vertical sections. A green glaze covers the stamped decoration. It is distributed in eight vertical panels, each one divided into five horizontal sections, three of which are decorated with friezes of poly-lobed arcatures. They are in turn separated by one section covered only by a green glaze and another with an inscription in cursive characters engraved on a green glaze. The inscription names the owner of the workshop and the date the coping was made. The inscription says: 'This was made in Haj Buluqin's house on the (…) day of the seventh of the month of *Rabi* II the last in the year five hundred eighty-six \[AD 1190\]'. The opening of the coping is crowned by several patterns, laid out in two superposed friezes. One is formed by squares filled with eight-pointed stars whereas the other is thinner and has a herringbone pattern.  
During the Almohad period, this type of coping was widely used in both the Maghreb and al-Andalus. They were built with the purpose of protecting the wells in the middle of the courtyards in houses. They also served as decoration, and that is the reason why ceramicists built them with special care and were proud to sign their work.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.short_description: This type of decorated coping, bearing the date and name of the workshop, was equally common in the Maghreb and al-Andalus. They were used to protect wells sunk in the centre of interior domestic courtyards, and to enhance their beauty.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.method_for_datation: The engraved inscription in cursive characters on the fourth section mentions the place of manufacture (the workshop of Haj Buluqin) and the date, the seventh day of the month *Rabi* II in the year 586 / 1190.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.method_for_provenance: Chance archaeological find in Sebta (Ceuta), at the place known as Llano de las Damas.

29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.name: Tankard.
29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.description: The tankard has a cylindrical body with a flat base and an angular handle. This characteristic shape found in a large number of mostly Iznik products attributed to the second half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century seems to be based on a leather or wooden original. The vessel is underglaze painted in two gradations of blue, diluted turquoise and opaque red on a white background. The decoration of the exterior shows a composition of elements used on Iznik ceramics and tiles throughout the AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries: large oval medallions filled with rosettes alternate with shrubs of flowers in two rows. The edges of spirals reflect Chinese influence. The origin of this abstract pattern was the 'waves and rock' motif, which was very common on the rims of Iznik plates. The tankard is marked on the foot with a crescent and an asterisk.
29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.short_description: Tankard with a cylindrical body and an angular handle. This shape, characteristic of many mainly Iznik products, seems to be derived from a leather or wooden original. Its underglaze painted decoration consists of medallions filled with rosettes and flowering shrubs in two rows.
29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.dimensions: Height 21 cm, diameter of rim 10.5 cm.
29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.method_for_datation: Unlike Iznik wares of the 10th–11th / 16th–17th centuries, this tankard is marked under the foot. The object was dated according to similar marks, which are known from Ottoman ceramics of the 13th / 19th century, for example, from Istanbul.
29500c62-a992-5094-94d4-fc5721242264.method_for_provenance: A vase housed in the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities also shows an imitation of Iznik pattern and a mark which is signed 'Istanbul' within a crescent. However, it was not possible to identify the workshop to which the mark of a crescent and asterisk on the bottom belongs.

296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.name: Jug.
296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.description: A stone-paste (fritware) jug with a bulbous pear-shaped body, resting on a low, circular foot-ring. The neck is cylindrical and widens towards a rimless mouth. An S-shaped handle is attached to the lip and shoulder. Both the neck and the body are covered with alternating blue and green fish-scale patterning; each area separated from the other by sinuous split-palmette borders. A guilloche border runs below the lip and around the lower body; a narrow white collar with dotted detailing sits around the lower neck. The all-over textural covering of this jug is akin to the engraved (repoussé) decoration of contemporary metalwork, and it therefore illustrates the extent to which designs were transferred between different media during the Ottoman period.
296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.short_description: Iznik pieces with a curious overall scale design are attributed to AH 987–92 / AD 1580–5. Such scale patterns are akin to the engraved or repoussé decoration of contemporary Ottoman metalwork, a fact that illustrates well the extent to which designs were transferred between the media in Ottoman times.
296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.method_for_datation: Iznik pieces with this characteristic overall fish-scale design are attributed to the period 987–92/ 1580–5.
296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.method_for_provenance: Ceramic wares of this style are known to have been produced in Iznik, Turkey during the period 987–92/ 1580–5.
296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.obtention: Bought from the Castellani Collection in 1884.
296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.bibliography:

296685d2-89a9-5e81-bce8-4114d2e64c21.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware), green, blue, black underglaze, bole-red underglaze slip, over which a clear glaze.

29723c0f-a1c2-5bb3-aa6b-3b7ef63ed1af.name: Ceramic vase
29723c0f-a1c2-5bb3-aa6b-3b7ef63ed1af.short_description: Kütahya was the second most important ceramic production centre after İznik due to the rich clay deposits in the area. Although there was a decline in ceramic production at the beginning of the 19th century, in the last quarter of the same century production was revived and new designs inspired by İznik ceramics were produced. This is a Kütahya-produced vase whose body enlarges toward the top. It has a floral design on a blue base. The inner part of the notched mouth is white.

29eaa974-bd2d-5ede-a8b9-1d1b993fec15.name: Bowl
29eaa974-bd2d-5ede-a8b9-1d1b993fec15.short_description: The thin-walled bowls with a decoration of blue stripes on white ground were revolutionary, formally and technically. It was the first time that the contrast of blue-and-white was employed as a stylistic means; also, firing technique was developed far enough so that the cobalt blue – applied before the glazing – stayed put and unfolded its full luminosity.
29eaa974-bd2d-5ede-a8b9-1d1b993fec15.bibliography: Mrazek, Wilhelm (ed), *Kunst des Islam. Teppiche, Keramiken und Fayencen, Gläser und Moscheelampen, Metallarbeiten aus den Sammlungen des Österreichischen Museums für Angewandte Kunst*, Vienna: Museum of Applied Arts, 1977.
29eaa974-bd2d-5ede-a8b9-1d1b993fec15.author: Mio Wakita-Elis

29f83378-fe07-5531-90be-4912dbf80f0f.name: Coffee Cup
29f83378-fe07-5531-90be-4912dbf80f0f.description: Tile red in colour and in the shape of a Bektashi headdress.
29f83378-fe07-5531-90be-4912dbf80f0f.owner: The Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism

2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.name: Tile panel.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.description: A panel of six wall-tiles, decorated with underglaze painting in the full colour range of the mature Iznik style. Wide green strips with meandering flowering vines form the side borders as well as a pointed-arch motif. The spandrels of the arch are filled with red and white arabesques on a dark-blue background, while the space beneath contains a masterful composition in which naturalistic flowers and large-scale arabesque motifs fill the brilliant white space without overcrowding it. The composition is abruptly cut off at the bottom, indicating that these six tiles formed the upper part of a larger tilework ensemble.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.short_description: A panel of six tiles, executed in the colour palette of the high Iznik style. The decoration features floral decoration beneath a pointed arch. This panel was the top section of a larger panel depicting a niche. It may have adorned an Ottoman palace.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.dimensions: Height 62 cm, width 102 cm, depth 3 cm.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.method_for_datation: Stylistic comparison: the use of green indicates that the tiles must date after the 1570s; while the high quality means they cannot be much later than the turn of the 17th century.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.bibliography: Lane, A., *A Guide to the Collection of Tiles*, London, 1960, p.21.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.author: Barry Wood

2ae3984e-4d68-5007-ab52-077d0d39f896.name: Alhambra vase
2ae3984e-4d68-5007-ab52-077d0d39f896.short_description: The Alhambra, the palace and fortress of the Moorish Kings of Granada, Spain, was founded in 1248 and largely completed by 1354. After three hundred years of neglect and destruction, restoration work began in 1828. Its sumptuous architecture excited a great deal of interest, dissemninated most notably by the *Plans, Details and Sections of the Alhambra* published by Owen Jones from 1836. Of the original furnishings of the Palace, some vases survive. The most famous was made before 1400 and is here copied relatively accurately by Deck. This vase was probably shown in the International Exhibition, London, 1862.
2ae3984e-4d68-5007-ab52-077d0d39f896.dimensions: Height: 107.0 cm, Width: 51.0 cm, Depth: 48.0 cm, Weight: 28.5 kg

2b7cc6a3-d756-5b6c-ae2c-9f1c0902b308.name: Bowl with fish design
2b7cc6a3-d756-5b6c-ae2c-9f1c0902b308.short_description: This slip-painted dish shows a broad band of six white and ochre fish 'swimming' anticlockwise around its inner walls. A large central interlace roundel in red and white and two borders with pseudo-*kufic* inscriptions complete the design, which may echo pre-Islamic customs and beliefs or astrological preoccupations.
2b7cc6a3-d756-5b6c-ae2c-9f1c0902b308.provenance: Eastern Iran, Afghanistan or Central Asia
keywords: Bowl; Kufic; Fish; Ceramic; animal decoration; pseudo inscriptions; calligraphy

2bf07354-1d19-5067-a7fe-bfedc33b8380.name: Small bowl with eagle.
2bf07354-1d19-5067-a7fe-bfedc33b8380.description: This poly-lobed bowl is decorated with the stylised figure of an eagle with its wings outstretched, painted in solid lustre with the exception of a few details left uncoloured, such as the eye and the neck. It is surrounded by small dotted panels and the edge is decorated with semi-circles.
2bf07354-1d19-5067-a7fe-bfedc33b8380.short_description: The shape and decoration of this bowl are influenced by a combination of different styles and traditions. Its shape is related to early Sassanid metalwork, while its decoration is reminiscent of a style used in late Abbasid figurative ceramics.
2bf07354-1d19-5067-a7fe-bfedc33b8380.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
2bf07354-1d19-5067-a7fe-bfedc33b8380.dimensions: Height 4.1 cm, length 12.5 cm, width 9.1 cm.
2bf07354-1d19-5067-a7fe-bfedc33b8380.method_for_provenance: The design of this piece derives from metallic prototypes of Sassanid origin via Chinese T’ang porcelain (618–906). The style used for the bird, however, is attributable to curvilinear stylisation typical of late Abbasid figurative ceramics.

2cc72222-bc92-577d-b037-11f94f619161.name: Two fragments of wall-cladding.
2cc72222-bc92-577d-b037-11f94f619161.description:
These two fragments of ceramic wall-cladding with a metallic sheen originally took the form of a cross.  
The geometric decoration consists of circles enclosing a motif that could be perceived as evoking either a fish or a flower on its stem, outlined in white with a paintbrush over an olive green background.  
The epigraphic decoration features the inscription '*al-yumn*' (prosperity), repeated several times, written in *kufic* characters and executed in white over a yellow background with a metallic sheen.  
According to G. Marçais, 'this ceramic draws inspiration from the 'Abbasid east which, itself, borrows from old Semitic or Byzantine civilisations'.  
In general, these crosses were linked to other elements, such as eight-cornered stars or lozenges, in order to form wall-cladding.
2cc72222-bc92-577d-b037-11f94f619161.short_description: Fragments of lustre-painted ceramic wall-covering, one decorated with geometric patterns including a fish or flower motif brush-painted in white on a green background, while the other has the *kufic* inscription *'al-yumn*' (prosperity) repeated several times in white on a yellow base.
2cc72222-bc92-577d-b037-11f94f619161.dimensions: Element with geometric decoration: length 15 cm, width 14 cm ; element with epigraphic decoration: length 17 cm, width 15.5 cm.
2cc72222-bc92-577d-b037-11f94f619161.method_for_datation: Fragments found in the Dar al-Bahr of the Qal'at Bani Hammad, which dates from the 5th–6th / 11th –12th centuries, according to Kitab al-Istibsar: 'The Banu Hammad built some important constructions in the *qal'a* … including \[the palace\] known as Dar al-Bahr, at the centre of which was a vast basin'.
2cc72222-bc92-577d-b037-11f94f619161.method_for_provenance: From the report of the De Beylié excavation, 1909.

2cc72222-bc92-577d-b037-11f94f619161.author: Houria Cherid

2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.name: Bowl.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.description:
The development of ceramics painted with metallic lustre was an important advancement in Islamic ceramic art. It was considered luxurious because it gave a metallic sheen, giving the impression of a precious metal. Such ceramics come in various types: normally the lustre is applied on to a transparent glaze; less frequently, it is found on cobalt-blue, manganese and turquoise glaze. This piece is one such example.  
A ceramic bowl with a cylindrical body and a columnar base, the bulk of the body decorated with a double border containing a band of repeating angular pseudo-*kufic* script and curling, stylised vegetal scrolls. Painted semi-circles are arranged around the rim. These designs are executed in dark, reddish-brown metallic lustre underneath a transparent layer of turquoise glaze. While the technique and the designs are familiar in other Fatimid lustre-ware, the shape is somewhat unusual. The emphasis on the decorative quality of calligraphy that this piece exhibits may be evidence of the influence of ceramics derived from the Eastern Samanid Dynasty, which is contemporary to the Fatimid period.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.short_description: The pseudo-*kufic* calligraphy and semi-circular rim decoration of this lustre-painted and transparent-blue-glazed bowl is most probably the work of Fatimid Egyptian potters who settled in Syria.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.dates: Hegira late 5th–early 6th century / AD late 11th–early 12th century.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.method_for_datation: The bowl was dated by comparison with similar pieces found in Tel Minis, a Syrian village near Ma'rrat al-Nu'man. The style was influenced by Egyptian Fatimid pottery of the 5th / 11th century.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.method_for_provenance: This bowl was found by a resident of Raqqa, but ceramic production in the region did not begin until the early 6th / 12th century. It is thought, therefore, that this piece may be either early Raqqa or Tel Minis ware. Lustre-ware production in Syria was prolific, but the provenance cannot be determined definitively.
2cd70993-c8a3-50ff-9205-453f52ff7756.provenance: Syria; possibly Raqqa or Tel Minis.
