2e402c4d-0004-5e48-84c2-e6f4b24d7d3e.name: Bowl with dark brown slip and white slip decoration
2e402c4d-0004-5e48-84c2-e6f4b24d7d3e.short_description: This earthenware bowl was covered in a dark brown slip before receiving an as yet unread, white floriated *kufic* inscription – possibly containing blessings. The secondary motifs evoking a textured background and rim, may suggest that the bowl was inspired by a metal prototype. Vessels like this have been associated with Nishapur and Afrasiyab.

2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.name: Plate with lotus leaves.
2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.description:
Plate with circular base and curved rim. The beige background is tin-glazed with no slip. The decoration is in green and yellow ochre with lively floral and geometric patterns. On the rim there are repeated sequences of two green and one ochre semi-circle. A similar juxtaposition of tones is used to great effect in the middle of the plate, where a central six-pointed star is surrounded by alternating spirals and lotus leaves.  
This striking combination of exuberance, richness and variety of ornamentation is rare in Oriental ceramics of this period. The colourful, stylised flora achieves a complex rhythmic effect.
2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.short_description: The floral and geometric decoration on this ring-based dish combines green and yellow ochre. The richness and variety of its ornamentation are typical of Aghlabid ceramics, with the colours, hues and stylised flora creating a very varied rhythmic effect.
2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.dates: Hegira, last third of the 4th century or beginning of the 5th century / AD 10th–11th centuries.
2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.dimensions: Height 7 cm, diameter 27 cm; diameter (of base) 10 cm, thickness 0.6 cm.
2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.method_for_datation: Raqqada, the Aghlabid capital, was built in 263 / 876. Since the plate was discovered on the excavation site, this date must be a *terminus ante quem*. Moreover, the colours and decoration of the piece are typical of the Aghlabid period, which ends with the advent of the Fatimids in 296 / 909. So it is probable that the latter date is the *terminus post quem* for the plate, even though the same type of work may have continued into the early Fatimid era.
2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.method_for_provenance: The discovery of this plate, made and painted in the Ifriqiyan manner, on site at Raqqada appears to confirm that it was produced locally in the pottery workshops of Kairouan or Raqqada.
2ee161bc-3657-5540-a52c-08980b1622cb.obtention: The plate was among objects discovered on site during the 1960 excavations at Raqqada. Initially kept on site, the piece was put on display in 1986 at the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada.

2f159199-c491-5bb7-b7b8-53c7b500249a.name: Panel decorated with a mosque.
2f159199-c491-5bb7-b7b8-53c7b500249a.description:
An Ottoman mosque with its typical truncated-cone minarets is painted within a horseshoe arch spanning two lateral columns. In the lower panel is a complex arrangement of flowers and leaves in a small vase. Tulips, sunflowers and carnations are intermingled with scrolled palm- and vine-leaves. These are arranged symmetrically and the whole pattern is contained within a second horseshoe arch.  
A broad selection of different foliated scrolls, leaves and flowers of all kinds decorate the lunettes, the arch-stones and the capitols. This great profusion of foliage is nonetheless cleverly organised.  
The main colours are the background beige (white lead or tin base), brown (manganese oxide base), yellow (antimony oxide base) green (copper oxide base) and blue (cobalt oxide base). Although the decoration is Ottoman-inspired the colours and techniques used in the production of this panel come from the Andalusian tradition. This combination of influences resulted in Tunisian ceramics taking on their unique character.
2f159199-c491-5bb7-b7b8-53c7b500249a.short_description: The decoration, colours and manufacturing technique used in this panel are typical of Tunisian ceramics, where Andalusian traditions mixed with Ottoman influences. An Ottoman mosque is painted inside a horseshoe arch, and the lower panel is decorated with a small vase containing a spray of flowers.
2f159199-c491-5bb7-b7b8-53c7b500249a.method_for_datation: The decoration, colours and manufacture of this panel are typical of the Qallaline workshops' production at Tunis during the 12th / 18th century.
2f159199-c491-5bb7-b7b8-53c7b500249a.obtention: This piece comes from the Bardo Museum and was acquired by the Sidi Qasim al-Jalizi Museum at the time of its inauguration in 1978.
2f159199-c491-5bb7-b7b8-53c7b500249a.author: Mourad Rammah

2fd59a40-4424-5f9b-820e-ab69e9b0306f.name: Jar
2fd59a40-4424-5f9b-820e-ab69e9b0306f.short_description: Bulbous, wide-mouthed jar with thick walls, four single and eight double handles; applied rope decoration on the shoulder. The jar is covered with a bluish-green glaze with large iridescent areas. Features such as the rope motif, the multiple handles, the colour of the glaze and the thick walls highlight the archaic character of the jar, and allow us to date it back to the later years of the Sasanian rule and the rise of the Islamic empire. Muslims borrowed extensively from the cultural heritage of the peoples they conquered, gradually integrating local traditions within the larger framework of Islamic civilization.
2fd59a40-4424-5f9b-820e-ab69e9b0306f.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
2fd59a40-4424-5f9b-820e-ab69e9b0306f.obtention: Purchased by a Romanian art collector in Paris  in 1926. Purchased by the Museum in 1960.

30241187-e18e-5731-96d9-ec8bc8d23e75.name: Tile picture of a Cuenca carpet
30241187-e18e-5731-96d9-ec8bc8d23e75.description:
An unusual “carpet,” this panel consists of 484 underglaze-painted tiles which together form the picture of a Cuenca carpet. The panel was probably intended as flooring, a kind of al fresco carpet which, when set into the ground, would add colour, pattern, and interest to an outdoor setting. Tiles would be decidedly more durable in inclement weather than a wool or silk carpet.  
In shades of blue, yellow, green and manganese on a white ground, the panel has a shield at centre bounded by the phrase "Ave Maria Gracia Plena Dominus Tecun." The shield is surrounded by a series of borders: the deepest interior border has mirrored, inverted, and repeated foliate scrolls; the outer borders feature patterned triangle, diamond, and oval motifs in a continuous repeat.  
Made about 1921, the tile panel’s design derives from a genuine Spanish carpet probably made in the 17th century. It is not known if the tile maker worked from the historic carpet itself or a photographic reproduction of it. An extant black and white image of the original carpet confirms the tile picture closely resembles the source. It is unclear, however, if the colours mimic it. A comparison between the two reveals that the tile maker opted to standardize colour usage across the tiles, whereas the carpet was woven with more variation.  
The tile picture was one of two that made its way to Florida, where it later came into the hands of Berberyan Galleries. Each shows a Cuenca carpet, although not the same carpet. Doris Duke purchased both panels for her home Shangri La, in Honolulu. Neither was used as flooring, but instead were wall mounted similar to hanging textiles. Later, Duke had one panel shipped to her home Rough Point in Newport, Rhode Island where it remains today. Ceramic may be an unusual vehicle for the display of the Cuenca aesthetic, but it was an aesthetic Duke adored. She purchased several Cuenca carpets for her collection, including a massive 17th century one for Shangri La’s Living Room.

30667b34-8461-5a17-8033-803fceee10dc.name: Dish.
30667b34-8461-5a17-8033-803fceee10dc.description:
The Iznik pottery dish decorated in cobalt-blue, thin pale green and relief red, with black outlines on a white background shows at the centre a dense floral design. The entire dish is treated as a single decorative surface. The flowers – red dotted tulips and carnations, a peony and a hyacinth spray falling across the centre of the plate – emerge from a leafy tuft and are adapted by curved and broken stems to suit the scale and surface of the dish. This style is called 'quatre fleurs' after the four principal types of flowers, the tulip, carnation, rose and hyacinth. It was promoted by the court painter Kara Memi in the second half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century and shows a greater realism in floral depiction than earlier styles. Feathered *saz* leaves combined with flowering sprays as can be seen next to the peony or with a simple leaf as above the tuft is a development of the last quarter of AH 10th / AD 16th century.  
The floral design at the centre of the dish is framed with a stylised Chinese wave-and-rock border on a flat sloping rim. The Chinese-influenced type of foliated rim, used together with the wave-and-rock motif, had been given up in the second half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century because of its costly freehand cutting.  
On the back the dish is painted with four blue-coloured spiral motifs alternating with four green trefoils on a white background. The transparent slightly turquoise glaze covers the back and bottom except for the foot-ring.
30667b34-8461-5a17-8033-803fceee10dc.short_description: Polychrome painted Iznik pottery dish. At the centre there is a dense floral design of various flowers of the so-called ‘quatre fleurs’ style emerging from a leafy tuft. The flat rim is decorated with a stylised Chinese wave-and-rock motif.
30667b34-8461-5a17-8033-803fceee10dc.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
30667b34-8461-5a17-8033-803fceee10dc.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.

30667b34-8461-5a17-8033-803fceee10dc.method_for_datation: The 'quatre fleurs' style was a development of the second half of the 10th / 16th century, and the feathered *saz* leaves combined with flowering sprays was a development of the last quarter of that century. 30667b34-8461-5a17-8033-803fceee10dc.method_for_provenance: The floral decoration and the shape are both specific for Iznik ceramics.

313aa86d-6ad7-502e-9d04-bd9dbded6167.short_description: The bowl shows a deer walking amongst flowering plants. Below its hooves are two fish decorated in blue. The lustre is light brown, enriched by blue underlinings.

315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.name: *Reposadero* or vat-base
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.description:
It has a cylindrical, hollow body with a straight base and a square-shaped rim, featuring a hole that would have served as a conduit for drainage. Both the base and the rim are slightly concave, the latter also has a whitish colour that could be interpreted as calcareous remains.  
  
The decoration is concentrated on the wall and consists of an epigraphic frieze between concave mouldings with marked edges. The central frieze is stamped with the inscription al-mulk with a six-pointed star positioned above the “m”.  
Functionally, the objects are known as *reposaderos* and served as supports for large water vats, which were both placed either in the courtyard or in domestic interiors. They preserved the water from impurities and kept it fresh, while also collecting any oozes liquid. By the spout of the *reposadero*, the water was transferred to basins or other vessels and could be used for washing hands or for human consumption. Furthermore, the stamped decoration, which repeats the word "*al-mulk*" or "the power", alludes to prophylactic practices of protection and praise of God.
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.dates: Second half of Hegira 6th century / AD 12th century
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.method_for_datation: Art-historical and archaeological studies have demonstrated the proliferation of different types of *reposaderos* in the domestic environments of al-Andalus from the end of the Hegira 6th / AD 12th and beginning of the Hegira 7th / AD 13th centurycenturies, following oriental models (Navarro 1995). This coincides with the generalisation of stamped decoration on ceramics for everyday use.

3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.name: Glazed bowl.
3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.description: A bowl with a circular mouth, a curved vertical rim with a triangular lip, a hemispherical body and slightly convex base with diagonal foot-ring. The exterior is glazed in honey-coloured monochrome and the interior presents an unusual decorative style which combines a frieze of small stamped rosettes with the decoration in *cuerda seca* in which the white, green, purple and honey colours of the glaze are separated by lines of manganese. The central theme is the tree of life formed by three lotus flowers in cross-section joined by a stalk, surrounded by a frieze of stamped rosettes. The composition is completed by a design on the rim in four parts, consisting of two pairs of alternating plant motifs. The 'tree of life' or 'tree of paradise' theme already appeared in metallic lustre-ware in the earthenware of AH 3rd -century / AD 9th-century Iraq (Grube, 1976). The object has been restored.
3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.short_description: Bowl decorated in *cuerda seca*. The central motif is a tree of life consisting of three lotus flowers seen from the side and joined by a stem, all surrounded by a rosette border. The decoration is completed by a four-part composition on the brim, formed by two pairs of alternating plant motifs.
3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.dates: Hegira second half of 6th century / AD second half of 12th century.
3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.dimensions: Height 8.5 cm, diameter (of mouth) 29.2 cm, diameter (of base) 11 cm.
3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated to the 6th / 12th century by comparison with objects of identical shape and decorative technique found, for example, in Ceuta and Alcazarseguir (Morocco) and in Cartagena, Málaga and Almería (Spain).
3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.method_for_provenance: The abundance of this type of ceramic in Málaga and Almería (Spain), where kilns have been found in which they were made, has led researchers to attribute its production to these towns.
3161f51d-fb30-50db-966e-808b130d86d6.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.name: Equestrian figurine.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.description:
A figurine of a bearded horseman with Asian Turkoman facial features, long braided hair and a helmet. Around the right front hoof of the horse is a snake that is climbing towards the rider from his left. The snake is shown opening its mouth to bite the rider through his armour, but he repels it with his shield. He carries a straight sword lifted into the air, ready to strike. There is a grooved cylindrical column coming out of the stomach of the horse that probably supported the statue, keeping it upright. The horse wears blue reins that are executed in relief. The reins continue around the horse's mouth and hang in front of its neck, then, like a harness, run across the sides of the horse's body down to the lower part of its hind legs.  
The object is glazed in off-white and blue and, therefore, can be compared to the laqabi-style ware of Persia, also known to have been produced in Raqqa. Laqabi ware is often seen as luxury bowls and dishes with moulded decorations. Production probably centred on the city of Kashan in Persia. Raised areas were often coloured in bright- blue, yellow, green, purple and pink to differentiate them from the white or off-white background.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.short_description: Known as the 'Horseman of Raqqa', this masterpiece of Syrian polychrome underglaze sculptural ceramics clearly displays the influence of the Central Asian military elite on artistic taste and local production.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.method_for_datation: The object is similar to wares produced in Persia during the Seljuq period in the 12th century; a period that saw significant trade activity and migration between Abbasid domains and those of the Seljuq and other Turkoman peoples.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this object is difficult to determine because there was substantial trade activity in ceramics between various centres of production and wealthy consumers. Therefore, it is impossible to determine whether it was made in Persia and imported to Raqqa, or made in Raqqa after exposure to wares from Seljuq Persia. Its “Eastern” features and its similarity to the *laqabi* wares reveals a strong Persian influence in either case.
32add590-3c53-51d7-af55-57212f399b39.obtention: Salim ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Haqq, Director General of Antiquities and Museums in the 1950s, referred to this figurine as the “Horseman of Raqqa” in the *Syrian Archaeological Annals*. It was found along with two others in a man-made pond during archaeological excavations in Raqqa. The pieces were then sold and taken to Paris where this figurine was deposited in a French bank. In 1949, after negotiations with the French government, the Horseman was returned to Syria and the National Museum of Damascus.

32b27ca0-4dc2-5e4e-a170-389deebd271f.name: Bowl with Design of Bird and Flowers
32b27ca0-4dc2-5e4e-a170-389deebd271f.short_description: A bowl made of reddish-buff clay, covered on the exterior, except for a few spots, with matt-white slip and, partially covering this, with glaze giving a creamy color. There are only traces of slip under the foot. The interior has the same cream-colored background, against which appears in profile a bird, having a green body and light brown beak, neck band, legs, and lower tail, decorated with dark brown spots, bands, and borders lightened with white dots. Additional decoration consists of three stylized flowers in the form of circular medallions, in brown and light brown with white dots as on the bird, as well as plant and tendril motifs in dark brown. This dark brown color has smeared over the background in several places. There is an incised circle around the interior of the bowl about one-third of the way up from the bottom. The bowl has been broken and mended, with some restoration in unimportant locations. Glaze and slip are missing from most of the rim.

32c00ce3-88f3-57c8-af19-222a4ef21303.name: Jug
32c00ce3-88f3-57c8-af19-222a4ef21303.short_description: The red slip - Armenian bole, introduced in workshops in Iznik in around 1560 – was used on this jug with a striking artistic force. The stylized tiger stripes – which together with the three spots comprise the classical chintamani pattern – hover all over the body of the jug like surrealistic lips. This pattern is found in variations on Turkish textiles and tiles.
keywords: 16th Century Iznik ceramics; Geometric patterns; Chintamani; cintamani

331c01a3-c119-5130-89aa-cbfe4030819b.name: Dish
331c01a3-c119-5130-89aa-cbfe4030819b.short_description: This deep dish features a spectacular centrally developed composition with four cusped medallions, stylized flowers, leaves and *çintamani* motifs. In combination with a restrained, yet impressive colour palette of dark blue, olive green and purple tones under transparent smoothly glittering glaze the décor can be considered as representing the so-called "Damascus" style in Iznik production, known for the first half and middle of the 16th century.

3370d63a-72ba-5b91-9038-50aa7d903914.name: Hookah bottle
3370d63a-72ba-5b91-9038-50aa7d903914.short_description: The new resurgence of lustre décor in Iranian ceramics took place in AD 17th century as a part of a general revival of culture and arts in the Safavid Iran. The patronage of the Iranian elite, who were fascinated with the splendour of Seljuq and Ilkhanid luxurious tableware, played a key role in the new renaissance of the tradition. The 17th century brought innovations to both the technology and the style of Iranian lustre painting. The stonepaste body became significantly whiter and denser in texture. The composition and quality of glaze also improved. Applied freely and richly on the surfaces of ceramic ware the lustre décor resembled in style the ornamentation on margins of books or album folios. In the repertoire of motifs, human figures have given way to floral patterns and landscapes, sometimes including animals. The garden, as a place of bodily solace and spiritual meditation, and a reminder of the heavenly Paradise promised by the Qur'an, became the key topic of the day. This small hookah bottle in a form of a gourd is a fine example of a new style of lustre painting. In its lower part birds and antelopes enliven favourite Safavid garden and flower motifs.

342ee59b-7d81-5295-82a8-47424a4bc175.name: Bowl
342ee59b-7d81-5295-82a8-47424a4bc175.short_description: The bowl is decorated in a golden brown lustre. Four seated figures are divided by a cross decorated with floral motif. The bowl is an example of the monumental style of Kashan.

343d8541-3a84-5139-8263-7b4033cb1128.name: Footed dish
343d8541-3a84-5139-8263-7b4033cb1128.short_description: Attributed to the “Gurgan hoard” in the past, this rimmed flat dish rests on three feet shaped as crowned sphinxes. The central field shows the depiction of an elephant carrying a palanchin (*hawda*) with a veiled figure, most likely a lady. Such theme is not unusual, and speaks of the intense political and cultural contacts with South Asia at that time. It may be an allusion to the story of Bahram Gur and Sapinud, his Indian bride, from the *Shahnameh*.

35b02f89-4d68-5272-8b1d-532de4511f6a.name: Pottery coffee-cup from Saudi Arabia
35b02f89-4d68-5272-8b1d-532de4511f6a.short_description: Cups like these were used predominantly to serve both *qishr* a drink made from the outer shells of coffee beans flavoured with cardamom or cinnamon as well as coffee made from toasted and ground coffee beans. They were frequently glazed in shades of green and yellow. Earthenware cups such as these were gradually replaced by finer porcelain cups during the middle and later parts of the 20th century.

35db2984-a03d-5306-8b35-2d8015d48fc3.name: Dish.
35db2984-a03d-5306-8b35-2d8015d48fc3.description:
A shallow, footed, stone-paste (fritware) dish belonging to the group of so-called 'Iznik'-style ceramics although its place of production was Damascus in Syria. The pale apple-green colouring – not the emerald-green of Iznik – is one of the distinctive features of this group of Damascus-produced 'Iznik' ceramics. This shallow dish is mounted on a cylindrical foot that flares slightly at the base. Both the underside of the dish and the surface of the foot are decorated. The pattern comprises a free naturalistic spray of pale aubergine-purple carnations, with pale apple-green stems and blue leaves. Two simple and very thin geometric bands surround the rim of the dish. The underside is decorated with four blue and green flower sprays, and the foot of the dish is decorated with a band of alternating blue flowers with green leaves.  
  
Ottoman architectural projects in Syria during the AH 950s / AD 1550s encouraged the establishment or an Iznik-offshoot ceramic-tiles industry in Damascus. Ceramic tiles were produced to decorate the Sulaymaniya Mosque, the Selimiye Madrasa, the Darwishiya Mosque and Shrine, the Sinaniye Mosque, and the Zawiya of Sa'd al-Din. These same tile-manufacturing workshops soon began to make tablewares too. It is thought that the potters recruited to decorate the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (completed in AH 963 / AD 1556), remained in Syria and played a role in the development of this local Syrian style of 'Iznik' ceramics.
35db2984-a03d-5306-8b35-2d8015d48fc3.short_description: When the Ottomans embarked on architectural projects in Syria, they set up potteries in Damascus to produced ceramic tiles for these monuments. The potters were resettled in Damascus for this purpose. In addition to tiles, a whole range of vessels including this dish was produced in the Iznik style.

3618877a-1f1a-5330-864f-53d4725fe233.description: This *mokhfia*, a conical dish on a short pedestal, is polychrome earthenware, with a design known as “turtle”. The example is characteristic of Moroccan ceramics in its shape and decoration.

36296e8f-2a4c-530e-a3d7-17c1732ee3a5.name: Jug.
36296e8f-2a4c-530e-a3d7-17c1732ee3a5.description: The body of this jug is elaborately decorated with a fish-scale patterned background upon which are arranged large white flowers with rosettes. The colourful palette of green, red, white and blue with black outlines on the outside of the jug, is contrasted by the plain white interior. The jug has an 'S-shaped' handle, and the neck of the jug is framed with two bands of geometrical ribbons. The jug can be specifically dated to the last quarter of the AH 10th / 16th century due to its colouring and style: the bright emerald green was used extensively from AH 977/ AD 1570; and the use of white highlights on the tips of the fish-scales was another common convention during the period. The use of fish-scales in decorating Iznik ceramics was a local innovation, first appearing on the fish motif in around AH 926/ AD 1520, and then subsequently used as background decoration and to fill-in other decorative objects such as pomegranates, clouds, and some floral shapes. The jug belongs to the so-called third phase of production (about AH 956–1111/ AD 1550–1700), when there were some 300 potters engaged in the manufacture of Iznik vessels and tiles.
36296e8f-2a4c-530e-a3d7-17c1732ee3a5.short_description: The ingenious fish-scale pattern on this jug is a local innovation by Iznik potters, which first appeared around AH 926 / AD 1520 on a ceramic fish motif, and was then used as background decoration or to fill in the surfaces of a variety of patterns including pomegranates, clouds and flowers.
36296e8f-2a4c-530e-a3d7-17c1732ee3a5.dates: Hegira last quarter of the 10th century / AD last quarter of the 16th century.
36296e8f-2a4c-530e-a3d7-17c1732ee3a5.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the jug can be specifically dated to the last quarter of the 10th / 16th century due to its colouring and style. For example the bright emerald- green was used extensively from 977 / 1570, while the use of a white highlight on the tip of the fish-scale pattern was another common convention during this period.
36296e8f-2a4c-530e-a3d7-17c1732ee3a5.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.name: Funerary stele ‘with ears’.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.description:
Fired-clay moulded funerary stele with a rectangular lower and rounded upper part and two appendages. It has been treated with an opaque, shiny tin glaze on to which the geometrical decoration and inscription in *kufic* characters has been applied using the metallic highlighting technique.  
The piece may have been mounted on the cresting of a funerary monument or fixed directly into the ground at the head of a grave.  
In al-Andalus, in accordance with Islam's sense of equality, tombs were characterised by their great simplicity. Nonetheless, we still find different types of burial. The most modest graves were usually marked with a single rough, unworked headstone, while stelae of a different type were used for people of higher social standing.  
Pieces of glazed and gilded clay were also produced for burials. Some are simple rectangular bricks, but the most important are the ones known as 'stelae with ears', which are made up of a rectangular part, the unglazed base of which was fixed into the ground, and a rounded part with two appendages, or 'ears', on top, hence the name. Some are tin glazed with an inscription in gold or cobalt on the front and a plant motif or 'hand of Fatima' (*hamza*) on the back.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.short_description: Funerary stele typical of the Kingdom of Granada said to have ‘ears’ due to the two appendages sticking out of the upper part. Sadly, some of its rich lustre decoration on a white base has been lost.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.dimensions: Height 30 cm, width 14 cm, depth 5 cm.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.method_for_datation: Parallels with similar pieces, kept in Huelva and the Institute of Valencia de Don Juan (Madrid), catalogued by Martínez Caviro as Nasrid from the 9th / 15th century.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.method_for_provenance: The piece is from Gibralfaro (Malaga), whose castle, built in the 8th / 14th century by Yusuf I (r. 734–55 / 1333–54), was built on top of an existing building erected by Badis al-Muzaffar (reign AH ?–465 / AD ?–1073) of the Zirid dynasty of Granada. From the 7th / 13th century, Malaga is mentioned in Arab sources as an important centre for the production of gold highlights.
36b1f585-6689-57a6-af25-716c209224fe.obtention: The piece was donated to the National Archaeological Museum in 1894.

370c5dcb-5b24-584f-9109-fe182b74b751.name: Long-necked amphora
370c5dcb-5b24-584f-9109-fe182b74b751.description:
This long-necked terracotta amphora from 19th-century Algeria is a prime example of impressive Kabyle pottery. These large terracotta amphorae are distinguished by their elongated necks, multilinear decorations, and distinctive horned handles.  
Even today, Kabyle women continue the tradition of coil-building and mould pattern techniques, decorating pottery with intricate geometric designs for household use.  
Skilled artisans create vessels of diverse sizes and shapes for storing water, milk, and oil, and for cooking and dining. The amphora’s decorative motifs, in black and brick red on a yellow slip, under a glaze, bear profound symbolic significance within Amazigh culture. These patterns, deeply ingrained in the Kabyle tradition, include a distinctive U-shaped design at the centre of the vessel that corresponds to the letter "ⵓ" in the Amazigh language, pronounced "oo" as in "moo". This symbolises either the moon, representing female fertility, or a horseshoe, symbolising fidelity. The firing process not only ensures the vessel’s durability, but also enhances the vibrant colours of the glazes, showcasing the exceptional skill and craftsmanship of Kabyle artisans. These artefacts speak to the cultural heritage and linguistic richness of the Amazigh people.

37eeebe2-30b7-5a11-b819-7445bc61c961.name: Tile
37eeebe2-30b7-5a11-b819-7445bc61c961.description:
Large rectangular ceramic plaque in a vertical arrangement. Its outer surface is completely covered with a symmetrical decoration based on scrolls twisted around themselves, from which different types of leaves emerge. The coat of arms of the Banda, characteristic of the Nasrid monarchy, is also found throughout the composition, flanked on all occasions by a pair of wading birds. The upper part and the right-hand side are framed by a gold herringbone motif, and the fact that the left-hand and lower sides do not have this border suggests that it was part of a larger ensemble. All the decoration on the tile is in blue, yellow and gold on a white background, although due to a manufacturing defect, the blue has run on part of the surface.  
  
Within this cultural context, water plays a prominent role in Andalusian architecture, often serving as a common thread. Present in numerous texts of Islamic sacred literature, it is presented as a symbol of life itself, thus reflecting the architectural design of the palace. We see it in ponds, fountains and irrigation channels with a practical, symbolic and aesthetic function, intertwining with the vegetation and evoking paradise. In this case, we are looking at a tile that was possibly used for a door jamb or a window frame, in which water is present indirectly, but its evocation is still clear: wading birds, vegetation and bluish tones contribute to an iconographic programme that revolves around this element.
37eeebe2-30b7-5a11-b819-7445bc61c961.method_for_datation: Comparative study with other similar pieces and iconographic analysis.

384dcfe8-dbaa-5658-9b1b-12f3a00fa9a4.name: Frieze tile
384dcfe8-dbaa-5658-9b1b-12f3a00fa9a4.short_description: The tile modelled in the form of a rectangle (almost a square) is adorned with a large cobalt-blue inscription in Persian standing out against a background of dense lustre-painted decor of floral curls, leaves, arabesques, birds and hares. At the top runs a border of relief palmette-patterned band. The tile once formed a part of a gorgeous frieze on walls of some early 14th century Ilkhanid palace. The art of lustre painting on ceramics was mastered by Iranian potters of Kashan in late 12th century. The technique involved application of metal-based pigment over already glazed and fired vessel.

3863e32d-5905-504c-b6f3-2271051d2c51.name: Dish with imaginary animal.
3863e32d-5905-504c-b6f3-2271051d2c51.description:
The dish, with curved sides, an out-curving brim and a ring-base, is decorated with a large, winged, imaginary animal with a bird’s head. It is notable that the motif of the imaginary animal is extremely frequent in the different manifestations of Islamic art, being associated with magic and apotropaism.  
A band adorned with peacock eyes runs along the length of the body, a motif that covers practically the entire surface of the huge wing, suggesting feathers. On the base there are small *kufic* inscriptions of the *baraka* (blessing) and *lisahibihi* ‘to the owner’) type. Large lance-shaped leaves masked from the unbroken lustre base decorate the brim of the dish. An inscription containing the word *baraka* can be read below the foot.
3863e32d-5905-504c-b6f3-2271051d2c51.short_description: This plate, decorated with animal motifs and *kufic* inscriptions on the bottom, includes a type of inscription uncommon in this sort of object.
3863e32d-5905-504c-b6f3-2271051d2c51.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
3863e32d-5905-504c-b6f3-2271051d2c51.method_for_datation: The dish is an excellent example of Iraqi production of monochrome lusterware from the 4th / 10th century.

38793766-f653-5775-9feb-93b915baf247.name: Ewer
38793766-f653-5775-9feb-93b915baf247.description: A ceramic ewer with a transparent turquoise glaze, painted in black and blue, in the form of a rooster. Composed of a base, body, neck, spout and handle, it is decorated with vegetal motifs. The circular base, which is smaller than the body, is glazed and undecorated. The body is pear-shaped, and adorned with vegetal motifs in black. The decoration begins at the lower body with a three-petaled leaf surmounted by a wide band, while the rest of the surface is adorned with vegetal designs composed of twisting branches sprouting bud-shaped leaves and half-palmettes. A plain band separates the body from the neck, which is short, cylindrical and decorated with impressed dots. Above it rises the spout in the form of a rooster’s head, featuring a comb, beak and circular eyes.

materials: Ceramic/Mold-formed, with underglaze decoration in black beneath a turquoise glaze

3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.name: Bowl.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.description: A bowl on a high foot-ring, painted in lustre on a white clay slip. The interior is decorated with a bold design of a robed and hooded figure, traditionally thought to be a Coptic priest, carrying a lamp or censer. Beside him stands an object often thought to be a cypress tree, but sometimes interpreted as an *ankh* or ‘key of life’ cross, an ancient Egyptian hieroglyphic sign which the Copts adapted for Christian use. The priest’s robe, his lamp, and the tree are all decorated with thin white lines scratched through the lustre to create spirals and other motifs. On the outside of the bowl, the word ‘Sa‘d’’ is written twice in *kufic* script. Oddly, the word is written in reverse, i.e. beginning with the last letter. It is unclear whether the word is a blessing (‘good luck, good fortune’) or whether it is the name of a particular craftsman or workshop. It appears on a group of similar Fatimid ceramics over a number of decades during the reign of the Caliph al-Mustansir (AH 427–87 / AD 1035–94).
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.short_description: A footed bowl painted in lustre with a picture of a robed and hooded figure holding a lamp or censer. He is a Coptic Christian priest, and his presence on such a fine object suggests the importance of this community in Fatimid Egypt.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.method_for_datation: This bowl belongs to a group of objects which all have the word ‘Sa‘d’ painted on them. These have been assigned to the reign of the Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir based on comparisons with other media such as textiles.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Fatimid capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.
3879f402-ef45-5009-af10-a145fd162aa2.obtention: In 1910 the art collector Dikran Garabed Kelekian placed his collection of Islamic ceramics on loan to the V&A.  Fifteen of the finest pieces, including this bowl, were purchased by the Museum (with the assistance of the National Art Collections Fund) after Kelekian’s death.

3952b5cc-0d6e-5e06-abfd-90c66456d559.name: Bowl with a throne scene
3952b5cc-0d6e-5e06-abfd-90c66456d559.short_description: The bowl is decorated in the *mina´i* technique, a term from the word meaning enamel. It features a seated figure on a throne surrounded by courtiers on horseback on a turquoise background. The *mina´i* technique flourished in Iran during the period before the Mongol invasion. Themes on such pottery are reminiscent of manuscript paintings.

397a2148-9a53-51ba-993d-0df58995eb61.short_description: In 1517, when Syria became part of the Ottoman empire, the great history of ceramics was over. But domestic and architectural ceramics arose, strongly influenced by Iznik, and much needed for numerous new buildings and renovations.

39ef25b0-8d27-55d5-b4e9-761de510e7f7.name: Bath scraper
39ef25b0-8d27-55d5-b4e9-761de510e7f7.description:
This object has been associated with a series of bath scrapers and pumice stones attributed to the Middle East of the AH 5th–6th / AD 11th–12th centuries. They were moulded in a variety of geometric shapes displaying animals in profile or facing each other.  
  
This piece shows two birds symmetrically placed around a central axis created by their almost-touching beaks, wings, and tails, along with decorative drop-shape motifs. Their bodies and legs face outward, creating a dynamic composition.  
  
This piece is left untreated to allow its abrasive surface to act as an exfoliating tool used in hammam rituals of purification of the skin.

3a31c191-2d71-5f90-af12-d4c3fb392a26.name: Glazed bowl with cobalt-blue and green decoration
3a31c191-2d71-5f90-af12-d4c3fb392a26.description: This high-walled straight bowl has a painted cobalt-blue and green decoration on a white opaque glaze. It has a repeated geometric pattern of alternating blue vertical lines and green shapes. The shape of this bowl and the colours used are highly typical of early Abbasid decorated glazed wares and were originally inspired by AH 2nd-3d / AD 7th–8th-century Chinese ceramics.

3a53b8ae-2e60-593a-a1f3-818f2f859a44.short_description: When Iraqi potters discovered the white-glazed pottery, later known as faience, they also began to use the luster technique. Luster consists of metal oxides applied to pottery that has already been fired. The piece is re-fired at a lower temperature in a reduced-oxygen atmosphere, and the thin decoration takes on a metallic look ranging from copper to gold.
materials: Earthenware, painted in luster over an opaque, white glaze

3ad498e2-1308-50b9-a3f2-b018a5be7ea1.name: Vase
3ad498e2-1308-50b9-a3f2-b018a5be7ea1.short_description: This small vase is an example of the elaborate production developed in the Eastern Iranian world. The vase has an elegant *kufic* character inscription – incomplete probably due to a restoration intervention – which bears, in its final part, a wish "In the name of God (for the) Blessing of its owner".
materials: Earthenware, white slip, black decoration under a transparent glaze

3b5f2dc7-2856-5500-bdbd-60cb4110286c.name: Oil lamp.
3b5f2dc7-2856-5500-bdbd-60cb4110286c.description:
This lamp is composed of a cubic oil compartment without a base, perforated on the side by a large hole that extends into a wide spout. The upper surface is pierced to form a filter composed of three triangular orifices through which the oil was poured. The lamp is equipped with an annular handle that is turned upwards.  
A mesh that absorbed oil would have emerged from the spout. This lamp would have formed part of rural daily home-wares and was used to light up houses.
3b5f2dc7-2856-5500-bdbd-60cb4110286c.short_description: A rural domestic object, this lamp consists of a cubic reservoir with a large hole in one side that extends into a wide spout. The oil was poured in through the top, which is decorated with openwork, and the ring handle faces upwards. An oil-soaked wick would have been placed in the spout.
3b5f2dc7-2856-5500-bdbd-60cb4110286c.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
3b5f2dc7-2856-5500-bdbd-60cb4110286c.dimensions: Height 4 cm, sides 4 x 5 cm, width of the spout 4.5 cm.
3b5f2dc7-2856-5500-bdbd-60cb4110286c.method_for_datation: The lamp was found on the Hammadid site (405–547 / 1015–1152) and has characteristics of Hammadid lamps: a long spout and an annular handle turned upwards.
3b5f2dc7-2856-5500-bdbd-60cb4110286c.method_for_provenance: The lamp was found in the Qal'at Bani Hammad.

3ba92e2d-8f97-58d9-9877-59445c525719.name: Bowl
3ba92e2d-8f97-58d9-9877-59445c525719.short_description: Earthenware hemispherical bowl covered with yellow engobe features a quatrefoil enclosed in a roundel (probably a blazon) and just below the rim seven evenly spaced titulatory inscriptions in *thuluth* script: "that which was made by order the revered, the magnificent, the respected, the well-served, the honoured 'ya aysa'".

3c4c41c9-f28c-54d5-b61f-8b68bcc06432.name: Bowl
3c4c41c9-f28c-54d5-b61f-8b68bcc06432.short_description:
This clay bowl is decorated with *kufi* calligraphy on the inner neck edge. While in Islamic pottery, one may expect an abundance of floral or geometric patterns, *kufic* ceramics feature a band of letters creating a central void.  
  
*Kufi* script originates from Mecca and Medina (625 AD) as one of the earliest forms of calligraphy in Islam, with its letters stretching to resemble one another.  
  
This plate originates from Iran and embodies a two-fold function. At first sight, the abstract script appears as a decorative design. The second sight reveals a hidden message to decode. The inscription on this bowl would read: “Planning before work protects you from regret; prosperity and peace.”

3d81aec6-b59f-5b48-b482-d6cde0cf5bda.name: Blue-and-white dish based on a Chinese model
3d81aec6-b59f-5b48-b482-d6cde0cf5bda.short_description: Chinese pottery had found its way into the Middle East before Islam, but its impact took on new importance shortly after the founding of the Abbasid Empire in 750 and the move of the capital from Syria to Iraq. Chinese shapes appeared in the 9th-century products of the kilns at Basra, Iraq, and potters emulated the white body by increasing the opacity of their glazes by adding tin. The impact of Chinese goods was especially felt during the Mongol period, when the Ilkhanids (1256–1353)—relatives of the Mongol rulers of China (Yuan dynasty 1279–1368)—ruled Iran. However, nothing compares with the overwhelming influence of Chinese blue-and-white porcelain imports on Persian pottery. From around 1600, a new boost to the porcelain trade came from the founding of the Dutch and English East Indies companies. Large quantities of porcelain, on its way to Europe from the Far East in their ships, were off-loaded in the ports of Iran. In response to this influx of Chinese porcelain, Persian potters made great efforts to simulate it.

3e22b1c1-3e48-51e8-aa1f-07a2f91c99b3.name: Star-shaped tiles.
3e22b1c1-3e48-51e8-aa1f-07a2f91c99b3.description:
These star-shaped tiles belong to a type probably developed around the end of the AH 7th–8th / AD 13th–14th centuries commonly known as *kashi* from the most famous production centre: Kashan in central northern Iran. These tiles, used as an architectural finish, almost ‘dematerialise’ buildings with their vibrant luminosity and polychromy.  
The decoration is based on central animals (felines, hares, elephants, etc.) above a background entirely covered with leafy bushes. Various epigraphic motifs run along the edge, and the hare tile bears a Qur’anic inscription that reproduces Sura 110 almost in full: ‘In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful / When triumph comes from God, and victory / You will see the people embracing God’s religion in throngs / You shall glorify and praise your Lord, and implore Him for forgiveness. He is the Redeemer’ while another, decorated with an elephant and a phoenix in flight and bearing the date AH 691 (AD 1291–2), includes a quotation from Firdausi’s Shahnama about the return of Isfandiyar of Gushtasp. The inscription reads: ‘Now we must drink joyfully / As from the river comes a smell of musk / The air is full of loud cries and the land is angry / Happy is he who is content to drink’.
3e22b1c1-3e48-51e8-aa1f-07a2f91c99b3.short_description: These star-shaped tiles, known as *kashi* after their most important centre of production (Kashan), were combined with cross-shaped pieces and used as a luxurious wall covering in palaces.

3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.name: Wellhead
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.description:
Wellhead in the shape of an external octagonal and internal semicircular prism, made of sifted reddish clay on which various decorative motifs have been stamped and complemented with green glaze. On a circular and smooth base, a prismatic shape rises, which is reinforced by the moldings that vertically decorate each of the walls, ending at the top with lobed modillions. Two decorative motifs alternate on its eight fronts. The first consists of a decoration of quadrilobed flowers included in a rhomboidal pattern, in the manner of the sebka network, all glazed in green and bordering its contours with manganese oxide. The second has a trilobed arch, whose central lobe is a sharp pointed horseshoe arch, and which houses a decoration with a mirror pseudoepigraphic motif ending in palmettes that end in a twisted stem. It ends, under the mouth of the border, with two borders: the lower one with a stamped seven-point star decoration, on which three bands with incised zig-zag lines and a central one with knife-corded thread, and the upper one contains a inscription in florid Kufic, transcribed by Sahwki Zayed (2015) as *at-tawfiq*, "The Providence", repeated five times on each side of the octagon. The presence of this inscription is confirmed in numerous Almohad works, and is common in the Merinid and Mudéjar works, but not in the Nasrid works. Its upper edge, thickened on the outside and rectangular in profile, is octagonal and smooth.  
  
Such wellheads can be understood within the broader development of water management systems in al-Andalus. Methods and objects were introduced and disseminated to optimise the water usage, an essential resource that significantly shaped everyday life. As part of these innovations, systems for water collection, distribution, and storage were devised. Among these, wells played a key role in accessing underground water, and wellheads such as this one were installed both in public spaces and in domestic courtyards.
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.initial_owner: Unknown / Daniel Aguilera Camacho (owner of the Córdoba house)
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.method_for_datation: The techniques of stamping and the *cuerda seca* technique (original and innovative technique, created in al-Andalus at the end of the 10th century that will continue to be used in later centuries), become widespread and reach their best expression in the AH 6th - 7th / AD 12th–13th centuries. Decorative motifs such as stars are frequent in pieces from the Almohad, Mudejar and Nasrid periods, throughout the AH 6th - 8th / 12th–14th centuries.

3fd8e824-1cbd-5b49-8dbd-ed37954052b0.name: Wall tile.
3fd8e824-1cbd-5b49-8dbd-ed37954052b0.description:
A colourful wall tile decorated with a geometric interlace pattern in white, honey-brown, dark-brown, and light copper-green glazes that are separated by unglazed well-defined borders, using a technique known as *cuerda seca*, meaning 'dry cord' in Spanish; the 'cord' referring to the unglazed borders separating the masses of coloured shapes making up the pattern. The *cuerda seca* technique involves pressing a patterned mould gently onto the surface of the clay; the outlines and boarders of the pattern are then coated with a mixture of manganese-oxide and grease to prevent the different coloured glazes from running into each other. After completing the application of the greasy substance and the coloured lead-based glazes, the tile is fired. While the coloured glazes fuse themselves to the body of the tile and harden, the greasy mixture burns away leaving a clearly defined unglazed outline, 'cord', round all the compartments that make up the design.  
  
Toledo was re-conquered by the Christians in AH 477 / AD 1085, but Mudéjar geometric designs remained popular, and continued to be made and used decoratively in a number of contexts in both secular and religious architecture right up to the beginning of the 10th century / 16th century.
3fd8e824-1cbd-5b49-8dbd-ed37954052b0.short_description: This colourful wall tile from Toledo is decorated using a technique known as *cuerda seca*, where the outlines of the embossed pattern are coated in a greasy substance to stop the paints of the different shapes from flowing over each other while being fired in the potter’s kiln.
3fd8e824-1cbd-5b49-8dbd-ed37954052b0.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
3fd8e824-1cbd-5b49-8dbd-ed37954052b0.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the reddish earthenware body of this tile and its thick multicolour glazing indicate that it was made in the 9th century / 15th century in Toledo, where some similar examples still survive in historical buildings.
3fd8e824-1cbd-5b49-8dbd-ed37954052b0.method_for_provenance: The reddish earthenware body of this tile and its thick multicolour glazing suggest it was produced in Toledo, where some similar examples still survive in historical buildings.
3fd8e824-1cbd-5b49-8dbd-ed37954052b0.obtention: Purchased by Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in 1883.

3fe11ec6-e560-5324-87a0-13f62820c8e3.name: Dish.
3fe11ec6-e560-5324-87a0-13f62820c8e3.description: A shallow dish with an upturned edge, painted under the glaze. The dish is adorned with a spray of flowers, painted in light- and dark-blue, sage-green, and greyish purple; they include tulips, lilies-of-the-valley, and hyacinths. The three largest flowers bear sinuous cloud-bands in their blossoms, which are reflected in the smaller cloud-bands flanking the base of the bouquet. As with the best of Iznik wares the artist has enlivened the composition by depicting the flowers swaying gently, thus avoiding a rigid and deadening symmetry.
3fe11ec6-e560-5324-87a0-13f62820c8e3.short_description: A shallow dish with an upturned edge, adorned with a spray of flowers including tulips and hyacinths. The distinctive cloud-band motif in each of the three largest flowers lets us relate this plate to several other wares made by the circle of an artist named Musli.
3fe11ec6-e560-5324-87a0-13f62820c8e3.method_for_datation: Details like the cloud-bands in the three largest flowers and the particular shade of sage-green allow us to link this dish to a group of wares associated with the circle of an artist named Musli, who also signed a mosque lamp dated 1549.
3fe11ec6-e560-5324-87a0-13f62820c8e3.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
3fe11ec6-e560-5324-87a0-13f62820c8e3.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, Istanbul/London, 1989, pp.246–7.
3fe11ec6-e560-5324-87a0-13f62820c8e3.author: Barry Wood

40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.name: Jug with Design of Five Sphinxes and a Standing Figure
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.short_description:
A biconical jug with handle and buff-colored composite body, wheel thrown with painted decoration and gilded highlights over white glaze. A straight collar rim sits on the large truncated biconical body on a small flared unglazed foot, a vertical strap handle with an applied flat disc thumb rest. There is a dark blue-gray scalloped band on the lip. The rim has a frieze of gray-blue rectangles outlined above and below in black and divided by vertical red lines; each panel is filled with delicate black arabesque patterns and a small square gold leaf central highlight.  
A red and black line defines the carination between neck and shoulder. The shoulder contains five spotted sphinxes with hats and collars, each a different color (blue, red, green, blue, red) walking to the viewer's left toward a vine or sprig with alternating red and blue buds. A figure in a long patterned blue robe and brown conical cap stands at the back of the procession. Gold leaf highlights the figure's shoulders, three areas on the body of each sphinx and the circular elements between them. A series of stylized buds in black and red sit below the top of the register and a second set rests on the decorative baseline. This decorative band is light green and filled with a pattern of red four-petaled rosettes drawn in black with white centers and blue dots above and below, separated by vertical blue lozenges. Some centers still preserve square gold foil elements.  
The bottom half of the body is undecorated except for a series of simple floral elements painted in black just under the band; a similar design is applied below the rim interior. The handle has a black *Kufic* inscription with blue highlights on the sides, the thumb rest is red. The glaze is badly cracked overall; six major areas of loss are in-filled and painted.
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.dimensions: Height: 13.7cm; Diameter of mouth: 8.3cm; Diameter of body: 14cm; Diameter of foot: 5.4cm
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.method_for_provenance: During the 12th and 13th centuries, the Persian city of Rayy was an important political, economic, and cultural center. It produced a variety of pottery, of which the most costly were called Minai wares.  These thin-walled vessels were first glazed with an ivory or white ground, although some have a turquoise or blue underglaze.  They are usually embellished with figural decoration not unlike contemporary manuscript painting.

40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.name: Bowl with horseman.
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.description:
The main decoration of the bowl consists of a large figure of a horseman, whose face clearly shows some Mongol features, on a background filled with plant shoots in relief.  
The decoration is characterised by a particularly delicate and elegant design painted in polychrome, with each colour requiring a separate firing.  
This piece belongs to a type known as *mina’i*’, in Persian ‘*haftrang*’(‘seven colours’). This technique effectively uses seven colours (red, blue, green, yellow, gold, white and black) applied on top of the glaze and occasionally, as in this case, with some details worked in relief and gilded.
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.short_description: This piece belongs to a type of ceramic known as *mina’i*, recognisable through the use of seven colours in its decoration. In antiquity, the main centre of production for *mina’i* ceramics was Kashan in central northern Iran.
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
40153d07-6252-5b57-89aa-964009f142c0.method_for_provenance: *Mina’i* ceramics were mainly produced in Kashan (central northern Iran) and in all probability would have been made by the illuminators of the manuscripts produced at that time that were lost with the Mongol invasion of 1220. Consequently, they are an important historical document for the study of illuminations of that time.

4159a293-3ddf-5001-9a68-0994c000b7d3.name: Tile
4159a293-3ddf-5001-9a68-0994c000b7d3.short_description: This tile belongs to the period of Timurid rule in Iran and Central Asia (Hegira 771-913/1370–1507 AD). The last great dynasty to emerge from the Central Asian steppe, the Timurids sponsored buildings that were often constructed on an enormous scale and sheathed in an elaborate decorative skin of brilliant glazed tile. Since the primary structural material was dun-colored baked brick, glazed tiles provided colorful embellishment. Elements of the floral design of this tile were cut from glazed tiles of different colors and assembled as a mosaic; it was set in place on the exterior of a building, where it joined others as part of a larger, more complicated design. Indeed, there are several nearly identical or related tiles in other museum collections in Berlin (MIA), Chicago (AIC), and Paris (MdL).
4159a293-3ddf-5001-9a68-0994c000b7d3.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
4159a293-3ddf-5001-9a68-0994c000b7d3.method_for_datation: The decoration, color scheme and technique closely relate to tiles still in situ in Timurid buildings, as for example, the mosque and madrassa complex of Gawhar Shad, Herat, Hegira 820-841/ AD 1417-38.
4159a293-3ddf-5001-9a68-0994c000b7d3.method_for_provenance: The technique of tile mosaic, a form of architectural decoration in which pieces of glazed ceramic of different shapes and sizes are assembled to generate a multicolored revetment, is especially associated with Iranian lands.

41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.name: Pear-shaped bottle.
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.description:
This piece is distinguished by its fine decoration painted in white, red and black with gold leafing on a blue background (*lajvard* in Persian, ‘lapis lazuli’) consisting of tiny stylised spiral motifs, large gold-leaf poly-lobed medallions and geometric decoration.  
Unlike *mina’i* ceramics, the decoration on lajvardina ceramics is mostly non-figurative and is characterised by the presence of floral, calligraphy and geometric motifs. This type of ceramic was used to produce elegant long-neck vases, polygon-sided recipients, cylindrical containers and diamond- or cross-shaped tiles.
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.short_description: This bottle is recognisable as an example of the type known as ‘lajvardina’ by its white, red and black paint with gold leaf on a blue base. This latter gives the style its name, as *lajvard* mean lapis lazuli in Persian.
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
41a3ec4b-1e2e-5b41-a889-b733678cd8fd.method_for_datation: Lajvardina work has been dated using the famous treatise of the techniques of Islamic ceramicists written by Abûl Qâsim of Kashan in 1301. By that time, the *mina’i* ceramic technique was no longer in use, with Kashan ceramicists appearing to prefer the lajvardina technique. Production of these ceramics must therefore have started before 1301, as suggested by archeological finds at Takht-i Sulayman in northwest Persia from the excavations recently carried out in the Palace of Abaka-Khan (1265–81).

41fe926a-f305-50a0-a6f2-3d275bd31f08.name: Bowl
41fe926a-f305-50a0-a6f2-3d275bd31f08.short_description: Kashan type fritware bowl covered with an opaque white glaze and painted in monochrome luster and cobalt blue. The interior is decorated with a large roundel bordered by bands of *naskhi* script giving the date in Arabic Shawwal 614 AH. The two Arabic verses are attributed to the Imam al-Shafi\`i: "Acquire learning, for Man is not born learned, the learned and the ignorant are of a different breed, a Man of the highest rank who reveals his ignorance loses his status." The exterior is occupied by a large benedictory *kufic* inscription.
keywords: Glaze; Luster; calligraphy; nashki; kufic; inscription; calligraphy

42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.name: Water pot.
42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.description: Water pot with everted rim with quadrangular lip, circular mouth, neck in the shape of an inverted truncated cone, globular body with two wing-form handles with an upper protuberance on the shoulder and a convex base. The neck and body are covered in a green glaze and profusely decorated with finger and nail impressions, and stamped with protective signs based on plants (rosettes, palmettes), calligraphic and architectural motifs (horseshoe and trefoil arches). The object has been restored.
42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.short_description: Almohad pitcher used to store water. The care taken to protect the content of the pitcher is evident from the profusion of prophylactic symbols stamped on it. It includes plant (rosettes and palmettes), calligraphic and architectural (horseshoe and trilobed arches) motifs.
42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.dates: Hegira second half of 6th or early 7th century / AD second half of 12th or early 13th century.
42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.dimensions: Height 70.5 cm, width 59 cm, diameter (of mouth) 28 cm.
42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.method_for_datation: It was dated to the Almohad period on the basis of stratigraphy, since it was found in the abandoned levels of one of the Almohad houses vacated after the Christian conquest of Mértola in AH 635–36 / AD 1238. This dating has been confirmed by comparison with similar decorative features on a water jar from Tetuan (Morocco) with an inscription dating it to AH 585 / AD 1190.
42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.method_for_provenance: Stamps used to decorate this type of water jar have been found in Mértola.
42311da9-1496-5d35-a0ea-56b7ce7ff0f7.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

materials: Ceramic made from compact greyish straw and paste mix, and made using a combination of coil technique for the lower part and thrown on a wheel for the upper part. It has a stamped decoration and is partially glazed.

4285852d-bdc9-521a-a814-ba8b902153a3.name: *Mihrab* (prayer niche)
4285852d-bdc9-521a-a814-ba8b902153a3.short_description: This mihrab, nearly 12 feet tall and dated 663/1265, is the masterpiece of the DDFIA collection. It is one of six surviving luster mihrabs made during the Ilkhanid period of rule in Iran (1256–1353) and one of only two of its type outside of Iran. Originally, it was located in the Imamzada Yahya, a tomb of a descendant of a Shi‘ite imam in Veramin, Iran. In the tomb’s prayer sanctuary, the mihrab was located on the qibla wall—the one indicating the direction of Mecca.
4285852d-bdc9-521a-a814-ba8b902153a3.type: Islamic, Indian & Southeast Asian works of art; tilework; ceramic
4285852d-bdc9-521a-a814-ba8b902153a3.holder: Shangri La, Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art
keywords: Ilkhanid; Iran; Kashan; stonepaste; moulded; overglaze-painted; lustre; underglaze; painted; cobalt; arabesque; inscription; Veramin; Imamzadeh Yahya; 'Ali b. Muhammad b. Abu Tahir; Qur'an; mosque interior decoration
materials: Stonepaste; molded, overglaze-painted in luster, underglaze-painted in cobalt and turquoise

42efdee4-d0a0-588e-8606-1ebc9cb0a6cb.name: Jar with green glaze
42efdee4-d0a0-588e-8606-1ebc9cb0a6cb.description: This jar is covered with a green glaze on the outside and inside. The jar has an annular base and two small handles attached to the base of the short neck. The clay used is red. This vessel would have been used to store liquids and food.

42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.name: Tile.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.description:
This moulded square tile of a hard yellowish paste shows a geometrical polychrome decoration of pinkish white interlacing bands forming green or pale blue glazed stars and dark brown or tan polygons in *cuenca o arista* technique. The central motif of the tile is a green eight-pointed star set in the middle of a cross composed of four opaque brown polygons. The latter divides the surface of the tile into four square compartments representing stellar and polygonal shapes. As the four green half-stars and brown half-polygons on the edges show, this tile was part of a repetitive design used in wall decorations.  
The *cuenca o arista* technique imitates tile mosaic. While the pattern of tile mosaic is made by cutting and assembling polychrome glazed tiles, the design of tiles worked in *cuenca o arista* technique is made by filling small pattern fields formed by thin strips of clay with different glazes. Where the glaze flowed over the frame, the design does not stand out clearly.  
The star and cross motif is one of the most common Islamic geometric decorative patterns continued in Mudéjar art.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.short_description: Moulded square tile with a geometrical polychrome decoration. Interlacing bands form green and pale blue glazed stars and brown polygons. Coloured glazes fill small pattern fields formed by thin strips of clay. This technique is called *cuenca o arista* and imitates tile mosaic.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.dates: Hegira end of 9th–beginning of 10th century / AD end of 15th–beginning of 16th century.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.dimensions: Height 15.0 cm, width 15.0 cm, depth approx. 1.9 cm.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.method_for_datation: Tiles similar in technique and design have been documented in buildings in Toledo dating from the end of the 9th / 15th century and the beginning of the 10th / 16th century, for example, in the monastery of San Clemente.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.method_for_provenance: Tiles similar in technique and design have been documented in buildings in Toledo, for example, in the monastery of San Clemente.
42f89df0-5a8b-5150-b126-94c092d264a5.obtention: The tile was purchased by the Museum of Cultural History in Lund, Sweden, from the Forrer collection in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, in 1922.

43631319-af52-5666-9856-e67b0498dfba.name: Tile Fragment
43631319-af52-5666-9856-e67b0498dfba.short_description:
The ancient city of Qalhat, known as the Twin of Hormuz, was the main port of northern Oman from the 7th to 9th centuries AH / 13th to 15th centuries AD. The Great Mosque was its most famous edifice. The mosque was built around 699 AH / 1300 AD by Bibi Maryam, the wife of Bahauddin Ayaz, King of Hormuz and Ruler of Qalhat. The Moroccan geographer Ibn Battuta visited Qalhat during his travels in the 8th century AH / 14th century AD and wrote a vivid description of the Great Mosque shortly after its completion:  
  
"Qalhat has fine bazaars and an exceedingly beautiful mosque, the walls of which are decorated with elaborate tile work."  
  
These fragments of opaque, turquoise-glazed *‘lajvardina’* (lapis lazuli) tiles were found on the surface of the mosque area. The tiles featured moulded *naskhi*\-style calligraphy under a raised band with interlacing arabesque patterns and were arranged in inscriptional friezes.
43631319-af52-5666-9856-e67b0498dfba.provenance: The Great Mosque, Qalhat (Oman). Origin: Kashan, Persia (Iran)
43631319-af52-5666-9856-e67b0498dfba.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
keywords: Tiles; Lajvardina; lapis lazuli; Hormuz; Qalhat; Arabesque

43c5ab5f-241d-5114-a0de-5364612ff8df.name: Jug with turqoise blue and brown glaze
43c5ab5f-241d-5114-a0de-5364612ff8df.description: This small jar was discovered during an excavation in a house in Murwab, northwest Qatar in AH 1402 / AD 1981. The jar was in fragments, but it was possible to piece together the top part and restore it. It has a slightly flared rim with a rounded end and a small straight neck. The jar widens into a rounded shape with two small handles that have brown spots of paint. The jar is painted in turquoise blue with drips inside and outside and is covered with an opaque glaze. The jar is made from beige earthenware and may have been made by potters in Basra or Samarra in Iraq or Susa in Iran during the early Abbasid period.
43c5ab5f-241d-5114-a0de-5364612ff8df.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

447ccade-689a-515e-9fad-173781b00ddb.name: Jug filter
447ccade-689a-515e-9fad-173781b00ddb.short_description: Pierced prior to firing and affixed to the truncated-cone neck of jugs, filters were designed to remove impurities, mostly insects. Alongside functional perforations, pierced decoration and purely ornamental incisions were used in geometric or animal compositions: here, a finely incised profile silhouette of a gazelle and its young, whose presence is merely suggested. The exquisitely elegant composition, which betrays a firm hand, is reminiscent of the design on a filter at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (inv. no. M.83.251.15), and is almost identical to that on a filter at the Museum of Mediterranean Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet) in Stockholm (inv. no. NM00428/1921).

45800acc-3f5e-5c55-89cc-238c62a3bdf9.name: Tile (*azulejo*).
45800acc-3f5e-5c55-89cc-238c62a3bdf9.description: Tile glazed in blue on a white background with vegetal decoration of the 'independent flower' type. The flower is seen from the front with its petals rounded, open and completely separated. The whole is derived from the simple division of the circumference into eight parts by two perpendicular centre lines and the lines that bisect the resulting angles. The flower model belongs in turn to a subgroup of tiles whose centre, the corolla, appears divided into eight parts by diagonals and axes joined together with arches. In this case, the outlines have been retained and each space has been filled with an unattached blue petal, which makes the flower extremely stylised. The four stems that shoot from the flower point towards the corners of the tile. Floral decoration was very prestigious in tile manufacturing, and some very simple examples, without separating lines between petals and corners decorated with small circles or entirely smooth flowers in white on a blue background, have survived. Tiles of this type are also held at other institutions, such as the National Museum of Ceramics and Sumptuary Arts González Martí in Valencia.
45800acc-3f5e-5c55-89cc-238c62a3bdf9.short_description: A number of different series of Mudéjar ceramics were produced in the Valencia region, and this tile glazed in blue on a white background belongs to the type known as ‘independent flower’ from the flower on its front, with its wide-open, completely separate, rounded petals.
45800acc-3f5e-5c55-89cc-238c62a3bdf9.dimensions: Height 5.5 cm, width 5.6 cm, depth 1.7 cm.
45800acc-3f5e-5c55-89cc-238c62a3bdf9.method_for_datation: From the style and from parallels with other similar tiles kept in Valencia.
45800acc-3f5e-5c55-89cc-238c62a3bdf9.method_for_provenance: Its origin is included in its file, and confirmed by the features described in detail above.
45800acc-3f5e-5c55-89cc-238c62a3bdf9.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from Apolinar Sánchez Villalba on 28 February 1933.

keywords: Tile; clay; firing; glazed; Mudéjar; Manises; Valencia; azulejo.

458f12d6-11aa-5aa1-8e81-ad3731f1366c.name: Panel of six tiles
458f12d6-11aa-5aa1-8e81-ad3731f1366c.short_description:
The panel depicts the holy sanctuary of the mosque at Mecca. Within the compound the Ka\`ba is shown in the centre among other sites such as the *minbar*, the well Zamzam and the structures of the different religious schools, all identified by their names.  
Such topographical works, with a votive or commemorative function, are typical of the Iznik workshops of the 17th century and follow analogous illustrations in manuscripts from the 16th century onwards.
458f12d6-11aa-5aa1-8e81-ad3731f1366c.type: Ottoman ceramic, fritware with polychrome underglaze decoration

45a31a2f-a589-5ebe-9521-9d4fb116c2ab.name: Tile
45a31a2f-a589-5ebe-9521-9d4fb116c2ab.short_description: This square tile is decorated with a black star-like shaped framed by decorative white lines. A star-like shape with yellow in the middle bears resemblance to a flower. The Victoria and Albert Museum holds identical tiles which were made in Toledo.
45a31a2f-a589-5ebe-9521-9d4fb116c2ab.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar objects e. g. Victoria and Albert Museum (see Ray 2000, p. 331).
45a31a2f-a589-5ebe-9521-9d4fb116c2ab.bibliography: Ray, A., *Spanish Pottery 1248-1898. With a Catalogue of the collection in the Victoria and Albert Museum*, London: Victoria and Albert Museum, 2000.

460f4b40-8466-573e-89cc-49b512d4d70b.name: Bowl with wing-shaped palmettes.
460f4b40-8466-573e-89cc-49b512d4d70b.description: The bowl, painted in brown and yellow-brown lustre, is decorated with two large wings filled with thin lines, which enclose an oval motif surrounded by vegetal elements. On the outside, there are four brown medallions with drop motifs. The decoration on the inside appears to be a variant on the tree of life consisting of wing-shaped palmettes, a Sassanid tradition.
460f4b40-8466-573e-89cc-49b512d4d70b.short_description: The decoration on this bowl is particularly interesting, with a traditional palmette motif, in this case in the form of wings, on the inside. This motif can be interpreted as a variant on the tree of life, a Sassanid tradition.
460f4b40-8466-573e-89cc-49b512d4d70b.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
460f4b40-8466-573e-89cc-49b512d4d70b.dates: Hegira second half of 3rd century / AD second half of 9th century.
460f4b40-8466-573e-89cc-49b512d4d70b.method_for_datation: The determination of the date and provenance of the piece is based on the analysis of the decoration of the bowl, which is characteristic of this type of 3rd / 9th century Iraqi ceramic painted with two-tone metallic lustre.

460f4b40-8466-573e-89cc-49b512d4d70b.author: Paola Torre

464d0c1e-ebf9-5c06-9946-277e345c0740.name: Tile
464d0c1e-ebf9-5c06-9946-277e345c0740.short_description: Square tile with cobalt blue and turquoise blue decoration. Painted with a lozenge-shaped compartment which contains eight lotus palmettes enclosing a central rosette; the corners of the tile are decorated with Chinese cloud motifs on a cobalt blue ground. The tile is illustrative of a stage preceding the floral style traditionally associated with Iznik pottery. The lotus motif and particularly the white clouds in the corners recall the long-standing influence of Chinese art. Turquoise was adopted by the Iznik potters in the first quarter of the sixteenth century; its presence here, associated with cobalt blue, has made possible a more accurate dating of the tile.
464d0c1e-ebf9-5c06-9946-277e345c0740.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
464d0c1e-ebf9-5c06-9946-277e345c0740.bibliography: Dunca, M., *Islamic Art at the National Museum of Art of Romania*, Bucharest: National Museum of Art of Romania, 2015: 102, no. 45.

4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.name: Dish.
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.description:
This Iznik pottery dish is underglaze painted in bright green, which dominates the composition, pale red and blue with black for the outlines, on a white background. The floral design at the centre is composed of tulips and roses on curved stems, all springing from a leafy tuft and a serrated *saz* leaf falling across the centre of the plate. A tulip on a curved *saz* leaf was one of the few stylistic developments in the traditional floral decoration of Iznik pottery in the last quarter of the AH 10th / AD 16th century. On the slightly curved rim, there are alternating blossoms of tulips and simple rosettes. The back of the dish is painted with ten green dots and transparent glazed. The glaze is heavily crackled. The foot-ring is pierced once for suspension.  
Iznik pottery of the AH 11th / AD 17th century is characterised by the increasingly inferior quality of colours and glaze as well as simplified and standardised designs, repeated in numerous examples of dishes. The artistic decline is due to the decline of Ottoman political and economic power. On the one hand the potters had to increase the production of vessels for the open market and on the other hand they had to make a profit by cutting costs.
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.short_description: Iznik pottery dish with polychrome underglaze painted floral decoration. The tulips and roses in the centre emerge from a leafy tuft. A serrated *saz* leaf falls across the centre of the plate. Alternating blossoms of tulips and rosettes decorate the rim.
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.owner: Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities, Stockholm. Since 1982 the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities.
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.dates: Hegira first half of the 11th century / AD first half of the 17th century.
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.method_for_datation: The 'quatre fleurs' style and the feathered *saz* leaves in combination with sprays of flowers occurred from the second half of the 10th / 16th century. However, the dish seems to be later because of the carelessly painted design and the green colour running into the glaze. These are significant features of polychrome underglaze painted ceramics of the 11th / 17th century produced for an increasing open market.
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.method_for_provenance: According to the floral decoration and the shape that are both specific for Iznik ceramics.
4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.obtention: On loan from the Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities, Stockholm.

4696d99f-fdbb-59ee-b765-d6c4a02eba6f.author: Friederike Voigt
