46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.description:
Like many other examples, these *azulejos* testify to the affinity between textiles and *azulejos* in Portugal during the 17th century. Such was the case with the embroidered Arraiolos rugs made in the Alentejo region where the same sort of patterns and even palette can be recognised.  
This pattern was relatively common in the *azulejos* used in Portugal during the first half of the 17th century. Because this is a 2 x 2 composition, four *azulejos* are required to make a pattern that can be repeated to infinity. Use of this sort of *azulejos* was mainly in the lower areas of architecture to allow viewers to approach the decoration more directly. In it, we can perceive a cross-like composition that is achieved by a much-intertwined element with a dense blue background, at the centre of which is an acanthus leaf motif. This rope-like cross composition is placed against a yellow background; here, a distinctive eight-point motif, which has its origins in leather- or metalwork, can be traced by the presence of nail marks left in all four of its extremities. The beautiful frame that can be seen in one of its borders is known in Portuguese as *rendas* or lacework, inspired by actual works.  
Some studies have shown that prints of these lace motifs could be made by the immersion of real lace in the pigments, which were then juxtaposed in the *azulejos*, or that these were painted using similar gestures as those used to make the real lace. This has not been the case for the motifs that decorate these *azulejos*, but nevertheless the elegance of this decoration gives a new and more regal understanding to this pattern type.
46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: 17th-century production of *azulejos* in Lisbon can easily be identified by the intense blue and yellow of the palette.
46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.method_for_provenance: The National Tile Museum holds a large number of *azulejos* of unknown origin, many gathered during the period of the destruction of the convents and palaces in the late 19th century, in the aftermath of the abolition of the religious orders in 1834.
46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.obtention: Probably salvaged during demolition of an unknown building where they had once been applied

4774c55a-a1aa-5860-91ed-a7105da0298d.name: Water bottle
4774c55a-a1aa-5860-91ed-a7105da0298d.short_description: This polychrome Iznik water bottle, *orsürahi*, is decorated with striking, stylised vegetal and arabesque motifs. The decoration was sketched out into the surface of the slip with a sharp instrument before the colours were applied, giving the artist a template from which to work but also allowing him to add additional painted details as he wished. The unusually large size of this bottle, and the spirited quality of its decoration, make it a particularly fine example of its genre.
4774c55a-a1aa-5860-91ed-a7105da0298d.obtention: Christie's London, Islamic Art and Manuscripts, 29 April 2003, Sale 6713, Lot 162 to Qatar Museums

47fcbd3c-bf49-59d2-b9ac-7634939dbb18.name: Islamic pottery from Ephesus
47fcbd3c-bf49-59d2-b9ac-7634939dbb18.short_description: Excavated by John Turtle Wood, an architect and surveyor. He was employed by the Ottoman Railway Company from 1858. Between 1863–1874 he excavated on behalf of the British Museum at ancient Ephesus, where he discovered the Temple of Artemis.

4890b1d8-3761-58e4-b21f-16c8c6e5cc7e.name: *Albarello* (pharmaceutical jar).
4890b1d8-3761-58e4-b21f-16c8c6e5cc7e.description:
Albarello with a pedestal base, a slightly concave cylindrical body and a long neck with an out-turned brim. Its surface is decorated with motifs in gold highlights on a tin white background. From top to bottom there is a band with geometrical decoration made up of rhomboids, a second band with flowers and volutes on white, and a lower band with vertical stripes and parallel, diagonal lines in blue and gold. In addition to its stylistic classification as a Manises product by the researchers mentioned below, recent analyses of the metals used in the decoration, essentially the cobalt that gives it its blue colour, have provided evidence of its Valencian origin. The intense blue tone, unlike the much lighter tone found in Malaga, is typical of this region.  
These types of object were used to store pharmaceutical products, hence their also being known as pharmaceutical pots or jars, a field in which Muslims excelled.
4890b1d8-3761-58e4-b21f-16c8c6e5cc7e.short_description: This Mudéjar imitation of the beautiful lustre-ware jars of the Nasrids differs from them in the greater intensity of the cobalt-blue typical of the potteries of Manises (Valencia).
4890b1d8-3761-58e4-b21f-16c8c6e5cc7e.dimensions: Height 29.4 cm, diameter of the mouth 10.7 cm, diameter of the base 10 cm, max. diameter 14 cm.
4890b1d8-3761-58e4-b21f-16c8c6e5cc7e.method_for_datation: Parallels with other objects, such as dish no. 51129 in the National Archaeological Museum, as well as other examples in the Institute of Valencia de Don Juan (Madrid).
4890b1d8-3761-58e4-b21f-16c8c6e5cc7e.method_for_provenance: Camps Cazorla places its origin in Manises, as does Martínez Caviró. Chemical analysis of the cobalt-blue confirms this hypothesis.
4890b1d8-3761-58e4-b21f-16c8c6e5cc7e.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological  Museum from Antonio Hidalgo in September 1882.

48af79f5-d145-59da-885f-a674a6c49de2.name: Dish
48af79f5-d145-59da-885f-a674a6c49de2.short_description: The Iznik potters’ enthusiasm for nature inspired them to develop new designs and to increase the colour palette. After being inspired by Chinese blue and white, Iznik potters introduced the Baba Nakkash style. Following the Chinese tradition of blue on white, it was also sometimes reversed. The designs consisted of stylised lobed leaves with curly tips. Initially these were in different shades of blue; small touches of turquoise were added as the style developed.
48af79f5-d145-59da-885f-a674a6c49de2.bibliography: Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, *The Essence of Iznik*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2011: 51-53.

49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.name: Dates group
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.description:
As a sign of hospitality guests are given *fuala* (light refreshments). Coffee, dates, *betheetha* (a sweet made of dates and fired flour), *khabees* (a sweet made of saffron, ghee and fried flour), leavened bread, and *dibs* (date molasses) were served on a *saroud* (palm mat) and covered with a *mechabeh* (palm food cover) to protect the food from dirt and insects.  
When guest finished eating they were offered a *ghasool* (a bowl of water) or a *maghsal al yad* (pitcher and vessel) to wash their hands. At the end of a visit, guests were perfumed with a *merash* (perfume sprinkler) filled with rose water and other fragrances. Guest were also perfumed with '*oud* incense'.
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

493fd5de-9ad8-584b-b87f-0c109a23012d.name: Tile Plate
493fd5de-9ad8-584b-b87f-0c109a23012d.description: The plate is coated with white clay and slip decorated with shades of grey and blue beneath a transparent colourless glaze. The plate’s scalloped, rimmed interior is adorned with a large medallion featuring flowers and leafy curling branches. The body is divided vertically into thirteen sections separated by grooves, each section decorated with a floral bouquet. The wide rim is encircled by a curving vine of alternating large and small flowers and leaves. The back of the plate is embellished with floral bouquets. The motifs are delineated in dark cobalt blue. Examples of this technique can be observed in the dull grey-blue flowers used in Chinese-influenced Iznik ceramics and pointed leaves seen on late 15th-century Ming porcelain. The production of plates in this style continued until the second half of the 16th century. In form and decoration these plates resemble Chinese porcelain of the Early Ming, Hsuan-te period (1426–1435).
493fd5de-9ad8-584b-b87f-0c109a23012d.dates: Hegira second quarter of the 10th century / AD first quarter of the 16th century

49ded692-84c0-5d04-b7b4-81eacbbca188.name: Ceramic fragment, base of a bowl
49ded692-84c0-5d04-b7b4-81eacbbca188.short_description: This sharp is part of a Kashan-style work which was found in Fustat, Cairo. The bright glaze of the ground shows an eight-rayed, blue star enclosed in a blue circle. Spiral decorations in brown lustre painting fill the blank spaces around and in the star, and the star’s outline is also traced in brown. On the back is a simple, wheel-like ornament with nine spokes in brown lustre painting.
49ded692-84c0-5d04-b7b4-81eacbbca188.bibliography: Watson, O., *Ceramics from Islamic Lands*, London: Thames & Hudson, 2004.

49f03f3b-5c62-50a6-af56-a99b7f0fe737.name: Niche tile with pair of lovers
49f03f3b-5c62-50a6-af56-a99b7f0fe737.description: The open-work niche tile with its green-glazed surface shows a pair of lovers in contemporary costume (Tracht). The young man with the curly hair is evidently a falconer, which indicates that the couple belongs to courtly society. The tile is one of the pottery masterpieces from 15th century Zurich. In addition to animal motifs and Christian symbols, courtly love of the late Middle Ages, with its main themes of love, faithfulness and adoration, was a popular topic. Hunting with falcons, a leisure pursuit exclusive to the nobility, also fell into this category and reflected the social status of the stove’s owner. Stove-tiles thus make an important contribution to cultural history and provide information on mediaeval costumes, hairstyles and accessories. Until the 16th century, potters did not sign their works. The names of many masters and the locations of the potteries are known thanks to documents and account books. In large towns such as Zurich and Basle, potters joined guilds.
49f03f3b-5c62-50a6-af56-a99b7f0fe737.obtention: Found in an excavation at «Moosburg» Effretikon 1953
keywords: Tile; Lovers; Falconer; Nobility; Moosburg; Effretikon; Zurich

4a14838f-3d68-55e8-8f84-cac452161836.name: Bowl with pod-shaped decoration.
4a14838f-3d68-55e8-8f84-cac452161836.description: The dish, painted in brown lustre on a cream background, is deep with vertical sides and a reasonably wide brim, decorated with pod-shaped swirls in relief. The decoration consists of tiny spike-shaped elements and small daisies that alternate with bands of solid and grid-pattern lustre. The centre of the boss is decorated with an animal, probably a hare. The inside bears a highly stylised epigraphic motif. On the outside, in the centre, there is a 16-point radial motif surrounded by a series of medallions with stylised fern leaves.
4a14838f-3d68-55e8-8f84-cac452161836.short_description: This bowl is an example of the metallic lustre-painted ceramics produced in Valencia. Zoomorphic and phytomorphic motifs, along with geometric elements, decorate the surface of the piece.
4a14838f-3d68-55e8-8f84-cac452161836.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
4a14838f-3d68-55e8-8f84-cac452161836.method_for_provenance: The dish belongs to a broad group of items that first appeared in Valencia towards the end of the 9th / 15th century and were extensively influenced by Renaissance metalwork.

4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.name: Plate.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.description: A deep dish with an underglaze-painted design showing a European-style sailing ship at sea, its sails billowing as it rides the cresting waves. Three tadpole-like fish are seen swimming below. In the rim of the dish, groups of simply drawn spirals, ultimately descended from the Chinese 'wave-and-rock' border pattern, reflect the oceanic theme. This dish is one of a number of similar pieces depicting sailing ships of either European or North African build. They were produced around the second quarter of the 17th century, when the Iznik ceramic industry had declined from its heyday of 50 or so years previous. Yet this plate retains considerable charm, especially the jaunty air the artist has given the ship.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.short_description: A deep dish with a representation of a ship at sea. Similar depictions of European and North African ships appear on a number of Iznik wares from the second quarter of the AH 11th / AD 17th century. Although the industry was in economic and artistic decline, examples like this retain a considerable charm.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.method_for_datation: Comparison with similar pieces of the same period.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

4a6e15bc-4e38-588d-8b7d-a1f2cb76b79c.name: Dish
4a6e15bc-4e38-588d-8b7d-a1f2cb76b79c.short_description: This dish is one of the finest known examples of the celebrated black-and-white wares, often referred to as "Nishapur ware". The inscriptions illustrate the social and literary interests of the dishes' owners. The text here is a proverb attributed to Yahya ibn Ziyad: "He who is unable to have an opinion will lose his chance". The inscription is revealed as the contents are eaten - providing an exemplary 'conversation piece' with which to conclude a social gathering of scholars.
4a6e15bc-4e38-588d-8b7d-a1f2cb76b79c.obtention: Forughi Collection, Iran; Private Collection, Geneva sometime before the Islamic Revolution, where it remained until it was formally acquired by the Museum of Islamic Art, Doha in 1999 from London Art Market

4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.name: *Madkhan* (Incense burner)
4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.description: The burning of incense is part of the routine for welcoming a guest. A *Mmadkhan* (incense burner) is used to hold a smouldering piece of charcoal on which incense is placed. The heat causes incense to burn thus, releasing its scent. The *madkhan* is passed around from person to person to share and perfume their clothing.
4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
4a7d2384-96d3-5574-ba51-84cb41cd1805.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

4b5af6a4-7de4-5e18-87de-8bf5e62763db.name: Dish
4b5af6a4-7de4-5e18-87de-8bf5e62763db.description: The Orientalism or Neo-Mudéjar style gave new light to old techniques such as ceramic with lustre decoration; the Manises workshops begun again to use lustre decorations and shapes from the Middle Age period.
4b5af6a4-7de4-5e18-87de-8bf5e62763db.author: Manuel Alonso

4b6b4cd7-723b-5fc1-9d39-214740318d2a.name: Panel
4b6b4cd7-723b-5fc1-9d39-214740318d2a.short_description:
William De Morgan designed and produced pictorial tile panels. The smaller versions were sometimes framed for display as pictures, or used in fireplaces. Larger panels, would have been used in architectural settings, grander fireplaces, bathroom walls, and for the decoration of smoking rooms on ocean liners of the P&O company.  
De Morgan had a great interest in Islamic tilework, much of which was thought to be Persian in the 19th century. The Islamic-inspired patterns and the dominant range of colours (turquoise, blue, green, purple), were also often termed 'Persian'. They were in fact more closely related to the tilework of Syria and Turkey. The different regional types of Islamic tile were little understood, despite the acquisition of large quantities of Islamic tiles by European collectors.
4b6b4cd7-723b-5fc1-9d39-214740318d2a.dimensions: Height: 61.4 cm panel, Width: 40.5 cm panel, Depth: 1.9 cm, Height: 20.6 cm each tile, Width: 20.6 cm each tile
4b6b4cd7-723b-5fc1-9d39-214740318d2a.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: Ceramic; earthenware; collector; collection; ceramic tile; tile panel; tilework; vegetal decoration; floral decoration; revival; Syrian tiles
materials: Buff-coloured earthenware, with painting over a white slip

4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.name: Ceramic tile.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.description:
A rectangular ceramic, glazed tile that was made during the restoration of the Dome of the Rock in AH 1233 / AD 1817 and with the name of one of the tile-makers inscribed on it. The inscription is composed within a 2.5 cm-wide frame of turquoise, undulating with an extremely light-green pigment, which is adjacent to another frame in dark-blue. The text, written in green and black against a pale-green background, reads: “Trust in God 1233 \[1817\] Mustafa Ali Effendi”. It is known that a number of tile-makers who worked on the restoration at the Dome of the Rock immortalised their names in a similar way, fixing the tiles in various places. The Museum has acquired another tile made by the same tile-maker, which reads: “Reckon with the One God and That is Enough, Mustafa Ali Effendi, 1233 \[1817\]”. The tiles are very alike; there is only a slight difference in the colour scheme in that the text and the “frame” of the second tile is decorated in dark-blue while the background takes on a very light-blue. There is a third tile by the same maker which was produced after those already discussed. This tile bears the text: “If you ask, Ask God 1234 \[1818\] Mustafa”. This inscription is written in light-blue against dark-blue.  
It is possible that these tiles formed the penultimate stage in the six stages of tile restoration at the Dome of the Rock, the final stage taking place in the 1970s. Despite the tireless attempts of the tile-maker to copy the tiles of former stages while replacing damaged tiles with new ones, one can still distinguish the different stages of restoration by means of the detailed workmanship, the colouration, glazing and in other artistic aspects, all of which help in ascertaining the dates of the restoration process. During the process of restoration a large number of tiles were made in Jerusalem; a number of them have been acquired by the Islamic Museum. However, some of the tiles required for the restoration were imported from Kütahya, or from Iznik in Turkey.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.short_description: A glazed ceramic tile which (like similar ones) records the name of the craftsman who contributed to the renovation of the Dome of the Rock in AH 1233 / AD 1817.  It is painted in a turquoise colour mixed with a light green. The name is written in green and black.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.dimensions: Length 36.5 cm, width 27 cm, depth 3 cm.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.method_for_datation: The tile inscription states the date of production.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.method_for_provenance: It is thought that kilns and ceramic workshops were set up at the Haram al-Sharif. However, the tile ceramicists would most likely have been from Damascus, for the names of a number of them repeatedly state the agnomen, “al-Dimashqi”, meaning “from Damascus”.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.obtention: The piece was transferred from the Dome of the Rock to the Islamic Museum during the restoration works of 1966.
4be93273-e1ba-5539-89c5-b15b9bf3f2d5.bibliography:

keywords: Ceramic tile; glazed tile; ceramic; glaze; faience

4c1c6011-7e32-57c2-ac90-5672e32a2457.name: Ewer
4c1c6011-7e32-57c2-ac90-5672e32a2457.short_description: The small ewer displays carved decoration under a thick cobalt blue glaze.
materials: Frit body, carved decoration under turquoise glaze

4c1d7376-2dba-5edb-8c50-24e7e3030900.name: Dish
4c1d7376-2dba-5edb-8c50-24e7e3030900.short_description: The dish is so-called "Sari" ware (production probably local to the town of Sari). Sari pottery's characteristic decoration is the figure of a big bird and "lollipop" flowers.
materials: Earthenware, white slip, underglaze polychrome decoration

4c2706b3-1aef-5df4-b5b2-4acc99b47143.name: Jar
4c2706b3-1aef-5df4-b5b2-4acc99b47143.description:
This transport jar was handmade and has a typical kitchenware profile. Its high neck with a wide rim allowed it to be covered with a lid (ceramic, wood, textile). Its ovoid body supports a single handle. The entire body is covered with a cream-coloured slip and geometric decoration painted in brown in a series of panels across the body.  
  
Although it was found in Al Zubara, in north-western Qatar, the characteristic grainy clay, as well as the manufacturing technique, shape and decoration, identify it as Julfar pottery. This type of pottery was made in Ras al-Khaymah (in the modern United Arab Emirates) and exported throughout the Gulf, particularly from the AH 12th-13th / AD 18th to the mid-20th century.
4c2706b3-1aef-5df4-b5b2-4acc99b47143.place_of_production: Julfar, Ras al-Khaymah Emirate, United Arab Emirates

4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.name: Tankard
4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.description: A cylindrical tankard with one handle. The body is decorated with a series of white flowers with a blue centre and green leaves on a red ground. On the top and bottom there is a band in the form of a chain. The handle is decorated in blue and white.

4d271fb9-86f6-54f6-8ff7-b1f5b8365eb6.name: Plate
4d271fb9-86f6-54f6-8ff7-b1f5b8365eb6.description: White clay and slip, decorated in yellow, green, blue, red and manganese purple tones under transparent glaze. The motifs are outlined in black. On the plate’s surface a female figure is seen from the front in a garden. She is wearing a yellow robe and blue and white striped shalwar. The shalwar, a garment of traditional Turkish origin, was made from the fabric called *selimiye*, which was widely worn in the Ottoman Empire during the second half of the 18th century. Figures depicted on Kütahya ceramics sometimes are presented in a schematic manner in traditional Ottoman attire. Female figures on these plates, which were mainly produced for export in the late 18th century, were sometimes referred to as concubines. In the years following the proclamation of the Republic, these plates, colloquially referred to as *kızlı tabak*, were included in the dowries of girls who were about to be married.
4d271fb9-86f6-54f6-8ff7-b1f5b8365eb6.dates: Hegira second half of the 12th century / AD Second half of the 18th century

4d52d723-2eaf-5fc7-ba06-13ce4807735a.name: Deep glazed bowl with pseudo-epigraphic inscription
4d52d723-2eaf-5fc7-ba06-13ce4807735a.description: This bowl was discovered on the site of a house during the Qatari-French archaeological mission in 2009. The bowl itself dates to the 9th century. It is covered in an off-white opaque glaze with a wide band of turquoise glaze or paint around the upper part. The black-brown paint around the outside resembles Arabic script, but it is unclear whether real words were intended or this is simply a design. This kind of stylised painting is known as 'pseudo-epigraphic' decoration and is particularly associated with workshops in Samarkand and Nishapur (present-day Uzbekistan and Iran, respectively). These types of wares illustrate the influence of Islamic design and Arabic script throughout the Muslim world during the early Islamic period.
4d52d723-2eaf-5fc7-ba06-13ce4807735a.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.name: Bottle.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.description: A pear-shaped bottle made of stone-paste with a tall elegant neck and flaring mouth. The body of the vessel is covered in a spiral pattern of tightly coiled floral stems, painted in cobalt-blue and turquoise. The same floral scrolls run horizontally around the neck. Placed throughout the design are diamond-shaped medallions. The break between the design on the neck and body may have been intended to make room for a gold mount. The distinctive spiral pattern can also be found on Ottoman manuscript illuminations, particularly as a background for the *tughra*, the sultan's official monogram. The shape of this bottle echoes a common Venetian glass form. Its exact function is unknown.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.short_description: An elegant ceramic bottle with blue and turquoise underglaze. While the shape may have derived from Venetian glass, the spiral pattern recalls Italian *tondino* ceramic dishes. There are also parallels between the tightly coiled floral stems and Ottoman manuscript illumination.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.type: Stone paste blue and turquoise painting
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.method_for_datation: This bottle can be dated to about 936 / 1530 due to its design which is similar to that of a cut-down bottle in the British Museum, with the same spiral pattern, bearing the date 935 (1529).
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.method_for_provenance: This type of spiral decoration is known as 'Golden Horn' ware, so called because of the number of sherds decorated in this style that were dug up at Sirkeci on the southern shore of the Golden Horn estuary in Istanbul. However, this bottle was probably made in Iznik, the main centre of production for ceramics in Ottoman Turkey in the 10th / 16th century.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.obtention: Part of the John Henderson bequest to the British Museum in 1878.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.bibliography:
Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, no. 147.  
  
Carswell, J., *Iznik Pottery*, London, 1998, pp.48–51, plate 26.  
  
Rogers, J. M., and Ward, R., *Suleyman the Magnificent*, London, 1988, p.195, cat. no. 136.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.author: Emily Shovelton
materials: Stone-paste with blue and turquoise painting under the glaze.

4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.name: Bottle vase
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.short_description: In the second half of the eighteenth century the neighbourhood of Tophane in Istanbul saw the establishment of the pipe makers’ guild. Most of the then existing sixty workshops produced a wide variety of objects such as coffee cups, writing sets, goblets, decanters, carafes, trays, etc. The high-quality red pottery manufactured here was often decorated with silver and gold highlights. Some of the dark brown vessels, such as the present one, had silver-inlaid decoration. The surface of this long-neck bottle vase is divided into sixteen vertical compartments filled with silver-inlaid vegetal and floral motifs. Incised vertical grooves bordered by rows of stamped circular motifs separate the compartments. The stamped motifs as well as the precious silver inlays recall the elaborate decoration of metal vessels and jewels.
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.method_for_datation: Stylistic comparison with Tophane wares from the Medelhavsmuseet in Stockholm donated to the Museum after the 1873 Vienna World Fair.
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.obtention: Transferred in 1949 from the National Museum Carol I in Bucharest.
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.bibliography: Dunca, M., *Islamic Art at the National Museum of Art of Romania*, Bucharest: National Museum of Art of Romania, 2015: 108, no. 49.
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.author: Mircea Dunca
materials: Earthenware, dark brown slip, silver inlays

4ee050c8-f860-5f8e-afca-7d0c987f64b7.name: Fragment of a dish
4ee050c8-f860-5f8e-afca-7d0c987f64b7.short_description: Fragment of a ceramic dish featuring a musician playing the lute (*\`ud*), surrounded by a jar and ewers with flowers and leaves. The musician’s garment is adorned with palmettes and his sleeves bear *tiraz* bands. Fatimid ceramics, such as this, often depict scenes from courtly life and provide valuable information on the painting tradition of the period.

4ef4f4cf-3d12-58c3-8cc2-6c635b02100f.name: Plate
4ef4f4cf-3d12-58c3-8cc2-6c635b02100f.short_description: Plain inverted rim, shallow body, ring base. Light brown paste, white slip, transparent glaze. Under glaze decoration in cobalt blue, turquoise, dark green, yellow, red and black with black outlines. At the centre of a scalloped sun-shaped medallion formed by intertwined *rumi* and palmette motifs is a star and crescent motif, itself at the centre of a scalloped nine-petal medallion. The remaining surface is covered with a geometric design composed of eight-pointed stars, and the rim is decorated with a wide border of rumi-palmette motifs. The reverse of the plate bears the inscription, *Kütahya Azim Çini Fabrikası Mamulatı* (Product of the Kütahya azim Tie Factory).

4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.name: Dish.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.description: A white dish with a foliate rim, painted under the glaze with a floral composition. Blue tulips, some with red dots and red rosettes sprout from emerald-green stems which grow out of a blue-and-green 'shrub' at the bottom of the composition. The outer rim of the dish is filled with tightly coiled black spirals surrounded with blue and enlivened here and there with green, a pattern descended from the Chinese wave-and-rock pattern. The freely designed, quasi-naturalistic floral spray relates this dish to a number of similar wares thought to date from the early years of the reign of Sultan Murad III (AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95).
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.short_description: A white dish decorated with freely rendered floral motifs, including tulips and rosebuds, in the brilliant colours associated with the peak of the Ottoman ceramic industry at Iznik.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.method_for_datation: Comparison with similar objects of the period.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, Istanbul/London, 1989, pp.246–7.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.author: Barry Wood

4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.name: Incense burner
4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.description: Incense burners like this are usually made of clay mixed with water and kneaded until it forms a mixture that can then be shaped. The burner is then adorned with engravings, intricate drawings, and different colors. The incense burners are then fired in a kiln, after which they are ready for use. Note the handle; it makes the burner safe to carry from room to room. Incense occupies a central place in Omani life, as the passing of a fragrant burner at the end of a visit is customary in every region of the country.
4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.holder: The National Museum - Sultanate of Oman
4f35a232-fd44-5945-a2d3-5c34f4b1ae6a.author: Noora Al Balushi

4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.name: Sphinx
4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.short_description: This sphinx was found in Rafiqa, Raqqa’s twin city, in 1924 together with the cock in the David Collection and the figure of a horseman in Syria’s National Museum. As ceramic sculptures, they are unique not only in Syria, but also in the rest of the Islamic world. They are fountain figures, and all have pipes to carry water up to the figures’ heads.
4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.dates: Hegira 2nd half of the 6th century / AD 2nd half of the 12th century
keywords: Syria; Fritware; zangids; imaginary animal; zoomirphic imagery
materials: Cast, modelled, and carved fritware painted in an opaque white and a turquoise glaze

50179dc4-4e0f-5796-85ea-539270a46a71.name: Cooking pot
50179dc4-4e0f-5796-85ea-539270a46a71.description:
This kitchen utensil was discovered at the al Wakra site during excavations carried out in 2011.  
It is a cooking pot that was made in Julfar (in the Emirate of Ras al-Khaymah) and used for storing and preparing foodstuffs and liquids. With a globular body and a flat base, this pot bears a grey slip, and some of the specific decoration painted in red from the Julfar production workshop can be discerned on the upper part of the body, neck and shoulder. This bears witness to the import of pottery and to Qatar's commercial links and activities.
50179dc4-4e0f-5796-85ea-539270a46a71.place_of_production: Julfar, Ras al-Khaymah Emirate, United Arab Emirates

5032bffe-ba78-553b-bd60-df9e0091fb80.name: Dish
5032bffe-ba78-553b-bd60-df9e0091fb80.short_description: In Turkey, underglaze-painted pottery, produced for the Ottoman court and wealthy patrons, is renowned for its unique style of motifs and colours, once again widely admired in Europe. Mostly fashioned into dishes, bowls and drinking vessels, these Iznik wares were another major influence on Western ceramic production. This Iznik dish with composite floral motifs is painted in underglaze cobalt blue, sage green, manganese and outlined in black is dated AD c. 1540.
5032bffe-ba78-553b-bd60-df9e0091fb80.bibliography: *Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia*, Volume 2, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2009: 155.

507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.name: Plate
507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.short_description: During the last third of the 16th century, a type of floral decoration emerged in Iznik ceramics known as “bouquets with bent flowers”. Blue tulips, red carnations and a blue blossom spray nestle in asymmetrical arrangement around the plate. The graphic quality in the rendering of the blossom spray is admirably enhanced against the white background. Stylized wave motifs in the border pattern have almost lost touch with their Chinese source.
507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.bibliography: Noever, Peter (ed), *Global:Lab: Kunst als Botschaft. Asien und Europa 1500-1700, Exh. cat. Museum of Applied Arts Vienna*, Ostfildern: Hatje Cantz, 2009.
507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.author: Mio Wakita-Elis
materials: Quartz frit ceramic, decoration: underglaze painting and so-called tomato red

5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.name: ‘Miletus ware’ bowls.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.description:
Inv. no. 3161: A bowl, the centre of which is framed by a circular band. Within it, dark-blue triangles are painted on a white ground. The points of the triangles meet, creating hexagons in the white space between them. These hexagons have dark-blue circles at their centres. The border is decorated with wave-and-rock motifs.  
  
Inv. no. 3174: A bowl; on a white ground, within dark-blue frames, stylised palmettes emerge from stalks, their centres filled with spirals. In the border, interlaced white motifs appear on a dark-blue ground. The outside is decorated with green spiralling tendrils.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.short_description: These two ceramic bowls have red paste, white slip and blue-and-white decoration. They are early examples of a ceramic group known as 'Miletus ware', which as a result of excavations at Iznik tile kilns is now known to have been produced at Iznik.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.dimensions: Inv. no. 3161: Height 14 cm, diameter 27 cm; Inv. no. 3174: Height 14 cm, diameter 34 cm.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.method_for_datation: As a result of the archaeological excavations at the Iznik kilns, many objects were found related to production of ceramics. These finds showed that ceramics variously classified as 'Miletus', 'Rhodian', and so forth were actually produced in Iznik, and they make it possible to establish a single classification and dating system for such wares.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.method_for_provenance: The bowls were found during the course of archaeological excavations at the Iznik kilns.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.obtention: The bowls were found during archaeological excavations at Iznik and brought to the Museum on 10 February 1967.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.bibliography: ölçer, N. *et al, Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, pp.244–5.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.author: Cihat Soyhan
materials: Red paste with white slip and blue-and-white decoration, a type known as ‘Miletus ware’.

512cb99c-ea37-501f-9c8b-da383856d20e.name: Moulded bowl with *kufic* inscription
512cb99c-ea37-501f-9c8b-da383856d20e.short_description: This moulded, facetted bowl of fritware shows a large benedictory *kufic* inscription enhanced by rabbits, birds and a large crowned sphinx. Cobalt blue streaks accentuate the decoration in the well and around the outside. The delicate body material was intended to imitate Chinese porcelain. The bowl’s shape may imitate a contemporary metal vessel.
512cb99c-ea37-501f-9c8b-da383856d20e.dates: Hegira late 6th century / AD late 12th century
keywords: Bowl; kufic; inscription; calligraphy; fritware; ceramic; animal decoration; bird; imaginary animal

525fce2f-a859-5439-8cdd-d1b640752ea5.name: *Ghotar* plate
525fce2f-a859-5439-8cdd-d1b640752ea5.description: In Morocco, the *ghotar* is a large dish for the presentation of food, such as *pastilla* (chicken cooked in pastry), or fruit.
525fce2f-a859-5439-8cdd-d1b640752ea5.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
525fce2f-a859-5439-8cdd-d1b640752ea5.dates: Hegira end of 12th century - beginning 13th century / AD end of 18th century

5280813d-cdb9-576e-8876-874404acb331.name: Bowl
5280813d-cdb9-576e-8876-874404acb331.short_description:
While the motifs on figurative bowls painted in luster in Abbasid Iraq were stylized, a number of quite naturalistic depictions of courtiers, dancers, wrestlers, etc. are known from Fatimid Egypt.  
There are many figurative elements in Fatimid art, something that should perhaps be seen in the context of the region’s Coptic Christian tradition.
materials: Earthenware, painted in luster over a white glaze

5319542a-7b08-534a-801f-e2b18cb78aef.name: Hemispherical plate.
5319542a-7b08-534a-801f-e2b18cb78aef.description: A fragment corresponding to a section of the body including part of the rim and the complete base. The rim has a lip semi-circular in cross-section and the base has a high foot-ring. It is made from pinkish beige paste. Both surfaces are coated in white enamel with a slight sheen. The interior surface has a motif of intersecting lines, painted green, creating eight equidistant spokes radiating from the centre. The quality and fine grain of the paste of this flattened hemispherical plate reflects the sophistication of domestic articles used in Silves in this period.
5319542a-7b08-534a-801f-e2b18cb78aef.short_description: Hemispherical bowl from the Almohad period. It is decorated with a star painted in green consisting of eight evenly spaced spokes radiating from the centre. The quality and finesse of this piece suggest a refined environment and probable domestic use in the town on Silves during that time.
5319542a-7b08-534a-801f-e2b18cb78aef.dimensions: Height 6.4 cm, diameter (of rim) 22.6 cm, diameter (of foot) 7.6 cm.
5319542a-7b08-534a-801f-e2b18cb78aef.method_for_datation: From its archaeological context, stratigraphy and style.
5319542a-7b08-534a-801f-e2b18cb78aef.method_for_provenance: Excavation carried out in the castle at Silves directed by Rosa Varela Gomes. Inventory number: Cast. Q 110/C3-3.
5319542a-7b08-534a-801f-e2b18cb78aef.obtention: It has been housed in the museum since the excavation carried out in the 1980s.

538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.name: Footed bowl.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.description:
A footed circular bowl with steep, curved sides that taper towards a flattened rim which projects towards the inside of the bowl. Underneath a clear turquoise glaze that stops short of the foot, the bowl is decorated extensively with black underglaze as seen for example on the rim: a succession of broad, black stripes. Around the interior wall of the bowl is a band that is defined only by borders composed of three fine lines above and below; individual lozenges have been disposed within this band at regular intervals. The wide base of the bowl is occupied by a roundel containing a large cursive inscription, set against a stylised scrolling background and enhanced by densely placed dots. The inscription reads: ‘*al-‘afiyah*’ (‘Good Health’). On the outside of the bowl there are short illegible cursive inscriptions.  
Other than Iran, the City of Raqqa was the centre for high-quality ceramics producing a sizeable quantity of artistically inventive and technically varied ceramic vessels and tiles during the late 5th–early 6th / late 12th–mid-13th centuries. The black-and-turquoise ware exemplified by this dish is typical of ceramics from Raqqa during this period. This group is characterised by a rather coarse and grainy stone-paste with a glaze that tends to deteriorate and, as a result, often shows varying degrees of iridescence.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.short_description: Syria was an important centre for the production of artistically inventive and technically varied ceramics during the AH late 5th–early 6th / AD late 12th and mid 13th centuries. Many pieces show black decoration under a turquoise glaze, often incorporating wishes for good health or blessings.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.dates: Hegira late 5th–early 6th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.method_for_datation: The bowl belongs to a well-defined group of late 5th–early 6th / late 12th–mid-13th-century Syrian pottery.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.method_for_provenance: Ceramic wares executed using this technique are currently attributed to late 5th–early 6th / late 12th –mid-13th-century Syria, with an active centre for the production of such wares attributed to Raqqa in Syria.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.obtention: Purchased by NMS in 1976 from Bluett and Sons Ltd in London, the item was had been on loan to the Royal Museum since 1960 from the Sir Eldred Hitchcock Collection, also based in London. During that time, the item was registered under loan number L.421.31. It was eventually bought by NMS in 1976 from Bluett and Son acting on behalf of the son of the owner.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.bibliography: Lane, A., *Islamic Pottery from the Ninth to the Fourteenth Centuries A.D. in the Collection of Sir Eldred Hitchcock*, London 1956, fig. 32, cat. no. 68.
538cb9d0-c759-560a-9e30-62d63b7ae0a5.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware) with black underglaze and clear turquoise alkaline glaze.

54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.name: Tile from ceramic inscription panel of the Dome of the Rock.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.description:
A tile forming part of a ceramic inscription panel that once decorated the exterior octagonal pinnacle of the Dome of the Rock. Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66) commissioned the panel while renovation work of the Dome of the Rock was being carried out, in around AH 969 / AD 1560. Each tile is 25 cm high by 25 cm long, and the whole inscription panel is 160 m long. The panel is decorated with a long Qur'anic inscription consisting of the complete text of the chapter “Ya-sin” (Chapter 36). The text is written in the Ottoman *thuluth* script in white against a dark-blue background. The inscription is interspersed with vegetal decoration consisting of intertwining spiralling stems, with blossoms and leaves. The tiles have a characteristic simplicity, and are of fine colouring and very detailed workmanship. The tiles represent an early example of Ottoman ceramics, used generally in architecture during the period, and more specifically in the Dome of the Rock. Buildings were often panelled with ceramic tiles during the Ottoman period, in fact, such tile work is a distinguishing trait of Ottoman contributions to the restoration and renovation of holy places, not only in Jerusalem but also in places such as Mecca and Medina.  
The Islamic Museum have acquired all sections of this inscription panel which was removed from The Dome of the Rock in 1960 during restoration works. The Museum has since housed and preserved the inscription panel as a witness to the first stage of ceramic-tile panelling on the outer walls of the Dome of the Rock. It is worth noting that previous to these tiles, the outer octagon of Dome of the Rock was covered with a glass mosaic, which had deteriorated badly due to age, until Sulayman the Magnificent ordered the removal of the damaged mosaic and replaced it with these tiles.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.short_description: A glazed tile from a band that wrapped round the exterior octagonal pinnacle of the Dome of the Rock, ordered by Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent during his renovation of the Dome. It is written in *thuluth* script in white against a dark-blue background. The verses are interposed with vegetal decorations.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.dimensions: Length (of a single tile) 25 cm, width 25 cm, depth 3 cm.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production for these tiles. This is supported by historical sources indicating the presence of a workforce and Ottoman ceramic tile-making kilns in the area.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.obtention: The piece was transferred in 1960 from the Dome of the Rock to the Islamic Museum.

5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.name: The ‘Lady of Sabra’ plate.
5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.description:
Round-based plate. It has a low, upstanding rim, slightly curved and sloping outwards. On the plate is drawn a female figure in profile with a large almond-shaped eye. The full mouth and the delicate nose are very finely drawn.  
The long hair starts in a pony-tail and ends in plaits hanging down to the knees. The figure is standing, wearing a brown-striped dress covered in fringes. She holds a glass in one hand and in the other a flower drawn in a naturalistic manner. The figure is surrounded by four stylised, fan-shaped flowers and by two rectangular shapes each containing a eulogy, probably ‘al-Mulk’ (Sovereignty).  
As from the advent of the Fatimids, Ifriqiyan ceramics began to show a preference for the figurative, showing a definite Mesopotamian influence. This trend is undoubtedly connected with the attitude of Shi'ite dogma towards the representation of the human form, more tolerant than that of the Malikite conformists.  
The face, with its huge eyes, is a common denominator of almost all human Ifriqiyan figures of the period, whether carved, modelled or painted, and seems to go back to a distant, Roman, North African past. By contrast, the style of the Lady of Sabra's dress had been in fashion since the Umayyad era and lasted right through the Abbasid period.
5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.short_description: This green bowl has a round base and depicts a female silhouette. The face is identified by an almond-shaped eye, a full mouth and an extremely fine nose. The profile is reminiscent of Ifriqiyan figures.
5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.dates: Hegira, second half of the 4th century / AD 10th century.
5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.method_for_datation: This object comes from the site of Sabra al-Mansuriyya, the short-lived capital of the Fatimids and then of the Zirids, which lasted just over 100 years (337–444 / 948–1053). It was retrieved from one of the oldest layers of the site, which dates it from the second half of the 4th / 10th century. The date is corroborated by the green colour and by the decoration.
5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.method_for_provenance: The discovery on the Sabra site of this plate and of two other identical plates, painted with Fatimid–Zirid decoration and made in the Ifriqiyan manner, suggests they were produced in series locally at the Sabra potteries or at those of Kairouan, the nearest economic capital.
5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.provenance: Kairouan or Sabra al-Mansuriyya, which both had potteries.
5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.obtention: The plate was among objects discovered on site during the 1979 excavations at Sabra al-Mansuriyya. It was acquired in 1986 directly from the site by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada.

5443b49b-dc27-5556-9034-4775ba220542.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Figurative decoration; women; Zirid; figurative representation

5518987f-66ff-5665-9182-5ca8e89a0429.name: Small jug.
5518987f-66ff-5665-9182-5ca8e89a0429.description:
This small jug, with a small circular base, a bulging belly, low neck and large opening, is composed of several pieces glued back together, with one piece missing from the neck. The handle that links the belly and the neck is surmounted by a thumb-piece that halps to lift the receptacle. The clay paste is covered by cream-coloured slip, which is visible on the inside and outside of the lower half and on the base. Horizontal grooves in relief can be seen on the belly, under the neck and on the inside. One part of the jug is varnished in green. The lower part and base remain bare.  
Given the dimensions of the jug, one supposes that it served as a kitchen utensil, used to hold milk and whey.
5518987f-66ff-5665-9182-5ca8e89a0429.short_description: This small, ring-base jug with a rounded belly, short neck and wide opening has been restored. The handle is fitted with a thumb hold. The clay was covered with a cream engobe (slip) that is still visible in places. It is decorated with horizontal grooves in relief. Part of the jug has a green glaze.
5518987f-66ff-5665-9182-5ca8e89a0429.dimensions: Height 21 cm, diameter of the belly 18 cm.
5518987f-66ff-5665-9182-5ca8e89a0429.method_for_datation: The jug was brought to light from the Muslim stratigraphic layer of Tiddis (Constantine); furthermore, formal characteristics (green glaze, handle with thumb-piece) very closely resemble those of Hammadid ceramic of the Qal'at Bani Hammad.
5518987f-66ff-5665-9182-5ca8e89a0429.method_for_provenance: According to the museum archives it was found in the archaeological site of Tiddis.

568ea72c-15dd-54c9-b0ee-2ca218f47449.name: Storage jar.
568ea72c-15dd-54c9-b0ee-2ca218f47449.description: A large ceramic storage jar decorated with blue and black underglaze painting. The jar is decorated all over with pseudo-calligraphic motifs of various sizes, including narrow bands around the shoulder and just above the base. The most prominent 'inscription' occupies the greater part of the jar; it consists mainly of dramatic verticals punctuated at nearly regular intervals with the letter waw. In this inscription, unlike the smaller ones above and below it, the letters have been left in relief to stand out against the dark-blue and black background, in which the spaces between the verticals are filled with scrolling vegetal ornament. The neck of the jar features a frieze of bird-silhouettes rendered in blue, with simple arabesque-like designs painted over them in black. Bold calligraphic inscriptions are a hallmark of Mamluk art, and examples like this jar show how that aesthetic made itself felt even in humble wares used for storage.
568ea72c-15dd-54c9-b0ee-2ca218f47449.short_description: A large ceramic storage jar, decorated in blue and black on a white ground. The decoration consists largely of pseudo-calligraphic inscriptions. This is a good example of how the Mamluk aesthetic extended even to humble wares used for storage.
568ea72c-15dd-54c9-b0ee-2ca218f47449.method_for_datation: Comparison with similar wares from the Mamluk period.
568ea72c-15dd-54c9-b0ee-2ca218f47449.method_for_provenance: Egypt and Syria were both Mamluk domains.
568ea72c-15dd-54c9-b0ee-2ca218f47449.bibliography:
Ayers, J., Oriental Art in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 1983, p.114.  
  
Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, pp.34–35.

5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.name: Panel of tiles.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.description:
A comprehensive group of ceramic tile panels in the form of a pointed arch. Apple-green is used for the background of the peripheral panels while a dark-blue dominates the central panels. Both the floral ornamentation and the calligraphic inscriptions are coloured white and carefully stencilled in black. The technique used to apply the colours is underglaze painting.  
These fine Damascene Ottoman tiles were found in the tomb chamber of the Mustafa Lala Pasha mosque, located above the window that overlooks the cemetery. The three lines of *thuluth* script translate as follows:  
(1) Protector  
(2) May the mercy of the Lord be upon him in every moment  
(3) Everything is mortal except for the countenance of God, He has the power of rule, to Him you will all return.  
The year AH 998 / AD 1590 was written in numerals in two locations between these lines. The spaces surrounding the inscription, as well as the space between the words, are filled with finely executed stylised vegetal motifs. The depiction of multiple flower varieties swaying in the breeze recalls the extent to which Chinese styles influenced the repertoire of Islamic ceramics. The choice of *thuluth* script for the calligraphy is a favoured ornamental script in tile work because of its monumental letter proportions and its curvaceous painterly quality.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.short_description: Ottoman style underglaze painted tiles made in Damascus display the painterly quality of *thuluth* calligraphy on a background of spiralling floral motifs.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.initial_owner: Probably a governor of Damascus during the reign of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 981–1003 / AD 1574–95).
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.method_for_datation: The inscription on the panel includes the date of its completion, 998 (1590).
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.method_for_provenance: The underglaze technique is consistent with local Syrian techniques of ceramics manufacture and distinctive from the Ottoman overglaze method. During this period, Damascus was a flourishing tile-production centre. It is therefore likely that the tiles were produced in Damascus.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.provenance: Mosque of Mustafa Lala Pasha, Damascus, Syria.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.obtention: The tile panels entered the Museum in 1919 when the mosque in which these tiles were originally located was demolished to make room for the Suq al-Hal, the Cardamom Market.

56fdf3b8-f3a7-5644-8aac-6ef2466a6f40.name: Panel of tiles.
56fdf3b8-f3a7-5644-8aac-6ef2466a6f40.description:
Panel made up of four *azulejos* (square tiles) and 12 *alfardones* (hexagonal tiles) glazed with cobalt-blue on a white background, the former decorated with blue-petalled flowers and white borders, and the latter with stylised Moorish plant motifs and banderols bearing the inscription in lower-case Gothic characters *fer be* ('do good'). Eight triangular pieces with stylised plant motifs are fitted into the corners and sides of the panel, three of which are decorated with the end of a banderol similar to the ones on the *alfardones*. They are in fact the ends of these tiles, cut off to form a triangular shape. Some retain the plant decoration and others part of a banderol. The panel is now framed with a line of smooth blue tiles.  
The panel was initially part of the decoration of the chapel of San Jeronimo of the Convent of Concepción Francisca in Toledo. The repetition of the text on the *alfardones* is an example of how, in the Mudéjar age, Manises ceramicists reinterpreted traditional inscription-based decorative schemes.
56fdf3b8-f3a7-5644-8aac-6ef2466a6f40.short_description: This set of tiles showing a complete decorative motif, was made in the potteries of Manises (Valencia) for the Chapel of San Jerónimo of the Convent of the Conception of St Francis (Toledo), which explains the repeated epigram *fer be*, ‘do good’.
56fdf3b8-f3a7-5644-8aac-6ef2466a6f40.method_for_datation: Part of a well-known and documented series from Manises.
56fdf3b8-f3a7-5644-8aac-6ef2466a6f40.method_for_provenance: The documentation kept in the National Archaeological Museum archive explicitly states that they come from the chapel of San Jeronimo of the Convent of Concepción Francisca in Toledo. This chapel was founded in 1422 by Gonzalo López de la Fuente.
56fdf3b8-f3a7-5644-8aac-6ef2466a6f40.provenance: Convent of Concepción Francisca, Toledo, Spain.
56fdf3b8-f3a7-5644-8aac-6ef2466a6f40.obtention: Obtained by the National Archaeological Museum as part of the collection of tiles sold by Anastasio de Páramo y Barranco in 1933.

5722c4e0-76c3-5fb1-8956-11019061b77b.name: Mosaic Tile Panel with Design of Flowers and Interlocking Vines
5722c4e0-76c3-5fb1-8956-11019061b77b.short_description: A kite-shaped mosaic panel, truncated at the bottom, is mounted into a framed, white plaster mold. Outlining the border on all sides except the bottom is a turquoise band, then a black band, then a golden-tan band, each progressively thinner. The main ground of the mosaic is royal blue in color, and is decorated with a series of interlocking vines in golden-tan, white, and turquoise, interspersed with various flowers with petals in pale pink or black, each outlined in white. Among the flowers and vines are leaves in forest green, outlined in golden-tan, ranging in saturation. The central element of the panel is a lobed pendentive with a black ground, surrounded in golden-tan, decorated with turquoise vines and flowers with pale pink centers, around a central flower outlined in white with a pale pink, teardrop center surrounded in royal blue outline, then pink teardrop petals, then royal blue pointed leaves.
5722c4e0-76c3-5fb1-8956-11019061b77b.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
5722c4e0-76c3-5fb1-8956-11019061b77b.method_for_provenance: This tile panel comes from the inner portal of the mausoleum of a holy man in Isfahan in central Iran.
keywords: Mosaic; Tile; Panel; Ceramics; Glazed; Fritware; Isfahan; Iran; Asia; Persian

5737c1ee-cc7f-51c5-a3a0-7d7bf8615842.name: Iznik bottle
5737c1ee-cc7f-51c5-a3a0-7d7bf8615842.short_description: An Iznik flask, with a spherical body and a long neck, is decorated with polychrome flowers: roses, hyacinth and carnations and the neck displays vertical panels. Bought by A. Benakis in Cairo in 1920 and according to the etiquettes under the base it was part of the 1885 exhibition at the Burlington Arts Club in London and of the 1925 exhibition in Alexandria. Ottoman c. 1575.

57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.name: Dish.
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.description:
The polychrome underglaze painted dish, with a broad slightly curved rim and a small flattened well, shows European influence. In the first half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century, Iznik ware, in seeking new sources of inspiration for designs and forms, included the tondino, a shape of Italian origin. The striking form of the dish under discussion derives from this type of maiolica (tin-glazed earthenware) and its Turkish imitations.  
The centre of the dish is decorated with a 'quatre fleurs' design of two tulips on short stalks, four roses on long curved stems and two sprays of other flowers, all springing from a leafy tuft. The roses with their large red blossoms dominate the centre of the dish and the decoration of the rim. The rim shows radiating floral stems of alternating tulips, roses and small flowers with red blossoms. Along the border of both rim and well, a red Chinese cloud and small forms derived from the motif of Chinese waves are set between the blossoms. The floral design with black outlines is coloured in a contrast of bright, slightly running blue and green with a thick raised applied opaque red on a white background. The outside of the dish is painted with ten blue flower-like motifs on white slip. The back and bottom of the dish, except for the foot-ring, are transparent glazed.
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.short_description: Polychrome underglaze painted dish with a broad rim and a small flattened well. Roses with large red blossoms dominate the pattern of the centre and the rim. Following the Iznik style other flowers and Chinese clouds are also included. The shape of the dish shows European influence.
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.method_for_datation: The 'quatre fleurs' style was a development of the second half of the 10th / 16th century. The slightly running colours suggest a dating at the end of the 10th / 16th century – beginning of the 11th / 17th century, but not much later because of the high quality of the glaze. Atasoy and Raby dated a plate of similar shape and decoration to 1009–19 / 1600–10.
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.method_for_provenance: The floral decoration and the shape are both specific to Iznik ceramics.
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.bibliography:

Carswell, J., *Iznik Pottery*, London, 1998.  
Müller-Wiener, M., *Türkisch-Osmanische Keramik*, Traunstein, 2004.
57c5b17a-cc28-503e-b6e8-63bb26227762.author: Friederike Voigt

5838c354-7008-5b83-99dc-80cbba207468.name: Egyptianising plate
5838c354-7008-5b83-99dc-80cbba207468.short_description: Plate with Egyptianising motifs and a copy of a drawing by Dominique Vivant Denon, *Voyage dans la Basse et la Haute Egypte, pendant les campagnes du Général Bonaparte*, 1802. Part of an Egyptian Service. Said to have been one of 3 Sevres plates which were thrown out of the windows of the Tuileries during the Revolution of 1848.

58b05d1c-5f36-5062-be5d-8dc0b6573bbf.name: Plate of polychrome ceramic from Fez
58b05d1c-5f36-5062-be5d-8dc0b6573bbf.description: This polychrome ceramic dish illustrates the refinement of Moroccan craftsmanship, especially that of Fez, a city famous for its pottery. In the centre, a six-pointed star outlined in yellow and blue immediately catches the eye. This motif is surrounded by rich floral and vegetal ornaments, arranged symmetrically, evoking the harmony and proliferation of nature. Stylised flowers, mainly blue and yellow, occupy spaces between the star’s branches, while green arabesques add dynamic and contrasting touches. The border of the plate is decorated with a multicoloured diamond pattern, alternating among blue, yellow and green, framed by a thin blue line. This detail gives a captivating finish to the whole, enhancing the composition’s effect.
58b05d1c-5f36-5062-be5d-8dc0b6573bbf.dates: Hegira mid of 13th century/ beginning of the 14th century - AD End of 19th century"
58b05d1c-5f36-5062-be5d-8dc0b6573bbf.dimensions: Diameter: 30 cm, height: 10.02 cm; base: 19.8 cm

58b37312-2a63-52d9-9118-d73987819f0b.name: Plate with metallic glaze.
58b37312-2a63-52d9-9118-d73987819f0b.description:
A bowl with a circular base and curved sides. The cruciform decoration is set off by four green areas glazed with copper oxide which cover the area outside the cross. The cross itself is decorated with dotted and stylised leaves and bordered with four twisted-rope motifs set within parallel lines.  
This plate is the only example of passementerie decoration that we have for this period. There are no other similar objects in Mesopotamian ceramics of this era, which could mean that this is an Ifriqiyan artefact. The floral decoration is quite similar to that of the wooden half-dome of the *mihrab* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan and also to the braiding found on Kairouanese bookbinding of the AH 3rd–5th / AD 9th–11th centuries. However, there is undoubtedly a connection in the colouring and the decoration between this piece and the façade tiles of the *mihrab* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The Mesopotamian origin of these tiles is firmly established. The metallic-glazing technique is a Muslim innovation which spread from Mesopotamia to Egypt in the early 3rd / 9th century and probably reached Ifriqiya in the second half of that century. It moved through the Maghreb and on to Spain before reaching Europe in the AH 6th or 7th / AD 12th or 13th centuries.
58b37312-2a63-52d9-9118-d73987819f0b.short_description: The lustre technique originated in Mesopotamia, spreading to Egypt and Ifriqiya, the Maghreb and Spain, before finally conquering Europe. The floral decoration and the colours used in this dish are reminiscent of the demicupola of the *mihrab* in the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
58b37312-2a63-52d9-9118-d73987819f0b.method_for_datation: This piece comes from the excavation sites at Raqqada, a city founded in 263 / 876, which survived until the middle of the 5th / 11th century. Unfortunately, the excavations were never published and the archives do not include the reports of the excavation which would have identified the different stratigraphic layers. However, the colouring and decoration of the piece are typically Aghlabid. It would appear from the evidence of this example and of mosaic flooring found on site that the ceramists had achieved a considerable mastery of the technique of metallic glazing, which could not have reached Ifriqiya before the middle of the 3rd / 9th century. This evidence would allow us to date the piece from the last quarter of the 3rd / 9th century.
58b37312-2a63-52d9-9118-d73987819f0b.method_for_provenance: As the decoration of this plate fits in the Ifriqiyan repertoire, it is plausible to consider that it was produced at the workshops in Kairouan
58b37312-2a63-52d9-9118-d73987819f0b.obtention: This piece was found on the site of the Raqqada excavations during the 1960s. From 1966 it was on display at the museum of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, transferring to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada in 1986.

590eb500-d496-5a10-9ce2-d253933322b6.name: Bowl with lovers in conversation.
590eb500-d496-5a10-9ce2-d253933322b6.description:
This piece is decorated by a pair of seated lovers in conversation on a background closely filled with palmette spirals, as was common in Kashan lustre-ware.  
An inscription runs along the outer edge of the bowl, almost certainly a good omen, that is unfortunately difficult to read as a result of the current state of preservation.
590eb500-d496-5a10-9ce2-d253933322b6.short_description: Bowl decorated with two figures in conversation. The decoration on this example from Kashan is typical of production from the early AH 6th / AD 12th century.

596c14fe-038a-5166-8b18-291ff7388f1d.name: Dish
596c14fe-038a-5166-8b18-291ff7388f1d.description: Large, white plate decorated with chequered pattern: squares painted either white with black dots, pale blue or green. Rim decorated with a twigs and simplified leaves. On the back side of the rim five blue spots.

59aacd3c-1eb0-50be-81af-310b08deaa40.name: Glazed and decorated bowl
59aacd3c-1eb0-50be-81af-310b08deaa40.description: This small open bowl was intended to serve food. The glaze and decoration remain only on the outside, with alternating vertically painted lines in red and yellow running from the lip to the foot. The glaze above the painted decoration is transparent. This particular combination of colours and patterns suggest that this bowl was a product of a workshop in Susa (Iran) or Samarra or Basra (Iraq).
59aacd3c-1eb0-50be-81af-310b08deaa40.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

59c2fb21-a451-5ddc-860d-380e07ae8190.name: Ceramic bowl
59c2fb21-a451-5ddc-860d-380e07ae8190.short_description: The bowl has a broad centre painted in underglaze blue with a round tripartite blazon showing in the middle a stemmed cup. This is the emblem of the office of the Mamluk cupbearer or *saqi*. Blazons are not often met on underglaze painted ware but are most commonly represented on metalwork and earthenware ceramics of the sgraffiato type from the end of the 13th century on.

59e80b7c-1bba-5071-b131-361159bba754.name: Dish
59e80b7c-1bba-5071-b131-361159bba754.description:
Istanbul was a lively center of trade, and many ships, both Turkish and Western, called at its harbor. Most of the Turkish vessels were light, fast ships with lateen sails, like the one depicted on a flask (11/1971). Western European galleys were much heavier, and this dish shows a monumental oceangoing three-master on the raging sea.  
  
What were presumably the muzzles of threatening cannons were transformed by the Turkish potter into flowerheads. An early example of the slogan Make Love, Not War?

5a5a6aad-8d85-5438-8174-be801759c798.name: Plate with phoenixes and deer
5a5a6aad-8d85-5438-8174-be801759c798.short_description: The well of this shallow plate shows two deer set against a background of lotus flowers and leafage, while the rim is covered with a band of flying phoenixes and parrots surrounded by similar floral and vegetal motifs. The design, painted in white slip on a grey-green ground, is directly inspired by Chinese silk textiles and lacquer wares.
5a5a6aad-8d85-5438-8174-be801759c798.dates: Hegira early 8th century / AD early 14th century
keywords: Plate; China; Ilkhanid; Ceramic; animal decoration; imaginary animal; zoomorphic imagery; phoenix; Chinese influence

5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.name: Footed dish or *tazze*.
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.description: A large circular stone-paste (fritware) dish set on a low, waisted foot-ring. It has a wide and shallow well forming into a curved concave sweep (*cavetto*) up to a broad, horizontal rim with a scalloped edge. The design in the well is contained within a roundel that is outlined by a double linear border. It consists of six flowers on curvaceous, leafy stems with tiny *fleur-de-lys* extensions, surrounding a small flower-head in the centre. The *cavetto* is decorated with seven sprigs that hold a central flower-head identical in style to the floral motifs in the well. The rim displays a debased wave-and-rock design. The underside of the *cavetto* is decorated with six floral sprigs.
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.short_description: Between the late AH 9th and 11th / AD 15th and 17th centuries Imperial Ottoman patronage ensured that Iznik stood out as the main centre of high-quality ceramic production in the empire. Many early Iznik wares attempted to imitate Chinese blue-and-white porcelains in body material, shapes and design.
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.type: Stone paste, two shades of blue
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.method_for_datation: This dish belongs to a group of Iznik wares identified by Atasoy and Raby (1989) as ‘flower scroll dishes’, which were produced in the workshops of Iznik between 931 and 998 / 1525 and 1590. Within this group the dish represents a late manifestation of the style, and Atasoy and Raby have dated this very piece to about 977–98 / 1570-90.
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.method_for_provenance: This dish belongs to a group of Iznik wares identified by Atasoy and Raby (1989) as ‘flower scroll dishes’; this very dish is dated to about 977–98 / 1570-90. It should be noted that this dish, as illustrated in Atasoy and Raby, is identified as having been sold at auction at Sotheby’s, London on 9 Mar 1974, lot 43, when in fact the dish was sold again at auction at Spink and Son, London, in 1979 and it was on this occasion that the item was purchased for the Royal Museum, Edinburgh.
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.obtention: Purchased from Spink and Son Ltd, London, in 1979.
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, p.123, fig. 202.
5abad405-1fc5-5ec3-bfc2-063b3b9fae2b.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware) underglaze painted in two shades of blue, over which a clear glaze.

5b5cf425-209d-5ed6-bf56-2f219440105b.name: Vase with cover
5b5cf425-209d-5ed6-bf56-2f219440105b.description: A vase with an octagonal base, short neck and cover. There are upright, narrow flutes across the entire surface. The plant ornamentation, painted in blue, red-brown and green is of Oriental inspiration. It is signed in red-brown: “APK” (in ligature) and engraved “X”.
5b5cf425-209d-5ed6-bf56-2f219440105b.short_description: A vase with an octagonal base, short neck and cover. The plant ornamentation, painted in blue, red-brown and green is of Oriental inspiration.

5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.name: Bowl with Epigraphic and Vegetal Decoration
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.short_description: This strikingly modern bowl is made from humble earthenware, disguised and beautified through the application of a white slip, a semifluid colored clay. Its interior is decorated with an encircling black inscription, and the spaces between the letters are filled by abstract decoration that is augmented by the color red, all covered by a transparent glaze. Read by turning the bowl counterclockwise, the Arabic inscription presents a proverb that retains some resonance even today: “Greed is a sign of poverty.” This proverb, which is inscribed on a number of Samanid bowls, is one of the sayings of the Shi’ite Imam ‘Ali ibn Abu Talib.
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.method_for_datation: The inscribed bowl exemplifies the elegant "black-on-white wares" excavated in the cities of Nishapur and Samarqand, both of which were governed by the Samanid dynasty beginning in Hegira 289 / AD 900.
5cf968b5-3058-5930-a6d0-15159faf8517.method_for_provenance: The material, technique and decoration are all consonant with Samanid epigraphic pottery.

5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.name: Mihrab
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.short_description: A mihrab is a characteristic architectural element in mosques and other places where Muslims worship. It serves to emphasize the direction of Mecca, toward which all prayer is oriented. Shaped like a niche, the mihrab is usually concave, but flat examples also occur, as here. This mihrab, which represents only the upper central panel of what was undoubtedly a larger ensemble, is inscribed with a passage from the Qur'an (15:45–47) that refers to Paradise, suggesting that it may have once graced a funerary monument.
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.dates: Hegira early 8th century / AD early 14th century
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.method_for_datation: This mihrab relates to several dated luster mihrabs, including one from the shrine at Qom from Hegira 734 / AD 1334 now in the Iran Bastan Museum in Tehran (3270). Such tile mihrabs and related tile ensembles were likely produced in Kashan rather than in situ. Luster tile production in Kashan seems to have come to an end around 1340, providing an approximate terminus ante quem.
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.method_for_provenance: Kashan was a major site of ceramics production in the 12th- 14th centuries (with a break during the Mongol invasions).
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.obtention: Kevorkian Collection (sale, Parke-Bernet, New York, December 18, 1970). Collection of Nasli M. Heeramaneck (1902-1971), New York, until 1973 (sold to); LACMA, The Nasli M. Heeramaneck collection, gift of Joan Palevsky.

5dee67a6-dec6-573e-b65b-409f8fb7b119.name: Tile
5dee67a6-dec6-573e-b65b-409f8fb7b119.short_description: The motif of three circles combined with paired wavy lines (possibly a much abstracted version of leopard spots and tiger stripes and probably originally a power symbol), was repeated in a variety of Ottoman media whether made for the court in Istanbul or produced in provincial centres such as Syrian Damascus. In this hexagonal tile, the Syrian artist has replicated the design but not the red and blue on a white ground colour scheme of the classic Iznik tile. Instead, the tile is boldly decorated in turquoise and black, a colour combination that typifies Syrian tiles in the Ottoman period.
5dee67a6-dec6-573e-b65b-409f8fb7b119.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
5dee67a6-dec6-573e-b65b-409f8fb7b119.dates: Hegira second half of the 10th century / AD second half of the 16th century
5dee67a6-dec6-573e-b65b-409f8fb7b119.method_for_datation: The paired wavy lines and groups of three large dots was a popular motif among a wide variety of Ottoman arts by the beginning of the 16th century, while the turquoise and black colour scheme specifically associate the tile with Syria.
5dee67a6-dec6-573e-b65b-409f8fb7b119.method_for_provenance: The turquoise and black colour combination typifies Syrian tiles in the Ottoman period.
5dee67a6-dec6-573e-b65b-409f8fb7b119.obtention: Collection of Maan Z. Madina (1926-2013), New York, until 2002 (sold to); LACMA, The Madina Collection of Islamic Art, gift of Camilla Chandler Frost.
