5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.name: Dish.
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.description: A circular stone-paste (fritware) dish with a shallow well, everted rim and low circular foot-ring. The dish has a busy floral composition, incorporating red roses, fleshy blue tulips with red detailing, and other blue and red flowers on stalks with green leafage, rising from a leafy tuft. A large serrated so-called *saz* leaf, rendered in blue with a white and red beaded centre, is placed obliquely across the naturalistically drawn flowers. The rim is decorated with a debased wave border, executed in blue and black. The *saz* leaf occurs repeatedly in later Iznik wares of the AH 11th / AD 16th-century but its origins lie within a decorative style developed in AH 9th- / AD 15th-century Iran and then subsequently adapted to all media within Ottoman art.
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.short_description: This type of dish, with its busy floral composition rendered in blue, green, black and the characteristic bole-red, its fleshy *saz* leaf and its debased wave border, is a typical example of the ceramics produced in Iznik during the AH late 10th–early 11th centuries / AD late 16th–early 17th centuries.
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.dates: Hegira, late 10th– early 11th century / AD late 16th– early 17th century.
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.method_for_datation: The style of this plate with its busy floral composition, fleshy *saz* leaf and debased wave border is consistent with a group of Iznik wares datable to the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.method_for_provenance: This type of dish with its busy floral composition rendered in blue, green, black and the characteristic bole-red, its fleshy *saz* leaf and its debased wave border are well known decorative elements among the ceramic wares produced in Iznik during the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.obtention: Bequest from Miss Campbell M. Currie in 1937.
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989 (for general discussion on Iznik wares).
5e07ad26-9889-5b0c-8700-7ac79e824fca.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware), black, blue, green and bole-red underglaze, over which a clear glaze.

5e17faa4-c7b3-5b94-a409-86fb692fc4f7.name: Bowl.
5e17faa4-c7b3-5b94-a409-86fb692fc4f7.description: A stone-paste ceramic bowl painted in brown, blue, green and red underglaze. Technically, the colourful decoration of a horseman imitates a type of Iranian ceramic known as *mina‘i* ware, ‘mina‘i’ meaning literally enamelled, a technique in which some of the colours were painted over the glaze and then fixed by firing. The Syrian potters were influenced by developments in Iran but lacked the technical knowledge of working with enamels on ceramics. They therefore imitated the style. This bowl mimics the type of design employed on minai wares with underglaze painting in similar bright colours to enamel. There is an illegible inscription on the underside of the bowl.
5e17faa4-c7b3-5b94-a409-86fb692fc4f7.short_description: The colourful decoration of the horseman on this ceramic bowl imitates a type of ceramic that originated in Iran. Enamelled ceramics, or *mina'i* ware, were exported from Iran to Syria, where potters imitated the style using underglaze painting rather than enamels.
5e17faa4-c7b3-5b94-a409-86fb692fc4f7.method_for_datation: Bowls of this style were probably created in the 7th / 13th century, soon after minai wares began to be produced in Iran.
5e17faa4-c7b3-5b94-a409-86fb692fc4f7.method_for_provenance: Syria was the obvious recipient of mina'i wares from neighbouring Iran.
5e17faa4-c7b3-5b94-a409-86fb692fc4f7.obtention: Acquired through the National Art Collections Fund in 1912.
5e17faa4-c7b3-5b94-a409-86fb692fc4f7.author: Emily Shovelton
materials: Stone-paste ceramic painted with brown, blue, green and red underglaze.

5e2de5b6-9e65-5cc0-b7c3-55df296ef3f6.name: Bowl
5e2de5b6-9e65-5cc0-b7c3-55df296ef3f6.short_description: The bowl shows decoration comprising a central stylised flower set in a square with corners sprouting shield-shaped leaves separated by trefoil motifs on arches. The overglaze decoration is painted in cobalt blue.
materials: Earthenware, opaque white glaze, blue decoration

5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.name: Water jar
5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.description: This piece belongs to a set that came from a Turkish shipwreck in the Red Sea, in the Gulf of Aqaba, near Sharm al-Sheikh, during the second quarter of the 18th century. The precise origin of these ceramics is not known, but these water jars are similar to those still used in Egypt today. After the Ottoman conquest, Sultan Selim I deported Egyptian craftsmen from various trades to Istanbul. As a result, ceramics declined irremediably, and production was limited to utilitarian objects such as this one, whose designs are incomparable to those produced from the 9th to the 15th centuries.
5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.dates: Hegira 2nd to 3rd quarter of the 12th century / AD 2nd quarter of the 18th century
5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.provenance: Near East, from a marine wreck
5e49717d-377e-51a8-a5cc-e5b4d8ad7979.obtention: Purchased from the Art Musulman gallery in 1985.

5f0f9d5c-e4b9-544a-a606-348a9bf33e9a.name: Dish
5f0f9d5c-e4b9-544a-a606-348a9bf33e9a.short_description: During the first half of the sixteenth century, artists of the royal design atelier of the Ottoman court developed a new decorative style characterized by its bright colours and naturalistic depiction of flowers. The floral composition on this dish with its tulips, carnations, and roses in red and blue on a white background is typical of the production of the Ottoman imperial kilns in the city of Iznik. Similar patterns of floral designs were used on textiles, carpets, book illuminations, and tiles, including some splendid examples in the Aga Khan Museum’s collection. The consistency of the Ottoman floral style helped establish a distinctive and singular visual brand for the Ottoman Empire and its arts. It is during this period that tulips caught Europe’s attention when they were first introduced there by Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, the Austrian ambassador to the Ottoman court.
5f0f9d5c-e4b9-544a-a606-348a9bf33e9a.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Dish; ceramic; floral; tulip; Fritware; underglaze-painted

5f65dbae-2362-5da9-a960-991cf65fb132.name: Lustre glazed bowl
5f65dbae-2362-5da9-a960-991cf65fb132.short_description:
The object is a wine bowl decorated with an image of a couple and with toasts and blessings. The technique used for producing this bowl is lustre with overglaze painting. Painted inside the deep bowl is a pair of seated figures, inspired by Persian illumination; the female figure holds a glass. The circumferential strip edging the bowl bears inscriptions which refer to wine drinking, confirming the vessel's function. It is an excellent example of ceramic glazed with metallic lustre, which was developed in Iran. In the late 12th century, subjects such as hunting scenes and human figures drinking wine appeared as decorations on objects. The bowl, with its high foot ring and the intricately-detailed decoration in the background, is typical for the wares produced in Kashan, where the lustre industry flourished in this period. The metallic, golden effect is created by painting with silver and copper oxide, which melts during the second firing. Excerpts from the inscriptions:  
Blessing:  
Honour and gladness, greatness and joy  
Be not distant from the owner of this bowl.  
Poem by Malek Fakhreddin Mubaraksah Guri:  
You said: Why were your tears the color of roses?  
Because you asked, I will tell you how it was:  
The blood-tinged tears surged up out of passion for you,  
And as my heart seethed, they boiled over.  
Toast:  
God, Creator of the World, protect the owner of this bowl wherever he goes.  
Poem by an unknown poet:  
Your face is always before my eyes.  
Beloved, do what seems right to you.  
Oh, soul and world, my heart is content,  
When it can only see him who has seen you.  
Poem by Afdaleddin Kashani:  
Oh Lord, do not expect help from any man!  
Do not look for shade under a branch without leaves.  
One wins honour through sobriety and contempt through greed.  
Be content with your honour and eschew contempt.

5fb9df90-7b26-5354-a02b-04f0411593be.name: Ka`ba tile
5fb9df90-7b26-5354-a02b-04f0411593be.short_description: This rectangular tile depicts a stylised view of Mecca, with the black-shrouded Ka‘ba in the centre of the *Masjid al-Haram*. It is part of a larger material corpus related to the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca and sites in the vicinity, which was a favoured theme in Ottoman workshops. Although this tile is painted in the traditional colour palette used by seventeenth century Iznik workshops, the bird’s-eye view, inspired by the European pictorial tradition, is a characteristic of later examples made at Tekfur Sarayı in Istanbul, a less well-known Ottoman ceramic workshop.

5fc4c91c-9fc3-5456-98a6-0dd4aa412e7f.name: Water jug.
5fc4c91c-9fc3-5456-98a6-0dd4aa412e7f.description: Fragment of a water jug with a curved everted rim, circular mouth and neck shaped as an inverted truncated cone with a central moulding, which is joined to the body by a vertical handle with an oval cross-section. The body is globular with a zoomorphic tubular spout rising from its shoulder. The overall design suggests the shape of an animal with a long narrow neck such as a camel or dromedary, whose hunched back forms the neck of the vessel. It is decorated with fine lines of white painted plant forms on a reddish background.
5fc4c91c-9fc3-5456-98a6-0dd4aa412e7f.short_description: Spout and neck from a water jug, whose shape is reminiscent of an animal with a long, thin neck such as a camel or a dromedary, with the hump being the neck of the jug. It is decorated with fine, phytomorphic lines in white paint on the red background of the piece.
5fc4c91c-9fc3-5456-98a6-0dd4aa412e7f.dates: Hegira end 5th – beginning 6th century / AD end 11th – beginning 12th century.
5fc4c91c-9fc3-5456-98a6-0dd4aa412e7f.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated to the 6th / 12th century by comparison with objects with similar decoration in the west of the Al-Andalus region.
5fc4c91c-9fc3-5456-98a6-0dd4aa412e7f.obtention: It was found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

5ffeeb7c-0b57-5dd4-a331-6d70ed986d0d.name: Bottle with wide rim
5ffeeb7c-0b57-5dd4-a331-6d70ed986d0d.description: This black glass bottle has a spherical body supported by a ring-shaped base. The tubular neck narrows slightly towards the top and ends with a flat rim. At its base it is circled by a twisting black glass ribbon overlay, the sole design element. Blown glass existed from the first century AD, making possible a considerable increase in the production of glass objects. The process became popular and played a significant part in the fabrication of vessels.

60e43904-297f-56d1-af8b-fa4776b2ccb3.name: Pitcher
60e43904-297f-56d1-af8b-fa4776b2ccb3.short_description: Çanakkale was a pottery production centre between the end of the 17th century and first quarter of the 20th century where pottery with interesting and original forms was produced. Mostly coarse red clay and sometimes beige-coloured paste was used. There are green, brown, dark yellow and under-glazed purplish brown, yellow, dark blue and white decorations made by a brush. This Çanakkale-produced pitcher is made of red clay; it has green and dark yellow glaze and a bulgy body with long, narrow neck. Its mouth has a stylized bird shape. It has a flat bottom and round handle. On the head, neck and body of the bird, there are raised rosette flower patterns. On the front part of the body, there is a cat and some cypress tree figures. The details were made with the barbotine technique.

611887bb-d44c-51a1-b6d3-d89221fb788c.name: Ewer
611887bb-d44c-51a1-b6d3-d89221fb788c.short_description:
The late 17th century witnessed the rise of Kütahya, the Ottoman second largest ceramic centre, situated in the south-eastern outskirts of Istanbul. Europeans, impressed by richness and refinement of its exotic patterns, called Kütahya "The Sevres of the East".  
This large egg-shaped ewer with strikingly thin walls belongs to rare samples of Kütahya ware. Painted with short rapid strokes of cobalt pigment on a snow white background it represents the best achievements of the second half of the 18th century.  
The original style of Kütahya décor genuinely combines different artistic traditions of East and West which were brought to the Ottoman culture due to trade activities of the Armenian community, settled in the town. Some researchers also suggest that the major part of the Kütahya ceramics was produced by Armenian potters.
611887bb-d44c-51a1-b6d3-d89221fb788c.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by M. Vyazmitina (examination, 1930, date, origin), Yu. Miller (publication, 1972, date specified).

611887bb-d44c-51a1-b6d3-d89221fb788c.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalized by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

612351f2-75a6-5485-beb3-2f66e1312be5.name: Ceramic floor
612351f2-75a6-5485-beb3-2f66e1312be5.description:
The Palatine Chapel, founded by King Dinis (1261‒1325, crowned 1279) in the early 14th century, contains one of the oldest ceramic floors in Portugal. This rare floor of the main altar probably dates from the 15th century, contemporary with the reign of King Afonso V (1432‒81, crowned 1438).  
The Chapel, a Christian religious space dedicated to the Holy Spirit, is characterised by the Mudéjar style, Hispano-Muslim ceiling decoration in *alfarge* carved wood and by the *alicatado* floor, formed from ceramic pieces of many colours and shapes. Both the mosaic floor and the wooden ceiling are among the oldest examples of Mudéjar craftsmanship in Portugal.  
The configuration and decorative composition used in the ceramic floor remind one of the Mudéjar-style carpets, decorated with a network of interlacement motifs containing geometric patterns, commissioned to embellish palaces and churches.  
Up until the second half of the 15th century, the term “*alicatado*” (Spanish for cut-tiles, derived from the Arabic verb qata’a, “to cut”) was given to the ceramic mosaics made in this technique. It requires piecing together monochromatic enamelled *tesserae* (small glazed ceramic pieces of various geometric shapes and colours that had been glazed and cut beforehand) to create decorative compositions with geometric patterns, a delicate, painstaking and expensive task, used mostly for paving floors, but also for wall surfaces.  
This ceramic floor might date from the same period as that of the room where King Afonso VI was imprisoned, one of the Royal Palace’s oldest rooms.
612351f2-75a6-5485-beb3-2f66e1312be5.method_for_datation: Other art historians have dated the Palatine Chapel ceramic floor to the 15th century, probably contemporary with King Afonso V (1432‒81; r.1438‒81). This monarch was born and died at the Royal Palace of Sintra and resided there frequently, as demonstrated by the countless documents signed by him here. Like King Duarte (1391‒38; r. 1433‒38), his father, King Afonso V seems to have held a special affection for the Palace at Sintra and carried out various improvements. He undertook the expansion and embellishment of the Palatine Chapel, probably from the mid-15th century (possibly between 1448 and 1476).
612351f2-75a6-5485-beb3-2f66e1312be5.obtention: In situ, commissioned by the king

612c0f2a-80e1-56d4-ad55-7c2f2f82cb8d.name: Bowl with golden-brown metallic glaze.
612c0f2a-80e1-56d4-ad55-7c2f2f82cb8d.description:
This deep bowl with round base and curved sides is decorated with scrolls of foliage and stems with palm leaves. They interweave exuberantly, revealing a bunch of grapes. Clearly defined rings divide the decoration into concentric areas, but the overall effect is one of unity and uninterrupted movement, enhanced by the harmony of the golden-brown motifs against the cream background. The space is well-covered but not overloaded.  
The formula for producing ceramics with a golden glaze has been roughly described since the AH 6th / AD 12th century. Red ochre (iron oxide or *almazzaron*) is added to a precisely measured mixture of copper and silver. This mixture is then diluted with vinegar. The golden-glazed ceramics which spread throughout al-Andalus from the AH 7th–8th / AD 13th–14th centuries were in vogue in Egypt at the same time. Both floral and animal decorations were used. The discovery of this bowl of al-Andalus origin in Tunis has highlighted the importance of the trade established from the AH 7th / AD 13th century between Ifriqiya and Muslim Spain.
612c0f2a-80e1-56d4-ad55-7c2f2f82cb8d.short_description: This is a typical example of the golden-glazed ceramics that spread through al-Andalus and Egypt from the AH 7th / AD 13th century, combining floral and zoomorphic motifs. The discovery of this dish of Andalusian origin in Tunis underlines the importance of trade between Ifriqiya and Muslim Spain.
612c0f2a-80e1-56d4-ad55-7c2f2f82cb8d.method_for_datation: This piece was discovered in a cistern during the digs at the *Kasbah* in Tunis in the early 1980s. It was found buried next to other Hafsid plates and bowls dating from the 7th and 8th / 13th and 14th centuries in a tank containing 270 pieces.
612c0f2a-80e1-56d4-ad55-7c2f2f82cb8d.method_for_provenance: Its Andalusian origin was established by comparison with other pieces. The workshops of al-Andalus were indeed producing similar bowls during the 7th and 8th / 13thand 14th centuries.
612c0f2a-80e1-56d4-ad55-7c2f2f82cb8d.obtention: After its discovery at the *Kasbah* excavations, this bowl was kept in Tunis at the National Patrimony Institute at Dar ibn Khaldun and then was selected for display at the Sidi Qasim al-Jalizi Museum in 1978.
612c0f2a-80e1-56d4-ad55-7c2f2f82cb8d.author: Mourad Rammah

6150a85a-81c3-563b-99dd-7601ebde8b0c.name: Ewer
6150a85a-81c3-563b-99dd-7601ebde8b0c.short_description: The achievements of old Samarqand (Afrasiab) pottery workmanship are exemplified by a separate type of unglazed and stamped tableware, mainly jugs and ewers, manufactured in moulds from an ash-grey clay. There were vast deposits of this clay near the town of Penjikent (60km to the east of Samarqand). Elegantly shaped thin-walled vessels with a polished surface and a delicate stamped ornamental pattern on shoulders and neck were probably designed to imitate valuable silver tableware. Historians suggest that the main function of these ewers was storing water that while steadily evaporating through the pores of the ceramic body remained fresh and cold for a long time.
6150a85a-81c3-563b-99dd-7601ebde8b0c.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by O. Bolshakov (examination, 1956, date and origin).
6150a85a-81c3-563b-99dd-7601ebde8b0c.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
6150a85a-81c3-563b-99dd-7601ebde8b0c.obtention: Acquired by the Khanenko Museum in 1921. From M. Stolyarov collection of pottery, made up during archaeological excavations at old Samarqand (Afrasiab) in 1914.

61f73c10-6b4a-575d-8580-f783f468119f.name: Bowl with a hare
61f73c10-6b4a-575d-8580-f783f468119f.short_description: By the 10th century, the Fatimid capital of Cairo had become the centre of production for ceramics decorated in a metallic paint with a golden lustrous sheen (known as lustre ceramics). The striking visual compositions on these ceramics portray men and women, acrobats, and animals—such as this jovial long-eared hare—painted in fluid lines and lively naturalism. Their relatively “ordinary” subject matter and the golden tone of the lustre sheen set them apart from the earlier lustre ceramics in Iraq and later examples from Iran. This type of Fatimid lustre-glazed bowl was highly appreciated as an export product throughout the Mediterranean, and several similar bowls can still be seen adorning the exterior walls of churches in Pisa, Italy, from the late 11th and early 12th centuries.
61f73c10-6b4a-575d-8580-f783f468119f.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

624c5039-aded-540a-9de4-63ad55600770.name: Lustre-painted ewer, rooster-shaped
624c5039-aded-540a-9de4-63ad55600770.short_description:
The ewer features a sparkling play of golden lustre arabesque of curls and dots painted over opaque white glaze. The design is on the brink of perfection: along with strokes a Persian ceramist left some elements of decor in white and filled up the surrounding surface. This "reserve" technique required a particular skill and carefulness from the master. The rooster was regarded by Iranians as a ritually pure and auspicious being since pre-Islamic times.  
The art of lustre painting on ceramics was mastered by Iranian potters of Kashan in late 12th century. The technique involved application of metal-based pigment over already glazed and fired vessel.

625168c1-5801-5ae1-8ba7-4afa5d4bee1c.name: Bowl with stylised bird
625168c1-5801-5ae1-8ba7-4afa5d4bee1c.short_description: This flat bowl depicts a stylized bird in olive green, red, and, brown with crown-like, three-dotted plumage on its head. The outer rim is decorated with a band of black and white triangles. The bird is possibly a depiction of the constellation of “Cygnus” (swan), widely used in other genres of Islamic art.

62a33986-22ab-54e6-b59d-861e59b608f3.name: *Khabia*
62a33986-22ab-54e6-b59d-861e59b608f3.alternate_name: Water storage jar; Large earthenware jar; clay cistern jar
62a33986-22ab-54e6-b59d-861e59b608f3.description:
The *khabia* is a large earthenware jar traditionally used in Morocco for the storage and preservation of drinking water. Handcrafted by skilled potters from the Marrakech region, the *khabia* was an indispensable element of both domestic and communal life before the spread of modern water supply systems. Its substantial size, often exceeding two metres in height, allowed families, mosques, or fountains to store large quantities of water drawn from wells or *khettaras*.  
The process of making a *khabia* required specialised knowledge—shaping and assembling clay coils, smoothing the surface, and firing in traditional kilns — reflecting centuries of artisanal heritage. Beyond its utilitarian role, the khabia embodied the cultural significance of water conservation in Moroccan society.  
The *khabia* displayed at the Mohammed VI Museum of Water Civilisation offers insight into vernacular technologies of storage and sustainability, serving as a reminder of how communities safeguarded water in arid environments long before industrial systems.

63941bb7-1c0a-5e01-8b06-e6ae1b313ece.name: Water bottle/jar
63941bb7-1c0a-5e01-8b06-e6ae1b313ece.description: A red pottery water jar used for filling and pouring water. It has a cylindrical body rounded at both ends, with a circular mouth at the centre flanked by two prominent handles, allowing it to be tied with ropes, hung, or carried easily - especially during travel. Due to the porous nature of pottery, the container also helped in cooling the water.

63bc371f-dee0-5a90-b7cb-1bb399d9c7f6.name: *Grande Panorama de Lisboa / Panoramic View of Lisbon*
63bc371f-dee0-5a90-b7cb-1bb399d9c7f6.description:
A tile panel *(azulejos)* painted blue on white that records Lisbon before the earthquake of 1755. A vast panoramic view of the capital and its outskirts, the panorama extends along the riverbanks from the Palace of the Counts of Miranda at the westernmost point to the Convent of St. Saint Francis in Xabregas, at the easternmost point.  
The focus is on the centre of political and economic power which included the city developments around the Royal Palace of Ribeira. This is immediately followed by the Palha Sea, flanked on the left by the Church of St. Gens and on the right by the Convent of St. Vincent de Fora. On the riverfront are the Terreiro do Paço and the Ribeira Velha Market. Nearby are the shipyard of Ribeira das Naus, the Royal Palace and St. Paul's Church.  
On the hills above are the convents of St. Francis of the City and Our Lady of Monte do Carmo; Loreto, Encarnação and St. Roch churches and the Convent of St. Peter of Alcântara.  
Along the foreshore are the palaces belonging to the Dukes of Aveiro, the Marquises of Abrantes, the Counts of Murça and the neighbourhood called Mocambo. The western area is more spacious. The Alcântara, Junqueira, Pocinho and Algés bridges cross the river defended by the forts of Alcântara, St. John of Junqueira, Our Lady of Conception and the imposing Tower of Belém. On a second plan the Sacramento, Livramento, Flamengas, St. Jerome, Our Lady of Bom Sucesso and Catarina-a-Velha convents are prominent as are the chapels of St. Christ and St. Hieronymus.  
Near the river are the royal palaces of Calvário, Santo Amaro à Junqueira Quinta, belonging to the Counts of Aveiro; Quinta da Calheta, the Palace of Quinta *da Praia* belonging to the Dukes of Cadaval, and the Palace of the Counts of Miranda.  
The eastern zone depicts the Church of St. Engrácia, the convents of Santos-o-Novo and Madre de Deus and, in a separate panel, the Convent of Saint Francis in Xabregas.
63bc371f-dee0-5a90-b7cb-1bb399d9c7f6.short_description: Lisbon is recorded on this tile panel measuring almost 23 metres wide, and produced before the earthquake of 1755. Depicting approximately 14 km of the riverbank, it shows a vast panoramic view of the capital and its outskirts between the Palace of the Counts of Miranda, the westernmost point, and the Convent of Saint Francis in Xabregas, the easternmost point.
63bc371f-dee0-5a90-b7cb-1bb399d9c7f6.method_for_datation: This panel is currently attributed by stylistic analysis to Gabriel del Barco, a Spanish tile painter and decorator who arrived to Portugal in 1669 and died probably around 1703.
63bc371f-dee0-5a90-b7cb-1bb399d9c7f6.provenance: Palace of the Counts of Tentúgal, Lisbon
63bc371f-dee0-5a90-b7cb-1bb399d9c7f6.obtention: Purchased by the Marquis de Sousa Holstein (1838–1878) for the Royal Academy of Fine Arts and incorporated into the Fine Arts and Archaeology collection at Alvor Palace in Lisbon, today known as Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga. Displayed there from 1903 until 1960, it was transferred to the Museu do Azulejo at that time the ceramics department of the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga.

63d3e691-fd6a-55ce-8dda-6da2acb434ea.name: Basin.
63d3e691-fd6a-55ce-8dda-6da2acb434ea.description: A very large basin (*ma'jna*) with a flat base and curved, sloping sides. In the centre, on the disc-shaped base, is a stylised decoration based on flowers and spreading palm-leaves. On the sides the *tawq* (necklace) motif is the main decorative component. Four *tawq*s adorned with stylised vegetation are drawn within arcatures. These arcatures alternate with others, containing medallions of diamond-shaped leaves. Just beneath the rim is a circle of dots. The decoration appears to be a mixture of surviving local influences like the *tawq*, which is found in Hafsid ceramics, and Ottoman influences, such as the arrangement of flowers. The main colours are the traditional yellow, green and brown, but with the addition of purple. The *ma'jna* is used for kneading pastry or rolling semolina but can also be a serving bowl for certain cooked dishes.
63d3e691-fd6a-55ce-8dda-6da2acb434ea.short_description: This large basin, known as a *ma'jna*, was used to knead dough or roll semolina, as well as to serve particular dishes. Its decoration combines surviving local elements with Ottoman influences. The composition is dominated by traditional colours: yellow, green, brown and blue-violet.
63d3e691-fd6a-55ce-8dda-6da2acb434ea.method_for_datation: The decoration, colours and manufacturing technique of this basin are all typical of the Qallaline workshops at Tunis during the 12th / 18th century.
63d3e691-fd6a-55ce-8dda-6da2acb434ea.obtention: This piece comes from the Bardo Museum and was acquired by the Sidi Qasim al-Jalizi Museum on its inauguration in 1978.
63d3e691-fd6a-55ce-8dda-6da2acb434ea.author: Mourad Rammah

6494cd55-e904-5563-a3a1-c84b7c6ea6dc.name: Poly-lobate bowl
6494cd55-e904-5563-a3a1-c84b7c6ea6dc.short_description: Seljuq production reached its height with *mina’i* ware, obtained using the technique of painting enamel over glaze. This poly-lobate cup is decorated in the centre with two horsemen surrounded by seated figures. The external wall of the cup is ornamented with a cursive inscription in black-brown.

650adcf4-9515-5259-9d51-4fbe7bcaddb6.name: Lotus tile
650adcf4-9515-5259-9d51-4fbe7bcaddb6.short_description: Two lotus blossoms painted in white and black on a cobalt blue ground. A half-blossom can be seen in the bottom right corner, while a complete blossom is shown on a stem to the left. On the back of the tile, the Arabic letters *lr lr* incised in the paste. Tiles with a similar restricted palette and a similar treatment of the stylised lotus blossoms were used for the redecoration of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, during the extensive restoration ordered by Süleyman the Magnificent. Therefore, the tile could have been made in an Ottoman workshop from Syria dating back to the mid-sixteenth century.
650adcf4-9515-5259-9d51-4fbe7bcaddb6.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
650adcf4-9515-5259-9d51-4fbe7bcaddb6.obtention: The tile belonged to Marcu Beza, writer and Consul General of Romania in Jerusalem between the wars. Purchased by the Museum in 1956.

65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.name: Bowl fragment.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.description:
An earthenware fragment that formed the centre and part of the rim of a footed and steep-sided bowl, showing a roundel embellished with an incised arabesque decoration; on the rim can be seen fragments of a band of Arabic calligraphic text. The technique, known as *sgraffito* (an Italian word meaning to scratch), involves dipping the vessel into a lighter coloured liquefied clay, known as a slip. With the aid of a pointed tool, the pattern is scratched into the slip, revealing parts of the clay as the design is drawn. The vessel is then glazed and fired. The incised pattern creates contrast; it reveals the colour of the darker clay, while the spaces between the lines show the lighter slip. The glaze on this bowl is a transparent ochre-yellow colour. This type of vessel was less costly to make than coloured ceramics, and therefore fulfilled the demands of the less affluent customers, who had just as much aspiration and taste for glazed wares with decorative texts and patterns, as did the wealthier customers.  
  
The city of Fustat continued to be an active commercial city during the Mamluk period (AH 647–922 / AD 1250–1517), although it had lost some of its fame to Cairo, which was established by the Mamluks and subsequently subsumed by her.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.short_description: This was once part of an impressive steep-sided bowl, decorated using an incising method called *sgraffito* – to scratch. It was less costly to make such monochrome ceramics in comparison to multicoloured ceramics, which made them more affordable to comparatively less-affluent people.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: comparable examples have been found in Fustat, Egypt, dating back to the 8th / 14th century.
65973130-c1da-546d-85a1-c58354b8bdfe.method_for_provenance: Comparable examples have been found in Fustat, Egypt, dating back to the 8th / 14th century.

6625424b-a321-5159-8e88-0b3b4f5cbefe.name: Unglazed bottle with lions
6625424b-a321-5159-8e88-0b3b4f5cbefe.short_description: This bottle type, common at the time, is constructed from several parts. The lions’ pounced bodies, striated legs and profiled palmette tails recall carved Fatimid rock crystals. Beasts with similar bodies also occur on unglazed wares from Syria and Northern Iraq. The central tree-of-life, finally, echoes contemporary Siculo-Islamic textiles.
keywords: Bottle; Lion; Ceramic; animal decoration; rock-crystal

66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.name: Cup with inscription.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.description: Cup with inverted bevelled rim, circular mouth, body in the shape of a bi-truncated cone with low carination, a vertical handle oval in cross-section which joins the carination to the rim, and a flat base with a diagonal foot-ring. The decoration was made using the partial *cuerda seca* technique, with the calligraphic motif drawn with a line of manganese and filled in with green glaze. The text is incomplete although we can read in *kufic* characters *baraka kamila \[wani\]ma ^sa\[mila\]* – 'full blessing and total happiness'. The sentence is not accompanied by any secondary motifs. This is one of the oldest objects with partial *cuerda seca* decoration conserved at Mértola and its ornamental and calligraphic style are somewhat different from the other objects which we can date to the AH 6th / AD 12th century. The object has been restored.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.short_description: Cup decorated in part using *cuerda seca* with a *kufic* inscription reading ‘*baraka kamila \[wani\]ma sa\[mila*\]’ (‘full blessing and total happiness’). It suggests the need to protect the content of this piece of tableware from Mértola Castle.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.dates: Hegira second half of 5th or beginning of 6th century / AD second half 11th  or beginning 12th century.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.dimensions: Height 10.2 cm, width 10.2 cm, diameter (of mouth) 9.1 cm, diameter (of base) 5.3 cm.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.method_for_datation: It was dated to either the end of the Taifa period or the Almoravid era through stratigraphy.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.method_for_provenance: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the Castle of Mértola.
66718328-7241-56c8-a45c-d60aff5e7c2d.obtention: This is a type of ceramic made in various regions of al-Andalus, but whose production has not yet been recorded in the west of the Iberian Peninsula.

66adc4ae-b72a-5645-9464-e6b42ed42fe6.name: Plate
66adc4ae-b72a-5645-9464-e6b42ed42fe6.description: Red clay with cream slip, decorated with purple-brown and mustard tones under a transparent colourless glaze. A traditional latticed decoration encircles the rim of the plate. The interior surface displays a particularly intriguing example of early Çanakkale ceramics. The centrepiece is a tow boat with waving pennant and regimental banners. In the 16th–18th centuries, depictions of the Ottoman navy can be found in various examples of ceramics, miniatures and wall paintings. These decorations are likely related to the city's seafront location and to Ottoman ships, of which the city's inhabitants were very proud. The unadorned lines of the oared and unmanned boats impart a naive quality to these plates, reflecting the diverse and creative enthusiasms of folk art.
66adc4ae-b72a-5645-9464-e6b42ed42fe6.dates: Hegira late 12th century / AD late 18th century

66c6e645-4939-52da-90c1-4d5b26b014bd.name: Bowl with Design of Radiating Panels Containing Floral Motifs and Calligraphic Inscriptions
66c6e645-4939-52da-90c1-4d5b26b014bd.short_description: A truncated conical fritware bowl with straight spreading sides and a straight vertical foot. The interior has radiating panels, six in blue containing floral scrolls in black, alternating with six black panels with carved-through *Naskh*\-script inscriptions in white. The exterior has a similar foliate design in black on white ground. The vessel is covered with an all-over transparent and crackled glaze except for the foot rim. There are slight chips on the top and foot rims.
66c6e645-4939-52da-90c1-4d5b26b014bd.dates: Hegira Late 6th to mid 7th century / AD early 13th century

66e51f17-108b-5591-b6b7-54ea9b37a8c1.name: Tile
66e51f17-108b-5591-b6b7-54ea9b37a8c1.short_description: This tile depicts geometric motifs on a white background. In each corner there are green fan-shaped leaf-like patterns, divided by a circle of geometric brown and black shapes. In the centre is a black leaf-like pattern around a green circle, forming a flower or star shape.
66e51f17-108b-5591-b6b7-54ea9b37a8c1.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar objects e. g. Victoria and Albert Museum (see Ray 2000, p. 331).

670eba93-83b0-54bf-987d-360af123a3ea.name: Coffee cups
670eba93-83b0-54bf-987d-360af123a3ea.description: Coffee in Oman is traditionally served in small cups without any added sugar or milk. The host holds the cup between the fingers of their right hand and pours in coffee from a *dallah* held in their left. Coffee is typically served first to the most honored guests.
670eba93-83b0-54bf-987d-360af123a3ea.holder: The National Museum - Sultanate of Oman

6737216e-9ec0-5301-bc44-aa17e6e3cff5.name: Yıldız Ceramic panel
6737216e-9ec0-5301-bc44-aa17e6e3cff5.short_description: Sultan Abdülhamid II founded in 1891 the *Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu* (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace in order to revive Turkish tile art and give it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. Many native and foreign artists have worked in the tile factory of Yıldız. One of them, Halid Naci received training in tile painting in Sevres, France after his education at the *Sanayi-i Nefise Mektebi* (School of Fine Arts) and he was assigned to be head painter of the tile factories after his return. In the middle of the porcelain plate are a herd of sheep, its shepherd and his dog, all drawn using natural colours.

676840b7-fa48-530f-8796-1f2f216489c5.name: *Quart*
676840b7-fa48-530f-8796-1f2f216489c5.description:
The *quart* is derived from an old Czech unit of volume of approximately 1.4 litres. The jug is decorated with a typical segmented strip with roses, and a central area featuring a landscape with fortified towns and a rider. Folk art characteristically disregarded the natural scale. For example, although it is in the background, the dovecote on the right is the same size as the spire of what appears to be a chateau.  
The shape and decoration of the object are based on Rococo faience following the tradition of Habán ceramics. The Habáns were Anabaptists driven out of Tyrol in the 16th century. They found refuge in Moravia – which was religiously tolerant at the time – and its clayey soil provided quality material for the production of faience. The Habáns had to leave Moravia after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 and many of them settled in adjacent territory of western Slovakia, where they gradually became assimilated into the local Catholic population. Some of the Habán potters returned to Moravia in the last quarter of the 17th century to practice their craft under more favourable conditions. The tradition of “folk faience” in Moravia goes back to this period.  
Jan Neumayer was said to have come from Pisa, but it is likely he only trained in Italy. He was one of the artists of the Olomouc workshop which, together with a counterpart in Šternberk, developed the folk faience tradition. The motifs of horse riders were frequently derived from J. Ridinger's engravings, many of which adorned chateau interiors. Ceramic and glass vessels sometimes featured production dates and the names of their owners, indicating that their manufacture was perhaps prompted by a “souvenir” value. Their ornamentation of multi-coloured floral patterns is found on folk ceramics and costumes to this day.

68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.name: Albarello
68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.description: An albarello (plural: albarelli) is typically an earthenware jar originally designed for medicinal purposes and used to hold apothecaries' ointments and dry drugs. The origins of this type of pharmacy jar trace back to the Islamic world. Its craftsmanship and design influence spread to Europe through Muslim-European interaction. This particular albarello exemplifies 14th-century AD Valencian ware by Muslim potters. It has a cylindrical body, tall neck, and slanting shoulder on a short foot. It is decorated in blue and lustre glazes, with seven horizontal geometric bands that include many abstract motifs favoured for pharmacy jars, including two bands bearing *al-afiya*, a stylised inscription of the Arabic word for health and happiness. While the albarello was originally used for medicines, glazed jars like this one were used for storing and transporting items like wine, water, butter, honey and olives.
68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.dates: Hegira second half of 8th century /AD second half of 14th century
68325b3d-407d-58cd-871d-f55852f7184e.author: Teslim Sanni
materials: Tin-glazed earthenware with lustre and cobalt blue decoration

6888b95a-b9b3-5ecb-b46a-031374206bdf.name: Bowl with Design of Vegetal Motifs
6888b95a-b9b3-5ecb-b46a-031374206bdf.short_description: A steep-sided bowl with lustrous white slip under transparent glaze covering the entire bowl inside and out except on the bottom and the short foot rim. The interior of the bowl has brownish-black and orange-brown slip ornamentation with design of stylized tree and flower motifs, dots, etc. at each side joined by a line of small dots; these alternate with a short broad line with dots below it (along the top rim).

68f3aad7-5032-554b-8430-789916bacd15.name: *Socarrat* tile.
68f3aad7-5032-554b-8430-789916bacd15.description: The term *socarrat* ('scorched') refers to large fired-earth tiles manufactured using the biscuit technique: the slab, once dried in air, is rubbed with white clay on its smooth side, then blue, red ochre and iron is painted onto this base. It is then fired, and the tile comes out coloured blue, vermilion and black on a white base. They were intended to decorate eaves and cornices, to which they afforded a colourful intensity, usually in mineral earthy black tones and iron or ochre reds dissolved in a lime milk that, once set, gave them consistency. *Socarrat* tiles are not glazed, a typical characteristic of *azulejos*. This *socarrat* tile combines black and red ochre, although this latter has lost its traditional flat colour quality so that the artist could treat it like a water colour and obtain a greater range of tones at will. It is decorated with a boat that is sliding through the water, accosted by sharks jumping at the bow and attempting to board it. The sails have been rendered realistically, taken in at the top and with edges that droop like a sunshade. The stars in the upper part suggest night-time. According to González Martí, the boat appears to be a caravel, as it fits the general description of a light vessel with a single deck, square stern, a castle at each end and three masts with sails. The prevalence of this type of vessel in late Gothic gold- and silverware attests to its popularity. More recently, the prominent bow and stern have identified it as a cog. In the centre, the coat of arms of the town of Paterna, where it was produced, has been stamped.
68f3aad7-5032-554b-8430-789916bacd15.short_description: Clay plaque fired just once having been decorated over a fine layer of white. It would have been placed between the wooden beams of a ceiling and the eaves. It was fire- and water-resistant and also had an ornamental value.
68f3aad7-5032-554b-8430-789916bacd15.dimensions: Height 41 cm, width 33 cm, depth 3 cm.
68f3aad7-5032-554b-8430-789916bacd15.method_for_datation: Through stylistic parallels with other *socarrat* tiles from the same period, published by González Martí (see bibliography).
68f3aad7-5032-554b-8430-789916bacd15.method_for_provenance: The piece bears a stamp of the coat of arms of the town of Paterna.

68f83415-d094-590c-bdae-7ff58905192e.name: Ewer.
68f83415-d094-590c-bdae-7ff58905192e.description: A ceramic ewer of rectangular shape, with four feet and a sloping shoulder. The original spout and handle have broken off and been replaced, probably in the 19th century, with silver mounts of European origin. The ewer is decorated with underglaze painting in blue and white. The wide sides are decorated with blue scrollwork designs set in a lobed diamond-shaped cartouche, from whose sides flowers grow out into the corners of the ewer. The narrow sides are painted blue and feature linked flower motifs in white. On the shoulder of the ewer, bands of blue scrollwork meander along a white ground. This decoration would have continued on the spout. The ewer's feet have been left white. This is one of a group of ceramic objects which represent the waning of the so-called 'Baba Naqqash' style. The arabesque patterns on the sides hearken back to the hallmark pattern of that style, while details like the scrollwork on the shoulder, or the chevron band around the neck, look forward to the next phase of Iznik decoration in the 1520s.
68f83415-d094-590c-bdae-7ff58905192e.short_description: A ceramic ewer of rectangular shape, with four feet and a sloping shoulder. The decoration in blue and white features both traditional and innovative elements. The original spout and handle have broken off and been replaced, probably in the 19th century, with silver mounts of European origin.
68f83415-d094-590c-bdae-7ff58905192e.dimensions: Height 23.8 cm, width 15 cm (including spout), depth 11 cm.
68f83415-d094-590c-bdae-7ff58905192e.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
68f83415-d094-590c-bdae-7ff58905192e.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, Istanbul/London, 1989, p.106, fig. 126.
68f83415-d094-590c-bdae-7ff58905192e.author: Barry Wood
materials: Painted and glazed ceramic; the mounts silver.

691ddce6-25f1-577a-8e88-7a0131702eef.name: Tile.
691ddce6-25f1-577a-8e88-7a0131702eef.description: Made of stone-paste, this hexagonal tile is painted with blue and turquoise in underglaze technique. Below large lotus flowers and fantastical so-called *saz* leaves sit a pair of ducks. This beautifully drawn design relates to 15th-century album drawings from Iran, used as sources for a range of decorative arts. During the 15th and 16th centuries Iranian potters travelled to Turkey to work for Ottoman patrons. This tile recalls certain motifs in the tile panels, also of blue and turquoise, in the Sünnet Odası (Circumcision Chamber) in the Topkapı Palace, Istanbul of about AH 933–4 / AD 1527–8. These compositions with large flowers, swirling leaves and animals may have been produced by craftsmen from Tabriz in Iran. Similar designs of leaves and animals can be found in a number of album drawings in the Topkapı Palace. Another abiding source of influence was Chinese blue-and-white porcelains which were imported to Turkey due to their popularity with Ottoman patrons. Despite these foreign influences the designs are adapted by Iznik potters to create a distinctive style of their own.
691ddce6-25f1-577a-8e88-7a0131702eef.short_description: Hexagonal tile with a design of ducks, flowers and *saz* leaves painted in blue and turquoise underglaze. Iranian or Chinese influence is apparent in many styles of Iznik ceramics; this composition echoes similar designs found in album drawings created by artists in Tabriz in Iran.
691ddce6-25f1-577a-8e88-7a0131702eef.method_for_datation: The blue and turquoise under-glaze ceramics were produced in the first half of the 16th century in Ottoman Turkey as seen, for example, in the tile panels in the Sünnet Odası (Circumcision Chamber) in the Topkapı Palace of about AH 933–4 / AD 1527–8.
691ddce6-25f1-577a-8e88-7a0131702eef.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the main centre of production for underglaze painted ceramics of this style, colour and technique during the Ottoman period.
691ddce6-25f1-577a-8e88-7a0131702eef.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by Augustus Wollaston Franks in 1892.

6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.name: Ceramic bowl.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.description:
The shallow shape of the bowl and the attempt to imitate the whiteness of porcelain are evidence of the admiration the Muslim potters had for Chinese ceramics. Early Abbasid potters created a tin-glaze or under-fired alkaline glaze in order to conceal the earthy colour of their wares with an opaque whiteness imitating Chinese porcelain. The decoration on this bowl includes four spontaneously flowing streams of green running from the border towards the centre. In the middle of the dish are three lines of angular Arabic *kufic* script that are decorative and not clearly legible.  
It is possible to read the first line as: “was made by which …" This is unusual as the proper phrasing should be "which was made by…". The second line is not entirely legible, but can be read as: “Muhammad”, possibly indicating the name of the craftsman. There are similar ceramic bowls exhibiting the same name. The third line reads: "enjoy your meal". Such wares were regularly decorated with aphorisms and good wishes to the owner.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.short_description: The fashion for Chinese ceramics among early Muslim potters is evidenced by the opaque whiteness and crackled effect of the glaze as applied on this Abbasid dish. Its designer, possibly named Muhammad, is trying to imitate Chinese porcelain.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.method_for_datation: The dating is approximated to the AH 3rd– 4th/ AD 9th–10th century or Abbasid period, based on stylistic and comparative evidence. Most bowls in this Eastern style are attributed to the period of the Buyid Dynasty, also known as the Buwayhids, an Islamic Dynasty of Persian origin and Shi'ite faith, who ruled in Iraq between 338–447/ 943–1055 while maintaining loyalty to the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.method_for_provenance: This type of ware was made in Mesopotamia and al-Jazira and shows Eastern influences. There were various centres of production.
6945b03a-e793-5c51-8b45-3e3ebf550370.provenance: Al-Jazira (the region located between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, hence known as “the island”; currently consisting of northeast modern Syria and northwest Iraq), or Mesopotamia.

69bd4624-b7de-55fb-85ce-4dbe6c7e46c2.name: Plate.
69bd4624-b7de-55fb-85ce-4dbe6c7e46c2.description:
Ceramic plate restored from a fragment that consisted only of a section of a plate's rim and base. The missing part was reproduced using plaster, enabling the general form of the plate to be restored. The original fragment is made up of a fine brown-coloured paste, which has been decorated along the edge of the rim with a green geometric design set within three concentric semi-circles, applied using a paintbrush. Some traces of paint have remained on the rim and on the base, suggesting that the decoration was repeated in a symmetrical fashion along its edge and at the centre of the plate, which sits on a ring-like base.  
The fine quality of the ceramic paste attests to it being a luxury item of crockery.
69bd4624-b7de-55fb-85ce-4dbe6c7e46c2.short_description: Ceramic, wheel-thrown dish that has been restored on the basis of a fragment of fine, brown clay brush-painted around the edge in green beneath a glaze. The decoration consists of three concentric semi-circles. The dish has a circular base.
69bd4624-b7de-55fb-85ce-4dbe6c7e46c2.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
69bd4624-b7de-55fb-85ce-4dbe6c7e46c2.dimensions: Height 4.9 cm, diameter of the base 6.2 cm, diameter of the rim 21.5 cm, thickness 0.6 cm.
69bd4624-b7de-55fb-85ce-4dbe6c7e46c2.method_for_datation: The fragment comes from the upper strata of a well, 14.5 m deep, full of ceramic shards and pottery that were piled up over four layers of earth, each corresponding to the Punic, Roman, Byzantine and Zirid eras. According to the chroniclers, Algiers was built during the Zirid era by Buluggin ibn Ziri (362–73 / 973–84).
69bd4624-b7de-55fb-85ce-4dbe6c7e46c2.obtention: Archaeological repository (Leschi and Le Glay excavations, 1952).

6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.name: Ceramic jar
6a082742-d8cb-5964-8ea7-e722c9a23660.description: A tall pottery jar with a flat base used for storage and short-distance transport, as indicated by its shape and four short handles. The handles are placed at the shoulder below a rimmed mouth. Under its yellow and pistachio-coloured glaze it is decorated with brown and green glazes in three horizontal registers. The band below the lip is delineated by a thin brown line at the top and a green stripe between two thin brown lines at the bottom, a motif that is repeated below the second and the third bands. It depicts a row of six-petalled flowers, outlined in brown, with a leaf on each side of the stem. The petals are decorated with a spot of green. In the second band, a brown-edged diamond pattern circles the body. The third band is decorated with a row of brown-edged leaves filled in with green. The pot is glazed inside in dark green. From historical documents (cookbooks or single recipes) we know some methods of traditional preservation; many of them remained in use in traditional communities in the 20th century, and even today. Meat or butter was preserved in relatively big pots, or salted in stoneware or earthenware jars. Curing with liquid and dry-curing were also used, the latter using salt mixed with other ingredients, such as spices, before smoking.

6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.name: Incense burner.
6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.description: An unusual incense burner made of earthenware. It has been thrown on a wheel and is perforated with leaf-shaped cut-outs in order to aid air circulation and maximum dissemination of the incense. The main body is divided in half by a perforated strainer-type horizontal partition where the burning incense would be placed. The vessel has a high lid that is also perforated, as is the lower part of the body, further increasing air circulation throughout the vessel. There are four handles on the axis of the main body, indicating that this incense burner would have been elevated, either hung from the ceiling or some other high place.
6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.short_description: Incense has held a special position in most if not all Islamic cultures, and has been mainly used to perfume interior spaces such as private rooms, mosques, shrines and religious schools. Vessels of all shapes and sizes, like this pottery burner, have been made to hold and burn incense.
6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.dimensions: Height (with lid) 23 cm, width (including handles) 20 cm.
6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the object was collected by the donor from Algeria along with other similar Ottoman ceramics.
6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.method_for_provenance: The object was collected by the donor from Algeria along with other similar Ottoman ceramics.
6aba1364-1271-56bc-8718-7c0b62b33f0d.author: Noorah Al-Gailani

6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.name: Vase.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.description: Vase with vertical bevelled rim, circular mouth, cylindrical neck, globular body, with two grooved strap handles with a pinnacle-shaped protuberance at the top which join the neck and belly of the vessel, and a convex base with diagonal foot-ring. It shows remnants of the base of a filter between the neck and body. The exterior is decorated using the partial *cuerda seca* technique, in which only some parts of the design are filled with green or greenish honey-coloured glaze and others with dotted lines. The decoration is divided into six successive horizontal bands of plant, wavy and calligraphic motifs. On the rim is a narrow border of schematic palmettes. Most of the neck is occupied by a wide band with large lotus flowers, and below this is a frieze of tooth-shaped motifs. On the shoulder is a calligraphic ornamental border in which the word '*baraka*' is repeated several times in florid *kufic* script and, on the belly, a band of phytomorphic medallions. Next to the base is a frieze of palmette leaves. The object has been restored.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.short_description: Almoravid or Almohad pot decorated in part using *cuerda seca*. The decoration is arranged into six successive horizontal bands with plant, undulating and calligraphic motifs. The lotus-flower motifs and the band inscribed with the word ‘*baraka*’ in flowery *kufic* script are particularly noteworthy.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.dimensions: Height 34.8 cm, width 32 cm, diameter (of mouth) 17.8 cm, diameter (of base) 13.4 cm.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated by comparison with objects of similar form, decorative technique and theme, in particular from Almería and Málaga.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.method_for_provenance: The abundance of this type of ceramic in Málaga and Almería (Spain), where kilns in which they were made have been found, has led researchers to attribute its production to these localities.
6ad7e7f5-5b8d-5bfc-afb9-c3c90a19d9a8.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

6b41f817-21dd-52c8-b611-243fb687aeb7.name: Pair of Ewers
6b41f817-21dd-52c8-b611-243fb687aeb7.short_description:
This pair of glazed ceramic ewers reflects some of the many changes that have taken place in the field of Islamic art history and perhaps also helps to broaden our understanding of modern art. Both bear labels indicating that they were lent to the first great exhibition of Islamic art, held in Munich in 1910. It is now more than one hundred years later, but they have actually grown even older during that time. Ascribed to eighteenth-century Turkestan in the 1910 catalogue, these ewers can now be assigned to the late Timurid period on the basis of art historical, scientific and archaeological evidence. Determining their likely place of production is perhaps more problematic.  
The site of Otrar as well as neighboring medieval settlements had begun to attract attention even prior to the first archeological excavations in 1904. It is therefore possible that the 1910 attribution of the pair of ewers to Turkestan (in the first half of the 20th century often used as a general designation for western Central Asia) may have some traction; perhaps Kirkor Minassian, the well-known dealer who loaned the ewers in 1910 (and whose name and Paris address are still preserved on one of the ewer’s exhibition labels) acquired them from some clandestine excavator active in the region.  
On the other hand, there is some evidence to link the two vessels with the northwestern end of the Iranian world—to Kubachi or elsewhere in Dagestan. The Oriental Museum in Moscow possesses a group of unpublished ceramic vessels with the identical decoration and color scheme as the turquoise-glazed ewer (no inv. numbers were available); these were excavated in the region of Dagestan. In addition, the State Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg, has a number of unpublished ceramic vessels that demonstrate the same color schemes and related decoration, which according to museum records were acquired from citizens of Kubachi in the first decades of the 20th century. One of them (VG-1611) is identical in shape and size to the Los Angeles ewers, although its decoration is coarser.  
This pair of ewers now provides a better understanding of late Timurid ceramics and their decoration at either the eastern or western-most extremes of the Iranian world. They also may enhance our appreciation of the “Orientalizing” themes in the work of Henri Matisse (1869-1954), who visited Munich in October, 1910, expressly to see the great Islamic art exhibition. It is easy to imagine that he also may have preserved a visual memory of objects such as these ceramic ewers whose colorful floral ornament is echoed in a variety of the artist’s works.

6b41f817-21dd-52c8-b611-243fb687aeb7.dates: Hegira late 9th-early 10th century / AD late 15th-early 16th century
6b41f817-21dd-52c8-b611-243fb687aeb7.method_for_datation: The art historical evidence for a Timurid date is substantiated on two further counts: one, the ewers were subjected to thermoluminescence testing in 2006 producing results entirely consistent with a late 15th – early 16th-century date, and two, excavations at Otrar, in southern Kazakhstan, especially from 1971-1985, have produced a wealth of related ceramic finds many of which date to the Timurid period, including single-handled vessels similar in shape to the present examples.

6c0d5ed7-f239-5a9e-b68f-3354fdd5c46c.name: Round-bellied vase.
6c0d5ed7-f239-5a9e-b68f-3354fdd5c46c.description:
This vase is glazed in yellow over a white slip. The belly is rounded and it has a long narrow neck with no handles ending in a prominent lip. The vase is quite crudely made but has a pleasing shape. The green and brown decoration is elaborate, consisting of a combination of domestic fowl and geometric motifs. Two stylised birds adorn opposite sides of the vase, one with its wings wide open.  
All over the rest of the vase, the artist has drawn wildly imaginative patterns; chequer-work, diamonds, circles and dots. Berber in inspiration, this decoration shows just how original Ifriqiyan art had become, in spite of its strong Oriental influences.
6c0d5ed7-f239-5a9e-b68f-3354fdd5c46c.short_description: The rich brown and green decoration on this vase, with its geometric motifs and domestic animals, is particularly noteworthy. Geometric motifs are dotted around the background. This ornamentation, inspired by Berber and Eastern art forms, is a good example of the singularity of Ifriqiyan art.
6c0d5ed7-f239-5a9e-b68f-3354fdd5c46c.dates: Hegira, last third of the 3rd century / AD 9th century.
6c0d5ed7-f239-5a9e-b68f-3354fdd5c46c.method_for_datation: Raqqada, where the piece was found, was the Aghlabid capital city, built in 263 / 876, which makes this date a *terminus ante quem*. Moreover, the vase is characteristic in its shape, colour and decoration of that of the Aghlabid repertoire, which we know well from the thousands of objects and fragments found at the Raqqada site. It appears that the same shapes, colours and techniques were carried over to beginning the Fatimid era, which means that we can date this piece from the last quarter of the 3rd / 9th century. But it was definitely produced in either the Raqqada or the Kairouan potteries.
6c0d5ed7-f239-5a9e-b68f-3354fdd5c46c.method_for_provenance: The discovery of this bowl on the Raqqada site would confirm that this was a local piece from the Raqqada potteries or from those at Kairouan, the nearest economic capital.
6c0d5ed7-f239-5a9e-b68f-3354fdd5c46c.obtention: This piece was found during the Raqqada site excavations in the 1960s. From 1966 it was put on display at the museum of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. In 1986 it was transferred to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada.

6c462380-2914-5cf9-9add-db9249d1c981.name: Ewer
6c462380-2914-5cf9-9add-db9249d1c981.short_description: Reticulated double-walled composite-bodied ceramic ewer, the openwork shell decorated with seated princely figures enclosed in curvilinearized dodecagonal compartments. The ewer was wheel-thrown and moulded, pierced, underglaze-painted in black, transparent turquoise glaze detailed with cobalt blue.

6ce7585a-6af3-5c01-acdf-e9095b77b4a9.name: *Batta* jug.
6ce7585a-6af3-5c01-acdf-e9095b77b4a9.description: With its shrunken neck and large hanging rim and spout, this small jug with a round belly is reminiscent of Phoenico-Carthaginian *bobeche* jugs. These *batta* jugs, commonly used to hold lamp oil in the AH 13th / AD 19th century, were made in Fez and Meknès in several sizes. This example is decorated with vertical flutes on the belly and a cord ribbon. Similar jugs could be decorated with two lines of small circles stamped above and below this ribbon. Jugs covered with green tin glaze like this one were intended for regions in the south of Morocco, in particular the oases of the Ziz Valley. For urban markets, Fez ceramicists made the jugs in the same shape but with much more elaborate polychrome decoration, using plant and flower motifs from the Moroccan-Andalusian repertoire.
6ce7585a-6af3-5c01-acdf-e9095b77b4a9.short_description: The neck and rim of this small jug, known as a *batta*, are reminiscent of Carthaginian *bobeche* jugs. This is a traditional shape for recipients used for lamp oil, and was made in Fez and Meknès for the southern regions of Morocco.
6ce7585a-6af3-5c01-acdf-e9095b77b4a9.method_for_datation: This type of jug was no longer produced in the early 20th century.

6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.name: Vertical-sided bowl.
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.description:
The decoration of the bowl, which is limited to the outside, consists of a large inscription in *kufic* characters with strokes finished with an apex and certain letters finished with volutes, all contained between two solid lustre bands. The main inscription is superimposed by four letters in cobalt-blue. Although very contemporary, the meaning of the inscription is related to the *baraka lisahibihi* type, ‘blessed be the holder’.  
It is relevant to note that decoration consisting of purely epigraphic motifs is quite rare in Mesopotamian lustre-ware, and thus it can reasonably be assumed that this piece was influenced by ceramics from the Samanid period in Khurasan and Transoxania (AH 4th–5th / 9th–10th centuries), to which significant production of non-lustre-ware china, decorated only with epigraphic motifs, is attributable.
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.short_description: This bowl is practically unique in its shape and decoration, with pieces decorated exclusively with calligraphy being rare in the early years of the Abbasid era.
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.method_for_datation: From stylistic analysis. The decoration is clearly influenced by ceramics from the Samanid period in Khurasan and Transoxania (4th–5th / 9th–10th centuries).
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.method_for_provenance: The simplicity of the piece is characteristic of objects from Samarra.
6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.bibliography:
Lane, A., *Early Islamic Pottery*, London, 1953.  
Philon, H., *Early Islamic Ceramics*, London, 1980.

6d275aae-efca-5e92-b1e9-cd4d92480102.author: Paola Torre
materials: Ceramic painted with metallic lustre and cobalt-blue.

6db232a1-1948-537d-8bad-3c92a264c7c0.name: Stucco panel
6db232a1-1948-537d-8bad-3c92a264c7c0.short_description: "Stucco" is a term used to describe the vast majority of decorations in Islamic Arts. White stucco, made from plaster stones, was used for column capitals, arcs, as well as sloped constructions such as roofs, as it is an incredibly supple, yet strong, adherent, durable and light material. Muslim artisans made countless constructions decorated with stucco. The 18th and 19th centuries, however, saw many constructions in carved golden plaster - both palaces and houses were elaborately decorated in this way. Floral motifs, closer to the Ottoman and Italian styles, soon overtook the geometric designs of previous centuries.
6db232a1-1948-537d-8bad-3c92a264c7c0.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
keywords: Carved plaster; capitals; palaces; Ottoman style; Italian-esque style

6db5dc26-a551-5750-a7ae-d8710e639fce.name: Water jug
6db5dc26-a551-5750-a7ae-d8710e639fce.short_description: This clay water jug with a handle is decorated with stamped patterns, painted golden motifs, and Arabic characters. Its long neck widens at the top and has remnants of a clay strainer inside. The curved base is decorated with a stamped floral pattern. The various types of décor—gold paint, geometric stamps, and floral stamps—divide the jug into several distinct decorative sections. The gilding of the jug is most likely an oil gilding. Some of the Arabic stamps read *tin makhtum*, a type of red clay believed to have a medicinal function in the Medieval period; the jug was most likely used for such purposes.
6db5dc26-a551-5750-a7ae-d8710e639fce.method_for_datation: Some of the stamps read *tin makktum*, a type of medieval medicinal clay.
materials: Clay, gold plated; probably oil gilding

6db950fc-93a3-5777-aada-7d4002b3f00b.name: Bowl with Design of Radiating Stripes
6db950fc-93a3-5777-aada-7d4002b3f00b.short_description: A deep bowl with flaring lip, set on a high ring foot. The surfaces are glazed primarily white, with royal blue glaze around the rim and vertical, alternating stripes of royal blue and olive green on both the interior and exterior. The stripes on the interior taper in thickness toward the *omphalos* area of the bowl, becoming notable thinner at a carination. The lines meet at a central blue circle enclosing a blue dot surrounded by two irregular green lines. The bottom of the short foot is also glazed white.
6db950fc-93a3-5777-aada-7d4002b3f00b.dates: Hegira Late 5th to late 6th century / AD 12th century
6db950fc-93a3-5777-aada-7d4002b3f00b.dimensions: Height: 10.2cm; Diameter of mouth: 20.3cm; Diameter of foot: 8.9cm
6db950fc-93a3-5777-aada-7d4002b3f00b.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
6db950fc-93a3-5777-aada-7d4002b3f00b.method_for_provenance: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.

materials: Glazed fritware with underglaze painted decoration

6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.name: Bowl.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.description: A thrown, earthenware bowl with a wide and flaring shape that sits on a small, round pedestal base; it has been moulded by hand around the rim to produce a ring of indentations. The bowl has been coated with a slip of liquefied clay and decorated with a simple flowing design on the inside with black and blue underglaze. It is glazed overall with a thickly applied glaze that is a transparent, intense yellow.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.short_description: This North African bowl would have been used for serving a vegetable stew with meat and couscous, a wheat product. Thrown on a wheel, it has a lid that matches it in shape but has a slightly smaller diameter. Vessels like this are still made today.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the object was collected by the donor from Algeria along with other similar Ottoman ceramics.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.method_for_provenance: The object was collected by the donor from Algeria along with other similar Ottoman ceramics.
6f45b4c6-e6d0-562e-aa92-b2efaf2a5915.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
materials: Earthenware decorated with black and blue underglaze, over which a transparent yellow glaze.

6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.name: *Stove*
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.description:
This stove once adorned the interior of the former Dietrichstein Palace next to the Franciscan Monastery, Brno. The palace, pulled down in a street development in 1906, was said to be one of the most beautiful in Brno.  
The bottom section features a scene in relief from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Venus and Adonis, with *putti* carrying a vase. The upper ledge bears the Dietrichstein coat of arms; the decoration climaxes in the figure of Ganymede kidnapped by Jupiter in the form of an eagle, another scene from Ovid. These myths frequently provided subject matter for the decoration of residences both secular and religious. They usually appeared as ceiling paintings and sculpted garden ornamentation, as well as on utility objects such as table crockery.  
The richly decorated stove manifests the span of work assigned to the sculptor employed by the imperial court. In the final phase of palace reconstruction by František Antonín Grimm, carried out from the early 1740s, Ignaz Lengelacher also created the ornamental stone vases on the entrance frontage. The stove is similar to those found in Klosterneuburg, near Vienna, designed by Donato Felice d'Alio, in whose studio Grimm worked.  
After the mid-18th century the Dietrichstein Palace was a major centre for the social life of Brno. Under the next owner, Count Salm-Reifferscheidt, it became a meeting place of the oldest Brno freemasonic lodge.
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.short_description: The richly decorated stove manifests the span of work assigned to the sculptor employed by the imperial court. Legends from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* were frequent subjects for decoration in residences both secular and religious. They often appeared in ceiling paintings, as well as in applied arts.
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.method_for_datation: The authorship of the image is defined by the work’s origin and the participation of Ignaz Lengelacher in the sculpted decoration of the Dietrichstein Palace.
6f7d1e22-4662-54e3-b5a0-d90fe53335a9.obtention: The Stove was acquired by the Museum of Applied Arts (Moravian Gallery, Brno since 1961) before 1928.

Miloš Stehlík, in Ivo Krsek – Zdeněk Kudělka (ed) – Miloš Stehlík – Josef Válka, *Umění baroka na Moravě a ve Slezsku*, Prague, 1996, p. 607, cat. 312, p. 613.  
Jiří Kroupa – Tomáš Jeřábek a kol, *Brněnské paláce. Stavby duchovní a světské aristokracie v raném novověku*, Brno, 2005, pp. 137–160.
