6fb6dc4e-a56b-544c-9b26-f00596b09c9d.name: Bowl with horserider
6fb6dc4e-a56b-544c-9b26-f00596b09c9d.short_description: This bowl shows a crowned horserider surrounded by birds, floral motifs and calligraphic elements drawn in black against a yellow background and further enhanced by individual dots of turquoise glaze. The style draws on both local Persian folk and royal traditions while the inclusion of *kufic* script signals awareness of a new, "Islamic" aesthetic.
keywords: Bowl; Kufic; Glaze; Ceramic; horsemanship; human representation; calligraphy

72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.name: Plate and ablution ewer
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.description:
The porcelain plate depicts a ritual washing ceremony, in which a servant pours water from an ewer for ablution. This scene illustrates the importance of cleanliness and ritual purity in Ottoman daily and religious life. The accompanying basin and ewer set, produced in the Süleymaniye workshop tradition, reflects the same function represented in the image. Such basin–ewer sets were commonly used indoors for ablution (*wudu*), particularly before prayer, as well as for washing hands after meals.  
  
Beyond their practical purpose, these objects held symbolic meaning, emphasising purity, hospitality and respect for religious practice. Through both the visual narrative on the porcelain plate and the physical form of the basin and ewer, the work highlights the central role of water in Ottoman ceremonial, domestic and spiritual culture.
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

72e174ad-f050-54f3-84a7-95a37e327e32.name: Jar
72e174ad-f050-54f3-84a7-95a37e327e32.short_description: Large earthenware jar of ovoid form that is slender at the base and is flaring at the shoulders, on which two curved handles extend to the bottom of the wide cylindrical neck. The exterior is decorated with streaks of green glaze and the interior is entirely glazed.

73a8c1a7-47a7-5ac2-8219-524e45f2889c.name: Basin
73a8c1a7-47a7-5ac2-8219-524e45f2889c.short_description: This large basin with a flat base and curved, sloping sides is also called a *maajna*. The feet of the basin are circular, and the centre is decorated with a highly stylised floral pattern with palms and winged shapes overlapping. The walls are mainly painted with a *tawq* (collar) motif. This style indicates a symbiosis between Ottoman influences and local traditions. The dominant colours are: yellow, green, brown, and violet. This basin was used to knead dough, roll semolina and as a serving bowl for certain ingredients, and shows traces of both Ottoman and Andalusian influences.
73a8c1a7-47a7-5ac2-8219-524e45f2889c.holder: Musée de la Céramique Sidi Kacem Jelizi

73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.name: Sugar bowl
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.description:
The master, Domokos Kuny’s father, founded a pottery in Buda producing faience and ceramics in what is today Christina Boulevard. Three masters and eight apprentices worked in his manufactory in the 1780s. The products of the workshop were extremely popular among the bourgeoisie and aristocracy of Buda and Pest in the late 18th century.  
The white glazed sugar bowl is decorated with floral motifs and on the base is the sign “OF” (Ofen=Buda). Domokos Kuny’s (1754–1822) father was Dominique Cuny who mastered the craft of ceramics in a Strasbourg manufactory before arriving from Baden-Durlach to Holics in Upper Northern Hungary. The commercial and economic development of Buda attracted him and he settled down in the city in 1784–85 and founded a manufactory. In the surrounding countryside were clay mines, perfect for the production of ceramics.
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.short_description: An object of everyday use from the workshop of the famous master Domokos Kuny (1754–1822).
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.method_for_datation: By historical documents and decoration and style of the object
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.obtention: Transferred from the capital’s collection in 1945
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.bibliography: *Budapest az Újkorban* (*Budapest in Modern Times*), (ed. G. Szvoboda Dománszky), Budapest, 1995, p. 27.
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.workshop: Ceramic workshop of Domokos Kuny, Buda
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.artist: Unknown, from the Domokos Kuny Workshop
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.author: Beatrix Basics
keywords: Pottery; ceramics; faience; sugar; applied art; manufactory; factory; workshop; bourgeoisie; aristocracy; Domokos Kuny; Ofen; Buda; Pest; domestic vessels

74522266-7a73-5544-925c-094de901d54c.name: Footed dish
74522266-7a73-5544-925c-094de901d54c.short_description: In the 1870s, blank spaces still existed on the map of the world. There was a great deal of interest in distant lands and in geographic observations. Scientific and commercial overseas missions under the Austrian Flag become more common. From 1873 to 1875 the corvette Helgoland of the Imperial and Royal Navy circumnavigated Africa. The staff included the naval officer, Lieutenant Commander (Linienschiffsleutnant) Leopold Freiherr von Jedina-Palombini. During a brief stopover in Tangier (Morocco) he purchased a selection of the famous blue and white Fassi ceramic ware which was very popular in that time. Pottery and ceramics produced in Fez are among the most beautiful examples of Hispano-Moresque art.
74522266-7a73-5544-925c-094de901d54c.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
74522266-7a73-5544-925c-094de901d54c.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.
74522266-7a73-5544-925c-094de901d54c.obtention: Estate Leopold Freiherr von Jedina-Palombini. Catalog entry: "Purchased from Baron Dr. Jedina, 1949."

749834b9-5f86-513c-a750-311aca2067e7.name: Deer-Figured Water Container
749834b9-5f86-513c-a750-311aca2067e7.description: The ceramic, off-white paste and one-colour turquoise glazed figurine has a navy blue glazed relief decoration with lines and dots on the back. The deer on a rectangular base has a hole in the back and on the head, and the three antlers are curved and joined at the top.

749ed869-f804-5e04-8571-0e4f75d67555.name: Bowl
749ed869-f804-5e04-8571-0e4f75d67555.short_description: Fritware *mina ´i* bowl with curved sidewalls gently flaring at the rim. The bowl is enamelled painted and gilded on an opaque white glaze.
749ed869-f804-5e04-8571-0e4f75d67555.dates: Hegira mid 6th–mid 7th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century

74cb07f0-79d7-57eb-be13-fe55793125ae.name: Milk jar
74cb07f0-79d7-57eb-be13-fe55793125ae.short_description: This butter jar with a *dagra* lid has a spherical body and rests on a small pedestal. It is decorated with a polychromatic pattern, organised in rows. Medallion shapes filled with flowers cover the lower half of the body, and the lid is also densely decorated with flowers, and framed by a lattice.

755aa26f-837b-56c6-a555-fffe8cf9d2d2.name: Dish with carnations.
755aa26f-837b-56c6-a555-fffe8cf9d2d2.description: Deep dish with curved sides and a flat base. The decoration, painted in red lustre, consists of a large, feathery bush with carnation flowers emerging from a small central vase, which is goblet-shaped and stands on a tall foot. Around this there is a typical frame of small concentric semi-circles from which feathered bushes spring, set uniformly between each carnation above a dotted background. The edge of the dish, marked with a slight inner groove, is outlined with a broad band of solid lustre.
755aa26f-837b-56c6-a555-fffe8cf9d2d2.short_description: This plate, decorated principally with a motif borrowed from Ottoman fabrics and ceramics, is an example of 18th-century late Valencian production. It was probably used as luxury crockery.
755aa26f-837b-56c6-a555-fffe8cf9d2d2.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
755aa26f-837b-56c6-a555-fffe8cf9d2d2.method_for_provenance: The dish comes from late Valencian production (12th / 18th century) whose distinctive features include the splitting up of decorative elements, the feathery look used in the plant decoration and the presence of carnations, a Turkish influence that reached the West in the form of both textiles and ceramics. Occasionally, as is the case with this piece, we see the almost exclusive use of this motif, according to a taste that was inspired by the famous Turkish ceramics of Iznik in which, among other things, the decorative use of flowers in vases is very common.

keywords: Dish; lustre; Mudéjar art; floral decoration

758017b1-e777-564d-bac6-2f8e62ea8bad.name: Bowl.
758017b1-e777-564d-bac6-2f8e62ea8bad.description:
An open bowl with a circular body on a flat base. The rim is semi-circular in cross-section, marked and slightly inverted.  
The ceramic is made from very light-coloured almost white paste, with a brown, almost sepia decoration. The surfaces have slips in the same colour as the paste.  
The decoration is centred on the inside of the object with a star-shaped or flower motif which spreads out from a broad circle decorated with a geometric pattern inside. Small semi-circles with a dot in the centre form a border around this circle, interspersed with groups of three lines which radiate outwards and are repeated seventeen times.  
The rim of the bowl was also decorated with stripes of the same colour, in seven sets of small dashes producing a very subtle effect.  
This type of decoration is common on the inside of similar pieces, but also on the outer walls of small pots. A very similar decoration has been observed on ceramics from Vilamoura (Loulé, Algarve, Portugal) and on ceramics unearthed in the Castle at Silves.  
In the archaeological excavations carried out at Silves, this type of ornamentation was not found in objects from archaeological levels dating after the AH 4th / AD 10th century.  
This may be a locally produced object.
758017b1-e777-564d-bac6-2f8e62ea8bad.short_description: The elegance of the geometric motif on the inside of this bowl is particularly noteworthy, depicting a star or flower in the centre radiating from a circle containing a geometric bar motif. The whole is reminiscent of traditional formulas from the region, characteristic of indigenous art.
758017b1-e777-564d-bac6-2f8e62ea8bad.method_for_datation: From its archaeological, stratigraphic and typological context. The date attributed (2nd–3rd / 8th–9th century) is disputed by Cláudio Torres, of the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola, who believes that it is probably a later piece, in comparison with others coming from the region of Gharb al-Andalus.
758017b1-e777-564d-bac6-2f8e62ea8bad.method_for_provenance: An excavation carried out in the courtyard next to the cistern in Silves, directed by Mário and Rosa Varela Gomes. Inventory number Q 41/C3-silo 1.
758017b1-e777-564d-bac6-2f8e62ea8bad.provenance: Courtyard adjacent to the cistern (now Silves Municipal Archaeology Museum), Silves.
758017b1-e777-564d-bac6-2f8e62ea8bad.obtention: Housed in the Museum after the excavation that was carried out in the 1980s.

75bb1422-0084-5c89-9bec-838982478b11.name: Double-shelled ewer, rooster-shaped
75bb1422-0084-5c89-9bec-838982478b11.short_description: A real masterpiece of the Iranian plastic art in ceramics is a double-shelled underglaze-painted ewer shaped as a rooster dating to the early 13th century. The openwork elements of décor (figures of winged sphinxes and floral motifs) are emphasized by painting in black under clear turquoise glaze. Double-walled tableware ewers and jugs were real technical breakthroughs of Kashanian potters. The rooster was regarded by Iranians as a ritually pure and auspicious being since pre-Islamic times.
75bb1422-0084-5c89-9bec-838982478b11.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by H. Rudyk (publication, 2017, date, origin).
75bb1422-0084-5c89-9bec-838982478b11.method_for_provenance: Arthur Sambon's auction catalogue (1914). Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927). Old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
75bb1422-0084-5c89-9bec-838982478b11.obtention: Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918. Previously purchased by the Khanenkos in Paris at the auction of Arthur Sambon collection in 1914.

77482de0-a383-587d-9e29-0206bf355536.name: Luster dish
77482de0-a383-587d-9e29-0206bf355536.short_description: Twenty-four pupils of both sexes are seated around a bearded teacher, who is wielding a cane. Everyone is looking the same way except the boy in the top left corner, who is looking at a girl. The scene has been identified as most likely being “the first meeting of Layla and Majnun at school” from Nizami’s famous book *Layla and Majnun*, written in the 1180s.
77482de0-a383-587d-9e29-0206bf355536.dates: Hegira end of the 6th century / AD end of the 12th century

78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.name: *Muqarnas* decoration
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.short_description: Developed in Iran, the *cuerda seca* technique was designed to produce multicoloured glazed tile decoration quickly, efficiently and cheaply. It was introduced to western Anatolia in the Hegira early 9th century / AD 15th century, probably by a group of Iranian master artists, whose work decorates the Ottoman royal mosque complex in Bursa known as the Green Mosque. An important example of *cuerda seca* tilework, possibly from the same building complex, is this ceramic revetment moulded in the form of *muqarnas* (stalactite- or honeycomb-like elements used as decoration in Islamic architecture). It is painted in a typical colour scheme of dark blue, turquoise, white and yellow. *Muqarnas* elements such as this one were produced in modular units and later set into place on building façades.
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.method_for_datation: The color scheme and cuerda seca technique relate this *muqarnas* element to the tile decoration of the Green Mosque Complex, Bursa, built between 822-827 Hegira / AD 1419–1424.
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.method_for_provenance: The glazing technique and colors are comparable with the tile decoration in the so-called Green Mosque Complex in Bursa.
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.obtention:
Possibly from the Green Mosque complex in Bursa, Turkey.

7892ac22-f1eb-5c25-a796-c350b3bd270a.name: Dish with floral decoration.
7892ac22-f1eb-5c25-a796-c350b3bd270a.description: Large plate with a broad flat base, curved sides and a narrow brim, painted in turquoise green, cobalt-blue and red lake in relief (Armenian bole) typically used with this type of dish. It consists of flowering stems that, like the central shoot with its blue campanulas, spring from a small bush with small alternating blue and red roses that is painted on the lower edge of the base of the dish. The flowers are dominated by three large peonies, tulips and hyacinths. The brim is decorated with the characteristic ‘wave-and-rock’ motif, highly stylised. The side is decorated with rose and palmette motifs that alternate between green and blue, with colour haloing.
7892ac22-f1eb-5c25-a796-c350b3bd270a.short_description: This plate, a typical example of work from the factories of Iznik in the AH late 10th–early 11th / AD late 16th–early 17th centuries, is richly decorated with floral motifs.
7892ac22-f1eb-5c25-a796-c350b3bd270a.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
7892ac22-f1eb-5c25-a796-c350b3bd270a.method_for_provenance: Careful examination of the details and the unlobed border of the dish reveal that this piece was produced in Iznik workshops around the end of the 10th / 16th and the beginning of the 11th / 17th centuries.

78c10c6a-90c0-51eb-966c-99cb0239f706.name: *Mina´i* painted bowl
78c10c6a-90c0-51eb-966c-99cb0239f706.short_description: Mina'i or haft-rangi ("enamelled", and "seven-coloured" in Persian) ceramics are a kind of Iranian figurative pottery that required technological knowledge and financial means to manage several rounds of firing. This bowl depicts an episode from the Shahnama: the presentation of the severed head of the general Ayin Ghashap to his opponent, the ruler Bahram Chubina. The head is presented by the soldier who murdered the general.

78fc4eee-3393-5086-bc09-000253cb480d.name: Figure on a horse
78fc4eee-3393-5086-bc09-000253cb480d.short_description: This statuette of an equestrian figure holds a basket or drums on each side. Though the body of the animal looks like a camel, the head is horse-like. Painted with a turquoise glaze, the contours are outlined in a dark blue colour. Figurative objects like this one have been manufactured since early Islamic times, with the heyday of production occurring during the Seljuq period. Fragments found in Raqqa, Rayy, Kashan, and Sultanabad indicate that workshops in these areas manufactured many of these objects. How and why these objects were used is uncertain, but this statuette most likely served a decorative function as its heavy weight restricts use.
78fc4eee-3393-5086-bc09-000253cb480d.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar objects, e.g. Museum of the Islamic Art in Berlin and the Museum of Glass and Ceramics of Iran in Tehran.

78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.name: Bowl with two dancing girls, a flowering tree and bands of script
78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.short_description:
This bowl was made in the *mina’i* technique, which was developed by potters in Kashan and was very popular in the late 12th century. *Mina’i* ware is identified by the use of coloured pigments under the glaze. Like many vessels made during this period, the bowl is coloured with muted colours and gold overglaze and was fired several times.  
The Inside of the bowl is decorated with two figures dancing around a small flowering tree, their headdresses flying. The edge of the bowl is inscribed in *kufic* script, wishing the owner happiness. The colourful picture resembles miniature paintings of the era and it is reminiscent of the rural life and cultural ceremonies of the region, possibly referring to Norouz, the Iranian New Year ceremony.
78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.dates: Hegira late 6th century-early 7th century / AD late 12th-early 13th century
78fd5c1b-903d-5e4d-a4fa-83c8d3da2f2e.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and by comparison with pieces from the Seljuq period.

79de590d-1ba1-5b9f-a1c0-57b81de273a9.name: Ten-pointed star-shaped tile
79de590d-1ba1-5b9f-a1c0-57b81de273a9.short_description: The ten-pointed star-shaped tile is decorated with arabesque motifs with alternating light-blue and ivory lanceolate patterns on black, interlaced across the entire surface around the small, six-pointed star in the centre, standing out from a cobalt-blue background. Such tiles were manufactured using the *cuerda seca* technique, in which the different colours of the glazing were separated by contour lines made from a blend of manganese and oily substances.
79de590d-1ba1-5b9f-a1c0-57b81de273a9.dates: Hegira mid-9th century / AD mid-15th century

7a68823e-191b-5fd3-bb5a-c45c2eb03deb.name: *Qolla* jar for provisions
7a68823e-191b-5fd3-bb5a-c45c2eb03deb.description: Directly inspired by the *khabiya*, a large jar for food preservation, this pot was used to store and preserve liquids such as oil or water, and various foods. The decoration includes a stylised branch motif with alternating leaves called *babbouch* (snail).

7ab9e067-b408-50a4-b58a-df8f27485caf.name: Bowl with laurel leaves
7ab9e067-b408-50a4-b58a-df8f27485caf.short_description: The bowl is painted in polychrome lustre colours achieved by using silver, copper and sulphuric oxides. It is decorated with laurel leaves on the rim and a geometric pattern with dots. The design reflects the connection of early lustre pottery with glass as motifs reflect those on late antique glasswork.
keywords: Bowl; Laureal leaves; Abbasid; Earthenware; vegetal decoration

7ad06476-d932-56f0-b128-ef8b7b5692e8.name: Lustre bowl
7ad06476-d932-56f0-b128-ef8b7b5692e8.short_description: The ceramic bowl is painted with monochrome lustre and displays a giraffe with its groom by a tree on a background filled with contour panels decorated with the so-called peacock’s eye design. The design is comparable to another bowl in Cairo with the same scene but in a double mirror image and signed by Muslim ibn al-Dahhan. Giraffes were regarded as exotic and prestigious animals and were paraded on festival celebrations.

7b2742c6-535b-5d12-97d6-c40de8fa7448.name: Water pitcher
7b2742c6-535b-5d12-97d6-c40de8fa7448.description: A fine example of Çanakkale pottery craftsmanship, characteristic of the region’s traditional ceramic art.

7bac3062-d8d3-5fab-a7f0-30acb10c03e0.name: Large bowl
7bac3062-d8d3-5fab-a7f0-30acb10c03e0.short_description:
The bowl is decorated with two large confronted birds, whose elongated bodies point in opposite directions. Their heads face backwards, which – together with their long, curved tails – creates a sinuous movement reminiscent of elegant calligraphic strokes.  
  
The centre of the bowl, which on many examples of this ware is left empty or accented by a small black dot, has been filled with a small bird with raised wings in the form of half palmettes. The exterior is undecorated.
7bac3062-d8d3-5fab-a7f0-30acb10c03e0.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art

7bb1e389-6b64-508c-be13-d7e4b898da6c.name: Footed bowl.
7bb1e389-6b64-508c-be13-d7e4b898da6c.description:
A large, footed bowl made of stone-paste ceramic and painted under the glaze with an array of leaves and floral devices. The colours used are manganese, sage-green, blue, and black. Around the outside is the serrated edged so-called *saz* leaf, an imaginary form that becomes popular on Iznik ceramics during the AH 930s to 50s / AD 1530s to 50s. Inside is a striking geometric arrangement of medallions containing cloud scrolls, enclosed between sprays of blue bells. This splendid bowl, with its bold painted design, was probably made for the Imperial court, perhaps for washing the feet of Suleyman the Magnificent himself (r. AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66).  
This footed bowl exemplifies a type of ceramic produced during the 930s to 50s / 1530s to 50s, known collectively as one of the ‘Damascus’ group, as it was once thought to originate there. It has since been proven that the Damascus variety originated from Iznik designs, characterised in particular by the introduction of certain colours – olive-green, black and manganese purple – and the appearance of the so-called *saz* leaf and fantastical flowers.
7bb1e389-6b64-508c-be13-d7e4b898da6c.short_description: Such a splendid footed bowl almost certainly belonged to the royal court, perhaps for storing water to wash Süleyman the Magnificent himself. Due to the sage-green, manganese, blue and black underglaze decoration of *saz* leaves and fantastical flowers, this bowl is grouped with so-called Damascus wares.
7bb1e389-6b64-508c-be13-d7e4b898da6c.type: Stone paste blue and turquoise painting, ceramic
7bb1e389-6b64-508c-be13-d7e4b898da6c.method_for_datation: A mosque lamp in the British Museum dated 955 (1549) provides the key to dating both this bowl and all other vessels employing a similar colour scheme and using such motifs as the cloud scroll. Another fixed point is a group of tiles both in the Yeni Kaplica *hammam* (baths) in Bursa dated 959–60 (1552–3), and in the Ibrahim Pasha Mosque in Istanbul, built in 956 (1550). These tiles have the same colours and decorative motifs as the 'Damascus' group of ceramic objects, such as this bowl.
7bb1e389-6b64-508c-be13-d7e4b898da6c.method_for_provenance: Iznik in Turkey was the main centre of production for underglaze painted ceramics of this style and colour, and using this technique, during the Ottoman period.
7bb1e389-6b64-508c-be13-d7e4b898da6c.obtention: Part of the Godman Bequest of 1983.

7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.name: Tile.
7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.description: A stone-paste (fritware) tile that has a stenciled, symmetrical design based on four arabesque cartouches and four rose-like flowers that spring from a central star motif. The cartouches extend towards the tips of larger arabesque medallions in the corners of the tile, while the flowers have two curved stems extending above, ending in half-flowers to the left and right. This tile was part of a larger overall tile scheme.
7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.short_description: Tiles like this one are typical of tile production in Ottoman Syria during the AH 11th century / AD 17th century. They were on the whole intended to echo the Iznik style, but a typical feature of Syrian pieces is a palette restricted to blue, green, turquoise without the addition of bole-red.
7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.method_for_datation: It is accepted that tiles such as this were produced in Ottoman Syria during the 11th / 17th-century.
7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.method_for_provenance: Tiles such as this one are typical of those produced in Ottoman Syria where the output was largely Iznik ware distinguished by a palette restricted to blue, green and turquoise without the addition of bole-red.
7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.obtention: Purchased from the Major W. J. Myers Collection in 1900.
7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, p.232, fig. 411 (For a similar Iznik-produced tile with virtually identical design and related to others placed in the mausoleum of Sultan Selim II in the Ayasofya).
7c54162f-752d-55a0-b15d-ba5049476e9d.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware) with blue, green and turquoise underglaze, over which a clear glaze.

7cea6ccf-c3e7-529b-8b69-b0d28db38eda.name: Excised *zellij* frieze.
7cea6ccf-c3e7-529b-8b69-b0d28db38eda.description:
This small fragment of wall covering is a specimen of excised or raised earthenware mosaic.  
This technique was used to introduce curved lines into ceramic decoration, notably to reproduce inscriptions and plant decoration. Mostly using black glazed tiles, craftsmen skilfully excised the glazed surface with a sharp hammer, taking care only to expose the fired clay where it was to be used as a background. Thus, the curved vegetal and written figures appear in low relief on the background of ochre fired clay.  
Here, inside a braided frame, cursive characters mix with spindly foliage dotted with nodes and bearing double palms and fleurons. The cursive inscription reproduces a pious formula: 'For me with the God of worshippers'.  
This type of inscribed band, originally from the Buinaniya Madrasa, was placed above the ceramic panelling and below a frieze of geometric motifs known as *charafa* (reminiscent of crenelations) which provided a transition between the earthenware decoration and the plaster panelling on the walls.
7cea6ccf-c3e7-529b-8b69-b0d28db38eda.short_description: This fragment, inscribed with a pious formula, is part of a glazed and excised earthenware mosaic in which it was possible to reproduce the curved lines of the inscription and the plant decoration, which is rendered in low relief on a background of ochre fired clay.
7cea6ccf-c3e7-529b-8b69-b0d28db38eda.method_for_datation: This architectonic element, originally from the Buinaniya Madrasa, was made at the time the monument was constructed.
7cea6ccf-c3e7-529b-8b69-b0d28db38eda.method_for_provenance: This frieze was salvaged during the restoration of the monument in the 20th century.

7cf9dbf7-35bc-5ff7-9f5e-d4b400e59363.name: Bowl.
7cf9dbf7-35bc-5ff7-9f5e-d4b400e59363.description: A tin-glazed bowl that depicts a stylised kangaroo-like animal with a pinecone behind it. The design of the pinecone is of Islamic origin. The small town of Paterna in Valencia was known not only as one of the most important centres for the production of unglazed and plain earthenware, but was also renowned for its tin-glazed pottery, painted in green and brown. This bowl was made by Mudéjar potters (Muslims living under Christian rule) living in Paterna.
7cf9dbf7-35bc-5ff7-9f5e-d4b400e59363.short_description: This popular ceramic bowl was made by Mudéjar potters (Muslims living under Christian rule) in the Valencian town of Paterna. The pinecone motif behind the unidentified animal is a typical design that appears on utilitarian ceramics, a sign of Paterna’s Islamic artistic heritage.
7cf9dbf7-35bc-5ff7-9f5e-d4b400e59363.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the distorted animal and vegetal designs on this dish are typical of this type of Mudéjar art; many similar examples have been found at Paterna.
7cf9dbf7-35bc-5ff7-9f5e-d4b400e59363.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

7dc4562d-82ce-50c5-a832-2096a508aa3d.name: Dish with artichokes and tulips
7dc4562d-82ce-50c5-a832-2096a508aa3d.short_description: Beginning sometime in the Hegira 950s / AD 1540s Iznik potters introduced manganese purple, sage green and black to their palette, while their decorative repertoire continued to focus on floral designs such as pomegranates, rosettes, tulips and artichokes. The latter two motifs form the main decoration at the centre of this large dish, where they are depicted in blue and green, while the cavetto and rim bear green pomegranates alternating with blue sprays of leaves or else tulips.
7dc4562d-82ce-50c5-a832-2096a508aa3d.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
7dc4562d-82ce-50c5-a832-2096a508aa3d.method_for_datation: Iznik wares with this specific color scheme, sage-green combined with more typical Iznik tones such as blue and turquoise, were produced for only a short period in the middle decades of the 16th century; the earliest dated example is the mosque lamp from Süleyman’s restoration of the Dome of the Rock (British Museum 1887,0516.1) dated Hegira 956 / AD 1549.
7dc4562d-82ce-50c5-a832-2096a508aa3d.method_for_provenance: The shape, technique, color scheme and decoration mark this dish as a product of Iznik.
7dc4562d-82ce-50c5-a832-2096a508aa3d.obtention: Collection of Dikran Kelekian (1867-1951) c. 1910. Collection of Maan Z. Madina (1926-2013), New York, until 2002 (sold to); LACMA, The Madina Collection of Islamic Art, gift of Camilla Chandler Frost.

7e112851-d569-579f-a466-578f55fc9c3a.name: Bowl with Design of Standing Figure and Four Birds
7e112851-d569-579f-a466-578f55fc9c3a.short_description:
A Nishapur-style bowl on a ring base has an exterior lip decorated with a band of dark triangles; below are horizontal, equidistant lines in the same glaze down toward the base. Also on the exterior are irregular areas of light red and yellow glaze. The interior of the rim has four horizontal dark lines outlining three bands of yellow, red, and white glaze. The rest of the interior has a bright yellow background. The central, male figure is thickly outlined in dark glaze and has a squared head, simplified eyes, nose, moustache, and mouth, and wears an ankle-length, belted garment with a black overlay. Above the waist the garment is red with yellow X designs. The skirt is decorated with patterned squares in dark outlines and a horizontal, blue band across the bottom; he also wears dark, pointed shoes. The figure is surrounded by numerous stylized, geometrical and vegetal designs, pseudo-*Kufic* inscriptions, and four long-necked birds with crests, possibly peacocks. Irregularly around the central field and edges of the bowl are intentional spots of turquoise glaze. The exterior and bottom of the bowl are covered in buff glaze and are undecorated. The bowl rests on a low foot, bottom slightly concave, covered in the same buff glaze.  
There is much chipping and cracking in the glaze, especially around the rim and over the entire exterior of the bowl; hairline cracks throughout. There are numerous, restored breaks, and chipping around the foot.
7e112851-d569-579f-a466-578f55fc9c3a.dates: Hegira Late 2nd to late 4th / AD 10th century

7ec4c61a-0b37-51f0-9e27-faeecc7abdb3.name: Dish with triangle decoration.
7ec4c61a-0b37-51f0-9e27-faeecc7abdb3.description: A bossed dish with a broad brim painted in brown lustre on a cream background. The main decorative motif is a ring of triangles around the inner edge of the brim, painted in solid lustre. The brim also bears another similar motif in carved lines that is for the most part separate from the painted decoration. Between the triangles there are, alternately, stars and dots, known as ‘*solfas*’ or musical notes, and spiral motifs on a striped background, along with large dots and curl patterns. In only one instance is the *solfas* motif repeated twice consecutively. A thick lustre band marks the outer edge of the brim. An inscription, contained by two thick bands of solid lustre, surround the hemispheric boss, which is decorated with a three-petalled flower. The outside of the dish is painted in brown-red lustre with concentric circles following a spiral pattern.
7ec4c61a-0b37-51f0-9e27-faeecc7abdb3.short_description: This bossed dish, produced in the Valencia area, is principally decorated with triangles and motifs known as *solfas* (musical notes).
7ec4c61a-0b37-51f0-9e27-faeecc7abdb3.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
7ec4c61a-0b37-51f0-9e27-faeecc7abdb3.method_for_provenance: The dish is one of a series of reasonably common Valencian products that were widespread in the second half of the 10th / 16th century. The style incorporates decorative themes belonging to fine dishes with pod-shaped decoration of the end of the 9th / 15th century and the beginning of the 10th / 16th century, simplified to suit popular taste.

7f3ad75b-9c30-59f5-bd90-9efafe607dc8.name: Bowl.
7f3ad75b-9c30-59f5-bd90-9efafe607dc8.description:
A shallow, stone-paste (fritware) footed bowl with a flat top rim: it is decorated with six rectangular rotating bands with heavy black outlines, which form a hexagon in the centre; the rim is decorated with pseudo-Arabic in *kufic* script. Organic decoration fills the background between the bands and in the centre of the hexagon.  
  
Raqqa was one of two major pottery-production centres in Ayyubid Syria, the other being Rusafah. In Raqqa there were a number of pottery workshops that produced a range of ceramics including lustre-painted, relief-moulded, and underglaze-painted vessels. The pottery ceased production when the Mongols razed the city to the ground in AH 657 / AD 1259.  
  
Syrian wares of this type were also found widely throughout Egypt, due to Fustat in Egypt being both a busy international port and due to the fact that Syrian potters settled in Fustat, establishing their own pottery workshops.
7f3ad75b-9c30-59f5-bd90-9efafe607dc8.short_description: Raqqa, where this bowl was made, was one of two major pottery-production centres during the Ayyubid period in Syria. The style and decoration of this dish, and the composition of the glaze and how it has deteriorated, are typical features of Raqqa pottery.
7f3ad75b-9c30-59f5-bd90-9efafe607dc8.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis, together with analysis of the material composition of the vessel's body which is distinctively that of Raqqa. Furthermore, the nature and extent of the deterioration of the glaze is also typical of Raqqa ceramics.
7f3ad75b-9c30-59f5-bd90-9efafe607dc8.method_for_provenance: The vessel is typical of Raqqa ceramics in both its material composition and in the nature of the deterioration of the glaze.
7f3ad75b-9c30-59f5-bd90-9efafe607dc8.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

80702cfd-ff0c-515c-86ba-e43978e9e1de.name: Figurine of a dromedary
80702cfd-ff0c-515c-86ba-e43978e9e1de.short_description:
The stonepaste vase is in the shape of a dromedary; there is a large vase on its hump and a few small ones on its body as well. The lustre-painted decoration includes the trappings and a saddlecloth, as well as a medallion with a harpy.  
Itinerant craftsmen from Fatimid Egypt or Ayyubid Syria may well have introduced lustrewares produced in the town of Kashan from the late 12th century onwards. It is now generally agreed that they these lustrewares are the work of different kilns within the town, produced over a continuous period of more than a century. Throughout this time, the town appears to have successfully maintained its monopoly and exported little if anything westwards to Anatolia, Syria or Egypt: finds outside the borders of present-day Iran (for example, in Central Asia or Afghanistan) have also been very few.

80cabe22-0796-50d8-b4b1-b4e1801d847c.name: Bowl.
80cabe22-0796-50d8-b4b1-b4e1801d847c.description: A stone-paste (fritware) bowl of flaring shape with straight sides, decorated with black painted stripes on the sides and a roundel of highly stylised calligraphy in the centre of the well, which may read: 'al-'izz … Muhammad' ('the glory... Muhammad'). The decoration is typical for this type of bowl where the body of the unglazed vessel is painted with black pigment, and a transparent glaze (in this case turquoise) is then subsequently applied overall. Raqqa was one of two major pottery-production centres in Ayyubid Syria, the other being Rusafah. There were a number of pottery workshops şn Raqqa that produced a range of ceramics including lustre-painted, relief-moulded, and underglaze-painted vessels. The pottery ceased production when the Mongols razed the city to the ground in AH 657 / AD 1259.
80cabe22-0796-50d8-b4b1-b4e1801d847c.short_description: The centre decoration of this bowl has a calligraphic inscription which may read 'al-'izz … Muhammad' ('the glory... Muhammad'), painted in black pigment under a transparent blue glaze. The popular use of good wishes inscriptions and blessings on Middle Eastern ceramics goes back to the earliest part of the Islamic period.

8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.name: Bowl
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.short_description: Some *mina’i* ceramics enjoy a particularly close relationship to poetry. Many examples are inscribed with verses, and others are decorated with figures referring to well-known poetic themes and tales. Several of these colorful wares, including this bowl, appear to depict the act of poetic recitation itself: taking place at a *majlis* (an assembly of courtiers and literati for the purpose of poetic recital), it can be imagined that the performer here, seated at the left before a courtly audience, is delivering the verses inscribed along the exterior rim of the bowl, which begin: "If the beloved leaves me, what am I to do? If s/he does not see the wisdom of our union, what am I to do?"
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.method_for_datation: The bowl is dated Hegira Muharram 583 / AD March 1187. It is one of five *mina’i* bowls dated to the month of Muharram in its inscriptions. Among these, three have very similar scenes of a literary *majlis*. Two of them, the LACMA bowl and another in the British Museum (1945,1017.261) are dated Muharram 583, the third, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (64.178.1), dated 4th Muharram 582 / AD 27th March 1186, is signed by Abu Zayd. Both the Metropolitan Museum and LACMA bowls share the same curious figure at far left, a young man standing with his right leg bent and foot pointing downward; in the former, the figure is clearly holding his leg as though tired from standing. The LACMA bowl can be attributed to Abu Zayd, who not only created works in both *mina’i* and luster but was a talented poet. He is known to have included some of his own verses among the poetic inscriptions on his luxury ceramic wares.
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.method_for_provenance: The bowl is decorated in the *mina’i* technique. A modern designation from the Persian word for "enamel", *mina’i* is almost entirely restricted to Seljuq Iran. While *mina’i* wares once were variously attributed to several sites on the basis of archaeological finds, the evidence demonstrates at present that the central Iranian city of Kashan was the nucleus for the production of these objects as well as contemporary luster wares; in fact, both types of wares were made by some of the same potters, in the same workshops. The *mina’i* technique involves the application of as many as seven colors, resulting in a well-controlled, polychromatic decorative surface not possible in other contemporary pottery types. The method for producing the polychrome enamel pigments is described in a treatise on pottery making by Abu’l-Qasim of Kashan, completed in Hegira 700/1301 AD, by which time *mina’i* or haft rang (“seven colors”) wares, as they are known in the textual tradition, were no longer being produced.
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.obtention: Possibly acquired by Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch (1864-1943, and 1863-1943, respectively) from MacDermid Parish-Watson, New York (d. 1948). Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch, until 1945 (gifted to); LACMA, gift of Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch.

81fcd4e9-7384-5569-aa53-bc862c54ad3f.description: A fine, pear-shaped pottery jug with two handles, in a characteristic cream colour, decorated using various techniques such as incising, perforations and knife scraping. The decorative scheme is composed of a combination of geometric and floral patterns which were common in Islamic art.
81fcd4e9-7384-5569-aa53-bc862c54ad3f.short_description: Pear-shaped, two-handled pottery jug from Tall Hisban, decorated using various techniques such as incising, perforations and knife scraping. The decorative scheme is composed of a combination of geometric and floral patterns.

81fcd4e9-7384-5569-aa53-bc862c54ad3f.method_for_datation: The jug was dated by stratigraphic context and comparison with similar jugs; Abbasid pottery is characteristically cream in colour.

820a47e5-8aaa-59ae-93fc-e4b386f5f8b4.name: Wellhead
820a47e5-8aaa-59ae-93fc-e4b386f5f8b4.description: It is made of terracotta. The rim protrudes very slightly. The body is encircled by five parallel chain-like incised lines. Between the two central lines are trapezoidal incisions arranged in a chain-like geometric pattern.

821515fd-cabe-5567-8bf4-25c6db38bf00.name: Three-handled jar
821515fd-cabe-5567-8bf4-25c6db38bf00.description:
Discovered in an unbuilt area adjacent to a complex of five houses, this three-handled transport jar was found during the 2007 excavation by the Qatari-French Mission. The unbuilt space between the houses served as an area with temporary installations, potentially functioning as open-air kitchens featuring fireplaces.  
  
Fashioned from red clay and enveloped in a cream slip, this jar exhibits a high neck atop a globular body. The body is adorned with horizontal and wavy incised lines, while three vertical leaf-like patterns are incised on the upper part, positioned between the handles. These leaf patterns feature short double lines incised within them. This jar would have been utilized for the storage, transportation, and serving of liquids.
821515fd-cabe-5567-8bf4-25c6db38bf00.dates: Hegira late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

8262afff-f5be-5577-ab18-a76c2170cb15.name: Plate.
8262afff-f5be-5577-ab18-a76c2170cb15.description:
A stone-paste ceramic plate painted with blue, turquoise and olive-green underglaze. Covering the centre of the plate is a vibrant design of so-called *saz* leaves, fantastical flowers and a pair of tulips. Around the rim is a more ordered arrangement comprising clusters of green leaves alternating with bunches of white and blue flowers. The tulips grow from a leafy tuft at one edge of the bowl, while the other flowers encircle them. Plates produced at Iznik often display plants springing from one edge, providing a vertical orientation for the design. This plate is a fine example of the ‘saz’, or ‘Damascus’ style that became popular in the AH mid-10th / AD mid-16th century.  
This plate exemplifies a type of ceramic produced during the 930s to 50s / 1530s to 50s, known collectively as one of the ‘Damascus’ group, as it was once thought to originate there. It has since been proven that the Damascus variety originated from Iznik designs, characterised in particular by the introduction of certain colours – olive-green, black and manganese purple – and the appearance of the so-called *saz* leaf and fantastical flowers.
8262afff-f5be-5577-ab18-a76c2170cb15.short_description: Tulips and fantastical flowers are depicted ‘growing’ from one edge of this ceramic plate, while *saz* leaves float around the bowl in a graceful arrangement. Ceramics of this type of design and palette were produced in Iznik although they were once considered products of the city of Damascus.
8262afff-f5be-5577-ab18-a76c2170cb15.method_for_datation: A mosque lamp in the British Museum dated 955 (1549) provides the key to both the dating of this plate and all other vessels employing a similar colour scheme and using such motifs as the cloud scroll. Another fixed point is a group of tiles both in the Yeni Kaplica *hammam* (baths) in Bursa dated 959–60 (1552–3) and in the Ibrahim Pasha Mosque in Istanbul, built in 956 (1550). These tiles have the same colours and decorative motifs as the 'Damascus' group of ceramic objects, such as this plate.
8262afff-f5be-5577-ab18-a76c2170cb15.method_for_provenance: Iznik in Turkey was the main centre of production for underglaze painted ceramics of this style and colour, and using this technique during the Ottoman period.

82635f79-7381-59a0-8cbe-e72a1b631f83.name: Dish
82635f79-7381-59a0-8cbe-e72a1b631f83.description: The Orientalism or Neo-Mudéjar style gave new light to different workshops, as Fajalauza in Granada. Following this revival, this workshop produced dishes and other object decorated with Alhambra motifs, in this case the gazelles from the very well-known "Gazelle Vase" from the Alhambra Palace, the inscriptions and interlaces.
keywords: Neo-mudejar style; Applied Arts; Production of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode

82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.name: *Habb* water cooler
82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.description:
The *habb* is a large ceramic water storage jar and filtration device, used in domestic and communal contexts throughout Iraq. It is known for being used in public spaces to provide water for travellers, an offering known as *ma’ al-sabil*, “the water of the way”.  
  
The ceramic structure is slightly porous, which has a cooling effect on the water inside due to evaporation from external surfaces. When it is placed on a metal or wooden support structure, Water drips slowly through the base and is collected in a container below, having been filtered by the clay. Placing charcoal inside the *habb* can also help to purify the water. Water ladles (traditionally made from basketry) and ceramic cups used with the *habb* are coated with pitch, which has antiseptic qualities.  
  
The form of the *habb* is evidenced since ancient times, for example in cylinder seal impressions; similar vessels were also used as fermentation vats for beer.  
  
The *habb* is still made in various parts of Iraq including Diwaniya, Najaf, Babylon and Baghdad, where traditional ceramic craft remains; the example in the collection of the Open Museum for Water Culture (Basra) was bought from a Basra street market but had been imported from nearby Iran.
82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.holder: Open Museum Initiative for Water Cultures
82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.author: Hannah Lewis, Rashad Salim

8360d938-1158-5dec-8d1b-26aa9fd74053.name: Pair of tiles
8360d938-1158-5dec-8d1b-26aa9fd74053.short_description: A key characteristic of Islamic art is to cover entire buildings with brightly coloured tiles. The pair of tiles provides a good example of how the walls of the sumptuous Safavid palaces must have looked.
8360d938-1158-5dec-8d1b-26aa9fd74053.dates: Hegira late 10th century / AD late 16th century

83d379f5-b3fb-5f8d-90e6-0d7825b5a477.name: Oil lamp.
83d379f5-b3fb-5f8d-90e6-0d7825b5a477.description:
A stone-paste (fritware) oil lamp with a long, open spout, cylindrical neck, looped handle and spherical body; an opaque turquoise glaze covers the whole lamp, inside and out. In style, this lamp is typical of AH 6th- / AD 12th-century Fatimid Fustat pottery. Fustat was one of the wealthiest cities in the Islamic world at that time, and was quite populous with many of its dwellings comprising of five to seven levels.  
  
This lamp and many others like it lit the interiors of Fustat's buildings, and testify to its position as one of the leading cities of the Middle East during the Fatimid period (AH 296–566 / AD 909–1171). A busy port, the residents of Fustat included tradesmen who dealt with a wide variety of goods that arrived from all over the world, from places as far away as China. Fustat was also an important manufacturing centre, accommodating craftsmen who produced fine ceramics, glassware, steel and copper products and textiles.
83d379f5-b3fb-5f8d-90e6-0d7825b5a477.short_description: The shape of this lamp is typical of those found at the city of Fustat in Fatimid Egypt. Fustat was a densely populated city, with craftsmen and artisans' workshops catering for the local and export markets. They were exposed to a wide range of artistic styles that came through goods from far lands.
83d379f5-b3fb-5f8d-90e6-0d7825b5a477.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
83d379f5-b3fb-5f8d-90e6-0d7825b5a477.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: comparable examples have been found at Fustat, Egypt, dating back to the 6th / 12th century.
83d379f5-b3fb-5f8d-90e6-0d7825b5a477.method_for_provenance: Comparable examples have been found at Fustat, Egypt, dating back to the 6th / 12th century.
83d379f5-b3fb-5f8d-90e6-0d7825b5a477.bibliography:

materials: Stone-paste (fritware), with an opaque turquoise glaze.

842a5200-0594-5a9c-bea6-e441fe3c4f78.name: Faience pottery tile
842a5200-0594-5a9c-bea6-e441fe3c4f78.short_description: This faience pottery tile is painted with a ship in a circle in its centre, surrounded by flying birds. The rest of the *zelige* tile is decorated with a stylised floral pattern in each of its four corners.
842a5200-0594-5a9c-bea6-e441fe3c4f78.author: Houria Cherid

8469840c-c735-573f-aef2-fdf1fcbc3556.name: Bottle-shaped vase
8469840c-c735-573f-aef2-fdf1fcbc3556.short_description: This nipple or bottle-shaped vase, with its central ring-shaped handle and turned-up base, resembles a closed coffin when seen from the side. Vases in this shape are very rare, and this particular one, which is decorated with the image of a great yellow and brown bird, was used for bottle-feeding infants.

84aca75b-106a-53be-b6ce-f390d4bbcb97.name: Pilgrim flask
84aca75b-106a-53be-b6ce-f390d4bbcb97.description: A round bodied pilgrim flask covered with intricate polychrome decoration and painted with floral motifs and circular medallions with checkered designs and red dots. In the centre, there is a stylised flower in yellow and dark blue.
84aca75b-106a-53be-b6ce-f390d4bbcb97.author: Mina Moraitou

852e199d-7836-57bb-b3ff-c9ab19231d89.name: Tile panel
852e199d-7836-57bb-b3ff-c9ab19231d89.short_description: This large polychrome tile mosaic panel has a central field of interlocking floral, arabesque, and geometric motifs that form an overall repeat on an indigo background. An everted border on three sides has alternating floral and serpentine forms in hexagonal medallions. A wide outer border has dense inscriptions with interwoven scrolling vines. Narrow brown and turquoise bands separate the three main sections. Purchased at auction in 1992.
852e199d-7836-57bb-b3ff-c9ab19231d89.type: Islamic, Indian & Southeast Asian works of art; tilework; ceramic

85f637f2-bdd8-5043-82c2-2e742768a71a.name: Inkwell.
85f637f2-bdd8-5043-82c2-2e742768a71a.description: Almost cylindrical inkwell with a convex base and raised rim with four circular-section handles. The exterior is glazed and decorated using the green and manganese technique. X-rays reveal that from the aperture there is a channel going down 2.9 cm into the receptacle for the ink. This channel is also glazed and was made separately and later joined to the aperture. Various similar pieces are known: one can be found in the Museum of the Alcazaba of Almería; another in Corbières (France); a third, made of glass, is in Iran Bastan Museum, Tehran. A fourth example, held in the Louvre Museum in Paris, is an interesting precedent, since it dates from the AH 3rd / AD 9th century and was discovered during an excavation at Susa. This last piece, from the same era as others found in Samarkand, Nishapur and Siraf (Persia), suggests that these inkwells originate from the Middle East, from where they would have spread to the West.
85f637f2-bdd8-5043-82c2-2e742768a71a.short_description: Portable inkwell worn from the belt. A duct, running from the opening down into the recipient, prevented the ink from spilling out. The calligrapher would have used it with a pen to write letters and documents for money, and it became the symbol of the writer.
85f637f2-bdd8-5043-82c2-2e742768a71a.method_for_datation: By its stylistic characteristics and its similarity to other inkwells of this era.
85f637f2-bdd8-5043-82c2-2e742768a71a.method_for_provenance: The source of the inkwell is not stated in its documentation. Production of this type of object was very limited, and its possible origin has been established by the clarity and austerity of its decorative design linking it to Madinat al-Zahra, a major centre of production of ceramics in green and manganese.
85f637f2-bdd8-5043-82c2-2e742768a71a.obtention: The inkwell was acquired by the State and placed in the National Archaeological Museum at an unknown date.

86a596e6-b986-58ee-a208-14ec3fe50206.name: Footed bowl (*tazza*)
86a596e6-b986-58ee-a208-14ec3fe50206.description: Footed bowl. A thick-walled vessel with scalloped rim which flares out from a deep cavetto (curved profile) bowl on a large, flared, hollow-pedestal base. Overall white underglaze decorated with deep blue designs. On the rim, a rock-and-wave pattern; on the interior wall, a band of trefoil arcades with small trilobed "cloud" patterns above the space between each arcade. Above each "cloud" element and arcade is a vertical L-shaped spike which fills the space. The trefoil arcade register surrounds the central medallion filled by a freely-drawn  bouquet with an elaborate central lotus surrounded by eight symmetrically arranged, stylized blossoms and leaves. The bundled stems grow from a cloud-like horizontal ground line with tendrils filling the space below. All registers are separated by concentric blue lines. On the exterior, horizontal lines define the changes in profile between rim, bowl and base while a freely drawn line traces the undulating curvilinear edge just under the scalloped rim. The body of the bowl and the pedestal foot are decorated with small circular sprays of stylized flowers surrounded by leaves and buds or fruit. Just above the bottom of the foot is a thickened horizontal rib thrown in the profile; this is highlighted above with a wide blue band. The underside of the pedestal foot is glazed overall, the juncture of the foot and body highlighted with a blue line and the bottom edge of the foot is unglazed. Some chips in the rim and foot have been filled and inpainted, while there is some wear on the interior glaze.

86c2720a-384b-58d3-92a2-3fc1aefd7f1c.name: Small earthenware jar
86c2720a-384b-58d3-92a2-3fc1aefd7f1c.short_description: This double-handled and oval-shaped *qolla* has a long neck and a bulging lip. The decoration is polychromatic and organised in rows. On vase's belly, a row of medallions filled with flowers are bordered by a lattice strip and a herringbone strip on either side. The neck is decorated with alternating yellow, blue and green vertical lines. This item shows traces of both Ottoman and Andalusian influences.

86fa6510-d51d-5f73-84cd-e89730dfb6c9.short_description: The Seljuq era is the golden age of Islamic ceramics, characterised by flourishing centres in what is now Iran capable of experimenting with different techniques.
86fa6510-d51d-5f73-84cd-e89730dfb6c9.dates: Hegira late 6th–early 7th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century

879d6d42-f66f-5915-91b7-d2443a989446.name: Tile with birds and rose
879d6d42-f66f-5915-91b7-d2443a989446.short_description: This colourful tile, rendered in yellow, pink, green, turquoise and manganese purple, is taken from a tile panel with a continuous repeat pattern. It shows two birds flanking a large rose, perhaps a reference to the mystical Persian story of the rose and the nightingale. In it the rose symbolizes God and the nightingale the yearning believer.

87c29ad1-e053-5d4e-8dd9-6ee3532db84d.name: Group of tiles
87c29ad1-e053-5d4e-8dd9-6ee3532db84d.description: A group of eight square wall tiles, mounted together a 4×2 grid. Each tile has a design of medallions, leaves, and seed pods, forming a repeating pattern in blue and green.

87ca58dd-ec81-5c67-8d08-0373d3c1c371.name: Large Bowl with Bird
87ca58dd-ec81-5c67-8d08-0373d3c1c371.short_description: This fritware bowl is decorated with a bird painted in cobalt blue, turquoise, and manganese purple under a glaze. It was made using the *laqabi* technique, which used lines, either incised or in relief, to prevent glazes from running together during firing. This allowed for the creation of intricate patterns and for glazes of different colours to be used side-by-side.
87ca58dd-ec81-5c67-8d08-0373d3c1c371.dates: Hegira middle of the 6th century / AD middle of 12th century

8825752a-6526-5ec0-8840-5242549e083b.short_description: Pear-shaped *huqqa* pipe reservoir, in Chinese style, covered with a cobalt blue engobe, painted in white and ochre slips under a transparent colourless glaze.

882edb61-7d84-519e-90cd-1e8568e3abc4.name: *Mokhfia* conical dish
882edb61-7d84-519e-90cd-1e8568e3abc4.description:
This conical plate, or *mokhfia*, is concave on a ring-shaped base. It has an arcade decoration called "turtle". In the centre of the dish a five-pointed star with green central point is inscribed in a double circle. Six blue dots are inside and five are outside of this star. From this central motif is a radiating design of five large green rounded forms, or scales, each with two dots on either side of a wide decorative stripe edged in yellow. The inside rim of the cup features a braided pattern enhanced with small blue strokes. This particular decoration and type of ceramic are characteristic of Moroccan work between the 17th and 19th centuries. They are widespread in Morocco and Spain. We note the Andalusian influence in certain motifs, such as the use of geometry.  
This piece cannot be attributed with certainty to a single production centre. However, Fes is the most important one of the period. The decoration with concentric arches called "turtle" is characteristic of these polychrome Moroccan ceramics. In the 19th century, the colours used were more assertive, the shapes heavier, and the designs less spontaneous than before.

8838f3d0-31b0-5466-9a13-570fd28e82f1.name: Jar fragments with incised décor
8838f3d0-31b0-5466-9a13-570fd28e82f1.description:
This fragment, a kitchen ceramic, was excavated in 2007 by the French-Qatari Mission in one of the houses in Murwab. The water jar features a globular body and a high, straight neck with an unpreserved rim. Crafted from creamy white clay with inclusions of sand and basalt, the porous nature of the material makes it well-suited for keeping water cool.  
A vertical decoration, created with a comb, adorns the entire upper part of the body up to the midpoint of the globular section. Additionally, a rounded handle was attached to the neck of the water jar.
8838f3d0-31b0-5466-9a13-570fd28e82f1.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

88af101d-92a2-5eaf-8d33-31977383ef1b.short_description: This bottle, painted with confident black strokes in reserve against a blue background, combines a Chinese shape and colour scheme with a Persian interpretation of Eastern motifs – three fat partridges alternating with large, fleshy lotus flowers. Such wares were designed to compete with Chinese porcelain in markets at home and abroad.
88af101d-92a2-5eaf-8d33-31977383ef1b.dates: Hegira second half of the 11th century / AD second half of the 17th century

88c3e9a5-4d43-5bac-af15-0e55e4b15da8.name: Two tiles.
88c3e9a5-4d43-5bac-af15-0e55e4b15da8.description: Two stone-paste (fritware) glazed tiles, tile no. 159 a horizontal composition of naturalistically drawn vines with green leaves and fleshy red grapes that flank a central branch that has small blue and red flowers growing on it. Tile no. 160 shows a dense floral design, with two curved so-called *saz* leaves superposed in the centre and surrounded by four fantastical half-flowers. The background is filled with sinuous red cloud-bands and delicate blue scrolling.
88c3e9a5-4d43-5bac-af15-0e55e4b15da8.short_description: Since the late AH 950s / AD 1550s tiles like these, commissioned by the Ottoman court for their extensive building programmes in Istanbul and elsewhere, are known to have become the major concern for the Iznik workshops and a large number of examples remain *in situ*.
88c3e9a5-4d43-5bac-af15-0e55e4b15da8.dates: Hegira, late 10th century / AD late 16th century.
88c3e9a5-4d43-5bac-af15-0e55e4b15da8.method_for_datation: The vine and flowering branch design on tile no. 159 relates to other examples dating to the second half of the 10th / 16th century, in particular those used in Takkeci Ibrahim Agha Mosque in Istanbul, dating to around 1000 / 1592 (see Atasoy and Denny, 2000). Tiles such as no. 160 were used in Murad III’s room in the Topkapı Palace in Istanbul in around 985 / 1578, and this design remained popular, if much simplified, until well into the 11th / 17th century.
88c3e9a5-4d43-5bac-af15-0e55e4b15da8.method_for_provenance: Ever since the late 950s / 1550s tiles like these were commissioned by the Ottoman court for their extensive building programs in Istanbul and elsewhere. Such tiles are known to have dominated output in the Iznik workshops and a large number of examples remain *in situ*.
88c3e9a5-4d43-5bac-af15-0e55e4b15da8.obtention: Purchased from the Major W. J. Myers Collection in 1900.

88d3503f-6102-578d-8dd9-c4a53576130e.name: Dish
88d3503f-6102-578d-8dd9-c4a53576130e.short_description: The design for the large dish is attributed to the circle surrounding the important illuminator and director of the court workshops Kara Memi (active AD 1545–1566).

88e1fa36-529e-53bc-bbcd-f2c0e91f810a.name: Jug.
88e1fa36-529e-53bc-bbcd-f2c0e91f810a.description: The shape of this jug probably copies a glass prototype, a probability further endorsed by the indentations that are arranged in a circular pattern similar to that found on contemporary Iranian glassware. The jug is moulded and glazed with an interesting opaque lavender-blue colour, but falling short of the foot, which has been left unglazed. The shape of this vessel shows the influence of Iranian ceramics on Raqqa's pottery industry. Raqqa was one of two major pottery-production centres in Ayyubid Syria, the other being Rusafah. Raqqa had a number of pottery workshops, which produced a range of ceramics including lustre-painted, relief-moulded and underglaze-painted vessels.
88e1fa36-529e-53bc-bbcd-f2c0e91f810a.short_description: The potters of the Middle East were frequently looking at other industries for artistic inspiration. The shape of this jug is moulded, copying a glass prototype. The circular indentations that decorate the belly of the jug are also found on contemporary Iranian glassware.
88e1fa36-529e-53bc-bbcd-f2c0e91f810a.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

891c65b9-b73d-5c4b-be2d-0e7198d79575.name: Dish.
891c65b9-b73d-5c4b-be2d-0e7198d79575.description:
An undecorated, thickly potted dish with a heavily applied deep-turquoise glaze that is typical of Raqqa ware in both its manufacture and shape. Though badly deteriorating, the glaze still indicates how beautiful this plain dish would have been in its time. The colour turquoise was appreciated aesthetically, and was thought to have protective qualities, rendering it popular in ceramics throughout the Islamic Middle East.  
  
Raqqa was one of two major pottery-production centres in Ayyubid Syria, the other being Rusafah. In Raqqa there were a number of pottery workshops that produced a range of ceramics including lustre-painted, relief-moulded and underglaze-painted vessels. The pottery production ceased when the Mongols razed the city to the ground in AH 657 / AD 1259.
891c65b9-b73d-5c4b-be2d-0e7198d79575.short_description: Though badly deteriorated, this turquoise dish would have looked strikingly blue when still new. Raqqa in Syria was an important centre for the production of ceramics during the Ayyubid period, generating many pieces with turquoise glazing, which was a popular auspicious colour in the Middle East.
891c65b9-b73d-5c4b-be2d-0e7198d79575.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis, together with analysis of the material composition of the vessel's body which is distinctively that of Raqqa. Furthermore, the nature and extent of the deterioration of the glaze is also typical of Raqqa ceramics.
891c65b9-b73d-5c4b-be2d-0e7198d79575.method_for_provenance: The vessel is typical of Raqqa ceramics in both its material composition and in the nature of the deterioration of the glaze.
891c65b9-b73d-5c4b-be2d-0e7198d79575.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

891d79a5-c271-5792-99f2-8c563766ed94.name: Dish
891d79a5-c271-5792-99f2-8c563766ed94.description: Large, white plate adorned with sophisticated floral motifs such as blue tulips, red roses and other flowers, which had both ornamental and symbolic meanings. Rim decorated with black spirals. On the back side of the rim eight green and pale blue spots.

894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.name: *Geometrical Elevation of the Building of the Chemical Laboratory* Azulejos
894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.description:
In 1772, under the educational reforms of King Jose I's Prime Minister the Marquis of Pombal, a new statute for Coimbra University emerged. The views of the Marquis and other Enlightenment figures replaced the Aristotelian school of thought previously taught by the Jesuits, who were expelled in 1759. The aim was to modernise teaching by basing it on practical experience and observation.  
In addition to hiring foreign teachers, buying new textbooks and the acquisition of specialised didactic teaching aids, the university replaced the Jesuit-built college with new buildings, one where the former College of the Jesus Society had been and another where the Paço das Escolas (School Hall) once stood.  
The buildings followed the designs of the English Engineer William Elsden, who was also responsible for the construction. The tile panel *Geometrical Elevation of the Building of the Chemical Laboratory* is one of nine panels decorating the Bishop’s palace.  
The building shown here was used by the science department, which had been newly created through Pombaline reform. Today the building hosts the Museum of Science, part of the University of Coimbra.  
The decoration of the Bishop's palace (today the Museu Nacional de Machado de Castro) was commissioned by the Bishop, formerly the Rector of the University. The panels were designed to celebrate the Pombaline reform of the University of Coimbra (1772–1777), and to mark the important role played by D. Francisco de Lemos de Faria Pereira Coutinho, known as “Reformer and Rector of the University of Coimbra”. He was picked out to lead local reform by the Marquis of Pombal.  
The panels were made at Nova Fábrica da Telha Vidrada, a factory founded in 1773 to meet the demands of (*azulejos*) required for the construction and renovation of the University buildings.  
The production of *azulejos* with repetitive patterns, single figures and ornamental and figurative panels are part of the second phase of the Rococo period (or Pombaline style) that occurred after the earthquake of 1755. In Coimbra this period was extended until the end of the century, whereas in Lisbon, *azulejos* from 1790 onwards had been designed in the Neo-classical style leaving the Rococo for the minor panels.  
The frames of bulky shell forms, similar to those present in some paintings of the period, probably belong to Salvador de Sousa Carvalho (1727–1810), who alternated with Manuel da Costa Brioso (1752–1776) as the director of the Nova Fábrica da Telha Vidrada.
894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.short_description: The panel is an excellent example of 18th-century quality ceramics produced in Coimbra. It represents a memorial of Pombaline reforms at the University of Coimbra depicting the façade of the Chemical Laboratory.

894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.method_for_datation: The date is set by analogy with other artist’s works and according to Salvador de Sousa Carvalho's presence at Nova Fábrica da Telha Vidrada during that period.
894c4ade-7fb1-538a-a14f-a5e4acebdcde.obtention: The *azulejos* are an integrated feature in the halls of the National Museum of Machado de Castro (Old Bishop's Palace).

8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.name: Tabla
8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.short_description: The *tabla*, also known as the *durbakke*, is a small hand drum very common in traditional Arabic music. It is shaped like a vase, and is covered at the top with goat skin. *Tabla*s are often beautifully decorated, with metal, bone inlay, or paint.

896034df-5b65-5b50-921e-f52b7e844979.name: Large Jar
896034df-5b65-5b50-921e-f52b7e844979.short_description: The origins of this object are from Southern Mesopotamia; it’s a complete pottery jar with rolled edges, a short-straight neck, and a globular body. This piece is considered rare, made from fine clay with opaque white glaze and copper, blue, and black manganese splashes on the sides. Archaeologists were able to find many different pottery pieces from different historical periods, and this piece dates back to the 9th century AD. A vessel like this is usually used as a goblet. Typically, it’s a multi-use jar which could have been used for storage and cooking or storing water to keep it cold or to drink from directly.

899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.name: *Fanayeel* or *Fanyaal* (Coffee cups)
899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.description:
*Fanayeel* (Coffee Ccups)  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving dallah referred to as a mezallah, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the mezallah with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
899ab17a-563d-52eb-b76f-6ab3b73e0e14.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

8a2ff55d-1f20-5c07-9cc0-adf4d8569dfe.name: Incense burner
8a2ff55d-1f20-5c07-9cc0-adf4d8569dfe.description: Incense burners like this are usually made of clay mixed with water and kneaded until a mixture is formed that can then be shaped. The burner is then adorned with engravings, intricate drawings, and different colors. The incense burners are then fired in a kiln, after which they are ready for use. Note the handle; it makes the burner safe to carry from room to room. Incense occupies a central place in Omani life, as the passing of a fragrant burner at the end of a visit is customary in every region of the country.
8a2ff55d-1f20-5c07-9cc0-adf4d8569dfe.author: Noora Al Balushi

8a443b74-27a8-5e30-8c10-9c63d1d95b0c.name: Storage jar
8a443b74-27a8-5e30-8c10-9c63d1d95b0c.short_description: The jar belongs to a larger group of ceramic wares very popular during the Qajar dynasty, which illustrate the development of the blue-and-white style; its shape, originating in Mamluk Syria, was adopted in China and in Safavid Persia. Used for the storage of food, including olive oil, they were known in Romania as ‘mutton suet jars’, because of the underglaze staining and the particular smell they have retained to this day. Here, the elegant outlines of the motifs, notably of those on the shoulder, the variety of the multilobed shapes and the dynamic composition are quite remarkable. In the twentieth century, such jars were occasionally turned into lamp bases, as the perforation and the groove for electrical wire on the bottom appear to suggest.
8a443b74-27a8-5e30-8c10-9c63d1d95b0c.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
8a443b74-27a8-5e30-8c10-9c63d1d95b0c.bibliography: Dunca, M., *Islamic Art at the National Museum of Art of Romania*, Bucharest: National Museum of Art of Romania, 2015: 97, no. 42.
8a443b74-27a8-5e30-8c10-9c63d1d95b0c.author: Mircea Dunca

8acf2eac-8e23-5efc-a927-dea5fc1c4c75.name: Bowl with radial decoration.
8acf2eac-8e23-5efc-a927-dea5fc1c4c75.description:
This piece, the shape of which is taken from contemporary Chinese porcelain from the T’ang period (AD 618–906), is decorated with blue cobalt paint with a large motif in the shape of stylised petals. In the background there is a star-shaped polygon, the points of which are hatched. In the centre there is a motif known as ‘Solomon’s Seal’, an extremely common decorative element in Islamic art.  
The bowl, decorated in a simple but pleasing style, could be considered typical of Mesopotamian pieces painted in blue cobalt only on a creamy white base. This type is of particular interest as it represents one of the oldest examples in the Islamic world of an imitation of the much-valued Chinese porcelain that was sent in significant quantities to Egypt and Iraq by sea and to Persia by land via the Silk Route.  
The imitation porcelain was produced using a heavy lead-oxide glaze to which was added tin oxide as an opacifier. The result is a consistent creamy white layer decorated with blue cobalt in an Islamic style.
8acf2eac-8e23-5efc-a927-dea5fc1c4c75.short_description: This piece is particularly noteworthy for its decoration inspired by Chinese porcelain from the T’ang period, evidence of contact and trade between China and countries such as Egypt, Persia and Iraq along the Silk Route.
8acf2eac-8e23-5efc-a927-dea5fc1c4c75.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”

8acf2eac-8e23-5efc-a927-dea5fc1c4c75.method_for_datation: Dating has been suggested on the basis of type (see description for analysis).
8acf2eac-8e23-5efc-a927-dea5fc1c4c75.method_for_provenance: It should be seen as a typical example of Mesopotamian pieces painted only in cobalt blue on a creamy white base.

8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.name: Cock
8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.description:
It was difficult to make and fire large ceramic figures like this one and the sphinx (Isl 56) with the technology of the day. They easily crackled or simply collapsed. The manganese, turquoise and blue glazes as well as the carved decoration are typical of laqabi ware, but while the glazes on a horizontal surface are kept in place by the carved decoration, this is not the case on an upright object like this one.  
  
Although both animals must be considered mythical creatures, the artist managed to depict the watchful and aggressive cock with all of this animal’s natural characteristics.
8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.dates: AH 2nd half of the 6th / AD 2nd half of 12th century

8b4cfd0b-0435-5653-9d1f-66f91996e7f4.name: Group of 5 1/2 tiles, formerly in the shrine of Imamzada Yahya in Veramin, Iran
8b4cfd0b-0435-5653-9d1f-66f91996e7f4.short_description: Two cross tiles and three and a half star tiles are joined to form two panels. Each panel features a cross tile with a central quatrefoil flanked by arabesque bands down each side. Inscriptions are located around the perimeter. On both sides of the cross are stellate tiles. Each eight-sided tile has inscriptions around the edge. The interiors of the tiles are not identical, but each has scrolling arabesque forms. All of the star tiles are cut in half vertically.

8b90eb6b-ced6-5988-a13e-7f83f166a462.description: It is made of Lüleci clay. The base is in the shape of a circle and has a rounded centre. There is a Mevlevi headdress on the cover. It is decorated with flowers and parallel lines.

8bc18f76-661e-508b-92b4-e262c93b5aa3.name: Jar with turquoise-blue glaze
8bc18f76-661e-508b-92b4-e262c93b5aa3.description:
This small ceramic jar is decorated in a turquoise-blue glaze. As the glaze covers the outside as well as the inside, liquids such as water, vinegar, oil and so on could be transported and conserved in the vessel. The jar has a short neck with a wide flat rim, allowing for a lid or flexible cover of fabric or leather to be fastened to it. Two small handles, one of which has broken off, indicate the jar could have been carried or suspended.  
  
This type of turquoise-glazed pottery is very common on archaeological sites dating to the early Islamic period. These wares were produced in the workshops of Basra in southern Iraq and then exported all around the Abbasid Empire and beyond. Examples have been found around the Indian Ocean region, including East Africa, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.
8bc18f76-661e-508b-92b4-e262c93b5aa3.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century
