8c014da5-017c-55b6-8f07-95eca4b0b551.name: Stalactite element (*muqarbas*).
8c014da5-017c-55b6-8f07-95eca4b0b551.description:
*Muqarbas* are ornaments with an alveolate structure in the form of stalactites that are used to decorate domes or corbels, notably within Arab–Maghrebi architecture. The ceramic pieces in the shape of parallelepipeds that compose the whole consist of two parts: one plain, and the other formed by four vertical flutes. The cruciform base of each piece and the fluted part are covered by very light-coloured green enamel; traces of yellow appear on some of the sides. The pieces are assembled together as a pyramid, with cement on the plain parts whilst leaving the fluted parts visible.  
This type of stalactite was the first vestige that was brought to light in the Muslim West that can be attributed to the Hammadid Calif al-Mansur (r. AH 481–98 / AD 1089–1105).  
This *muqarbas* element was probably used to ornament the upper part of the exterior wall that looked onto the courtyard of the Dar al-Bahr; undoubtably, the decoration was applied.
8c014da5-017c-55b6-8f07-95eca4b0b551.short_description: This *muqarbas* is an ornamental wall-covering in the form of a four-level parallelepiped made up of a number of ceramic pieces and divided into two parts: one full and the other fluted, with traces of green enamel. The pieces are bound to one another using cement.
8c014da5-017c-55b6-8f07-95eca4b0b551.dimensions: Total height 41 cm, total length 21 cm, height of each piece 16 cm, dimension of each side of the pieces 5 cm.
8c014da5-017c-55b6-8f07-95eca4b0b551.method_for_datation: Stalactite found in the Dar al-Bahr of the Qal'at Bani Hammad (5th–6th / 11th–12th centuries), according to Kitab al-Istibsar: 'The Banu Hammad built some important constructions in the *qal'a*…including \[the palace\] known as Dar al-Bahr, at the centre of which was a vast basin'.
8c014da5-017c-55b6-8f07-95eca4b0b551.method_for_provenance: From de Beylié documents, which indicate that these stalactites were recovered from the foot of the wall looking over the southern side of the Dar al-Bahr courtyard.

8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.name: Cup/Bowl.
8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.description: An open vessel, hemispherical in shape. It has a slightly everted semi-circular rim, a foot-ring, and is made from light-coloured paste. The surfaces are enamelled with polychrome decoration. In the centre there is a simple and charming depiction of a lotus bulb which is a symbol of eternal life. This type of piece, from its shape, especially its ring foot, indicates Iberian production in imitation of an oriental style. In addition to the decorated base the rim of the object also has a discontinuous decorative wavy line interrupted in three places.
8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.short_description: Bowl made in the Iberian Peninsula based on oriental models. This AH 4th / AD 10th century piece has a quite naïve representation of a lotus bulb in its centre, a symbol of the eternity of life.
8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.dimensions: Height 4 cm, diameter (of rim) 15.6 cm, diameter (of base) 6.8 cm.
8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.method_for_datation: On the basis of its archaeological context and ceramics of a  similar style.
8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.method_for_provenance: Excavation carried out in Silves in the courtyard next to the cistern, directed by Mário Varela Gomes. Inventory number Silves 3, Q37 – C3.
8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.provenance: Courtyard adjacent to the cistern (now the site of Silves Municipal Archaeology Museum), Silves.
8c32bee4-0f68-56fc-9da8-59caa6e72f6d.obtention: Housed in the Silves Municipal Archaeology Museum after the excavation carried out in the 1980s.

8c95b79c-1630-52c9-b76b-3d50a79d2673.name: Dish.
8c95b79c-1630-52c9-b76b-3d50a79d2673.description: A circular stone-paste (fritware) dish that has a shallow well, an everted, flat rim and a low, circular foot. The well shows a young man wearing a green kaftan with a red belt, a blue undershirt and trousers, red boots and a green turban. In his raised right hand he holds a scroll. To the right of the figure is a tall spray of blue hyacinths and a red rose, to his left a blue iris and a blue hyacinth. There is additional floral detailing behind and above the figure, and the rim has a debased wave border executed in black. The underside of the dish is enhanced by an alternating pattern of three blue sprigs and three green sprigs with black outlines. A group of related dishes with similar figures survives, and it has been suggested that the man depicted may be the fictional young lover named Ibrahim, known from popular Ottoman literature. It has been suggested that such plates were produced on the Golden Horn in the 17th century on order from ordinary citizens. A very similar plate is in Château d’Ecouen, Musée de la Renaissance.
8c95b79c-1630-52c9-b76b-3d50a79d2673.short_description: Plates showing individual figures flanked by flowers mark the last phase of Iznik production for the popular market, starting in the early AH 11th / AD 17th century. It has been assumed that the man depicted may be a young unfulfilled lover named Ibrahim, known from popular Ottoman literature.
8c95b79c-1630-52c9-b76b-3d50a79d2673.dates: Hegira, early 11th century / AD early 17th century.
8c95b79c-1630-52c9-b76b-3d50a79d2673.method_for_datation: Plates like this one, showing individual figures flanked by flowers, mark the last phase of Iznik production starting in the early 11th / early 17th century.
8c95b79c-1630-52c9-b76b-3d50a79d2673.method_for_provenance: Stylistically related pieces are known to have been produced in Iznik during the early 11th / 17th century.
8c95b79c-1630-52c9-b76b-3d50a79d2673.obtention: Purchased from Bluett and Sons, London, in 1967.

8cac8019-a3fa-5a86-bdc9-c979d80c824f.name: Tankard
8cac8019-a3fa-5a86-bdc9-c979d80c824f.short_description:
Such stonepaste tankards with straight cylindrical bodies and applied flat angular handles were produced in the workshops of Iznik from the second half of the 16th century onwards. The specific shape most likely originated from Eastern European or Balkan leather, wooden or metal prototypes. Such tankards could probably serve both as vessels for drinks and as flower vases or interior decorations.  
The Khanenko Museum tankard is painted in fine free "calligraphic" manner with repetitive motifs of tall greyish blue tulips and two kinds of red flowers entwining with their naturally bent stems the body of the vessel. Two ribbons of a meandering pattern run around the rim and at the foot of the tankard. The style of the painting and its colour gamut suggest considering the piece was produced in the first half of the 17th century.
8cac8019-a3fa-5a86-bdc9-c979d80c824f.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by Yu. Miller (examination, 1961, date, origin).

8cd96f1a-abb6-5bcf-809b-2f3caf95df11.name: Bowl.
8cd96f1a-abb6-5bcf-809b-2f3caf95df11.description: An incised (sgraffiato) splashware (or slipware) bowl with green, brown and manganese glaze that was used popularly as ordinary tableware. Drawn with incised lines under the glaze there is a striking depiction of an archer, mounted on a rearing horse, and drawing his bow and arrow. The splashware technique with polychrome glaze was derived from Chinese T'ang pottery. The incised or sgraffiato technique was widespread in the medieval world – both Christian and Islamic – but relates more specifically to the sgraffiato Aqhkand ceramics produced near Tabriz in Iran in the 12th and 13th centuries. The Iranian product is characterised by a central bold motif with vigorous drawing of incised lines that would have been used to keep the glaze from running outside the design. The system was eventually carried to regions of Italy via Anatolia and then to the Byzantine provinces. Polychrome sgraffiato wares were also popular in Mamluk Egypt, where the technique was used for inscriptions and heraldic devices rather than for figurative designs.
8cd96f1a-abb6-5bcf-809b-2f3caf95df11.short_description: A bowl with incised, or *sgraffiato*, decoration of an archer on a rearing horse, drawing his bow and arrow. The technique of polychrome glaze splashed onto the surface was derived from Iranian ceramics, in their turn inspired by Chinese T’ang pottery.
8cd96f1a-abb6-5bcf-809b-2f3caf95df11.method_for_datation: The piece relates to wares discovered in excavations that can be dated to the AH 7th / AD 13th century, for example that found at Qal'at Jabar, where the archaeology belongs to the period AH 6th and 7th / AD 12th and 13th centuries only.
8cd96f1a-abb6-5bcf-809b-2f3caf95df11.method_for_provenance: The bowl was found in Aleppo and stylistic analysis confirms that it is from northern Syria.

8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.name: Cooking pot.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.description: Pot with vertical straight rim with flattened lip and external flange, circular mouth and cylindrical neck. The body is shaped like a truncated cone with sharp carination close to the base. It has two strap handles with a central ridge and convex base. There are horizontal incisions around the rim, neck and body and fire marks indicate that it was used in cooking. The object has been restored.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.short_description: Kitchen implement with an extremely simple form and very little decoration. This type of pot was found in an Almohad oven excavated in Mértola and appears almost exclusively in this region, which helps to identify it as a local product.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.dates: Early Hegira 7th century / early AD 13th century.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.dimensions: Height 21.5 cm, width 35 cm, diameter (of rim) 23.5 cm, diameter (of base) 19 cm.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.method_for_datation: It was dated to the Almohad period on the basis of stratigraphy, since it was found in the abandoned levels of one of the houses of the citadel vacated after the Christian conquest of Mértola in AH 635–6 / AD 1238.
8d436c70-8d15-5b93-b5b5-044a974ad60d.method_for_provenance: This type of pot has been found in an Almohad kiln excavated in Mértola and is almost exclusive to this region. This indicates that it was produced locally.

8d76b341-a93b-5d3a-8003-baf0071d63f7.name: Vase
8d76b341-a93b-5d3a-8003-baf0071d63f7.description: The Orientalism or Neo-Mudéjar style gave new light to old techniques like decorating ceramic with lustre; new ceramic artisans such as Pickman, in Seville, produced pieces in Neo-Mudéjar or Orientalist style. This piece won an award in one of the International Exhibitions. It reproduces the shape of the vase known as "The Alhambra vase" in lustre decoration.

8dfc5c9a-d7a1-5ca9-b551-ffaee845f356.name: Decorated ceramic wares from Asyut
8dfc5c9a-d7a1-5ca9-b551-ffaee845f356.short_description: In the second half of the 19th century, a cruise along the Nile was one of the highlights of a trip to Egypt for prosperous Europeans. In Asyut, en route from Cairo to Aswan, tourists purchased the typical products of the pottery metropolis. In hundreds of houses potters created wares for local demand, for tourism, and for export: incense vessels for the mosques of Asyut, flacons for rose water, or crocodile shaped foot rasps. Previously, vases from ancient Egypt influenced the form and decoration of silver and porcelain wares in Europe. At this time, silverware from France and Vienna began to serve as models for the potters in Asyut. In the wake of tourism and transnational trade, a mixture of local pottery art and European expectations was created. These new wares were sufficiently "Egyptian" to appear exotic, while remaining trusted and inexpensive to be brought home as  "typical" souvenirs. Today, no one in Asyut remembers the once flourishing pottery industry.
8dfc5c9a-d7a1-5ca9-b551-ffaee845f356.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.

8e119327-6e4c-5502-ac20-00d69c2be9c3.name: Calligraphy bowl
8e119327-6e4c-5502-ac20-00d69c2be9c3.short_description: This bowl presents a reddish clay body coated with white slip to create a uniform background ornamented with elegant calligraphy carrying an auspicious message in black *kufic* script.

8e2d8258-5733-5cff-a71b-a0329ecb34b2.name: Portable stove.
8e2d8258-5733-5cff-a71b-a0329ecb34b2.description: A portable stove consisting of an upper or fire chamber, a grate and a lower chamber or ash collector. The upper chamber has a vertical rim or moulding into which another object is fitted, a circular mouth, a cylindrical body with sharp carination, holes to ventilate the fire and two vertical strap handles with a conical protuberance at the top. The grate is convex with circular openings between the upper chamber and the ash collector, which is almost cylindrical with an oval opening and flat base. It is decorated with a cord of impressed fingernail marks at the point of carination, three parallel wavy incised lines and white paint on a reddish background which traces interlacing vertical and horizontal lines. The object has many fire marks from its use as a portable stove for cooking or heating. The object has been restored.
8e2d8258-5733-5cff-a71b-a0329ecb34b2.short_description: Kitchen utensil from the Almohad era, probably produced locally. The stove consists of an upper (or fire) chamber, a grill and a lower (or ash) chamber. This type of item has been used up to the present day in this region.
8e2d8258-5733-5cff-a71b-a0329ecb34b2.dates: Hegira early 7th century / AD early 13th century.
8e2d8258-5733-5cff-a71b-a0329ecb34b2.dimensions: Height 22.2 cm, width 33.5 cm, diameter (of mouth) 29.2 cm, diameter (of base) 15.6 cm.
8e2d8258-5733-5cff-a71b-a0329ecb34b2.method_for_datation: It was dated to the Almohad period on the basis of stratigraphy, since it was found in the abandoned levels of one of the houses of the citadel vacated after the Christian conquest of Mértola in AH 635–6 / AD 1238.
8e2d8258-5733-5cff-a71b-a0329ecb34b2.method_for_provenance: This type of object was usually traded locally. Moreover it is a very common form in the region, with technical and formal characteristics typical of items produced in Mértola.

8e67c517-318a-50e5-bf21-5fd465b11ddd.name: Nine-tiled panel
8e67c517-318a-50e5-bf21-5fd465b11ddd.short_description: The panel reproduces the transversal section, stylised, of the Mosque of the Prophet in Medina. Below the upper tier, a central cuspid arch and two lateral arches supported by four elegant spiral columns, crowned by a crescent. Three mosque lamps are suspended in correspondence to the centre of the vaults of the arches. In the middle, a central scroll displays the inscription "Glory to Allah".

8ebb69af-e6c3-5fed-b470-2f450f6466b1.name: Bowl
8ebb69af-e6c3-5fed-b470-2f450f6466b1.short_description:
The bowl displays the characteristic polychrome decoration of in and overglaze colours, which were occasionally expertly finished off by partial gilding after the second firing. This technique is known as *minaʿi*, the Persian word for enamel. Alternatively, the term “seven colours” (Pers. *haft rang*) is used.  
  
The base of the bowl is dominated by an enthroned ruler sitting with legs crossed on a low throne, complete with a backrest. On his flanks, two attendants who are traditionally interpreted as ministers or counsellors accompany him. Symmetrically arranged peacocks, symbolizing the magnificence of the ruler, occupy the free area above and below this group. Meanwhile, the wall of the vessel presents twelve seated men, some of whom have recognisable attributes like falcons and a tambourine whilst others appear to be engaged in conversation. Courtly entertainment like music, the reciting of poetry, drinking of wine, and hunting had been part of classical courtly iconography since the seventh century. Such iconography was not only witnessed in Iran but throughout the entire Islamic world and further influenced secular Christian art in the Mediterranean region.
8ebb69af-e6c3-5fed-b470-2f450f6466b1.dates: Hegira end or 6th-beginning of 7th century / AD end of 12th-beginning of 13th century
8ebb69af-e6c3-5fed-b470-2f450f6466b1.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar dated objects
8ebb69af-e6c3-5fed-b470-2f450f6466b1.method_for_provenance: By comparison with stylistically similar works

8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.name: Strainer.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.description:
The greyish earthenware fragment showing openwork at the centre was part of a jug with strainer. The slightly convex strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the vessel and was intended to protect the stored liquid from pollution and insects. Its design is inscribed in a circle and shows a quadruped passing to the left. The motif is set against a filigree background of rhombs. The major outlines of the animal, usually called a gazelle, are incised into the material. The remaining surface of the body is left plain. A striated zigzag line between two circles surrounds the quadruped.  
Decorated strainers are known from excavations of sites dated to the AH 2nd–9th / AD 8th–15th century. Strainers of the Fatimid period, which was the high point of their development, show not only the most varied patterns, but also the most elaborated compositions and the finest execution. As well as gazelle-like quadrupeds, other zoomorphic motifs such as elephants, lions, hares, birds or fish are depicted on the strainers.  
The strainers are only small fragments of vessels, but they call attention to themselves. One reason might be the unexpected combination of simple earthenware, mostly undecorated on the outside, with costly designs inside the neck of the jugs. Another might be that the potters created a highly aesthetic form for a simple utilitarian object. The complex patterns of the openwork carried out within small areas reveal the skills of the craftsmen.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.short_description: Earthenware fragment which was integrated in a vessel as a strainer. The latticework displays a quadruped, possibly a gazelle, passing to the left. The strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the earthenware vessel to protect the stored liquid from insects and pollution.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.method_for_datation: A strainer also showing a gazelle was excavated at al-Fustat and dated according to numismatic evidence of undisturbed loci to the 5th / 11th century.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.method_for_provenance: Similar strainers were excavated at al-Fustat and their place of manufacture ascribed to the city. According to F. R. Martin, this strainer comes from excavations at al-Fustat.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.obtention: Purchased from the collection of the Swedish art dealer and art historian F. R. Martin in 1921.

8f458da9-54d7-5f9f-b148-b999f3b4cd27.name: Ablution Ewer
8f458da9-54d7-5f9f-b148-b999f3b4cd27.short_description:
Geometric patterns and floral motifs in red and liquid gold adorn this white porcelain ewer from Ottoman Turkey. The bird-shaped body is reminiscent of similar pieces from the Umayyad dynasty. These types of vessels would pour water, often scented, for ablution purposes or to clean guests’ hands before a feast.  
  
While borrowing elements such as flowers, the paisley leaf and fruit from the Iznik art, a craftsman likely designed the ewer for the Hungarian market. With growing interest in Asian and Ottoman ceramics in 19th century Europe, craftsmen from Italy, France and Hungary attempted to imitate Iznik pottery. Meanwhile, Turkish artisans wished to suit the European palate, tailoring the typical Ottoman production.  
  
This ewer embodies the lavish Ottoman trend of blending influences from China, the Italian Renaissance, the Balkans and Iznik style. From this imitation of art through mutual admiration, new objects were created. Their unique interplay of styles is studied until today.

8f8ea92e-671e-5c67-8e28-151c8dfb79b3.name: Dish with stylised bird.
8f8ea92e-671e-5c67-8e28-151c8dfb79b3.description: A deep dish with curved sides and a flat base, decorated with a large figure of a stylised bird with filiform, almost plant-like, long wings. The body is rendered using a series of rectangular panels filled with thick zigzag lines. The base of the dish is mostly decorated with large flowering bushes, palmettes and clusters of small dots within a frame consisting of a fringed motif that runs below a brim painted in solid lustre.
8f8ea92e-671e-5c67-8e28-151c8dfb79b3.short_description: The decoration of this deep dish is typical of late Valencian production, characterised by flowering bushes, large birds and red lustre.
8f8ea92e-671e-5c67-8e28-151c8dfb79b3.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
8f8ea92e-671e-5c67-8e28-151c8dfb79b3.dates: Hegira end of 12th century / AD end of 18th century.
8f8ea92e-671e-5c67-8e28-151c8dfb79b3.method_for_provenance: The dish belongs to late Valencian production in the 12th / 18th century characterised by specific decorative motifs such as the carnation plants and large birds, as well as a vivid red lustre.

8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.name: Hanging lamp.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.description: A ceramic lamp with bulbous body and flaring neck, painted blue-and-white. The neck bears an inscription in angular *kufic* script between friezes of geometric knotted designs. Small split-palmette tendrils emanate from some of the letters. The words are illegible but may derive from the phrase 'wa-asu Sahwan' ('and they grieved distractedly'). Around the main body is a scroll of lotus blossoms with the distinctive 'tadpole' leaf common to a number of blue-and-white ceramics of this period. The row of elongated pointed panels around the shoulder of the lamp is a design that is also found on Ottoman silverware, and a motif that recalls Balkan silverware. This presents an interesting example of the innovative exchange both artistically and culturally that saw shapes, designs and patterns shift between different materials and between the cultures of Europe and Asia.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.short_description: Around the neck of this blue-and-white ceramic lamp is a *kufic* inscription of illegible words. Although modelled on a glass prototype, this ceramic lamp would clearly give little light. Its function must have been more symbolic or decorative than functional.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.method_for_datation: It is thought that this lamp came from the Turbe of Bayezid II (d. 917 / 1512), because of its close resemblance to a group of four lamps made for this building.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the main centre of production for ceramics of this quality in Ottoman Turkey.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by John Henderson 1878.

900e462b-7bd7-52b5-bff8-75c6f5cccaf4.name: Vase.
900e462b-7bd7-52b5-bff8-75c6f5cccaf4.description: A magnificent flower-vase with a circular body, flaring foot and tall, flaring neck with curved arms. The construction of this type of vase is complicated and very few have survived. Covering the entire vase is a vine-leaf pattern painted in blue and brown lustre. Displayed in a roundel on the main body is the coat of arms of Piero 'Il Gottoso' ('the Gouty') de Medici (AD 1414-69), or his son, Lorenzo 'Il Magnifico' ('the Magnificent', AD 1449-92). This comprises seven circular shapes, one of which is painted with lilies, the symbol of the Kings of France that was added to the Medici arms in AD 1465. On the reverse of the vase is another roundel with the Medici symbol of a diamond and gold ring, painted in gold lustre, symbolising eternity, and two feathers. Lustre was made by applying iridescent metallic decoration to twice-fired pottery, which was then fired for a third time. This technique was first introduced to craftsmen in Malaga, southern Spain. Throughout the AH 9th / AD 15th century Valencia was a thriving centre of lustre-ware manufacture; Valencian wares soon becoming renowned throughout Europe. Italy had a particularly active trade with Spain and also began to manufacture luxury ceramics in direct competition with Valencian wares. Although largely a Christian area, both Christians and Muslims were said to have been employed as potters during this period.
900e462b-7bd7-52b5-bff8-75c6f5cccaf4.short_description: A spectacular vase covered in a repeat vine-leaf pattern in blue and brown lustre. On one side of the body is a roundel with the coat of arms belonging to the Italian Medici family. On the reverse of the vase is another roundel with a Medici symbol of a diamond and gold ring with two feathers.
900e462b-7bd7-52b5-bff8-75c6f5cccaf4.method_for_datation: The coat of arms belongs to Piero de Medici (816–73 / 1414–69). In 869 / 1465 King Louis IX of France granted Piero the honour of including the lilies of France in the Medici arms. Lilies are included in the design of this vase which means it must have been produced between 869 / 1465 and Piero's death in 873 / 1469.
900e462b-7bd7-52b5-bff8-75c6f5cccaf4.method_for_provenance: The shape and technique are typical of ceramic wares produced in Valencia during the 9th / 15th century. Large quantities of lustre-wares were exported to Italy, particularly to the wealthy families of Tuscany. Furthermore, during the 9th / 15th century Valencia was the major centre for the production of ceramics in Spain.
900e462b-7bd7-52b5-bff8-75c6f5cccaf4.obtention: Part of the Godman Bequest to the British Museum in 1983.

90313d34-f14e-568c-b0bd-898e9a4aef37.name: Bowl
90313d34-f14e-568c-b0bd-898e9a4aef37.description: This bowl was made using the *mina'i* enamel technique. Patterns and figures are depicted in cobalt blue, brown, green, red and black on a white primed surface. The centre of the bowl depicts a round-faced, almond-eyed, human figure with arched brows holding a goblet while seated cross-legged on a throne. On each side of this figure is a person standing with folded arms.

9143cd75-c9e3-5465-8800-1db8617ff642.name: Dish.
9143cd75-c9e3-5465-8800-1db8617ff642.description: An example of an early blue-and-white Iznik 'grape dish', the design for which is based on a 15th-century Chinese prototype of three bunches of grapes amid vine leaves. The original Chinese porcelain designs had grapes and vine leaves surrounded by 12 sprays of flowers; this Iznik example has only 11 sprays of flowers. It is also interesting to note that the Iznik potter has chosen not to copy the original early 15th-century Ming-style wave pattern on the rim, but has used instead a 14th-century Yuan-style rim. The potters of Iznik had access to, and were influenced by, Chinese porcelains. This was especially so after Sultan Salim the Grim (r. AH 917–26 / AD 1512–20) conquered Tabriz in Iran, Damascus in Syria, and Cairo in Egypt, where he obtained large quantities of Chinese ceramics which were brought back to the Ottoman capital, Istanbul, between AH 919 and 922 / AD 1514 and 1517.
9143cd75-c9e3-5465-8800-1db8617ff642.short_description: Although it may look Chinese, this dish was made in the town of Iznik in Turkey during the AH 10th / AD 16th century. The Ottomans loved Chinese ceramics, especially the blue and white ones. They commissioned the potters of Iznik to reproduce these designs with some adaptations to suit Ottoman taste.
9143cd75-c9e3-5465-8800-1db8617ff642.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: examples of the original Chinese versions of the Yuan- and Ming-period dishes survive, and examples are to be found in the ceramic collections of the Topkapi Palace, Istanbul.
9143cd75-c9e3-5465-8800-1db8617ff642.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

915b2a0a-3698-5292-bb7d-21c5904180f8.name: Jar.
915b2a0a-3698-5292-bb7d-21c5904180f8.description: A virtually undamaged jar with a swelling body and a narrow neck with an everted rim. Except for the foot-ring the whole jar is glazed and decorated with lustre painting. The lustre decoration begins about a third of the way up from the foot and is divided into horizontal bands. The bottom band features interlaced ribbons painted in reserve; above them, a wider band has heart-shaped palmettes. At the top is a band which displays five fish, their scales and other details scratched through the lustre to appear in white. The neck is decorated with a band of triangles and dots. The jar’s decoration is reminiscent of Coptic art: fish are a traditionally Christian motif, and motifs using repeated fish (and birds) are found in early Coptic textiles.
915b2a0a-3698-5292-bb7d-21c5904180f8.short_description: A large vase with extensive decoration in lustre, including a band of prominent fish around the shoulder. The presence of the fish may indicate that the vase was made for use in the Coptic Christian community, as early Coptic textiles feature similar repetitions of fish-motifs.
915b2a0a-3698-5292-bb7d-21c5904180f8.method_for_datation: A very similar jar (although with no figural decoration) was found in Fustat in 1966 and was dated to the first quarter of the 11th century.
915b2a0a-3698-5292-bb7d-21c5904180f8.method_for_provenance: The object was found at Fustat (old Cairo).
915b2a0a-3698-5292-bb7d-21c5904180f8.obtention: In 1910 the art collector Dikran Garabed Kelekian placed his collection of Islamic ceramics on loan to the V&A.  Fifteen of the finest pieces, including this jar, were purchased by the Museum (with the assistance of the National Art Collections Fund) after Kelekian’s death.

925c28b8-4c6f-550b-8808-705ed2594359.short_description: The centre of the bowl is decorated with fine precise motifs in black under a brilliant glaze and underlined in blue.  An elegant inscription runs along the inner rim.

92d942fe-2bc5-5d4f-9f93-e15c911e7d1c.name: Footed bowl.
92d942fe-2bc5-5d4f-9f93-e15c911e7d1c.description: An incised, circular earthenware bowl with steep flaring sides, a rimless lip and a flat base that is supported by a high, splayed foot. Inside the bowl, just below the rim, are fish alternating with brief inscriptions in *thuluth* script. On the outside, underneath the rim, is a scroll band and beneath this, above the foot, is a pseudo-epigraphic frieze. This bowl is a typical example of *sgraffito* earthenware produced in Mamluk Cairo, being a rather crude utilitarian ware, the reddish body of which is covered with a white slip with *sgraffito* decoration under a yellow, or sometimes green, glaze. Additional elements of the design, particularly epigraphic details and blazons, are generally highlighted in brown slip, an approach that echoes, conceptually at least, the metal inlay on contemporary brass vessels. Many pieces of this type have been attributed to one particular contemporary potter named Sharaf al-Abawani.
92d942fe-2bc5-5d4f-9f93-e15c911e7d1c.short_description: The potters of Mamluk Cairo produced much utilitarian ware from coarse red clay, a white slip through which the decoration was carved and a yellow-green glaze. Epigraphic details and blazons are often highlighted in brown slip, an approach that echoes the metal inlay on contemporary brass vessels.
92d942fe-2bc5-5d4f-9f93-e15c911e7d1c.dates: Hegira, mid-8th century / AD mid-14th century.
92d942fe-2bc5-5d4f-9f93-e15c911e7d1c.method_for_datation: This bowl belongs to a well-known and chronologically defined group of Mamluk ceramics that date to around the mid-8th / 14th century.
92d942fe-2bc5-5d4f-9f93-e15c911e7d1c.method_for_provenance: Items of this type are known to have been produced at Fustat in Cairo during the Mamluk period. Large quantities of complete vessels and sherds are held by museums worldwide and many sherds have been found at Fustat.
92d942fe-2bc5-5d4f-9f93-e15c911e7d1c.obtention: Purchased by NMS from Spink and Son Ltd, London, in 1981.

92faf071-041f-5e86-a8af-4013003f481e.name: Water jar, with one handle
92faf071-041f-5e86-a8af-4013003f481e.description: The upper section of this water jar, discovered in one of the houses at Murwab, was found during the Qatari-French Mission's excavation in 2007. This kitchenware features a globular body paired with a high, straight neck. The neck is adorned with incised horizontal lines, and the lip is simple with a rounded end. Crafted from red clay, the surface is covered with a thicker, darker red slip, albeit significantly damaged over most of the surface.

934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.name: Mosque lamp.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.description:
A large ceramic mosque lamp with a high flaring neck and a bulbous, almost pear-shaped body on a low foot. The lamp is divided into three registers by thin white bands. In the top register, around the neck, a Qur'anic inscription features part of the famous Light Verse (24: 35), which, because it likens the light of God to a lamp, was often used on mosque lamps. The lower two registers are decorated with floral motifs on the body which are painted under the glaze in turquoise, cobalt-blue, black, and red. Curiously, the floral motifs, most noticeably the large bisected quatrefoil motifs in red, do not line up between the middle and lower registers; perhaps the painter was working from a design not originally meant for an object of this shape. Around the middle of the lamp are large bosses alternating with handles, one of which is now missing. The loss of one handle may be the reason that the suspension chains have been riveted directly to the lamp's body.  
  
This 'lamp' – which would have shed no light, being made of ceramic, and is thus clearly meant to be symbolic – is reputed to have been made for the mosque complex in Istanbul built by Sultan Süleyman 'the Magnificent'. This complex was an important act of architectural patronage which provided a major stimulus to the Ottoman ceramic industry, centred at Iznik. One result was the addition of a brilliant red to the colour range of Ottoman ceramics. The clearly tentative quality of the red on this lamp, the thin and uneven application of the pigment, indicates that it comes from the early phases of the Ottoman potters' experimentation with the colour.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.short_description: A ceramic ‘lamp’ with a bulbous body and flaring neck. Although clearly meant to hang from a ceiling like a regular lamp, it would have shed no light, and is thus clearly meant to be symbolic. It is reputed to have been made for the Süleymaniye mosque complex, which was completed in AH 963 / AD 1557.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.method_for_datation: The lamp is supposed to have been made for the mosque complex built by Sultan Süleyman in around 963 / 1557.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

93aea7f2-ded4-548e-b4d4-d89f40968a55.name: Tile panel.
93aea7f2-ded4-548e-b4d4-d89f40968a55.description:
The rectangular panel is composed of square tiles dominated by a white and brown horseshoe-shaped arch (*mihrab* – prayer niche) with a yellow half-moon on it. The arch is supported by two columns, decorated with a zigzag pattern in turquoise, opaque yellow and light blue, each standing on a base and with a capital. A dense, symmetrical floral design fills the area under the arch emerging from a large footed bowl supplemented by a second smaller one and a vase above. The bowl is flanked symmetrically with cypress-like trees with half-moons on the top and two birds beside the foot. Two other birds are shown on the rim of the large bowl from which also spring two sprays of flowers. From the centre of the vase a fantastic composite-blossom emerges with the stems of other flowers on its point. The sprays of flowers growing out from the stems of the central axis fill the field within the arch. Two sprays with blossoms like carnations and peonies and two serrated-edged leaves in combination with sprays of white flowers take up the remaining area under the arch. The spandrels are symmetrically filled with half-palmette motifs and scrollwork in reverse against a blue background. Although the potters used a standardised repertoire of decorative elements such as the *mihrab*, vase motifs and symmetrical composed flowers, the decoration of these tile panels is individual.  
In the AH 11th and 12th / AD 17th and 18th centuries, faience (glazed coloured earthenware) became the dominant element of Tunisian architectural decoration. After a first firing the tiles are covered with an opaque white tin glaze. The mineral pigments used for the polychrome decoration are applied over the dried glaze. In a second firing, glaze and pigments are melted together. The colours used – antimony yellow, copper turquoise, cobalt-blue and manganese brown – are typical for faience, suitable for withstanding high temperatures.
93aea7f2-ded4-548e-b4d4-d89f40968a55.short_description: Rectangular panel of faience tiles painted with a horseshoe-shaped arch. A dense floral design, emerging from a footed bowl, fills the area under the arch. In the AH 11th–12th / AD 17th–18th centuries, faience (glazed coloured earthenware) became the dominant element of Tunisian architectural decoration.
93aea7f2-ded4-548e-b4d4-d89f40968a55.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
93aea7f2-ded4-548e-b4d4-d89f40968a55.method_for_datation: This tile panel shows close similarities to panels made by a faience atelier working from about the mid-12th–mid-13th / mid-18th–mid-19th centuries.
93aea7f2-ded4-548e-b4d4-d89f40968a55.method_for_provenance: The style of decoration was characteristic of ateliers in Tunis.
93aea7f2-ded4-548e-b4d4-d89f40968a55.obtention: There is no information about acquisition.

93c26b61-bb1e-54cf-b39b-ecc84bcbe143.name: Bowl with polo player
93c26b61-bb1e-54cf-b39b-ecc84bcbe143.short_description: The bowl depicts a mounted equestrian figure, along with birds and flowers, on a yellow background. To the left of the figure, along the rim, there is a pseudo-*kufic* inscription. The bowl’s decoration in yellow, green, and black is typical of Nishapur buff ware. Representations of similar figures are often linked to a Sassanid hunting motif, but the image could also depict a polo player. Later, in the Seljuq period, representations of polo were frequently used in both lustre and *mina'i* ware.
93c26b61-bb1e-54cf-b39b-ecc84bcbe143.method_for_datation: By comparison with other objects excavated in Nishapur.

93c34ced-5cb1-5c21-8d26-5401ec1708ee.name: Coping from a well.
93c34ced-5cb1-5c21-8d26-5401ec1708ee.description:
An octagonal coping of a well, in green-enamelled ceramic. The embossed decoration is distributed over five registers that extend above a base that juts out slightly and a remaining segment of edge. The lower register features arches adorned with cells that are bordered on three sides by rosettes. The second register is embellished with rosettes that have four petals each and are surrounded by foliage, forming a square, the corners of which are decorated with flowers. The third register is replete with interlacing foliage that end in flowers. The fourth and fifth registers are decorated with palmettes that have diverging lobes.  
This type of well was often used in houses.
93c34ced-5cb1-5c21-8d26-5401ec1708ee.short_description: Octagonal ceramic well-coping painted beneath a green glaze with a protruding base and the remains of a rim. The stamped plant decoration is divided between five sections. This object was placed above wells inside houses.

93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.name: Incantation bowl
93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.description: The bowl is inscribed in Mandean script, in Aramaic Mandean dialect. The text spirals from the bottom of the bowl about fifteen times around. The beginning of the text is unreadable because of a crystal deposits and blackening. The name of the sponsor, the beneficiary of these incantations, which is typically stated at the beginning of the text, remains unknown here. The remaining lines consist essentially of a repetition of names of demons exorcised by linked formulas, including the female demon Lilith, her ancestors (“all her families and lineages”), and her offspring. The Aramaic communities of Mesopotamia are heirs to ancient beliefs dating back to the Akkadian and even Sumerian texts, according to which demons were of an inexhaustible variety. The Mandean, because of his dualistic faith, believes in evil spirits whose harmful actions he dreads. Magic is therefore an essential aspect of his religious life. This practice, consisting in burying the cups thus inscribed at the four corners of the house, was widely diffused among the various religious communities of Mesopotamia until the Muslim conquest and beyond.

94f76ace-8af6-5ec8-aec6-d15a08b2f250.name: *Albarello*
94f76ace-8af6-5ec8-aec6-d15a08b2f250.short_description: This *albarello*, or pharmacist vessel, is decorated with vertical blue stripes. The transparent, colourless glaze applied after painting has turned into a patchy, mother-of-pearl layer. The simple stripe decoration was very popular during the period in Iran. Although *albarello* has a Latin root, the shape originated in the Middle East and was introduced to Europe sometime around the 15th century. *Albarelli* were used as both functional and decorative objects in traditional pharmacies. The jars were generally sealed with a piece of parchment or leather tied with cord.
94f76ace-8af6-5ec8-aec6-d15a08b2f250.dates: Hegira late 6th century-early 7th century / AD late 12th-early 13th century

94fe0097-4bb5-5659-a22f-0a97faeb593d.name: Jug
94fe0097-4bb5-5659-a22f-0a97faeb593d.short_description:
Towards the end of the Hegira 5th (AD 11th) century, Egyptian potters tried out a new material that revolutionised ceramic production in the Middle East: they mixed a small amount of the traditional white potter’s clay with quartz and glass powder (the so-called frit) and obtained a glass-hard, sugar-white body. The effect of this technique was a quality of ceramique more akin to that of Chinese porcelain. From Egypt, the new material reached Persia via Syria in the first half of the Hegira 6th (AD 12th) century and gradually replaced the traditional clays. The turquoise-coloured glaze was also new and related to the new material quartz frit.  
  
The novel properties of this innovative material quickly led Iranian potters to experiment with it, and the large jug with a handle bears witness to this burst of creativity. Its melon-shaped body, the thin handle and the beak-shaped spout are elements that could not be made in ordinary clay. Similar jugs made of metal, often copper or brass, served as models.
94fe0097-4bb5-5659-a22f-0a97faeb593d.dates: Hegira end or 6th-beginning of 7th century / AD end of 12th-beginning of 13th century
94fe0097-4bb5-5659-a22f-0a97faeb593d.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar dated objects

9550bb5f-dcd9-54bc-a521-b59609c24581.name: The Tavira Vase.
9550bb5f-dcd9-54bc-a521-b59609c24581.description: Vessel made from red clay.The sides, sloping slightly outwards, become thicker at the top to form an invisible channel through which water could pass after having been poured into a kind of funnel-neck which stands out clearly from the overall piece. The water would run through the channel and then be poured into the interior of the vase through eight of the 14 figurines standing around its edge.Two armed and mounted knights, accompanied by a dismounted archer, stand on either side of a woman also on horseback. Then come two musicians, who would have been part of a quartet, now incomplete. This set of human figures was followed by five animals, four of which remain: a bovine, a camel, a deer or gazelle, another camel and a lion. A flock of doves is perched on the funnel-neck.This is an extraordinary piece of popular art probably representing the ceremonial abduction that took place before a wedding ceremony, in which the animals are intended to be an allegory of good fortune for the couple. The water coming from the eight gargoyles would be for a shrub planted in the vase, possibly basil as this plant was associated with the cult of love in Iberian and Mediterranean traditions.
9550bb5f-dcd9-54bc-a521-b59609c24581.short_description: This pot, an example of popular art, represents the ceremonial abduction enacted before a wedding ceremony. The human figures (woman, crossbowman, knights and musicians) are accompanied by animals, intended as a good omen for the newly weds. The pot would have contained a plant.
9550bb5f-dcd9-54bc-a521-b59609c24581.dates: Hegira end of 5th or beginning of 6th century / AD end of 11th or beginning of 12th century.
9550bb5f-dcd9-54bc-a521-b59609c24581.method_for_datation: By stratigraphic references and typological comparison with related artefacts.
9550bb5f-dcd9-54bc-a521-b59609c24581.method_for_provenance: Collected during archaeological excavations directed by Maria and Manuel Maia, near the Porta de D. Manuel in Tavira.

95b8eda9-e7cf-5537-afd3-f65ff7d2e85d.name: Lajvardina bowl
95b8eda9-e7cf-5537-afd3-f65ff7d2e85d.short_description: At the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries a new type of luxurious enamel-painted ceramics called '*lajvardina*" emerged in Ilkhanid Iran. The Persian word "*lajvard*" means "lapis lazuli", which pointed in this case to the specific deep blue colour of the vessel background provided by cobalt-based glaze. The bowl, presumably made in Kashan, presents an impressive sample of this showy and costly technique. The polychromous decor of floral motifs arranged overglaze in a cross pattern is supplemented by the elements of gold foil. The hemispherical shape of the bowl reveals artistic influence of Yuan porcelain ware of China.
95b8eda9-e7cf-5537-afd3-f65ff7d2e85d.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by V. Krachkovskaya (1926, origin), Leon Guzalian (1953, date),  H. Rudyk (publication, 2017, specified date and origin).

9649e657-d081-5990-b3dd-ee2b6d2ee696.name: Washing Set (Pitcher and Wash Basin) with Chamber Pot
9649e657-d081-5990-b3dd-ee2b6d2ee696.description:
The 19th century witnessed major changes in the political, social, cultural, and economic spheres in Serbia. The uprisings against centuries-long Ottoman rule, in 1804 and 1815, led to the enactment of Sultan Mahmud II’s hatt-i sharif in 1830, the establishment of the autonomous Principality of Serbia, Serbia’s full independence, confirmed at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and the proclamation of the Kingdom of Serbia in 1882. The transition from a feudal to a capitalist society was accompanied by cultural pluralism, which implied the establishment of new cultural models with a local Ottoman-Balkan imprint, as well as the adoption of cultural models common in bourgeois Europe. In this context, the items imported from Central and Western Europe got a significant place in everyday life and the visual culture of Serbia. While European influences in Serbia signified a gradual breaking up with Ottoman traditions, at the same time, due to the extensive reforms that permeated all spheres of society, they also significantly shaped the visual culture of the Ottoman Empire.  
The washing set with a chamber pot originates from the renowned ceramics production centre of Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire, England. This area was home to a collective of workshops that produced majolica, stoneware, and porcelain. One of these manufacturers was S. Fielding & Co. Adapting to fashion trends and market demands, the company exported high-quality ceramic pieces worldwide from 1870 to 1982.  
The wash set preserved in the Museum of Applied Art, and created in the Historicist style, is characterized by its subtle decoration and the combination of a green pastel ground with floral motifs. A floral garland follows a restrained black line running along the central section of each vessel. The black band is edged with delicate touches of gilding. On the bottom of the pieces is the mark of the workshop: Crown Devon, Fieldings, Stoke-on-Trent, England, indicating that the set is part of the Crown Devon collection, which was produced from 1880, while from 1912 onward, the items were made in series.

96cf4210-b3bc-5e9b-8016-56c054beba7c.name: Jug.
96cf4210-b3bc-5e9b-8016-56c054beba7c.description: A medium-sized jug that has a spherical-shaped body and a small 'S-shaped' handle. The body rests on a small, unglazed, foot. The jug is typically decorated with simple horizontal zigzag bands, painted with black pigment on the body of the unglazed vessel, and then glazed with a transparent turquoise glaze. Raqqa was one of two major pottery-production centres in Ayyubid Syria, the other being Rusafah. Raqqa had a number of pottery workshops, which produced a range of ceramics including lustre-painted, relief-moulded and underglaze painted vessels.
96cf4210-b3bc-5e9b-8016-56c054beba7c.short_description: The black decoration under the transparent turquoise glaze is typical of ceramics made in Raqqa during the Ayyubid period. Raqqa was one of two major production centres in Syria, the other being Rusafah. Both were located near the river Euphrates.
96cf4210-b3bc-5e9b-8016-56c054beba7c.dimensions: Height 15 cm, diameter (of rim) 6.5 cm, diameter (of base) 7 cm.
96cf4210-b3bc-5e9b-8016-56c054beba7c.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis and analysis of the material composition of the clay body, which resembles in type that typical of Raqqa pottery.
96cf4210-b3bc-5e9b-8016-56c054beba7c.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

98bd70b5-7a3c-5e69-8bad-62f096449b47.name: Jug
98bd70b5-7a3c-5e69-8bad-62f096449b47.short_description:
This jug has a straight, slightly flared body with a clear carination above the foot and a sharply bent shoulder. The high, narrow neck is provided with a long raising tubular spout. A slim handle with a thumb knob connects the rim with the shoulder of the jug. The form but also the structured body with regular vertical grooves and the applications on the neck are derived from metalwork jugs. Especially the suggested ring-knob is an imitation of rings on metalwork jugs.  
Slightly smaller jugs with similar neck and spout but globular body are frequently produced in earthenware with a simple brown or turquoise glaze. These belong to the simple mass-produced wares for daily use, as water jugs for example.  
The fritware material allows a more refined elaboration of the appliqué details as well as of the object shape. Although the general appearance of our object is sober, the few details such as the grooved body and the applications on the neck are thoroughly worked out and may have belonged to the fine equipment of a household.

98bd70b5-7a3c-5e69-8bad-62f096449b47.method_for_datation: Similar jugs in earthenware were produced from the 10th to 12th century. Simple comparable.

9912e075-4003-59ba-9165-47ab7ab42398.name: Dish.
9912e075-4003-59ba-9165-47ab7ab42398.description:
An Iznik ceramic dish decorated with a cruciform arrangement of tomato-red, blue and green floral clusters surrounding a central rosette and alternating with brackets of arabesque decoration. The outer rim of the dish is decorated with a Chinese-style wave-and-rock border. The brilliant tomato- red used on this dish (painted under the glaze) has a distinctive body and rises slightly once fired; this gives Iznik dishes like this one a distinctive texture. This dish belongs to the third phase of Iznik pottery manufacture, which lasted from AH 956 to 1111 / AD 1550 to 1700 and which saw the development of new techniques, such as underglaze painting, and a greater variety of colours, such as the brilliant tomato-red, known also as Armenian bole.  
  
Iznik ware of this period became so very popular in several regions of the Ottoman Empire and some parts of Europe, that for a long time it was mistakenly attributed by European scholars to potters on the Island of Rhodes. This was mainly due to the extensive use of Iznik dishes in decorating the walls of Rhodian homes, thus giving the false impression that the ceramics had been made locally.
9912e075-4003-59ba-9165-47ab7ab42398.short_description: This Iznik ceramic dish with its brilliant underglaze red colour belongs to the third period of Iznik pottery production, which was very popular in several regions of the Ottoman Empire and parts of Europe, including the island of Rhodes where such dishes were used to decorated domestic walls.
9912e075-4003-59ba-9165-47ab7ab42398.dates: Hegira last quarter of the 10th century / AD around 1575–1580.
9912e075-4003-59ba-9165-47ab7ab42398.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the distinctive texture of the brilliant underglaze bole-red indicates that this dish was definitely produced by an Iznik workshop in the third period of Iznik pottery manufacture, which lasted from AH 956 to 1111 / AD 1550 to 1700. The style and layout of the floral decoration is also typically Iznik.
9912e075-4003-59ba-9165-47ab7ab42398.method_for_provenance: The distinctive texture of the brilliant underglaze bole-red indicates that this dish was definitely produced by an Iznik workshop; the style and layout of the floral decoration is also typically Iznik.

99eb7578-9253-520d-8e15-f2005c79e229.name: Table jar with blue glaze
99eb7578-9253-520d-8e15-f2005c79e229.description: This table jar, unearthed in 1981 during the French mission at the Murwab site in one of the houses with a plaster floor, exhibits a well-recognized design inspired by early Islamic metal needles. Featuring a notably tall (10cm) and wide (11cm rim diameter) straight neck with a slightly projecting rim, the jar boasts a mildly globular body that accommodates two handles on its upper portion. The straight handles suspend from the upper part of the neck. Although the blue glaze is considerably damaged, it reveals a very fine cream paste akin to eggshell. This artefact likely originated from the workshops of Basra.

99f71437-c1aa-557c-a1a0-065a2171dd10.name: Star dish.
99f71437-c1aa-557c-a1a0-065a2171dd10.description:
This deep dish, painted with blue on a stanniferous (tin-bearing) white base, has no inner brim and belongs to the group of utensils known as *tabsil*, which were used to serve dishes in sauce. Its classical geometric composition is based around a centrepiece consisting of a blue circle surrounded by festoons and small dots that link to a six-pointed star. Three lines of intertwined circles radiate from this star, which is highlighted with a blue braid and a white ribbon, before opening out into a six-petal corolla. The spaces in the intertwining pattern, alternating between strong and faded blues, contains small snake motifs left in reserve and half-flower motifs inspired by the efflorescence of blue-and-white Chinese dishes, which were known at this time in Morocco as a result of trade with the Far East.  
The decoration is completed on the curved brim of the dish with small bouquets of flowers and foliage coloured deep blue. The six medallions placed on the points of the central star are inscribed in reserve with two Arabic letters and four numbers indicating the year when the object was made (AH 1274 / AD 1857–8). This very elaborate composition, based on different shades of blue on the brilliant white background, makes this dish particularly interesting. It is one of five known pieces of this type of ceramic to be dated.
99f71437-c1aa-557c-a1a0-065a2171dd10.short_description: This bowl, from a group of utensils known as *tabsil* used to serve dishes with sauce, is one of five pieces to be dated. Its highly elaborate, classical composition radiates from the centre. The small, blue seedlings are reminiscent of certain motifs on blue Chinese dishes.
99f71437-c1aa-557c-a1a0-065a2171dd10.method_for_datation: The two Arabic letters, *s* and *ain*, the first letters of the words *souni'a'* and *'am* meaning 'made in the year', and the numbers 1, 2, 7 and 4 painted inside the six medallions indicate the Hegira date 1274 (AD 1857–8).
99f71437-c1aa-557c-a1a0-065a2171dd10.method_for_provenance: The town of Fez was known for its production of this type of ceramic.

9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.name: Dish with anthropomorphic moon.
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.description: Dish with slanted sides and a ring-base. The decoration, painted in a typical red lustre, as was common in later Hispano-Moorish products, consists of a large rhomboid motif containing a circle whose profile, accentuated by a slight groove, serve to link the brim and the side of the dish. In the spaces between the rhombus and circle there are 'feathered triangles' made up of a series of thick, opposed, parallel lines, producing an effect similar to stylised leaves. The brim, the edge of which is closed with a think band of solid lustre, depicts typical leafy shoots with a central element that appears to be a large round fruit (possibly a pomegranate). The leaves are rendered with a characteristic series of curved parallel lines that evoke the idea of metal springs. Practically identical plant shoots (missing only the central fruit) are repeated in the decoration of the base of the dish where, beside a popular anthropomorphic moon motif, two characteristic 'grotesque lions' confront one another.
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.short_description: This plate is attributable to late Hispano-Moorish production by virtue of its typical red-lustre decoration, which consists of geometric shapes and an anthropomorphic moon flanked by grotesque lions.
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.method_for_provenance: This type of decoration is fairly common in Valencian products from the first half of the 11th / 17th century and is used without significant alterations on a range of different objects (dishes, long-neck vases, handled jars, jugs).

9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.description:
The widespread use of *azulejos* ‒ that were initially produced in Seville during the first half of the 16th century ‒ in Portugal, allowed those involved in the placement of them in architectural settings many ways to experiment with a new decorative expression, giving an early original use to something that was previously foreign to Portuguese culture. In the 16th century, Spanish *azulejos*, like large tapestries with respect to the pattern, were used to create large walls expanses filled with the same motif.  
In the beginning, the Portuguese used the *azulejos* from Spain in the same way, but as time went on they started to become less concerned about the patterns in the *azulejos* and more interested in creating compositions. These compositions could be more architecturally related, like imitations of stained-glass windows, doors and *mihrab*s, or with the intention to re-create carpets, not by the repetition of the pattern, but by juxtaposing different decorations and thus creating something new, like this panel. This early and original understanding of the potential of *azulejo* became the basis for a tradition that has remained in Portugal to this day. This panel uses 16th-century *azulejos* in a composition that can be seen in the architecture of the church of Sé Velha in Coimbra.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: in the 16th century, the *azulejos* in the techniques of *arista* or cuerda seca were imported to Portugal, because at that time there was no production of this type in Portuguese workshops.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.method_for_provenance: The National Tile Museum holds a large number of *azulejos* of unknown origin, many collected during the period of the destruction of the convents and palaces in the late 19th century, in the aftermath of the abolition of the religious orders in 1834.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.obtention: Probably salvaged during demolition of an unknown building where they had once been applied
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.bibliography: Meco, José, *O Azulejo em Portugal*, Lisbon: Publicações Alfa, 1989.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.author: Alexandre Pais

9c0d7e7b-502c-5d62-8588-ba4d3901df58.name: Camel figurine
9c0d7e7b-502c-5d62-8588-ba4d3901df58.short_description: The pottery of Dhofar is, like the region itself, quite distinct from the rest of the country in terms of form, producer and technique. Dhofari pottery can be broadly divided between Salalah ware and the combined ware of the coastal villages of Taqah and Mirbat. The key differences noted are the type of clay used and the featured stylistic forms. The simple terracotta camel figures made in the coastal villages of Dhofar bear a resemblance to pre-Islamic forms. However, modern potters attach neither spiritual nor religious significance to their use of ancient forms. Beyond their use as decorative objects, spiritual and religious significance has long since been lost in time.

9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.name: Footed dish or *tazze*.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.description: A circular stone-paste (fritware) dish with a shallow well, curved sides (*cavetto*), an everted scalloped rim and a low, circular foot-ring. The well is filled with a naturalistic arrangement of flowing flower stalks, rising from a tuft of green leaves. The flowers include red carnations, red roses, blue tulips, with red dotted detailing, and blue hyacinths, all of which are executed in order to exploit the shape of the well. The scalloped rim carries a wave border in blue and black. The underside is decorated with ten floral motifs disposed at regular intervals, consisting of an alternating pattern of five blue flower-heads with green centres, and five bouquets of three blue tulips.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.short_description: Ottoman Iznik was most famous for the production of brilliant polychrome wares revealing an exuberant naturalism which was influenced to a considerable extent by the innovative drawings of the leading Ottoman court designer Kara Memi. The best pieces were executed between AH 956 and 982 / AD 1550 and 1575.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.method_for_datation: This dish belongs to a group of Iznik wares characterised by a naturalism that was influenced by the innovative drawings of the leading Ottoman court designer Kara Memi and datable to between 956–82 / 1550–75.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.method_for_provenance: Dishes of this naturalistic, floral decorative style are known to have been produced in Iznik during the second half of the 10th / 16th century.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.obtention: Bought from J. M. Whitehead, London in 1883.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, pp.222–30, fig. 397 (for a related piece and discussion of this type from Iznik).
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware) with a blue, green and black underglaze, and bole-red underglaze-slip, over which a clear glaze.

9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.name: Jar with lid.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.description:
The spherical jar stands on a high foot and has a cylindrical rimless neck with a flat lid with a knob. The body is covered inside and outside with an opaque, pale turquoise-coloured tin glaze. In the lower part the glaze is not thick enough so that the reddish colouring of the body shines through the glaze. The abstract decoration of the jar is mainly composed of a series of vertical stripes alternating with dotted lines, called 'millipedes', around the neck and a scale pattern filled with stylised half-carnations on the spherical section of the jar. The foot-ring is undecorated. The colours used are a deep limonite yellow, two gradations of brown, a light one of iron oxide and a dark one of manganese, and cobalt-blue and copper green. The use of brown, yellow, blue and green as full, unmixed tones is the characteristic colour scheme of Moroccan polychrome faience. Faience is the type of decoration: after a first firing the potters put on the opaque tin glaze on the earthenware vessel; the mineral pigments used for the polychrome decoration were applied over the dried glaze; in a second firing glaze and pigments melted together.  
The small and large red dots irregularly spread over the whole outside surface of jar and lid are a striking feature. It is a paste with a base of red lead applied over the glaze by fingertip. After drying, the paste appears like red wax. However, this kind of decoration was not executed by the potters themselves. It was done by the faience traders, at first to cover the traces of the firing tripods on plates and later on all kinds of pottery vessels.  
Faience was an urban ceramic in Morocco whose most important centre of production was Fez. The objects made by the faience potters were mostly functional and for everyday use. This pot was possibly used for storing fat or yeast. Unlike other examples of this kind of stock pot, however, this one does not have the usual two handles.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.short_description: Jar on a high foot and with a flat lid with knob. The decoration is composed of vertical stripes alternating with dotted lines and stylised half-carnations. The colour scheme is characteristic of Moroccan polychrome faience. This pot might have been used for storing fat or yeast.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.dimensions: Height approx. 21.3 cm, diameter of rim 10.5 cm.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.method_for_datation: Dating is difficult. There are only a few dated faiences and the same forms and patterns were used throughout various periods. The red dots were probably common from the end of the 12th / 18th century.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.method_for_provenance: On the basis of the pattern, the technique and the colour scheme.

9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.name: Dish.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.description: A circular stone-paste (fritware) dish with a shallow well, broad, everted rim and a low, circular foot-ring. The well is decorated with seven bouquets, comprising one at the centre, surrounded by six others. The flowers are naively drawn and the pigments overall very pure: red, green and blue with black. The rim has a white, cusped zigzag band, reserved against a green ground; a narrow blue line accentuates the zigzag patterning and contrasts with the white and green.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.short_description: Towards the end of the late AH 10th century / AD 16th century the artistic quality of Iznik wares began to decline. Raw materials were less refined, colour schemes duller and designs simpler. Dishes with simple floral bouquets were made between the AH late 10th / AD last quarter of the 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.dates: Hegira, late 10th century / AD late 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.method_for_datation: Dishes with similar floral designs have been attributed to the late 10th / late 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.method_for_provenance: Ceramics of this type are known to have been produced in Iznik during the late 10th / late 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.obtention: A gift from Miss Beatrice Danford, Newton St. Boswells, in 1953.

materials: Stone-paste (fritware), red, blue, green and black underglaze, over which a clear glaze.

9e38c5ee-2be1-5810-be6d-783f681533c7.name: Ceramic dish.
9e38c5ee-2be1-5810-be6d-783f681533c7.description: A large round ceramic dish glazed in blue, green and manganese-purple with incised decoration, known as 'laqabi ware', or polychrome carved pottery. The figure dominating the centre of the dish is a harpy, a fantastical animal with the body of a bird and a human head. The first stage in the production process comprised cutting the overall design into the unfired ceramic: the harpy, the swirling vegetal scroll behind the figure, and the border pattern. After the first firing, the glaze was applied to the incised lines which were intended to stop the glaze from running. The design around the border is a simplified version of the rope motif typical of 'laqabi ware' ceramic dishes. Dishes of this type would have been used as tableware and were a cheaper alternative to metal plates and bowls.
9e38c5ee-2be1-5810-be6d-783f681533c7.short_description: A large, round ceramic dish with a picture of a harpy, a fantastical animal with the body of the bird and a human head. The very specific technique of this dish – with incised decoration and polychrome glaze – is known as ‘*laqabi* ware’, and was produced in Raqqa, Syria.
9e38c5ee-2be1-5810-be6d-783f681533c7.method_for_datation: By comparison with other objects excavated in Syria.
9e38c5ee-2be1-5810-be6d-783f681533c7.method_for_provenance: Lane (1947) attributed 'laqabi ware' to Iran, but Porter (1981) has shown that in terms of shape, body and design this type of ceramic was more likely to have been produced in northern Syria.

9fb409e3-528f-533c-9017-82d63273b965.name: Bowl
9fb409e3-528f-533c-9017-82d63273b965.short_description: The Seljuq era was distinguished by its extensive use of lustre techniques – painting with metal oxides then fired in a reduction kiln – to produce fine ceramics. The high quality achieved by the ceramic painters is borne out by countless bowls, bottles and vases decorated with thin brushstrokes that outline geometric shapes, floral patterns and human figures.

9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.name: *Ataifor* (bowl).
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.description: This *ataifor* is a dish with a convex base, curved sides and a smooth rim. The piece is made from reddish clay; the outside is covered with a honey-coloured greenish glaze and the inside with a white glaze. The inside of the receptacle is decorated with elements in green and manganese on a white base. The large circular border that runs round the edge of the plate, with fan-shaped palmettes joined by undulating stems, gives the piece a tri-lobed appearance. The central strip completes the decoration with an inscription in archaic *kufic*, where the phrase ‘al-Mulk’ (power) is repeated. The letters outlined using dark manganese lines are filled with copper green, creating a contrast with the white base that was common in the ceramics of the era.
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.short_description: This bowl or *ataifor*, produced in the palace workshops of Madinat al-Zahra, is thought to have symbolic significance: the word ‘al-Mulk’, ‘the power’, represents sovereignty, while the white, green and black represent the Umayyad dynasty, Muhammad, and the austerity of the Qur’an respectively as well as the sovereignty of the caliph.
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.method_for_datation: The writing style could date it to the second third of the 4th / 10th century. The simple *kufic* inscription belongs to an initial stage of production at Madinat al-Zahra, before the reign of al-Hakam II (350–66 / 961–76).
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.method_for_provenance: The *ataifor* came from archaeological excavations at Madinat al-Zahra. Both its shape and decoration are characteristic of palatine production at Madinat al-Zahra.
9fd48483-773e-56ef-a4ac-80ac9b4f89d0.obtention: The *ataifor* was given to the National Archaeological Museum by the State on 5 February 1943.

9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.name: Irrigation bucket
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.description:
The cylindrical object features a straight mouth and pointed base, with retaining recesses located at the start of the mouth and base. The surface shows traces of hand modelling, leaving indentations on the body in the form of perimeter circumferences and on the base in parallel lines following the conical shape.  
  
Made of whitish porous, unglazed clay, it retains traces of *almagra* (reddish pigment) drips on both the exterior and interior. Functionally, such objects can be understood within the context of irrigation and hydraulic systems in al-Andalus. Their development enabled the introduction of new plant species, the expansion of arable land, and the diversification of the diet. These innovations changed working methods, the agricultural cycle, and the landscape.  
  
Waterwheels spread throughout the Iberian Peninsula. The waterwheel buckets, which were secured with ropes at the top and halfway down their cylindrical body, underwent technical improvements. These elements reflect a series of small but significant technical advances. The earliest ones, with an annular or pointed bottom, gradually were replaced by others with a perforated bottom that prevented their tilting and breakage in addition to the backward movement of the wheel.
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.method_for_datation: Comparative study of typologies; references provided by previous owner.
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.method_for_provenance: References provided by previous owner on file.
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.obtention: The bucket was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 1 January 1987.

a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.name: Alhambra vase.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.description:
This piece is one of the so-called 'Alhambra vases'. Formally, all of these are similar: a large egg-shaped body and a narrow, unglazed base from which two large, flat handles emerge, and an octagonal neck reinforced with vertical mouldings.  
The decoration of pale gold on a white base is arranged horizontally in broad bands of different widths that are separated from one another by other smooth, narrower bands. The central, and widest, band contains vegetal motifs and an inscription in *kufic* characters in white on a golden background, in which the word 'forgiveness' is repeated several times. Both above and below the central band there are other similar bands decorated with plant arabesques and gold circles, all joined by a thread. The decoration of the main body is completed by another two bands, one on the lower part with small arches and another nearer the neck with a *kufic* inscription, now almost completely disappeared.  
The neck, which has eight sides separated by mouldings, is decorated with stylised vegetal motifs. The handles, attached close to the body, are decorated with the hand of Fatima (*hamsa*) on each side.  
The Alhambra vases constitute the most important examples of Nasrid ceramic production. These pieces became extremely well known for their delicate decoration and large size, and were exported to other places. The best-preserved examples are to be found in Palermo (Regional Museum of Sicily), St Petersburg (Hermitage), Stockholm (National Museum of Fine Arts) and Madrid (Institute of Valencia de D. Juan and the National Archaeological Museum). Some are decorated exclusively in gold and others in gold and cobalt-blue, always on a tin-glaze background.  
Although its form derives from large storage vessels, its cumbersome size and the absence of any strengthening elements in the handles suggest a purely ornamental function.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.short_description: The so-called ‘Alhambra vases’ were luxury items because of the technical complexity of their manufacture and the beauty of their decoration and lustrework. The intended use is not known, but their renown led them to be exported to Sicily and Mamluk Egypt.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_datation: It is difficult to determine the date of manufacture of these vases. Nonetheless, all writers agree that, on the basis of the inscription, the oldest examples are those decorated solely with gold on white, which were produced from the last third of the 7th / 13th century and, in particular, during the 8th / 14th century.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_provenance: Although all of these pieces are known generically as the Alhambra vases, they were produced in Malaga and exported. From the 7th / 13th century, Arab writers begin to mention Malaga as a large centre for the production and export of ceramics with gold or metallic highlights.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.obtention: The piece was found by chance at the beginning of the 20th century during work to shore up vaults in the monastery of Santa María de la Defensión in Jerez de la Frontera (Cadiz). It was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 29 July 1930.

a15286eb-a10a-5ff6-92f0-7aa1105bf571.name: Sherds
a15286eb-a10a-5ff6-92f0-7aa1105bf571.short_description: Lustre painting is an elaborate technique requiring several firings, the last one without oxygen. Used to decorate ceramics but also glass, it was much appreciated for its luxurious, iridescent effect suggestive of glittering gold and silver, the more so since Islam prohibited vessels made from precious metals. The present sherds illustrate the wide variety of motifs, colours and designs used by the potters of Fustat during the Fatimid dynasty.

a16c230e-422f-5bde-8b7a-803161b630d9.name: Grenades.
a16c230e-422f-5bde-8b7a-803161b630d9.description:
A cone shaped vessel with a pointed base and a small opening, 3 cm in diameter. Made of thick black or gray burnished pottery ware, the vessels are decorated with almond-shaped designs in relief which are arranged into nine segments and divided by straight lines, starting at the neck and ending at the pointed base.  
  
Scholars differ in opinion as to the function and use of these vessels. Some think they were used as containers for perfume or other precious liquids, while others believe they were filled with naphtha and used as grenades.
a16c230e-422f-5bde-8b7a-803161b630d9.short_description: Cone-shaped vessels from Ajlun Castle made of thick grey or black pottery. Their function and use are not certain; some scholars think they were containers for perfume or precious liquids, while others believe they were filled with naphtha and used as grenades.
a16c230e-422f-5bde-8b7a-803161b630d9.dimensions: Height 12 cm, width 14.7 cm, circumference 29.5 cm.
a16c230e-422f-5bde-8b7a-803161b630d9.method_for_datation: The vessels are dated by stylistic analysis and by the fact that they were found as part of the archaeology of a dated building.
a16c230e-422f-5bde-8b7a-803161b630d9.method_for_provenance: The provenance is unknown but the grenades were probably produced in Syria.
a16c230e-422f-5bde-8b7a-803161b630d9.obtention: The vessels were collected during an archaeological excavation carried out in the Castle of Ajlun.
