a1ecccac-7c93-51a2-925d-06173dfe0ef5.name: Merlon.
a1ecccac-7c93-51a2-925d-06173dfe0ef5.description:
This merlon, with its rectangular base prolonged on both sides by two projecting notches, is crowned by an element in the shape of a leaf whose concave surface has two perforations at its centre. The green-coloured enamel that covers the surface runs over the edge onto the lateral sides. Fragmented into two parts, the piece was restored with plaster on its posterior side.  
This merlon, along with other similar elements, constitutes one of the friezes that crowned the summit of the façades of Hammadid palaces.  
The holes that can be seen on the surface of the leaf might have been used to accommodate the fixing of bolts.
a1ecccac-7c93-51a2-925d-06173dfe0ef5.short_description: Rectangular-base merlon topped with a leaf-shaped object, the concave surface of which has two holes for attaching it. It is coloured with a blue-green glaze that has disappeared in places. This merlon was part of a frieze used to adorn Hammadid palaces.
a1ecccac-7c93-51a2-925d-06173dfe0ef5.dimensions: Height 64 cm, width 24 cm, depth 7.5 cm.
a1ecccac-7c93-51a2-925d-06173dfe0ef5.method_for_datation: Merlon was found in the Qal'at Bani Hammad (5th–6th / AD 11th–12th centuries).
a1ecccac-7c93-51a2-925d-06173dfe0ef5.method_for_provenance: The merlon was found by Golvin in the palace of Manar. Furthermore, these merlons have appeared in abundance in the palace of Manar, but have not appeared elsewhere.
a1ecccac-7c93-51a2-925d-06173dfe0ef5.provenance: Qasr al-Manar, Qal’at Bani Hammad, Algeria.

a21ffaa4-2f94-5760-8200-a9816e236687.name: Eight-pointed star-shaped tile
a21ffaa4-2f94-5760-8200-a9816e236687.short_description: Tile in the shape of an eight-pointed star with a blue border. It is decorated with an eight-pointed star featuring a design in low relief: a running deer in a field of vegetation reserved in white against the lustre-painted ground. The text of the first Sura, *Fatiha* (*The Opener*), in Arabic, is inscribed between the parallel sides of the concentric polygons. The inscription, in *naskhi* characters, is painted in lustre on a white ground.

a2dc11cb-45ba-5aad-a8e3-58331496893b.name: Bowl.
a2dc11cb-45ba-5aad-a8e3-58331496893b.description:
An example of underglaze polychrome lustre-ware, specifically the type renowned in the area of Raqqa and neighbouring Rusafa during the AH 6th / AD 12th century. Stylistically this type of ceramic follows the trend in Persian *mina'i* ware that is characterised by prominent colours and gilding applied over the glaze. As Syrian potters were not familiar with the technique of applying overglaze enamels, they used their habitual underglaze method while adopting the iconography and style of *mina'i*.  
The piece is a semi-spherical bowl with a tall base. Its interior is decorated with an illustration of a person – either a man or a woman, it is difficult to tell – who wears a small hat, has a halo surrounding her Turkoman moon-like face and a beauty spot on her left cheek. She carries in her right hand a cup. The clothing is decorated with embroidery consisting of stylised vegetal patterns; similar vegetal decorations also surround the figure.  
Along the inside rim of the vessel are stylised geometric designs. The outer surface of the vessel is decorated with a band of almond-shaped motifs. The whole decorative scheme has been executed in blue, black, red, green and brown on a background of ivory-beige; a light-green transparent glaze covers the vessel overall.
a2dc11cb-45ba-5aad-a8e3-58331496893b.short_description: The westwards movement of the Seljuqs from Central Asia brought a fashion for Iranian iconography. Syrian potters used their local method of underglaze polychrome painting while executing Eastern-inspired figurative images.
a2dc11cb-45ba-5aad-a8e3-58331496893b.method_for_datation: The bowl is dated by comparative analysis of similar finds from Raqqa believed to be of the Ayyubid period (6th–7th / 12th–13th centuries). Production of ceramics ended after the Mongol invasion and destruction of the city in 656–7/ 1258–9.
a2dc11cb-45ba-5aad-a8e3-58331496893b.method_for_provenance: Raqqa and Rusafa were known as centres for the production of wares of this type, specifically polychrome ware with underglaze painting in five or six colours and figural representation showing strong Persian or Central Asian influence.

a37a77c0-be32-5414-8a2a-ad1daa8bf28a.name: Star tiles.
a37a77c0-be32-5414-8a2a-ad1daa8bf28a.description:
The star and cross tiles in underglaze and lustre techniques, respectively, that once decorated the walls of the Kubadabad Palace in Beyşehir are rare examples of Seljuq tile art in regards to their decoration and symbolic meanings. The star tiles were produced using the underglaze technique, while the cross tiles were produced using the lustre technique. Representing a wide range of figurative imagery, the tiles are decorated with scenes from the daily lives of the sultans and of the palace in general. In addition, talismanic fantastic animals that were believed to protect the palace, as well as various domestic animals and game (e.g. sphinxes, sirens, peacocks, lions, double-headed eagles, birds, foxes, rabbits, wolves, horses, goats, camels, and ducks) were also depicted.  
  
In the Kubadabad Palace, the eight-pointed star tiles were placed together with cruciform tiles to form large panels. While the star tiles have mostly figurative decoration, the cruciform ones generally have vegetal decoration. The underglaze painted examples are decorated in black, turquoise and dark-blue under a colourless transparent glaze.  
  
The figurative decoration shows good observation of nature, a lively imagination and a realistic style. The double-headed eagles are depicted in profile and cover the entire surface of the tile. Their bodies, in frontal view, bear cartouches with inscriptions reading 'al-sultan', 'al mu'azzam' ('the great'), etc. Generally framed with plant motifs, the double-headed eagles are thought to bear symbolic meanings. Used in various periods as both a coat of arms and a totem, the image of the double-headed eagle is ascribed many meanings such as strength, power, protective spirit, nobility, and wisdom. The double-headed eagles on the Kubadabad Palace tiles are thought to symbolise power, most likely representing the sultan with inscribed panels on their bodies.
a37a77c0-be32-5414-8a2a-ad1daa8bf28a.short_description: One of the most important palaces of the Anatolian Seljuq period, the Kubadabad Palace is renowned for its wall tiles. The main theme of the tiles is the daily life of the sultan and his entourage and courtly life in general They reflect careful observation of nature and a wide-ranging imagination.
a37a77c0-be32-5414-8a2a-ad1daa8bf28a.dates: During the reign of Sultan Alaaddin ('Ala al-Din) Keykubad I (r. hegira 616–35 / AD 1220–37).
a37a77c0-be32-5414-8a2a-ad1daa8bf28a.method_for_datation: The Kubadabad Palace in Beyşehir was built by the Seljuq Sultan Alaaddin ('Ala al-Din) Keykubad I (r. AH 616–35 / AD 1220–37). Inscriptions and written documents show that the palace was completed in 634 / 1236. The tiles of the palace are dated to the same year.
a37a77c0-be32-5414-8a2a-ad1daa8bf28a.method_for_provenance: The tiles were found *in situ* at the palace but the place of production is not known. However, it is highly likely that they were produced at Beyşehir or Konya. The latest finds during the ongoing excavations suggest that they might have been produced on site at the palace.
a37a77c0-be32-5414-8a2a-ad1daa8bf28a.obtention: Initiated in the mid-20th century, the ongoing archaeological excavations at the Kubadabad Palace have brought to light a considerable number of tiles. Once forming the decoration of the walls of the palace, the tiles were taken for public display to Karatay Madrasa Museum in Konya after they had been studied.

a3dac180-1eea-5814-9963-a2c290044228.short_description: The bowl is decorated in turquoise, blue, and purple in a opaque white glaze. The decoration in black and red is overglaze. The bowl is embellished by leaf gilding decoration.
a3dac180-1eea-5814-9963-a2c290044228.dates: Hegira late 6th–early 7th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century

a4216aec-61b4-5519-bef1-4a5dd8bcb4b4.name: Tile panel in the form of a doorway
a4216aec-61b4-5519-bef1-4a5dd8bcb4b4.short_description: This large mosaic tile panel is installed on the east wall of the dining room lanai at Shangri La. To produce a panel such as this, a potter cut small shapes out of glazed and fired tiles, then fitted the small pieces together to produce a mosaic effect. Each shape had to be precisely cut to align perfectly with the surrounding shapes glazed in contrasting colors. The technique was often used in Iran and Central Asia to adorn buildings and other architectural structures such as gateways.

a422b89c-541c-5d0c-b8ef-5292227a2201.name: Pilgrim’s Flask.
a422b89c-541c-5d0c-b8ef-5292227a2201.description:
This canteen, often described as a pilgrim's flask, is a container used to carry water while travelling, on pilgrimage, or hunting trips. It is manufactured using a mould and its body is in the form of a disc with a mouth and a pair of loops attached to the side. To keep water from spilling out, the mouth is elongated by a tube of earthenware resembling a set of gradually narrowing rings stacked one on top of the other. The two loops flanking the flask's mouth can be strung by a rope to hang on the hip while travelling on foot, horse or camel-back.  
The surface of the body is decorated with a moulded imprint boldly portraying a Mamluk blazon, known in Arabic as 'rank'. The open-winged eagle on top of a chalice that is flanked by flowers is known to be the blazon of Prince Toquztimur. It is believed that he started out as an official cup-bearer and his blazontherefore displays the cup. When he rose to the rank of governor for Sultan Nasir al-Din Muhammad (r. AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40), he added the symbol of the eagle as a tribute to the Sultan. The six-petal roses that appear underneath the eagle may signify a tribute to Nasir al-Din's family, the Qalawun.
a422b89c-541c-5d0c-b8ef-5292227a2201.short_description: This flask decorated with an emblem, a fashion that became popular during the Mamluk period, carries a symbol of an eagle and identifies the owner as Prince Toquztimur, the Mamluk Governor of Hama and later Aleppo.
a422b89c-541c-5d0c-b8ef-5292227a2201.initial_owner: Prince Toquztimur (r. AH 742–6 / AD 1341–5), Mamluk Governor of Hama and then Aleppo.
a422b89c-541c-5d0c-b8ef-5292227a2201.method_for_datation: The canteen is datable by the blazon that identifies it with Prince Toquztimur (r. 742–6 / 1341–5). Similar objects have also been dated to this period.
a422b89c-541c-5d0c-b8ef-5292227a2201.method_for_provenance: This object was found in Aleppo, but since Prince Toquztimur was the Governor of Hama and then of Aleppo, it is also possible that the flask was produced in Hama. Similar objects, in respect of both style of decoration and function have been given Syrian provenance.

a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.name: Tile Panel for a Spandrel
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.short_description: Buildings in Isfahan, capital of the Safavid dynasty in the seventeenth century, were lavishly decorated with tilework. An innovation of this period, found in palaces and other secular structures, was the use of individually painted square tiles, which were combined to form a larger pictorial scene and employed the *cuerda seca* technique. First developed in Iran in the later 14th century, *cuerda seca* was designed to produce multicolored glazed tile decoration quickly, efficiently, and cheaply. To prevent the different glazes from running during the (single) firing process, the decorative motifs were outlined with a greasy pigment that burned off in the firing, leaving behind a dull, dark line. This tile panel is half of a pair of spandrels that was once set above an archway in a palatial pavilion known as the Hasht Bihisht, completed in Hegira 1080 / AD 1669-70. Here, amid a tranquil floral landscape filled with birds, a lion attacks a stag, a motif that can perhaps be interpreted as a visualization of a contemporary poetic metaphor for the arrival of spring. Other contemporaneous spandrels from the Hasht Bihisht on the eastern facade include animal combats, for example, a leopard and a gazelle and a tiger and a gazelle.
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.method_for_datation: The tile panel is very closely related in terms of style, subject matter (animal combat), technique and dimensions to other spandrels still in situ at the Hasht Bihisht pavilion in Isfahan, which dates to Hegira 1080 / AD 1669-70. It may have come from the western façade of the structure.
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.method_for_provenance: The technique, style, and dimensions are consonant with tilework from the Hasht Bihisht.
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.provenance: Iran, probably Isfahan, Hasht Bihisht, West façade

a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.name: Bowl painted in blue and black
a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.short_description: The type of thin-walled bowls of an elegant bi-conic shape/decorated with refined blue and black painting belongs to the best achievements of Iranian ceramics of the AD 12th–13th centuries. The inner surface of the museum bowl is decorated with a cross-shaped composition with radial inscriptions in Persian, scratched on black ribbons in the "dry kalam" technique. The inscriptions make up a love poem: "Since you cannot love me for a moment / Do not break further my wounded heart. / Be less cruel, less tyrannical to me, / Until my heart slowly leaves you". Masterly drawn flowers, long-tailed birds and "willow branches" betray the hand of a subtle artist.
a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.method_for_datation: Arthur Sambon's auction catalogue (1914, origin, inscription reading). Stylistic analysis by  V. Krachkovskaya (1926, date); T. Starodub (1976, specified origin).
a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.method_for_provenance: Arthur Sambon's auction catalogue (1914). Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927). Old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
a49a47fe-f470-5805-9a91-aceb1f2dd325.obtention: Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918. Previously purchased by the Khanenkos in Paris at the auction of Arthur Sambon collection in 1914.

a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.name: Dish.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.description:
'Brazier' dish with a large, flat circular base and straight, shallow sides finished with a narrow brim. The piece is made of red clay and covered with a tin glaze. It is decorated with gold and cobalt-blue lustre on a creamy white background. The base of the dish, decorated with interlaced, small and stylized vegetal patterns, is divided into quadrants with alternating blue and golden motifs. The brim is decorated with the traditional ‘fish-like border’ pattern. Golden spirals fill and break up the white background throughout the piece.  
Technically, ceramics from the AH 8th and 9th / AD 14th and 15th century are no more than a continuation of the Almohad tradition. However, the incorporation of cobalt oxide into the glaze in the Nasrid era gave rise to a wide range of blues, and the application of copper sulphate, silver and red ochre to achieve metallic highlights resulted in some exceptional pieces. Centuries-old gilded Andalusian ceramics had their heyday during the Nasrid reign in Granada.  
The manufacture of this type of ceramic required three firings. The final firing, in a reduction kiln, was the most delicate as it required perfect control of the kiln and its temperature. The mix of metal sulphides had to adhere to the piece without the glaze from the previous firing melting again.  
The importance of the pottery workshops of the kingdom of Granada, and specifically of Malaga as the main centre of production, caused the expression *obra de maliqa* (made in Maliqa) to be used, with some variations, to refer to gilded ceramics regardless of where they were produced. This term was also used in the Christian world for pottery workshops of Nasrid origin that, from the late AH 8th / AD 14th century, began to move to various places on the east coast of Spain, of which Manises was the most important centre for highlighted ceramics produced in the Malaga style for Christian customers.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.short_description: This enormous dish represents a continuation of the technique and decorative style of Nasrid ceramicists in Mudéjar workshops to meet the needs of their Christian clientele, who wanted new shapes like this shallow dish with its flat base, straight sides and horizontal rim.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.dimensions: Height 4.5 cm, maximum diameter 41.5 cm, base diameter 34.8 cm.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.method_for_datation: The perfect development of the technique, the type of decoration and the style of the plant arabesques are characteristic of ceramics with golden highlights from the first third of the 9th / 15th century.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.method_for_provenance: The growing decadence of the Nasrid kingdom, along with the development of the maritime power of the kingdom of Aragon and its control over the trade routes of the Mediterranean resulted in Mudéjar centres, contemporaries of the Nasrid producers that used the same traditional procedures and decorative styles, springing up around the east coast. The intense colour of the cobalt and its shape are more characteristic of Valencian pieces, but only an analysis of the clays could determine the precise origin of the piece.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.provenance: Nasrid kingdom of Granada or Christian kingdom of Valencia, Spain.
a4a2465e-0ea9-5fe8-9719-b7e20f0986e6.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum by the State on 6 June 1875.

a52ea6dc-cf4f-5836-a534-c806ce30745b.name: Tile Bowl
a52ea6dc-cf4f-5836-a534-c806ce30745b.description: The bowl’s surface is coated in white clay and slip and decorated in blue and white under a transparent colourless glaze. On the exterior a dark grey-blue ivy branch, reminiscent of a Chinese cloud, is adorned with large stylised flowers and shoots in cobalt blue. The contours are grey-blue. The exterior of the rim is encircled by a band of short angled lines, and the interior by a band of half rosettes. Inside the bowl is a medallion featuring a large stylised flower with six petals in the centre. This is a unique example of the influence of Chinese porcelain.
a52ea6dc-cf4f-5836-a534-c806ce30745b.dates: Hegira second quarter of the 10th century / AD second quarter of the 16th century

a5329f82-997c-5624-abe3-aed18ec8753c.name: Jar.
a5329f82-997c-5624-abe3-aed18ec8753c.description: Jar with an ovoid belly, with no neck or foot, resting on a narrow base. A roll acts as a spout. The marks left by the removal of the handles suggest that they were flat and perhaps wing-shaped like the famous jars of the Alhambra. The upper third of the belly is decorated with four horizontal strips covered with a green-bronze glaze. These strips have stamped motifs and are delimited by clay cordons with incised chevron patterns. The repetitive motifs that decorate the strips are plant-like (palm leaves and fleurons) or epigraphic. On the top strip, stylised patterns seem to reproduce the word 'Allah' or *al-yumn* (happiness), to express God's omnipresence and to have it protect the food kept in the jar. This form of decorative jar is frequently found on the archaeological sites from the Nasrid period of al-Andalus.
a5329f82-997c-5624-abe3-aed18ec8753c.short_description: This egg-shaped jar was used to store foodstuffs. The marks left when the handles were removed suggest that they were flat, possibly wing-shaped, like the famous 'Alhambra jars'.
a5329f82-997c-5624-abe3-aed18ec8753c.dimensions: Height 59.5 cm, base diameter 12 cm, max. diameter 58.7 cm, neck diameter 16.6 cm.
a5329f82-997c-5624-abe3-aed18ec8753c.method_for_datation: From stylistic and comparatives studies with the Nasrid work.
a5329f82-997c-5624-abe3-aed18ec8753c.method_for_provenance: Discovered during chance excavations in Salé.

a55c2ebe-979d-535b-8bc8-31f893bda658.name: Cup with *rubab* player.
a55c2ebe-979d-535b-8bc8-31f893bda658.description:
The cup is decorated in the centre with a figure playing a *rubab*, a traditional Iranian stringed instrument. The background is filled with dotted panels and the edge is decorated with semi-circles.  
The *rubab*\-player motif, shown here seated as was the custom among nomads, appears frequently in Islamic art and seems, like the figure of the drinker, to evoke court scenes in celebration of the life of the sovereign. The musician, depicted in a style similar to that used in figurative Nishapur ceramics from the same period, is wearing characteristic headgear that was common among Turco-Mongolian people in Central Asia.
a55c2ebe-979d-535b-8bc8-31f893bda658.short_description: This piece is decorated with, among other things, a male figure playing a stringed instrument, the *rubab*. The figure of the musician is common in Islamic art and, like the figure of the drinker, appears to evoke the splendour of court life.
a55c2ebe-979d-535b-8bc8-31f893bda658.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
a55c2ebe-979d-535b-8bc8-31f893bda658.method_for_provenance: Many of the decorative elements, such as the dotted panels that make up the background, are typical of Iraqi ceramics of the 4th / 10th century.

a5defb3f-7271-5a06-9b25-33267fdf495e.name: Vessel
a5defb3f-7271-5a06-9b25-33267fdf495e.description: The vessel is cream-coloured, with a ring base, convex body, long thin neck and scalloped rim. The figural, stylised geometric and floral decorations in a lustre technique cover the entire surface.
a5defb3f-7271-5a06-9b25-33267fdf495e.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts

a6a01024-6733-5cbd-9746-7f832e8a4d36.name: Vase.
a6a01024-6733-5cbd-9746-7f832e8a4d36.description: This small pot, with a spherical body and a cylindrical neck fitted with two handles and a ring-foot, would have been used as a drinking vessel. The neck and upper part of the belly are covered in dark manganese-oxide paint and carved with decorative motifs. The motifs appear in a frieze on the neck and on the upper part of the belly. Horizontal and vertical dividing lines as well as a braid motif known as the 'eternity braid' are drawn on the neck. A pseudo-epigraphic motif, representing the name of Allah embellished with plant motifs and framed by a panel of horizontal volutes, can be seen on the belly. The handles are decorated with scattered oblique lines and with small painted disks. This type of decoration, reminiscent of metalwork, is typical of Almohad produce from North Africa and al-Andalus.
a6a01024-6733-5cbd-9746-7f832e8a4d36.short_description: This small pot with a rounded belly, cylindrical neck and two carrying handles, would have been used as a drinking vessel. The neck and upper part of the belly are covered in brown paint with excised decorative motifs: an 'eternity' plait and pseudo-epigraphic motifs.
a6a01024-6733-5cbd-9746-7f832e8a4d36.dimensions: Height 12 cm, base diameter 5.4 cm, max. diameter 13 cm, aperture diameter 9.9 cm.
a6a01024-6733-5cbd-9746-7f832e8a4d36.method_for_datation: Found in the rubble of a medieval bourgeois house on the archaeological site of Lixus. The date has been confirmed by stylistic and comparative study with reliably dated objects discovered in Murcia and Huelva in Spain from the end of the first third of 7th / 13th century.

a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.name: Jug
a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.short_description: Jug with rounded carination and flaring neck. The handle connects Jug with rounded carination and flaring neck. The handle connects the rim with the largest diameter of the body and is topped with a thumb rest. The object is entirely covered with an off-white slip. The rim is accentuated with a black slip painted band. The vessel is decorated with a purplish-black inscription band around the largest diameter of the body – reading *al-hamdu lillah* – the neck and along the handle. The inscription on the handle reads *Allah al-ʿalim bi-l-umur* (God is omniscient on all things). Also on the inner side of the neck we find a short illegible epigraphic decor. The combination of the widespread form with floriated *kufic* inscriptions is unusual. The small jug could be a drinking vessel.
a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
a6d99b72-8bf4-59da-85c1-3680ed3adc6d.method_for_datation: Comparable script design is found on large conical bowls in the Nishapur excavations and in the Khalili Collection. Many examples of similar script but with inverted colours (white script on black slip) are found in Iranian museums. This type is common in Central and Northern Iran, but not found in Central Asia.

a6fb95de-a396-5ed1-a364-2182f9ed0860.name: Dish
a6fb95de-a396-5ed1-a364-2182f9ed0860.short_description:
A splendid example of the early Iznik ceramics is a big deep dish painted with vine or plane-tree leaves and the Chinese "chi" clouds. The dish is dated to the first half of the AD 16th century.  
Refined painting in two different hues of cobalt-blue, dark and light, as well as the “chi” cloud motif point to the influence of Chinese Ming porcelain on the early Iznik ware. At the same time, the free composition of décor, with no distinct division on central field and border, reveals the inherent Turkish artistic traditions.
a6fb95de-a396-5ed1-a364-2182f9ed0860.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by Yu. Miller (publication, 1961, date, origin).
a6fb95de-a396-5ed1-a364-2182f9ed0860.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927): the Khanenkos' collection. The entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946.

a7fd98fa-f450-5ba3-b6d2-3909a56326ac.name: Decorated panel featuring a mosque
a7fd98fa-f450-5ba3-b6d2-3909a56326ac.short_description: An Ottoman-style mosque, identifiable by its cone-shaped minarets, sits in the middle of this horseshoe arch supported by two columns. The lower panel contains a vase with various flowers emerging from it, such as carnations, tulips, and vine leaves. A dense rinceau pattern with flowers and leaves fills the gaps in the arch and the keystone and decorates the capitals of the columns. The main colours are yellow green and blue, although beige and brown also feature. This item shows traces of both Ottoman and Andalusian influences.

a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.name: *Ataifor* (bowl).
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.description:
This *ataifor*, with a ring in the base and curved sides, is made of yellowish material and coated with a white glaze. The inside is decorated in green and manganese. The decorative theme is made up of a large circular border running round the edge of the plate in which it is possible to see the remains of a *kufic* inscription with the phrase ‘al-Mulk’ (power). The decoration is finished with two narrower strips that cross in the centre, with markings that appear to be a simplification of *kufic* writing but that are in fact meaningless. The decorative technique used, epigraphic motifs in copper green and manganese black visible through the white glaze, produces an impressive chromatic effect.  
Madinat al-Zahra was the most important centre for the production and distribution of ceramics glazed and decorated in green and manganese during the Caliphate. Ornamentally, the clarity of the design and the austerity of the compositions, with extensive areas of the base undecorated, differentiates them from other works produced at the same time in al-Andalus.  
The function of this type of ceramic is still unclear, but what is clear is that production at Madinat al-Zahra constituted a fundamental technological advance. The use of copper and manganese oxides in the decoration and the glazing, which made the containers waterproof and stopped liquids soaking the earthenware, created a type of special crockery which was considered a luxury.
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.short_description: Found in an archaeological dig at the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahra, this bowl or *ataifor* would have been part of the domestic crockery at the caliph’s home. This can be inferred from the inscription ‘al-Mulk’, ‘the power’, presumably referring to the power of the caliph.
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.method_for_datation: The *kufic* script belongs to an initial stage of production at Madinat al-Zahra, before the reign of al-Hakam II (350–66 / 961–76).
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.method_for_provenance: The piece came from archaeological excavations at Madinat al-Zahra. Most of the ceramics are characterised by an open not a closed shape, and the majority of them are *ataifors*. The phrase ‘al-Mulk’, related to Umayyad power and legitimacy, is the inscription most frequently found in this type of ceramic.
a80ae3b6-0e85-5e1b-93e6-f4552c3eac51.obtention: The *ataifor* was given to the National Archaeological Museum by the State on 5 February 1943.

a842940f-0cc2-5088-a04d-869d51b9464b.name: Pitcher, with one handle
a842940f-0cc2-5088-a04d-869d51b9464b.description:
Uncovered in an unbuilt area adjacent to a cluster of five houses, this pitcher was discovered during the 2007 excavation by the Qatari-French Mission. The unconstructed space between the houses featured temporary installations, potentially serving as open-air kitchens, marked by ash and fireplaces.  
This jar features a single handle, a flared globular body, and a small flat base. Its body is adorned with a horizontal incised line as a decorative element. Crafted from red clay and adorned with a cream slip, the entire lower section of the body retains traces of red pigment. This kitchen vessel likely served the purpose of storing and transporting liquids.
a842940f-0cc2-5088-a04d-869d51b9464b.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

a8732393-9f73-5349-bf08-2e06bf17b6f1.name: Jar with animal decorations
a8732393-9f73-5349-bf08-2e06bf17b6f1.short_description: This oval-shaped double-handled *charbiya* has a long neck, a curved rim and a flat bottom. The main colours of the decorations are yellow, green and brown. On the shoulders, a strip of leaves in green and yellow are superimposed on a paler green background. A second strip of brown herringbone sits above a yellow and brown spotted cheetah, painted in profile with its head turned in full face and its big green eyes wide open. Its back is raised and topped with a ribbed crest. This item shows traces of both Ottoman and Andalusian influences.

a8912ca5-9dcf-581c-885c-df8260626ef3.name: Plate with battle scene.
a8912ca5-9dcf-581c-885c-df8260626ef3.description:
Round-based plate. The rim is ribbed on the outer wall and slopes slightly outwards. The glaze has been applied direct onto the grey clay with no slip coating. Shape and technique are typical of Ifriqiyan ceramics of the high Middle Ages.  
The plate is illustrated with a battle scene in which horsemen at the gallop brandish shields in their left hands. This stylised, imaginative decoration is Mesopotamian and was very much in vogue in the Fatimid era. Although seeming to derive from contemporary Oriental sources, it probably has its origin in a distant, Roman, North African past. In fact, the horses drawn on this plate are less naturalistic, more stylised than those of similar Mesopotamian artefacts. From their freedom of line and their particular decoration they are more reminiscent of contemporary Ifriqiyan plates. Moreover, the riders' faces possess that huge eye which is a common denominator of almost all Ifriqiyan human figures of the time and which would confirm the fundamental North African influence behind the decoration of this plate.
a8912ca5-9dcf-581c-885c-df8260626ef3.short_description: This dish has a round base and sloping sides. It is illustrated with a war scene, suggesting a North African influence, while the stylised, fantasy decoration suggests a link with contemporary Eastern decoration. This type of decoration was extremely popular during the Fatimid era.
a8912ca5-9dcf-581c-885c-df8260626ef3.dates: Hegira, second half of the 4th–first half of the 5th century / AD 10th–11th centuries.
a8912ca5-9dcf-581c-885c-df8260626ef3.method_for_datation: This object comes from the site of Sabra al-Mansuriyya, the short-lived capital of the Fatimids and then of the Zirids, (337–444 / 948–1053). This dates it from the second half of the 4th / 10th century to the first half of the 5th / 11th century. No publication exists identifying exactly the stratigraphic layer the object came from and so a more precise dating is not possible.
a8912ca5-9dcf-581c-885c-df8260626ef3.method_for_provenance: The discovery of this plate on the Sabra site painted with Fatimid–Zirid decoration and made in the Ifriqiyan manner suggests it was produced locally at the Sabra potteries or at those of Kairouan, the nearest economic capital.
a8912ca5-9dcf-581c-885c-df8260626ef3.obtention: The plate was among objects discovered on site during the 1979 excavations at Sabra al-Mansuriyya. It was acquired by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada where it has been displayed since 1986.

a8a6f9eb-3333-5602-8d2c-2c290373e727.name: Jug with lustre decoration
a8a6f9eb-3333-5602-8d2c-2c290373e727.short_description:
The shape of the jug, with its angular shoulders, low feet and animal-shaped handle, derives from early Islamic metalwork. The exterior is decorated with a honeycomb pattern, filled with stylised floral motifs and wings that recall the Sasanian royal crown.  
  
The technique of lustre painting was used initially on glass. By applying a combination of metallic oxides, sulphur and other substances to the glazed surface and firing in an oxygen-poor muffle kiln, a thin metallic layer of gold, silver or copper was deposited on the surface. The process was difficult to control, as over-firing tended to dull the colours. Abbasid potters initially aimed for polychrome decoration but later monochrome yellowish lustre became popular. Lustre-painted vessels and tiles were a luxury, but fragments have been excavated all over the Middle East, northern India and Brahminabad in Sind.

a8a6f9eb-3333-5602-8d2c-2c290373e727.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on the shape of the vessel and the techniques used in its production.

a8cad3b1-e877-5fbf-9d11-982f19d43ae1.name: Ewer
a8cad3b1-e877-5fbf-9d11-982f19d43ae1.short_description: Fritware ewer with a pinched funnel like neck and crozier-shaped handle painted in black cobalt blue, turquoise, and ceiling wax red under a transparent colorless glaze. a96b9761-d3ff-5abd-8595-89489283b72f.name: Bowl
a96b9761-d3ff-5abd-8595-89489283b72f.short_description: Chinese porcelain from the Tang Dynasty was traded as luxury ware across the Indian Ocean into Iraq. Iraqi potters quickly began to develop local equivalents. They imitated the white colour by inventing an opaque white glaze to and embellished them with a cobalt blue inscription or design, most inscriptions refer to good fortune or the name of the potter. This bowl is an exceptional example of the so called “blue and white ceramics”, bearing a single bold line of kufic script.

a9ca5e93-6181-5581-a2a1-a5d53df76069.name: Bowl
a9ca5e93-6181-5581-a2a1-a5d53df76069.short_description: Grape motifs – symbolising wealth – can be found during the late Ming Period as decoration on porcelain bowls, which were also exported to the Ottoman court. Like  many other motifs, they were copied and varied in Iznik ceramics, most notably through the typical "tomato red".

aa0b309d-187e-51f6-a380-037fc3e58964.name: Dish.
aa0b309d-187e-51f6-a380-037fc3e58964.description: A small dish with decoration painted under the glaze. The central design features a finial-like motif in blue, white, and red, highlighted with black outlines. Its cresting outline is silhouetted against a background of tightly nested spirals. Four overlapping-rosette patterns with bold red centres are placed around the edge of the central circular area. Round the outside of this circle runs a series of emerald-green tri-lobed motifs. The rim of the dish is decorated with two rows of similar spirals interrupted by five large abstract wave-like forms tinged with green. Between these waves are set small red motifs which provide a subtle but effective contrast against the blue, black and white background. Although it is unknown for whom such a fine little dish would have been produced, since at this time the potters of Iznik were working for both imperial and popular (and even foreign) patrons, the quality of its decoration shows that the Ottoman ceramic industry was still at the height of its greatness.
aa0b309d-187e-51f6-a380-037fc3e58964.short_description: A small dish with a finial-like motif at the centre, on a background of tightly nested spirals. It is unknown for whom such a fine little dish would have been produced, since at this time the potters of Iznik were working for both imperial and popular (and even foreign) patrons.
aa0b309d-187e-51f6-a380-037fc3e58964.method_for_datation: The use of a distinctive turquoise, as well as a ground covered in closely packed spirals, was favoured by a certain Iznik workshop during the 1580s and 90s.
aa0b309d-187e-51f6-a380-037fc3e58964.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

aa2e3644-d6c0-5118-9a8c-3a9e9c44a8d0.name: Dish
aa2e3644-d6c0-5118-9a8c-3a9e9c44a8d0.short_description: This early sixteenth-century Manises dish is among the most individualistic examples preserved in the DDFIA collection. It features a single leaping deer (or goat), whose general outlines have been incised into the ceramic body. Other incised wares with similarly large lions, bulls, birds, and rabbits are known to exist, but it was more common for the undersides of Manises dishes to be painted with oversized birds and animals.

aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.name: *St. Francis of Assisi* Azulejos
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.alternate_name: *St. Francis of Assisi* Blue-and-white tile panel
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.description:
Our Lady of the Visitation Convent in Vila Verde dos Francos is a Franciscan Convent of the third order and, therefore, part of a noble residence where a few Franciscan friars lived a monastic life. D. António de Noronha, the owner of the residence, along with other nobles – both men and women – often went there to retreat.  
Society life necessarily followed strict social rules, which were taken very seriously. As part of the social mores was the struggle of the Christian soul against the Devil – Psychomachy – fundamental to salvation. Updated continuously up until the end of the Baroque period, the Hagiography (example of life) of St. Francis of Assisi was used as a didactic tale to explain to men, and especially to women, how to behave in society. As shown here, St. Francis was a sinner during his youth and, like him, people have the opportunity to resist temptation.  
The remarkable blue-and-white tile composition, by an artist from the Oliveira Bernardes' workshop circle, reveals a sophisticated technique and an artistic capacity to transform these moralising figurative *azulejos* into impressive iconographic themes.  
Handling the use of engravings in a most creative way, the artist adapted those compositions: pilasters with angels and *albarradas* (vases with flowers), to the wall covering as if it were a scenic architectural stage.  
This particular chancel panel recounts the episode of St. Francis converting Muslims in Syria during the Fifth Crusade. On this journey a woman with a lovely body but a "filthy soul" tried to tempt him. Feigning acceptance of her sinful offer, he took off his clothes and leaped into a fire, inviting her to follow him. He miraculously survived, having overcome the temptation and led the woman to salvation.
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.short_description: In this *azulejos* panel, St. Francis of Assisi is tempted by Evil, symbol of vanity and lust, one of the most regrettable sins of women. Evil Is conveyed here by a half-naked, half-devil woman.

aae1befb-bde5-5b51-b06a-8f5f49582dd4.name: Azulejo (glazed tile)
aae1befb-bde5-5b51-b06a-8f5f49582dd4.short_description: Apart from its utility function and use for cladding façades, the azulejo is, at the beginning of the 20th century, an iconic expression of Portuguese art. This panel, produced by the Faience Factory of Caldas da Rainha, depicts tiles made in Seville in the 16th century for the Palace of Sintra.

ab21cc92-59d1-559f-ab5b-149da55c95bd.name: Vase
ab21cc92-59d1-559f-ab5b-149da55c95bd.short_description: In 1891 Sultan Abdülhamid II founded the Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace for the purpose of reviving Turkish tile art and giving it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. A vase with conical body with wide mouth and round foot. There is a landscape painted on its body. The rest of its body has an intricate floral design painted on a green base. On the base a stamp of the star and crescent and dates of 1312-13 written in Arabic can be seen.

ab2ad44c-568d-5824-b3c4-9961e9edec7a.name: Ceramic Floor
ab2ad44c-568d-5824-b3c4-9961e9edec7a.description:
One of the oldest and rarest ceramic floors in Portugal, possibly dating from the building campaign promoted by King Afonso V (r.1438‒81), in the mid-15th century.  
Tradition has it that King Afonso VI (r.1656‒83) wore down the floor as he walked back and forth from his bed to the window overlooking the Sintra mountains. The truth, however, is that this floor was already more than two centuries old when he was imprisoned here, between 1674 and 1683, by order of his brother, King Pedro II (r.1683‒1706).  
The rare and valuable floor in this room presents a composition that combines various types of ceramic techniques and decorative styles, imbuing the tile set with dynamism, colour and originality.  
This is one of the oldest rooms in the palace and the only compartment of the palace that has an iron-barred window. The Palatine Chapel’s ceramic floor may date from the same period as this one.
ab2ad44c-568d-5824-b3c4-9961e9edec7a.method_for_datation:
Other art historians have dated the Palatine Chapel ceramic floor to the 15th century, probably contemporary with King Afonso V (1432‒81; r. 1438‒81). This monarch was born and died at the Royal Palace of Sintra and resided there frequently, as demonstrated by the countless documents signed by him here. Like King Duarte (1391‒38; r. 1433‒38), his father, King Afonso V seems to have held a special affection for the Palace at Sintra and carried out various improvements. He undertook the expansion and embellishment of the Palatine Chapel, probably from the mid-15th century (possibly between 1448 and 1476).  
The absence of cobalt blue in the ceramic floor reinforces the theory about its age.

ab2b67d7-838e-59c7-9a3d-24e8458ff5d8.name: Tankard
ab2b67d7-838e-59c7-9a3d-24e8458ff5d8.description: Iznik pottery, originating from the town of Iznik in western Anatolia, emerged during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II (AD 1451–1481). Initially influenced by blue and white Chinese Ming porcelains, Iznik ceramics evolved to incorporate vibrant hues. This cylindrical tankard, adorned with intricate carnations and tulips in blue, green and red, likely hails from the mid- to late 16th century, a pinnacle era for Iznik pottery. The distinctive red pigment, introduced circa 1570, possibly originated from iron-rich Armenian clay. Notably, cross-hatched black lines on the tankard suggest it was crafted based on a leather prototype.

materials: Stonepaste painted in blue, green and red under a transparent glaze

ab6e3c86-7858-5c43-a23c-f3a2d298a83f.name: Tile
ab6e3c86-7858-5c43-a23c-f3a2d298a83f.short_description: Toward the mid-10th / mid-16th century the colour scheme of Iznik wares expanded to include a brilliant red and a bright grass green, along with a blue deep. The magnificent tile with sumptuous flowers and lower border painted to imitate breccia marble probably comes from the royal living quarters at the Topkapı Sarayı Palace, Istanbul, from the time of Murad III (Hegira 982-1003 / AD 1574-95). This sultan’s expansion of his living quarters, from Hegira 986-996 / AD 1578-1588, included a bedroom pavilion decorated with Iznik tiles embellished with blossoming trees, flowers, and illusionistically painted imitation breccia marble, very similar to the LACMA tile. Objects of this type, both tile revetment and vessels, demonstrate the great variety of ornament used by Iznik potters; they also help to illustrate the different stylistic phases of Iznik wares, which in turn reflect the evolution of Ottoman taste in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries in a variety of media.
ab6e3c86-7858-5c43-a23c-f3a2d298a83f.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
ab6e3c86-7858-5c43-a23c-f3a2d298a83f.method_for_datation: The tile is similar to others in Murad III’s bedroom pavilion at Topkapi Saryi, Istanbul, completed in Hegira 996 / AD 1588.
ab6e3c86-7858-5c43-a23c-f3a2d298a83f.method_for_provenance: The tile represents the classical type of Iznik ceramics, in which the palette is comprised of red, blue green and white.
ab6e3c86-7858-5c43-a23c-f3a2d298a83f.obtention: Possibly Topkapi Saryi Palace (commissioned under the reign of Murad III), Istanbul, until 17th century. Possibly removed, seventeenth century. ab764cb9-de88-533a-9da2-2f302eeac364.name: Bowl with Design of Two Equestrian Figures, Two Seatd Figures, Tree, Birds, and Inscriptions
ab764cb9-de88-533a-9da2-2f302eeac364.short_description: A bowl, the interior with turquoise blue matte ground with polychrome decoration of two mounted horsemen flanking a tree. There is also a seated figure above each of the equestrian figures. There are three birds in the tree and another three birds below the horsemen. The blue border near the mouth rim forms a background for a repeated inscription in stylized *kufic* script, with tiny blue scallops along the edge. The exterior is turquoise blue with a *naskhi* inscription in black. Blue glaze covers part of foot. The bowl has been broken and repaired. Glaze has been lost from triangular area adjacent to the bird at lower right of the horsemen. Restored area includes part of seated figure at left.

ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.name: Qibla directional plate.
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.description:
Muslims must face the *qibla*, the direction of the Ka'ba in the city of Mecca, while praying. They therefore often need instruments to help pinpoint the direction of the Ka'ba. This plate is one such instrument. Its base is a round and flat area that has a circle of semi-vertical columns on it. Recorded around the centre of the circle is the name of the craftsperson and the place in which it was made (“made by Sayyid Thabit in Damascus”). Emanating from the centre towards the rim are tables in the form of a sequence of rings. These rings contain the names of a number of cities in three bands (Damascus, Baghdad, Constantinople, Jerusalem, Tehran, Kabul …), in addition to alphabets corresponding to numbers that indicate degrees of angles. The inner circumference of the plate's rim is marked by units, each of which is equivalent to five degrees and also the four cardinal directions (east, west, north, south), which are set in half circles.  
The exterior surface of the rim contains a two-line explanation in Arabic on how to use the instrument. In between these two lines are four medallions in which it is indicated that the plate was made by order of Sultan Salim I "the triumphant champion of justice and supreme ruler \[khaqan\] who is the son of the supreme ruler, king of the two lands and the two seas, and servant of the two sanctuaries, may God immortalise his rule". All this information is registered in black *kufic* script on a white background, and is covered with a transparent glaze.
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.short_description: The scientific diagram inscribed on this ceramic dish served an important function. A schematic arrangement of city names and trigonometric data help the user to establish the orientation of the Ka'ba in Mecca and thus the direction of prayer. It was especially useful when travelling.
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.initial_owner: Sultan Salim I (also Selim, r. AH 918–26 / AD 1512–20).
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.method_for_datation: The inscription on the plate indicates that it was made by order of Sultan Salim I, (r. 918–26 / 1512–20).
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.method_for_provenance: The inscription on the plate indicates that it was made in Damascus.

ab971419-834f-5843-8c6d-6b6cb9c2104a.name: Bowl.
ab971419-834f-5843-8c6d-6b6cb9c2104a.description: A large bowl on a high foot. The decoration, painted in cobalt and turquoise under the glaze, consists of long, continuous stems which coil into tight spiral roundels. This is a decorative style which flourished in Ottoman ceramics between about the 1520s and the 1550s. It is often called the 'Golden Horn' style in reference to the area in Istanbul where such wares were once thought – probably erroneously – to have been made. Another name, less frequently used, is the 'tuğrakeş spiral' style. This term was devised to emphasize the apparent connection between this style of decoration and that found in products of the Ottoman imperial chancery, whose expert illuminator, the tuğrakeş, was entrusted with decorating the sultan's imperial monogram or *tughra*. The extraordinary size of this bowl, as well as the skill with which it is decorated, suggests production for the highest levels of the Ottoman hierarchy, although direct evidence for this is lacking.
ab971419-834f-5843-8c6d-6b6cb9c2104a.short_description: A very large footed bowl on a high foot, decorated with the tightly coiled spirals sometimes called the ‘Golden Horn’ style. The size and quality of this bowl suggests that it was made for a high-ranking Ottoman official, possibly for washing the feet during ablutions.
ab971419-834f-5843-8c6d-6b6cb9c2104a.method_for_datation: Stylistic comparison with other, similarly decorated wares and with the illumination of imperial monograms in the period mentioned in the description.
ab971419-834f-5843-8c6d-6b6cb9c2104a.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

ac7d2e08-3036-5085-bcc1-db471ce20950.name: Bowl
ac7d2e08-3036-5085-bcc1-db471ce20950.short_description: Shallow earthenware bowl, with slightly everted rim, is glazed and overpainted with luster. The bowl has central rosette surrounded by a *kufic* inscription bearing the artist's name: "Blessing to the owner/the work of Sulayman, pupil of Abu Khalidan or Khaiikan/forbearance is a virtue". It is attributed to Nishapur.
keywords: Earthenware; Glaze; Luster; Rosette; calligraphy; kufic; inscription

acffa1ff-e78f-59cd-a3d3-aa606fa1ebc7.name: *Burma* (Camel milking bowl)
acffa1ff-e78f-59cd-a3d3-aa606fa1ebc7.description: The camel is the symbol of Bedu life. Offering both essential transport and milk, without camels, the Bedu would not have been able to survive in the desert. Camel milk is said to test saltier and more acidic than cow’s milk. Camels need milking two to four times per day. Milking bowls were traditionally made from clay.
acffa1ff-e78f-59cd-a3d3-aa606fa1ebc7.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century
acffa1ff-e78f-59cd-a3d3-aa606fa1ebc7.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

ad093485-bbc5-5ffd-9337-e1db1372739f.name: Tile panel
ad093485-bbc5-5ffd-9337-e1db1372739f.short_description: The primary decoration of this tile panel is the elegant inscription reserved in white against the blue ground. Although incomplete (the blue vertical bands represent areas of loss) the text is nonetheless readily recognisable. It is from the opening section of a particularly powerful chapter of the Qur’an (al-Fath: 4): “He it is who sent down tranquility upon the hearts of the believers that they might add faith to their faith – to God belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth, and God is All-Knowing, Wise…” The panel is very similar in dimensions, color scheme and calligraphic style to one in the Metropolitan Museum, which provides the information that it was made for an unidentified mosque.
ad093485-bbc5-5ffd-9337-e1db1372739f.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
ad093485-bbc5-5ffd-9337-e1db1372739f.dates: Hegira early 11th century / AD late 16th-early 17th century
ad093485-bbc5-5ffd-9337-e1db1372739f.method_for_datation: The cartouche-like frame and white on blue ground color scheme relate the panel to large Ottoman-era Syrian calligraphic friezes such as those in the Umayyad Mosque, Damascus, probably dating to the mid-16th century (e.g., south wall of the prayer hall). The LACMA panel probably also was created for a mosque.  The LACMA tile panel is very similar in style, color scheme and dimensions to one in the Metropolitan Museum (58.90.1a–g) dated Hegira 1000 / AD 1591–92, which was made for a mosque.
ad093485-bbc5-5ffd-9337-e1db1372739f.method_for_provenance: Syrian tiles of the Ottoman period though related to Iznik wares do not contain red in their palette. The cartouche-like frame and white on blue ground color scheme relate the panel to large Ottoman-era calligraphic friezes in the Umayyad Mosque, Damascus, among other buildings.
ad093485-bbc5-5ffd-9337-e1db1372739f.obtention: Collection of Maan Z. Madina (1926-2013), New York, until 2002 (sold to); LACMA, The Madina Collection of Islamic Art, gift of Camilla Chandler Frost.

ad2cb375-808c-5067-aa87-d73fb88bbe79.name: Bowl
ad2cb375-808c-5067-aa87-d73fb88bbe79.short_description: The bowl painted in lustre on an opaque white glaze is a typical example of the miniature style of Kashan. The decoration is riders on horseback and cypresses.

ae298707-a316-526f-bd3e-9e589dc8eee0.name: Wall tile
ae298707-a316-526f-bd3e-9e589dc8eee0.short_description: Inscription: Qur´an, *sura* 23, Vers 81 "... distinction of the night ..."
ae298707-a316-526f-bd3e-9e589dc8eee0.author: Mio Wakita-Elis

aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.name: Bowl with stand
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.short_description: This bowl with a bulging rim sits on a stand. The decoration is made of two layers of concentric patterns around a central circle, filled with winged motifs. These green and brown patterns are painted on a yellow background. Although this kind of bowl is usually used to serve couscous, in the town Nabeul, and particularly for the occasion of Islamic New Year, each child is presented with a *methred* bowl, filled with golden couscous, dried fruit, dates, a hard-boiled egg and sweets. This all surrounds a statuette made of sugar, moulded and coloured to resemble an animal (such as a rooster or a gazelle) or a figure, like a doll or cavalier.

keywords: Floral motifs; winged motifs; cermaics from Nabeul

aee0d03f-b711-5643-8552-3ef51656eff4.name: *Jarrita* vase with two handles
aee0d03f-b711-5643-8552-3ef51656eff4.description: This drinking vase has a pear-shaped body and two rounded handles that join a short neck that widens toward the top; it rests on a low base. The decoration, painted in dark blue and a beautiful shade of bronze-gold on the ivory opaque glaze, is placed symmetrically on both sides of the handles. A frieze of pseudo-epigraphy whose drawing seems to recall the word *al-'afiya* (good health)... is drawn in blue on the neck over a glossy background of a wormlike pattern. On the body, eight-lobed medallions in bronze-gold have a blue pseudo-epigraphic pattern in the centre. On each side of the handles is a scalloped almond composition. Directly below each handle is another pseudo-epigraphic motif against a glossy background. A series of horizontal lines rings the lower part of the body. The lustre decoration with metallic reflections is a process peculiar to the arts of Islam. The technique is seen as early as the eighth century on fragments of Egyptian glasses; it was later applied to ceramics, beginning in the ninth century in Mesopotamia under the reign of the Abbasids. It is a decoration painted on a glazed piece that has undergone a first firing. The lustre consists of a mixture of copper and silver oxides to which are added sulphur and red ochre, and a binder to permit a brushed application. A second firing in an oxygen-poor atmosphere results in the incorporation of the oxide particles, now reduced to a metallic state in the softened glaze. Quite characteristic effects are produced when the pieces are observed in light. The secrets of this complex and sometimes unpredictable technique were jealously guarded in pottery workshops. Nevertheless, the process spread to both the East and the Muslim West, and in Spain its development was encouraged by the Nasrid rulers, especially in Malaga. Since the Reconquest, the craze for Hispano-Moorish ceramics (*loza dorada*), continues, since production is exported to Muslim countries and Christian Europe. Cobalt blue and brown lustre, combined in bold compositions, as here, give a characteristic identity to a process that is still used, for example in Manises (in Valencia).

af2360cf-273b-5cf6-9a61-60adaa53198d.name: Dish
af2360cf-273b-5cf6-9a61-60adaa53198d.short_description:
A few types of the AD 17th century Persian ceramic ware, painted in a free expressive style and covered with cracks, were traditionally known as “*Kubachi*” ceramics. This conventional name came from a village in Daghestan, where in the 19th century huge amounts of Iranian Safavid pottery were concentrated. However, the production centres of various "*Kubachi*" wares are still to be specified.  
The innovations in the 17th -century Iranian miniature painting, and particularly in the portrait genre, were reflected in décor of ceramic ware. A large plate, decorated in multicoloured painting, represents the favourite motifs of the Safavid era. Images of the lush garden with birds symbolized the joy of earthly paradise and the promised enjoyment of heavenly paradise. A handsome young dervish meditating in the blooming garden stood for the Divine Beloved in the symbolic language of Islamic mystics.  
Multicolour painting of various plants, rendered in natural bends of their sprouts and branches, was inspired by the style of Turkish Iznik ceramics of the late 16th century. Such kind of ware was probably produced in the workshops of Qumisheh (now Shahreza), a small town near Isfahan.
af2360cf-273b-5cf6-9a61-60adaa53198d.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by I. Rapoport (examination, 1963, date, origin), H. Rudyk (publication, 2017, date specified).
af2360cf-273b-5cf6-9a61-60adaa53198d.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
af2360cf-273b-5cf6-9a61-60adaa53198d.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalized by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

b0765880-f23a-5f96-bc55-a402dfeabde4.name: Vessel.
b0765880-f23a-5f96-bc55-a402dfeabde4.description: A stone-paste (fritware) vessel with an arabesque decoration on the top half of its baluster form. Painted in black and blue under a transparent glaze; the glaze has deteriorated rather badly. The shape is similar to Iranian pottery vessels and is indicative of the close artistic relationship between Syria and Iran during this period, especially between Raqqa and Kashan as, with the exception of the *mina'i* wares produced in Kashan, Raqqa produced more or less the same type of ceramics. Raqqa was one of two major pottery-production centres in Ayyubid Syria, the other being Rusafah. In Raqqa there were a number of pottery workshops that produced a range of ceramics including lustre-painted, relief-moulded, and underglaze-painted vessels. Pottery production ceased when the Mongols razed the city to the ground in AH 657 / AD 1259.
b0765880-f23a-5f96-bc55-a402dfeabde4.short_description: Raqqa potters had a close artistic relationship with those of Iran during the late Abbasid period, and especially during the Ayyubid period. The shape and the style of the blue and black arabesque decoration of this vessel are similar to vessels made in the city of Kashan in Iran.
b0765880-f23a-5f96-bc55-a402dfeabde4.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis, together with analysis of the material composition of the vessel's body which is distinctively that of Raqqa. Furthermore, the nature and extent of the deterioration of the glaze is also typical of Raqqa ceramics.
b0765880-f23a-5f96-bc55-a402dfeabde4.method_for_provenance: The vessel is typical of Raqqa ceramics in both its material composition and in the nature of the deterioration of the glaze.
b0765880-f23a-5f96-bc55-a402dfeabde4.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

b0765880-f23a-5f96-bc55-a402dfeabde4.author: Noorah Al-Gailani

b09ccbac-3e92-56ec-95ea-6a58eb8d70a9.name: Dish (*tondino*).
b09ccbac-3e92-56ec-95ea-6a58eb8d70a9.description: A dish in the Italianate form known as tondino, with a narrow, deep well and a wide rim, decorated in two shades of blue on a white ground. The centre of the bowl features a medallion with a 'bouquet' of five flowers growing from a small mound. This pattern is repeated around the rim, in round spaces created by triangle-like indentations in dark blue; these spaces are linked by six-pointed stars at their intersections. Although the bouquet pattern is repeated, a close look reveals that no stencil was used – the artist drew the pattern freehand each time. This dish is one of a group of wares thought to represent a point in the history of Iznik pottery when the potters themselves, rather than painters, took over the decoration of the ceramics. This may have been a reaction to falling demand from the Ottoman court; by applying the designs themselves, the potters could lower the prices of the objects, and thus sell them to a broader market. The result of this change of approach was a simpler, more spontaneous style than the studied and meticulous designs found on previous Iznik wares. While the 'Potters'' style did not last long, giving way during the decade AH 950 / AD 1540 to the nascent classical Iznik aesthetic of brilliant polychrome floral designs, it does represent an important moment in the history of Ottoman ceramics.
b09ccbac-3e92-56ec-95ea-6a58eb8d70a9.short_description: A dish in the Italianate form known as *tondino*, with decoration based on a repeating pattern of a bouquet of five flowers. This dish is one of a group of wares thought to represent a time when the potters themselves, rather than painters, took over the decoration of Iznik ceramics.
b09ccbac-3e92-56ec-95ea-6a58eb8d70a9.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

b1b31d42-2423-51e8-9e8c-0117ff7b0186.name: Cylindrical tankard.
b1b31d42-2423-51e8-9e8c-0117ff7b0186.description: A cylindrical tankard with an angular handle, decorated with stems of tulips, hyacinths and other flowers in light blue, green and red on a white background. The vertical stems are gently curved. The edges of the rim and base are bordered with wave patterns. The model of this tankard, taking its inspiration from the art of metalwork of the Balkans, became widespread in Ottoman Turkey in the second half of the AH 10th / AD16th century. This piece may also have been used as a flower vase.
b1b31d42-2423-51e8-9e8c-0117ff7b0186.short_description: Tankard inspired by the Balkan metalware popularised in Ottoman Turkey in the second half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century. This piece is decorated with bunches of tulips, hyacinths and other flowers in light blue, green and red on a white background.
b1b31d42-2423-51e8-9e8c-0117ff7b0186.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis. The broadening of the range of colours with the introduction of red, Armenian bole, indicates production in the second half of the 10th / 16th century.
b1b31d42-2423-51e8-9e8c-0117ff7b0186.method_for_provenance: By expert examination, stylistic and comparative analysis and exhibition catalogues written by international specialists, mentioned in the bibliography.
b1b31d42-2423-51e8-9e8c-0117ff7b0186.obtention: From the Jeuniette collection, it was purchased through M. Stora & Co. on 10 April 1919.

b1c9d73d-7178-5324-9b0c-d946356b48ab.name: Plate
b1c9d73d-7178-5324-9b0c-d946356b48ab.description: Red clay, cream slip, decorated in purple-brown and mustard tones under a transparent colourless glaze.  It is one of the few surviving examples of a plate used on a daily basis. In a naive manner the giraffe is depicted tied to two trees. The rim is decorated with an intermittent lattice pattern. The model for the giraffe was sent as a gift to Sultan Mahmut II in 1823 by the governor of Egypt, Kavalalı Mehmet Ali Pasha. It was kept on a ship anchored in Çanakkale harbour that was being resupplied on its way to Istanbul. Upon seeing the giraffe in the harbour, ceramic masters were inspired to produce a new motif in their workshops by reproducing the giraffe on plates.
b1c9d73d-7178-5324-9b0c-d946356b48ab.dates: Hegira 1st half of 13th century / AD early 19th century

b1ea078d-e766-5285-80c6-1d829833078f.name: 26 clay screens for water jars
b1ea078d-e766-5285-80c6-1d829833078f.short_description: These clay screens served as enclosures for water jugs and are decorated with various patterns. The decoration is either drawn into the damp clay with a thin wire or cut out of the clay. Some of the screen closures hold fragments of the neck of the vessel.

b1fe1635-a0ea-5d86-871f-4148f5ba34cc.name: Plate
b1fe1635-a0ea-5d86-871f-4148f5ba34cc.short_description:
The genuine enthusiasm that Chinese blue-and-white porcelain aroused in Iran since AD 14th century led to various attempts of Persian potters to unravel the main Chinese secret and to devise ways to simulate the unparalleled effects of porcelain.  
Along with plates and bottles that more or less closely imitated Chinese porcelain in the motifs and style, an authentic Iranian style of cobalt-blue décor developed in the 17th–18th century. This plate depicting tigers and birds in dense thickets of forest or garden, freely arranged in a decentralized composition, was possibly made in Kerman of the early 18th century.
b1fe1635-a0ea-5d86-871f-4148f5ba34cc.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by I. Rapoport (examination, 1963, date, origin).
b1fe1635-a0ea-5d86-871f-4148f5ba34cc.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).

b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.name: Hornos vase
b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.description: Pear-shaped vase with a narrow base decorated with six rings. It has a tall, faceted, flared neck, a wide, protruding rim, and wing handles. The decoration combines gold and cobalt on a cream ground, forming segments of blue listels on the main body which are filled with vegetal compositions based on palms, palmettes, and pines. This vertical partition is repeated on the neck where, over two friezes framed in blue and decorated in reserve over a gold ground, salient edges are added. The first of the friezes features a cursive calligraphic inscription; the second, interlaces. The wing handles also feature small-scale vegetal decoration, overlaid with palmette scrolls. Reflecting the splendour of the Nasrid courts, the so-called Alhambra vases were considered luxury items. They were frequently mentioned as gifts and praised in the chronicles of Medieval travellers. These vases were manufactured in specialised workshops using complex lusterware techniques in gold and cobalt blue; they often included short poems of the fajr genre, or boastful style, reflecting on the object's beauty, contents, and use. Specifically, as translated by Eduardo Saavedra in 1875, the inscription around the neck of the Vase of Hornos praises the value of water: "Every fountain springs forth, resembling the most perfect stream, and increases abundant kindness and excellent joys. And it affirms the memory of happiness and poverty that faded away morning and evening with the fortune of time."
b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.provenance: Church of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, Hornos (province of Jaén, Spain)
b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.obtention: Unearthed during plowing, the vase was moved to the Church of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, where it served as holy water stoup. First acquired by V. Juan y Amat, then deposited at the Valencia Institute of Don Juan. Later purchased by the Spanish State for the National Archaeological Museum.

b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.name: Pilgrim bottle.
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.description:
The heavy, pinkish-grey earthenware flask belongs to the group of the so-called pilgrim bottles. The body of this type of pilgrim bottle is commonly composed of two flat circular sides, each with a broad, flanged edge and an unornamented strip of earthenware in the middle connecting the two side parts. This connecting strip is slightly concave so that the flask stands in a safe upright position on the edges of the side parts. Above, the bottle has a flared neck consisting of two sections separated by a ring in relief. The rim of the neck is damaged. For carrying and suspension, there are two handles fixed to the neck and to the shoulders. The bottle shows identical moulded decoration on both sides. At the centre there is an eight-petalled rosette surrounded by an arabesque scroll. The four double-framed leaf forms of the outer zone are set against a dense background pattern of tiny rhombs.  
On similar bottles the centre of the sides often bears an emblem easily recognised as belonging to one of the Ayyubid or Mamluk sultans and amirs. These emblems were attributes of their dignity. A rosette might not appear to be a specific emblem but it does actually belong to them. It is actually one of the oldest devices used under the Ayyubids and early Mamluks. They usually chose six-petalled rosettes. Only one amir, Musa bin Yaghmur (AH 599–663 / AD 1203–65), seems to be known whose emblem was a white eight-petalled rosette as seen on this bottle. He was governor of Cairo under the Ayyubid al-Malik al-Salih and in AH 648 / AD 1250 under al-Malik al-Mu'azzam governor of Damascus.  
Judging by the unglazed body, this bottle could have been used for storing liquids such as water. The porous material allowed evaporation to keep the liquid stored in it cool.
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.short_description: Earthenware flask. Characteristic are two flat circular sides and handles for carrying and suspension. Both sides are decorated with an eight-petalled rosette at the centre. This is the place where Ayyubid and Mamluk sultans and amirs usually marked their bottles with their own emblem.
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.dimensions: Height 26.5 cm, diameter of body 13.6 cm, diameter of rim 7.9 cm.
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.method_for_datation: An Ayyubid amir, Musa bin Yaghmur (599–663 / 1203–65), is known to have as an emblem the eight-petalled rosette without shield.
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.method_for_provenance: There are different clues. Musa bin Yaghmur to whom the bottle may be ascribed was governor of Damascus. Other pilgrim bottles of this type come from Syria and Jordan. This bottle is supposed to have been excavated, probably in Syria, since it was bought by the Swedish Crown Prince in Aleppo.
b233b9f9-606a-5020-b525-f2dfcb494a75.obtention: Gift of the Swedish Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf in 1935.

The ceramic ewer is decorated with underglaze ground cobalt blue pigment and two-tone rosettes outlined in over glazed white enamel and gold leaf.

b2a64729-0616-53e6-bc8d-4d7583ceac8c.name: Plate
b2a64729-0616-53e6-bc8d-4d7583ceac8c.short_description: Sultan Abdülhamid II founded in 1891 the *Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu* (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace in order to revive Turkish tile art and give it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. This plate features a dark green background on which there is a *tuğra* (monogram) made of gilding and a border around the edge.

b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.name: Raqqa lustre bowl.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.description:
The thin wall of the bowl is decorated symmetrically on the inside with a quatrefoil motif that covers its entire surface. A stylised trefoil leaf is painted within each of the four petals. Corkscrew tendrils, each with a bifid leaf, occupy the spaces between the outer contours of the petals. The outer edge is emphasised with a lustre stripe.  
A collection of about 100 pieces of pottery, to which this piece belongs, was found at Tell Minis in Syria. At first it was thought that such pieces were imported into Syria from Egypt, but the discovery at Tell Minis confirmed that they were made in Syria. Meanwhile, the findings gained from excavating in the urban area of Raqqa have confirmed that a large number of these ceramics were produced in Raqqa. Some of these feature inscriptions. The decoration is very reminiscent of Fatimid ceramics, modified by the introduction of lustre painting and the use of quartz fritware. It can be assumed that, following the end of the Fatimid dynasty (AH 564 / AD 1169), Egyptian manufacturers of ceramics moved to Syria, where they introduced the new techniques. The existence of identical ceramic pieces strongly suggests that pattern drawings were used in the workshops.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.short_description: Small thin-walled bowls with figurative or vegetal patterns in a reddish colour are typical of Syrian lustre-ware pottery of the Ayyubid period. The design of this bowl with four petals in ovals and arabesque leaves in the spandrels is very clear and perfectly fits the round shape of the bowl.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.dates: Hegira late 6th–early 7th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.method_for_datation: The excavations in Raqqa confirm that lustre ceramics glazed with reddish-brown lustre were made in Syria during the Ayyubid period. The technique was brought over by potters from Egypt following the downfall of the Fatimids.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.method_for_provenance: Findings made in Tell Minis and in Raqqa have led to the conclusion that this type of ceramic originated in Syria.
b35798dc-77ea-5958-913f-2fb174b5a6c6.obtention: From a private gallery in London, 1992.

b3d75056-35c3-5258-acbf-bbe88d25a45b.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
b3d75056-35c3-5258-acbf-bbe88d25a45b.description:
Although many people believe the word *azulejo* derives from the Portuguese word *azul* (blue), this is a misconception. The use of this colour in *azulejos* can be limited to a very narrow timeline of approximately 60 years (c. 1690‒1750) in a larger history of more than 500 years of uninterrupted use in Portugal.  
Nevertheless, there are some exceptions for the single use of blue in Portuguese *azulejos* outside this chronology, one of which can be seen in this panel. In this complex pattern of 6 x 6 *azulejos*, 36 pieces are required to obtain a single motif that can be reproduced to infinity, whereby its intertwined double four-lobe design has a lighter dimension on account of the monochromatic use of blue. Although complex, the blue gives a subtlety to the design of this motif, and in this way focuses the attention rather than tiring the senses.  
By contrast, the frame uses a different kind of composition. Instead of the motif in blue over the white background, it opens the decoration in white over a dense blue using a decoration that can be compared to woodcarving or some jewellery of this period. By this, the contrast between a very dense frame and the motif is lightened by a less compact pattern, creating equilibrium between elements, which provides the viewer a harmonious sense of beauty.
b3d75056-35c3-5258-acbf-bbe88d25a45b.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: 17th-century production of *azulejos* in Portugal, of this intense blue, was accomplished only by the Lisbon workshops
b3d75056-35c3-5258-acbf-bbe88d25a45b.method_for_provenance: The National Tile Museum holds a large number of *azulejos* of unknown origin, many gathered during the period of the destruction of the convents and palaces in the late 19th century, in the aftermath of the abolition of the religious orders in 1834.
b3d75056-35c3-5258-acbf-bbe88d25a45b.obtention: Probably salvaged during demolition of an unknown building where they had once been applied
