b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.name: Dish.
b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.description:
The polychrome underglaze painted dish with a sloping rim and a deep well shows a male human figure outlined in black on a white background. The man is dressed in uncoloured wide trousers, a pale blue jacket and a white blouse with green sleeves. His hat and shoes and the flower that he holds in his right hand are of thick pale red. Five flowers on thin curved stems – two red-dotted blue tulips and three smaller ones with red blossoms – fill the area around the man. The rim shows a zigzag pattern composed of almond-shaped leafs. The triangular areas are coloured alternately in light blue and a bright green and filled with half-rosettes, each with a red dot at the centre. On the back the dish is painted with three large blue dots under a transparent, light turquoise coloured glaze. The foot-ring is pierced once for suspension.  
Figurative depictions on Iznik ceramics were inspired by the popular imagery of miniature costume albums, many of which were produced for sale to Europeans from the beginning of the AH 11th / AD 17th century. The standardised painting of the man and the formulaic character of the flower decoration are due to the mass production of the open market.
b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.short_description: Polychrome painted dish with a deep well showing a human figure on a white background. The area around the man is filled with flowers. The rim shows a zigzag pattern. Figurative depictions on Iznik ceramics were inspired by the popular imagery of miniature costume albums.
b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.dates: Hegira first half of 11th century / AD first half of the 17th century.
b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.method_for_datation: The object was dated from its decoration. Figurative depictions, frequently in combination with a zigzag pattern on the rim, occurred in great number on Iznik ceramics from the beginning of the 11th / 17th century. They were inspired by single-figure costume studies such as the Album of Sultan Ahmed I (r. 1011–25 / 1603–17) and its popular copies.
b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.method_for_provenance: The zigzag pattern on the rim in combination with the human figure occurred in great number on Iznik ceramics from the beginning of the 11th / 17th century.
b4039c69-caaf-5330-a68e-4354845b82a9.obtention: Bequest of the Hungarian scientist, Nobel Prize winner and art collector, Georg von Békésy (1899–1972).

b44570b2-8918-5357-94ca-bfbb2096bf44.short_description: Small bowl decorated with an incised design of spiralling scrolls ending in palmettes and two green splashes. The shape of the vessel, resting on a foot-ring, and the slightly everted rim, recalls Chinese prototypes.

b458ec48-6ce3-5cb1-a3f6-348c8e7108e6.name: Ceramic tile panel.
b458ec48-6ce3-5cb1-a3f6-348c8e7108e6.description:
A panel of ten ceramic tiles, a product of the Maghrebi School of ceramists who travelled to Egypt and settled in coastal cities such as Alexandria, Rashid (Rosetta) and Damietta. The piece is decorated with overglaze paintings in blue, yellow and green. In the lower portion of the panel there is the shape of a pair of feet coloured in blue, above which are architectural forms, made up of a group of small domes, and other decorative elements in the Ottoman style. Towering over them is a single large semi-circular dome. It is flanked on either side by the forms of pencil-shaped minarets in the Ottoman style. The dome is framed at the top by a lobed arch, whose pinnacle is crowned by a crescent-shaped motif. It is possible that the feet and the architectural forms symbolise the *Mi'raj* where the Prophet Muhammad ascended the heavens accompanied by the Angel Gabriel from the site of al-Haram al-Sharif in the sacred precinct of Jerusalem. It was there that he met the prophets and the number of mandatory prayers for all Muslims were ordained to be five daily.  
It is known that the ceramists of the Maghrebi School migrated to Egypt in the second half of the AH 12th / AD 18th century and settled in coastal cities, producing wares that were influenced by the styles and techniques used in the ceramic workshops of the Maghreb and al-Andalus. This might explain the widespread use of the term, *Zilizli*, which is used by the inhabitants of Rashid (Rosetta) for ceramic tiles, as it is derived from the word, *zillij* meaning ceramic tiles in colloquial Maghrebi Arabic. Among the most famous of the Tunisian ceramists who migrated to Egypt and settled in Alexandria was al-Hajj Mas'ud al-Sab'a whose signature is found, along with an inscription: 'The work of the master al-Sab'a', on the ceramic tiles that embellish the Dar Jalluli in Tunisia. This ceramist also established a distinguished school in Egypt in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. A number of his ceramics were utilised in the decoration of some contemporary buildings in Alexandria and Cairo.
b458ec48-6ce3-5cb1-a3f6-348c8e7108e6.short_description: Artisans moved freely from one country to another in the Islamic world. Artisans from Mosul came to Egypt after the Mogul invasion of Baghdad. Maghrebi ceramic artisans, likewise, brought their style influenced by the Andalusian style. This ceramic tile panel follows the Tunisian school.
b458ec48-6ce3-5cb1-a3f6-348c8e7108e6.method_for_datation: Some of the most prominent ceramics produced by al-Hajj Mas'ud al-Sab'a is the tile-panelling that embellishes the Mosque of Abd al-Baqi Georgi (Chorbagi) in Alexandria, (built 1171 / 1757). His name, which is incorporated into the tilework, includes the words, 'work of the master al-Sab'a'. This extensive tile panelling, which covers both the walls of the mosque and the *mihrab,* consists of ceramic tiles in the Maghrebi style. In the decorative scheme, the base of the composition comprises vases from which flowers, stems or depictions of buildings and architectural components emerge; domed buildings and minarets in the Ottoman style, as well as crescent shapes, which complete the decoration at the top of the composition. The architectural and vegetal decoration in the tiling of the Mosque of Abd al-Baqi Georgi resembles to a large extent the decorative scheme of the tiles we are discussing here. In view of the great similarity in style, the similarity of decorative components, and the fact that the signature of the craftsman is on the tiles of the Mosque of Abd al-Baqi Georgi, we may deduce that these tiles are his work, or at the very least, of his school.
b458ec48-6ce3-5cb1-a3f6-348c8e7108e6.method_for_provenance: It is highly probable that this tile panel is the work of al-Hajj Mas'ud al-Sab'a. That he was prolific in Alexandria, Egypt, is verified by the presence of his work in the Mosque of Abd al-Baqi Georgi (Chorbagi).
b458ec48-6ce3-5cb1-a3f6-348c8e7108e6.obtention: It was housed in the museum as part of the *waqf* of Prince Yusuf Kamal in the year 1923. Prince Yusuf was a prince of the Muhammad 'Ali family and he donated a large collection of his acquisitions especially jewellery, textiles, ceramic and wooden pieces to the museum.

Atil, E., *Ceramics from the World of Islam*, Washington D.C., 1973.

b5902a63-cea0-5cad-8814-d54861e5f719.name: Dish
b5902a63-cea0-5cad-8814-d54861e5f719.short_description: Ceramics with a molded or stamped decoration in relief inspired by Roman or Sasanian metalwork is known from as early as the Umayyad period. This flat dish, with its distinctive Arabic inscription in *Kufi* calligraphy, is a further development of this type and is also an example of a pure and harmonious Islamic style that was found in Abbasid Iraq.
materials: Earthenware with molded decoration covered by a yellow and green glaze

b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.name: Tile (*azulejo*).
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.description:
Square tile cast from whitish clay with decoration in relief covered with a tin glaze showing two long-legged birds facing each other before a tree with intertwined branches. The coat of arms of the Nasrid dynasty sits on top of the tree and another two birds are to be found in the top corners, one almost completely missing due to a break suffered by the tile. Some of the decorative motifs were realised in blue and gold, although the gold has almost completely disappeared.  
Nasrid ceramics are considered to be a continuation of Almohad ceramics. Glazed clay had already been used in this period in exterior decoration, but it was during the Nasrid age that its use inside palaces reached its peak, mainly to decorate plinths and floors. The more sumptuous finishes were made using tiles with metallic highlights in gold or gold and blue on a white background.  
In terms of decoration, panels with figurative motifs are also to be found in the Palace of the Alhambra, from where this piece originates, although they are a minority. This tile belongs to a type in which influences from the Christian world are beginning to become apparent. The use of vegetal as well as zoomorphic and heraldic motifs are closely related to Gothic models.  
With regard to the origin of the Nasrid coat of arms, there is no doubt that heraldry as ornamentation comes from the Christian and not the Muslim world. Most researchers concur that it originated with the coat of arms of the Order of the Band founded by Alfonso XI in 1330. The Nasrid kingdom, as a vassal of Castile, used this coat of arms, incorporating the motto of their dynasty 'There is no conqueror but God'.
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.short_description: The inclusion of the coat of arms of the Nasrid sultans on the ‘tree of life’ suggests that this tile was intended to decorate the Alhambra. It is an example, albeit a faulty one, of an exquisite lustrework technique using blue cobalt, enhanced in this case with figures in relief.
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.dates: Around the turn of the Hegira 9th century / AD 15th century.
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.dimensions: Height 22.5 cm, width 22.5 cm, depth 2.8 cm.
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.method_for_datation: This piece belongs to a series of Nasrid tiles with the same decoration that are kept in the National Museum of Hispano-Muslim Art in Granada, the Institute of Valencia de Don Juan, Madrid and the National Archaeological Museum. They all originate from the Palace of the Alhambra and were dated by Martínez Caviro to around the turn of the 15th century.
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.method_for_provenance: The Nasrid coat of arms indicates that it came from the Kingdom of Granada, but there is some doubt about the exact place where the tiles were produced. The first examples may have been made in Malaga, with later pieces being made in Granada. Ceramicists would commonly move to work on large projects such as the Palace of the Alhambra.
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.provenance: Palace of the Alhambra, Kingdom of Granada, Spain.
b5db61c2-f435-5ed6-87a3-c6bbd6e5f917.obtention: The piece was deposited with the National Archaeological Museum by the State on 1 July 1941.

b6227f02-1142-5b04-b3af-734ad8573ce6.name: Drums
b6227f02-1142-5b04-b3af-734ad8573ce6.short_description: The two drums are part of the flourishing tradition of enamelled ceramic in Fez, in production since the Middle Ages. Cobalt blue and white decorations identify Fez products dating to the second half of the 19th century. The drums belong to the ethnographic collections of the Pigorini Museum founded between the 19th and the 20th century. The origins of scientific activity and conservation of Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the "Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography in Rome" within the buildings of the Roman College.

b66de1ea-876e-5dc1-93b3-a69ada001076.name: Stove
b66de1ea-876e-5dc1-93b3-a69ada001076.description: A stove on an iron pedestal and composed of two main parts, the lower has a scalloped design; the walls of the corpus are green and decorated with white sculptural and relief decoration (bunches of flowers, volutes and *Rocaille*). In the centre of the lower part are elongated cartouches with scenes in relief. In two of these cartouches ladies and gentlemen are ambling in the countryside with shepherds' crooks in their hands, while in the third there is an idyllic picture of music-making under a tree. The top of the stove ends with a three-dimensional figure of a female shepherd with a lamb in her arms. The firebox is at the rear.
b66de1ea-876e-5dc1-93b3-a69ada001076.short_description: A white and green stove richly decorated in the lower part, with a three-dimensional figure of a female shepherd at the top.

b6b54e1a-238d-59fb-8fc0-bf1b0cd6d93c.name: Pitcher.
b6b54e1a-238d-59fb-8fc0-bf1b0cd6d93c.description:
A pitcher offering an example of Syrian polychrome underglaze pottery. It follows the trend in Persian *mina'i* ware that is characterised by prominent colours, and gilding, applied over the glaze. As Syrian potters were not familiar with the technique of applying overglaze enamels, they used their habitual underglaze method while adopting the iconography and style of *mina'i*. This type of enamel ceramic decoration flourished during the AH 6th / AD 12th and AH 7th / AD 13th centuries in Persia with contemporary imitative wares in Syria, The increased flexibility in paint application and colour has characterised these wares with more figurative and even narrative representations.  
This small pitcher is outfitted with a handle and has a simple circular base. The lip of the vessel opens out slightly towards the exterior presumably to ensure liquids poured efficiently, and is decorated with geometric and stylised vegetal ornamentation. Most of the body is decorated with a group of sitting women, some of them playing musical instruments. Their clothing, accessories and hairstyles may indicate the fashions of the day, and provide insight into what were seen as the ideals of beauty by contemporary society; the trend for vertically striped fabrics in alternate colours is an example. The decoration of the pitcher is executed in black, burgundy, and dark blue on an ivory-yellow base, and traces of gilding are also evident.
b6b54e1a-238d-59fb-8fc0-bf1b0cd6d93c.short_description: This exquisite little pitcher with polychrome underglaze decoration is an example of a popular style of ceramics from the AH 6th and 7th / AD 12th and 13th centuries in Syria. It reveals a scene of Eastern-featured women playing various musical instruments.
b6b54e1a-238d-59fb-8fc0-bf1b0cd6d93c.dates: Around hegira late 6th century / AD 12th century.
b6b54e1a-238d-59fb-8fc0-bf1b0cd6d93c.method_for_datation: Through stylistic comparisons with similar objects made in Syria most of which date to the late 6th / 12th and early 7th / 13th centuries.
b6b54e1a-238d-59fb-8fc0-bf1b0cd6d93c.method_for_provenance: Many similar pieces of polychrome underglaze pottery have been found in the regions of Jazira and Raqqa. Furthermore, scholars have noted the lack of enamel or overglaze painted pottery found in the region. Hence it is thought to be a Syrian production and not an Iranian import.
b6b54e1a-238d-59fb-8fc0-bf1b0cd6d93c.provenance: Jazira (the region located between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, hence known as “the island” and currently consisting of northeast modern Syria and northwest Iraq), or Mesopotamia.

b6ddda27-c0ff-5f0f-b4b1-bb06af0f4dc4.name: Vase with lid.
b6ddda27-c0ff-5f0f-b4b1-bb06af0f4dc4.description: Lidded vase, with medallions painted in blue under the transparent glaze and metallic lustre decoration. On the white background motifs are arranged in compartmented horizontal rows, composed of pseudo-inscriptions in a flowery *kufic* script interrupted by circular medallions containing floral motifs and scrolls. The lid follows the same decorative design as the vase itself. It cannot be stated with certainty what function the object served; it might have been a utilitarian or a decorative object, or possibly both.
b6ddda27-c0ff-5f0f-b4b1-bb06af0f4dc4.short_description: Ayyubid lidded pot from Raqqa in Syria. Motifs consisting of pseudo-inscriptions in flowery *kufic* script are arranged in compartmented horizontal strips on a white background, interrupted by circular medallions with floral motifs and scrolls.
b6ddda27-c0ff-5f0f-b4b1-bb06af0f4dc4.dates: Hegira end 6th century / AD end 12th century.
b6ddda27-c0ff-5f0f-b4b1-bb06af0f4dc4.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and by comparison with objects from the same period.
b6ddda27-c0ff-5f0f-b4b1-bb06af0f4dc4.method_for_provenance: By expert examination. In correspondence relating to the object, Antoine G. Brimo refers to having received from Calouste Gulbenkian a specific sum for his expert's report on the object in question, in which he confirms its authenticity.

b7aafb59-ff4c-5242-9b12-fb975a73f3bf.name: *Zellij* panel.
b7aafb59-ff4c-5242-9b12-fb975a73f3bf.description:
This *zellij* panel, which covered the entrance wall of the Bouinaniya Madrasa, is decorated with *testirs*, geometric motifs often used in earthenware tile facings.  
Each element is known by a particular name, and the stucco craftsmen memorised the particular proportions, motifs and dimensions corresponding to each figure. The motifs were first drawn on the tile then carved using a mallet. They were carved in the fired clay beneath the glaze so as to give each piece a corner-shaped profile. Once assembled, they created a polychrome mosaic with large and simple motifs dominated by white, yellow ochre and black. The panel includes a thick white line tracing rectilinear knotwork, a method introduced in the AH 7th / AD 13th century by the Almohads in their architectural decoration, and polychrome filling made up of small elements whose specific shapes are matched exactly to the voids left in the design. This knotwork rises from small white columns encircled with a green band and finishes in half knots. It encloses a network of concentric diamonds made up of elements in yellow ochre, violet black and emerald green or yellow ochre, black and lavender blue, all with a black piece in the centre.  
This fragment illustrates the mastery of the *zellij* craftsmen in the Marinid era who, like their Nasrid counterparts, produced op art masterpieces before their time.
b7aafb59-ff4c-5242-9b12-fb975a73f3bf.short_description: This *zellij* panel covered the entrance wall to the *madrasa*. It is decorated with *testirs*, or geometric patterns that are the pre-eminent decorative motif for earthenware-tile facings. It consists of a network of lozenges surrounded by an interlacing design.
b7aafb59-ff4c-5242-9b12-fb975a73f3bf.method_for_datation: The panel comes from the Buinaniya Madrasa (AH 751–7 / AD 1351–6).
b7aafb59-ff4c-5242-9b12-fb975a73f3bf.method_for_provenance: The panel was salvaged during the restoration of the monument in the 20th century.

b7cc9c16-b067-5542-91fe-67d7377310ad.name: Jar
b7cc9c16-b067-5542-91fe-67d7377310ad.short_description: This Iznik jar belongs to an early stage in the development of Ottoman pottery, possibly the early 10th century / second decade of the 16th century as suggested by its decoration and colour scheme, which employs a lighter shade of blue, along with the deep cobalt. The dynamic floral decoration inspired by Chinese designs is boldly painted on the white ground, or else, as on the foot and shoulder, it is reserved in white against blue. Jars of this type, which were made for courtly or urban patrons and were most likely used as storage containers, testify to the high aesthetic standards of the day.

b7cc9c16-b067-5542-91fe-67d7377310ad.method_for_datation: The jar belongs to the end phase of a subgroup of Iznik ware sometimes referred to as “Baba Nakkaṣ” around the 1520s, based on its colour scheme, alternating blue and white ground, and curvaceous juxtaposition of the floral designs, which have a compositional relationship to Chinese blue-and-white porcelain.
b7cc9c16-b067-5542-91fe-67d7377310ad.method_for_provenance: Shape, colour scheme and decoration are typical of Iznik ware.

b7ce4f8c-eeaa-5739-a40e-36309170d6fc.short_description: Fez is an important centre for Moroccan pottery and is particularly associated with a distinctive form of blue and white ceramic ware which became popular in the late 19th century. This bottle was donated to the V&A by George Maw, founder of Maw & Co., a British manufacturer of ceramic tiles. The company won many medals and awards at the international exhibitions which were a feature of the late 19th century. This bottle was displayed at the 1871 Annual International Exhibition held in London.

b822c95a-a322-5a1f-a599-8e7881c43da8.short_description: This small bowl with a spout presents a bird surrounded by pseudo-geometric patterns painted in black with white and red dots. The decoration is made with coloured liquid clay.

b86322b9-31bb-52dc-86d7-821809e043fd.name: Pottery bowl
b86322b9-31bb-52dc-86d7-821809e043fd.description: A glazed small pottery bowl decorated under a blue, light green, and brown radial design under a greyish glaze. The rhythm of the five colours evokes the five pillars of Islam, elevating the object from an ordinary houseware to a spiritual level. The radials point to a blueish spot in the middle of the bowl. The rim is lined with the same blue as one of the radials inside the bowl. We see the radial underglaze or lustre design in some beautiful AH 6th / AD 12th-century Kashan Iranian pottery bowls.

b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.name: Tankard.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.description: A tall, stone-paste (fritware) tankard of cylindrical shape with a flat angular handle with curved projections at the top and bottom. The tankard is decorated with an undulating succession of tall red tulips and blue-green so-called *saz* leaves that alternate with smaller red and blue flowers. All the flora springs from a decorative band around the lower body, enhanced by blue and red detailing. This decorative band is repeated around the lip. The handle shows crude abstract detailing. This type of tankard first appears in Ottoman ceramics in the AH late 10th / AD mid–late 16th century and was widely exported. Metal prototypes of this type are known from the Balkans. Leather or wood models may also have contributed to the development of this ceramic type.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.short_description: This type of tankard first appears in Ottoman ceramics in the AH 10th / AD 16th century and was widely exported subsequently. Metal prototypes of this type are known from the Balkans. Leather or wood models may also have contributed to the development of this type in ceramics.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.dates: Hegira, late 10th century / AD mid–late 16th century.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.method_for_datation: Iznik tankards with this particular type of decoration have been attributed to the late 10th / mid–late 16th century.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.method_for_provenance: It is known that tankards of this type and decorative style were produced in the workshops of Iznik during the late 10th / mid–late 16th century.

b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.name: Ceramic bowl.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.description: Glazed bowl with vertical rounded rim, circular mouth, body shaped as inverted truncated cone with low carination and base with diagonal foot-ring. Covered with honey-coloured monochrome glaze and decorated in *cuerda seca* with white, green and honey colours separated by lines of manganese. The central theme is the word '*baraka'* written in *kufic* characters, surrounded by a frieze of palmette leaves which runs around the rim of the bowl. The object has been restored.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.short_description: Bowl decorated entirely using *cuerda seca* from the Almoravid or Almohad periods. The central motif is the word ‘*baraka*’ written in *kufic* characters and surrounded by a frieze of palmettes that runs around the brim of the bowl. Similar pieces have been found around the western Mediterranean.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.dimensions: Height 8 cm, diameter (of mouth) 25 cm, diameter (of base) 10.3 cm.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated to the 6th / 12th century by comparison with objects of similar form, decorative technique and theme, in particular from Almería and Málaga.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.method_for_provenance: The abundance of this type of ceramic in Málaga, in which very similar calligraphy is found, and Almería (Spain) where kilns have been found in which objects with this type of decoration were made, has led researchers to attribute its production to these localities.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.name: Plate.
b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.description:
A ceramic plate decorated with geometric designs in yellow pigment on a brown background and under a transparent glaze.  
  
The inner surface is divided into four zones, each pair corresponding with each other. One pair consists of curved triangles filled with crossed lines forming, net-like, small indented squares; the other two zones show crisscrossed curved lines which form an arrow–head design.

b9280ed6-19f0-55b4-a602-5d1098d3ab59.short_description: Composite-bodied ceramic dish, the centre with a configuration of six circular dense foliated and floriated scrolls and five stylized palmettes, bordered by eight paired Chinese-style cloud devices, the rim with a border of small flowers on thin scrolling stems; exterior with alternations of two types of Chinese-inspired cloud motifs. It was wheel-thrown, covered with white engobe, painted with cobalt blue stain, and transparent colourless glaze.

ba61949f-4fe6-55e5-a72f-065204514600.name: Long-necked bottle
ba61949f-4fe6-55e5-a72f-065204514600.description: This monochrome bottle with a long neck has a facetted design, imitating metal bottles. This type of object appears in painted miniatures in which the cupbearer pours wine from an identical bottle. Prohibited by the Qur’an, wine nevertheless could have medicinal and digestive virtues, according to Al-Râzî: “the usefulness of wine for the preservation of health, and the improvement of digestion, is certain if it is given its rightful place, and if its quantity, quality, and timing are in accordance with the rules of the art".

ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.name: Stand.
ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.description: A rectangular stand with four legs and two holes in the top, made with slabs of moulded clay, decorated in relief and 'lustre-painted'. The relief design on each of the wider sides of the stand comprises pairs of griffons surrounded by swirling arabesques. 'Lustre-painted' pottery was produced in Abbasid Iraq before the technique appeared in Fatimid Egypt and was possibly introduced by migrating craftsmen. After the end of the Fatimid dynasty, the lustre technique sprang up in Ayyubid Syria, again probably brought by craftsmen who moved to areas where they would find the greatest patronage. Lustre painting was one of the most popular decorative techniques of 'Raqqa ware'; a type of pottery produced in AH 6th–7th- / AD 12th–13th-century northern Syria. The original use of objects similar to this stand is not certain although the turned legs on some objects of this type imply that they were adapted from wooden models, making it possible, therefore, that the stand was used as a table and that the holes in the top were used to hold bowls, drinking vessels, oil lamps or ink pots.
ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.short_description: The exact use of this lustre-painted ceramic stand is unknown. It may have been adapted from a wooden table; the holes at the top could have been used to hold bowls, drinking vessels, oil lamps or ink pots.

ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.method_for_provenance: The style and technique correlate with similar ceramic objects produced in Raqqa. Furthermore, this stand was found in Raqqa, Syria.

bbeb7fe5-88d9-5182-83a9-e637b3a17a0b.name: Tile panel
bbeb7fe5-88d9-5182-83a9-e637b3a17a0b.short_description:
The architect of Membland Hall in Devon commissioned this sumptuous design for bathroom tiles from William Morris. Morris had the tiles painted in the studios of William de Morgan (1839-1917). They represent a rare collaboration between these two creative geniuses.  
Edward Charles Baring, 1st Baron Revelstoke, was the builder of Membland Hall. He was a merchant banker. The hall was later demolished.

bc05121b-1942-54f8-ba62-84b29282f089.name: Tile Panel
bc05121b-1942-54f8-ba62-84b29282f089.short_description: Kütahya was the second most important ceramic production centre after İznik due to the rich clay deposits in the area. Although there was a decline in ceramic production at the beginning of the 19th century, in the last quarter of that same century production was revived and new designs inspired by İznik ceramics were produced.

bc0e1083-d95d-5698-ab89-71d2e2154a4d.name: Bowl from Nishapur
bc0e1083-d95d-5698-ab89-71d2e2154a4d.short_description:
The bowl has a heavy body and a slightly concave base, its centre filled with a grid pattern on which a curved interlacing band forms six circles. They are attached to a central circle that is decorated with a pseudo-*kufic* inscription. The vegetal circles are alternately filled with the same pseudo-*kufic* inscription and a grid pattern with green and yellow dots. The outside walls of the bowl are decorated with black lines.  
The decoration depicted on this bowl relates to a corpus of pottery found in Nishapur where arrangements of the circle-shaped vegetal ornament in black, yellow and green colour are a common motive. Based on the extensive excavations conducted by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in Eastern Persia, Nishapur has been a centre of well-designed polychrome pottery made during the Islamic period. However, vessels with this kind of pseudo-*kufic* inscription seem to be rare.
bc0e1083-d95d-5698-ab89-71d2e2154a4d.method_for_datation: By comparison with other objects excavated in Nishapur.

bc1be694-23e7-57dc-8d0e-5dd013cff796.name: Bath scraper or pumice stone
bc1be694-23e7-57dc-8d0e-5dd013cff796.description:
This object has been associated with a series of bath scrapers and pumice stones attributed to AH 5th-6th / 11th-12th century Middle East. They are characterised by an animal shape or motif made from a coarse material.  
  
This model represents a rodent or a hedgehog recognisable by its long ears and the spines on its back. The bottom of the piece is incised with a grid that would have accentuated its abrasive quality. Deliberately left unglazed and unrefined, such scrapers were used during hamam rituals to exfoliate and purify the skin.  
  
This bath scraper could be considered an early version of the traditional exfoliating washcloth (ar. *kessa* , tr. *kese*), an emblematic item from the hamam. It is also plausible that they coexisted, given that the *kessa* was made from natural perishable material that would have disappeared in places where ceramic has survived.
bc1be694-23e7-57dc-8d0e-5dd013cff796.bibliography:
Peteet, J., *The Hamam through Time and Space* , New York: Syracuse University Press, 2024.  
  
Rugiadi, M., ‘Bathing and the Hammam’, in *Court and Cosmos. The Great Age of the Seljuqs*, New Haven and London: Yale University, 2016: pp. 107-108.

keywords: Water; pumice stone; bath scraper; Iran; ceramic; ablution
materials: Unglazed ceramic with molded and incised overlay decoration

bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.name: Fragment of a pottery bowl.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.description:
The Raqqa region contains a group of Abbasid palaces that have been labelled with the letters A, B, C and D. This ceramic fragment was found during archaeological excavations carried out in Palace A. The fragment is part of a delicate bowl that was made in a mould and decorated around its girth with Arabic *kufic* script that reads: “from the work of Ibrahim al-Nasrani that has been made in Hira for the Amir Sulayman, son of the Commander of the Faithful." The Commander of the Faithful, or Caliph, in question is the Abbasid Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (r. AH 136–58 / AD 754–75). The text indicates that this piece was made in Hira by Ibrahim al-Nasrani and transported to Raqqa. The name of the craftsperson (al-Nasrani, i.e. the Christian) indicates that he was probably a master craftsman in the Christian ceramic-producing quarter of al-Hira.  
The base of the bowl was stamped with geometric and stylised vegetal motifs including palm trees.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.short_description: Although this bowl is delicate and fragmented, its moulded band of early *kufic* inscription has mostly survived. It includes the name of the craftsman, Ibrahim al-Nasrani, evidently a Christian, the place of production in Hira and the dedication to Sulayman, '\[son\] of the commander of the faithful'.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.initial_owner: Prince Sulayman (son of the Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (r. AH 136–58 / AD 754–75).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.method_for_datation: The inscription on the fragment associates it with the rule of the Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (136–58 / 754–75).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.method_for_provenance: The text inscribed on the vessel fragment specifies Hira, in Mesopotamia (Iraq) as the place of production.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.provenance: Produced in Hira in southern Mesopotamia (Iraq).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.obtention: The fragment was found during an archaeological excavation carried out in 1948 in Palace A by the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities under the direction of archaeologist Nasib Salibi.

bc4af44a-740c-54ce-806a-021695934601.name: Yıldız Ceramic vase
bc4af44a-740c-54ce-806a-021695934601.short_description: Sultan Abdülhamid II founded in 1891 the *Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu* (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace in order to revive Turkish tile art and give it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. The vase has yellow covers and two handles. There is a landscape of a tree and a house near the water on the vase.

bd228d18-d160-5fd5-95ad-52e75e120f02.name: Welcoming Person (*Azulejos*)
bd228d18-d160-5fd5-95ad-52e75e120f02.description:
The Halberdier (here shown isolated) is the first of three welcoming halberdiers painted on tiles (*azulejos)*, which decorate the main staircase of the Mitra or Patriarch's Palace in St. Antão do Tojal (now Casa do Gaiato). The elaborately decorated *trompe l'oeil* *azulejos* were meant to transform an ordinary staircase into a magnificent one. Since the 16th century, tiles were used in Portugal to decorate churches, palaces and gardens; in the first half of the 18th century the most sophisticated colour used on tiles was cobalt blue. The artist used architectural drawing, ribbons of foliage and flowers, and little exotic pets such as monkeys and birds, to make visitors believe they were in a splendid garden guarded by halberdiers. To enhance the *trompe l'oeil* illusion, the halberdiers are drawn to natural scale, as if they were actors on the set of an opera.  
Designed to create the ambiance of a splendid welcoming ritual for those visiting the palace, all three characters exhibit magnificent Baroque outfits: the fabric of the jackets are embroidered with gold thread. These particular halberdiers display details that represent military dignity, such as the *écharpe* diagonally draped over the bust of one, or that used as if it were a belt, or a *cravat* attached to the button hole of a jacket (this one probably represents King João V's special German or *Tudesco* guard). Painted *azulejos* on staircases or patios, with welcoming personages such as personal guards, are characteristic of Palaces in Lisbon and are often seen in religious buildings such as, Setúbal, Corpo Santo Brotherhood or Évora University (Saint Spirit Convent).  
The artist who invented this iconography signed some of his works with the letters "P.M." or "P.M.P.", which is thought to be linked with Father Manuel Pereira, an amateur painter and architect who lived in the kingdom of Pedro II and his son João V.  
The Ancient Patriarch's Palace in Lisbon dates back to the 17th century and was renovated in the 18th century. The work is likely to be by the Italian Architect Antonio Cannevari, who constructed the new Palace Church, a nearby Fountain, the Aqueduct, and also a new small Palace with an exterior fountain. The patron responsible for all these new urban structures and the decoration of the old Palace was the Lisbon Patriarch Tomás de Almeida. These artworks were designed to receive King João V and his entourage when they were on their way to visit the most important project of his reign – the Mafra Convent and Palace – which was under construction at that time.
bd228d18-d160-5fd5-95ad-52e75e120f02.short_description: The first of the three welcoming halberdiers painted on a life-size scale on tiles, decorating the main staircase of Mitra or Patriarch's Palace in St. Antão do Tojal. The *azulejos*, painted in cobalt-blue with gold detail on the halberdier's outfits, were designed to transform a simple staircase into a magnificent one in order to receive guests such asliliguest King João V and his courtiers.

bda8c465-9ce4-5191-8783-1d1baf8d0177.name: Bowl
bda8c465-9ce4-5191-8783-1d1baf8d0177.short_description: The bowl shows a simple decoration which is enriched with splashes of colours under a transparent glaze.

bdb59a8c-f1cd-55ee-bcbc-1e82a6258ce8.name: Tile panel.
bdb59a8c-f1cd-55ee-bcbc-1e82a6258ce8.description:
The rectangular panel composed of square tiles is dominated by a yellow and brown horseshoe-shaped arch supported by two columns and two capitals. A dense, symmetrical floral design fills the area under the arch emerging from a vase standing on a base. The vase is flanked by cypress trees. Three lotus-like flowers on sturdy stems, one on the top of the other, form a middle axis. On each side of the axis a tendril composed of three scrolls emerges from the vase. Each scroll is filled with a large blossom, of which the two that face each other are similar: the lower pair are rosettes, the two in the middle are lotuses, and the top pair are peonies. The remaining surface under the arch and the spandrels above are filled with sprays of various flowers. Above the arch is a circle containing a motif of a half-moon. The design is painted in an opaque orange-yellow, two tones of green, dark and light blue and brown on an opaque white glaze. The panel is set in a wooden frame.  
In the AH 11th and 12th / AD 17th and 18th centuries, faience (glazed coloured earthenware) became the dominant element of the Tunisian architectural decoration and the horseshoe-shaped arch called *mihrab* (prayer niche) an unmistakable feature of most tile panels. The more naturalistic floral decoration and the representations of cypresses are due to the influence of Ottoman art.
bdb59a8c-f1cd-55ee-bcbc-1e82a6258ce8.short_description: Rectangular panel of faience tiles painted with a horseshoe-shaped arch. A dense floral design, emerging from a vase, fills the area under the arch. In the AH 11th–12th / AD 17th–18th centuries, faience (glazed coloured earthenware) became the dominant element of Tunisian architectural decoration.
bdb59a8c-f1cd-55ee-bcbc-1e82a6258ce8.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
bdb59a8c-f1cd-55ee-bcbc-1e82a6258ce8.method_for_datation: This tile panel shows close similarities to panels made by a faience atelier working from about the mid-12th–mid-13th / mid-18th–mid-19th centuries.
bdb59a8c-f1cd-55ee-bcbc-1e82a6258ce8.method_for_provenance: The style of decoration was characteristic of ateliers in Tunis.
bdb59a8c-f1cd-55ee-bcbc-1e82a6258ce8.obtention: There is no information about acquisition.

c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.name: Lustre bowl with a sun motif.
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.description:
A large dark-brown lustre bowl from Qal'at Ja'bar, which is a particularly remarkable example of so-called Raqqa-ware. It was uncovered in the 1973/4 archaeological excavations by the Syrian Directorate of Antiquities within the medieval fortress of Qal'at Ja'bar on the left bank of the Middle Euphrates, thus making it one of the few pieces that reached the Museum not via the art market but from a particular archaeological site.  
The decoration of this piece is highly original: it is dominated by an impressive sun with a female face, almond-shaped eyes, beauty marks on the cheeks and loosely curled hair. The solar-shaped face is framed by two halos of radiating rays which cover the central surface of the bowl.  
The astrological sign of the sun is a common iconographic motif on contemporary metalwork where it is usually surrounded by the planets and signs of the zodiac forming a cosmic circle. On medieval Syrian pottery, however, such a depiction is unique. Interestingly enough, the potter replaced the circle of planets with eight medallion-like ornaments – alternating red-on-white vegetal motifs with white-on-red lunar cartouches. This must be a specific “Raqqa” variation on the metalwork theme. The rim of the bowl is freely painted with dotted and curvilinear motifs that are regularly punctuated by a pair of vertical lines, a feature echoing calligraphic decoration.  
The dish belongs to the rare group of lustre-painted pieces with figurative decoration. Its shallow shape with convex profile, flat, everted rim and flaring foot is standard and particularly popular with lustre-wares. Its exterior is undecorated. The greenish transparent glaze covers only the top two-thirds of the vessel in typical Raqqa manner.
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.short_description: This Raqqa-ware was found during excavations at the Ayyubid fortress Qal'at Ja'bar. Decorated in characteristic brown metallic lustre, the dish portrays a radiating sun with feminine facial features and jewellery. Planetary symbols were a common feature on Islamic luxury items, particularly on inlaid metalwork, more rarely on ceramics.
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.holder: National Museum of Aleppo, Islamic Department
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.dates: Hegira early 7th century / AD early 13th century.
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.method_for_datation: Stylistic considerations and archaeological excavation point to the region of Raqqa in which the production of lustre-painted pottery flourished during the 6th / 12th century up until the Mongol invasion of 655–6 / 1258–9.
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.method_for_provenance: It is unlikely that the bowl was made *in situ*, although archaeological excavations have recently uncovered evidence of fritware production in Qal'at Ja'bar. Rather, the high quality of the piece points to a manufacture in a more specialised centre, most likely in one of the thriving pottery workshops in nearby Raqqa.
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.obtention: The bowl was uncovered during archaeological excavations led by the Syrian Directorate of Antiquities in 1973/4.
c01c0ea8-09eb-5aa5-9b63-e27164389d77.bibliography:

c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.name: Earthenware dish.
c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.description: Medium-sized circular earthenware dish, with the surface line slightly broken. It is decorated in chestnut colour on a white background with metallic lustre. It is one of the Persian-style *pardalot* series, whose central theme is a stylised bird surrounded by plant decoration. The bird is contained within a central area bounded by triple concentric lines, alternating with a band of interlacing. Its rim is rounded, accentuated by a wide continuous band, crossing over to the back of the dish. This is not decorated, but has drips resulting from the volatilisation of metal oxides during firing. Three equidistant spurs are still visible resulting from the mark left by the trivets. This dish is designed to resemble and substitute for tableware which was previously made of metal; it is nevertheless also considered a luxury object.
c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.short_description: This ‘cuenco’ dish from Manises, decorated in brown on a white lustre background, is part of the Persian-style *pardalot* series. The central motif is a stylised bird surrounded by plant decoration. This plate imitates, and was used instead of, metal tableware.
c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.dimensions: Height 6 cm, diameter (of rim) 28 cm, diameter (of base) 9 cm.
c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.method_for_datation: Probable dating by stylistic analogy with the class of gilded lustre-ware ceramics from Manises produced in the 15th–18th centuries. The Muslims of Valencia continued its production until the 18th century, introducing more varied profiles and new shapes, as well as variations in its decoration, especially in the use of polychromy. For this reason it is thought that this object may belong to the early period of production at Manises. The Persian-influenced shape and the popular nature of the central subject of the piece, characteristic of the first half of the 15th century, add strength to this dating.
c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.method_for_provenance: Manises is the source of the metallic-painted lustre-ware which developed a large market as luxury objects all over Europe during the 15th century.
c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.obtention: It was obtained in 1915–16, and appears on the list of property transferred from the Episcopal Palace.
c14e61c4-a9ad-5af3-bb2d-94ef6f7c83f0.author: Ana Alcoforado, António Pacheco
keywords: earthenware dish; Mudéjar; Manises; modelled; clay; glazed; lustre; pardalot; Persian style
materials: Clay modelled on the wheel and glazed (lustre-ware).

c19090c2-9f5c-5b91-8652-fc049332fd82.name: Jug.
c19090c2-9f5c-5b91-8652-fc049332fd82.description: The jug has a squat globular body, a high concave neck with a flared rim and a low foot. It has underglaze painted in a bright blue, a thick opaque red and a diluted turquoise-green on a white slip. The design outlined in dark blue appears in two horizontal registers alternating tulips and carnations, referring to the floral style of the Iznik ceramics of the AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries. However, as well as an obviously different kind of slip and glaze, the motifs are simplified and schematically executed. The handle and the narrow bands edging the floral depictions are ornamented with geometrical patterns. The jug is marked under the foot with a crescent and an asterisk.
c19090c2-9f5c-5b91-8652-fc049332fd82.short_description: Jug of polychrome painted pottery. The motifs of the decoration – tulips and carnations – refer to the floral style of Iznik ceramics. The handle shows a geometrical pattern. The jug is marked under the foot with a crescent and an asterisk.
c19090c2-9f5c-5b91-8652-fc049332fd82.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
c19090c2-9f5c-5b91-8652-fc049332fd82.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
c19090c2-9f5c-5b91-8652-fc049332fd82.dimensions: Height 18.6 cm, diameter of rim 8.3 cm.
c19090c2-9f5c-5b91-8652-fc049332fd82.method_for_datation: Unlike Iznik wares of the 'quatre fleurs' style of the 10th–11th / 16th–17th centuries, this jug is marked under the foot. c1a94556-7d78-595d-a94f-93dcbfdaae91.name: Tile with a rider on a camel *(Bahram Gur Hunting)*
c1a94556-7d78-595d-a94f-93dcbfdaae91.short_description:
The gem of the museum collection, this tile is today the only known dated object of Iranian lustred ceramics from AD 1220–1260. The artistic merits of the piece are unmatched. Sophisticated composition is perfectly aligned with the octagonal star plane. Delicate painting in amber-gold lustre is supplemented by soft tones of turquoise and blue applied to a background of ivory tint, the resulting colour combination producing a striking decorative effect.  
The scene on the tile deserves particular interest. According to Vera Krachkovskaya and Leon Guzalian, it probably illustrates one of the legendary episodes from *Shahnamа* (Book of Kings) epic by Ferdowsi, namely King Bahram Gur hunting.  
The border of the tile is inscribed in Persian, containing three verses by an unknown poet dedicated to unrequited love. Also here the date of the Muslim Hejira calendar is indicated: "in the safari of 624". This corresponds to the period from late January to the end of February AD 1227.  
Such tiles, alternating on the walls with diagonal or straight blue or turquoise crosses, decorated room interiors of Iranian elite.

c1dc368c-d1ca-53c8-a0da-a63bd4ed9f6b.name: *Jobbana* covered pot
c1dc368c-d1ca-53c8-a0da-a63bd4ed9f6b.description: The word *jobbana* comes from the Arabic word *jben*, which refers to cheese. This lidded jar was originally used in Morocco to curdle milk, but was used also to preserve butter or serve *harira*, a soup with which the Ramadan fast is broken in the evening. The delicacy of the decoration of this pot is characteristic of the workshops of the city of Safi, a city on the west coast, whose name is inscribed under the base. The tone of blue reflects the use of a handmade nickel-based pigment. Ceramic production development in Safi would result from the arrival of potters from Fes who appreciated the quality of clay in banks near the city.

c2c6489a-b997-5d3e-a98c-d31891a7ba03.name: Large *khabiya* jar
c2c6489a-b997-5d3e-a98c-d31891a7ba03.description: This large jar, *khabiya*, is intended for the storage of grain, semolina, oil, or water. Its motifs are typical of Tunisian craftsmanship, whose main production centre was in the pottery district (Qallaline) of Tunis. These motifs, the *taouq* (rim decoration), the strip of vertical hatching, and the band of ovoid kernels (*qloub*) are linked by similar designs. The composition is arranged in parallel bands, with the repeated use of yellow, green and brown.

c2d89824-82fc-5b0b-b842-57fa1d2f9bf8.name: Ceramic boat model
c2d89824-82fc-5b0b-b842-57fa1d2f9bf8.description: This is one of many clay models of flat-bottomed boats with vertical sides found at Ur, of varying shapes and sizes. It is among several examples that bear a resemblance to the *isbiya* barge (see item 2024.8.2 in the collection of the Open Museum Initiative for Water Culture), particularly in the lip protruding from the bottom edge of the boat. This feature is called *leffa* in Hit, where *isbiyas* were traditionally made, and is unique to the *isbiya*.
c2d89824-82fc-5b0b-b842-57fa1d2f9bf8.obtention: Transferred to Basra Museum from the Iraq Museum by Ministry of Culture. Originally excavated from the Royal Cemetery of Ur by Sir Leonard Woolley, 1920s.

c360d26b-9b7f-5e18-8e84-14c2c3fee2ec.name: Dish (charger).
c360d26b-9b7f-5e18-8e84-14c2c3fee2ec.description: A wide flat dish in a form known as a charger, with decoration painted under the glaze in black and blue. The decorative motifs, which include scrolling arabesque stems and sinuous cloud motifs, are a distinctive combination of traditional arabesque (*rumi*) and Chinese (*hatayi*) styles, so this style has been dubbed *rumi-hatayi*. This style characterises the early phase of Iznik ceramics, when the potters were forging their own decorative idiom out of influences from Iranian and Chinese art, contemporary Ottoman metalwork and manuscript illumination, and others. The *cavetto*, or curve of the dish between the rim and the bottom, has been left blank, creating a zone of transition which sets off the decoration of the rim.
c360d26b-9b7f-5e18-8e84-14c2c3fee2ec.short_description: A wide flat dish in a form known as a charger, decorated with scrolling arabesques, floral motifs and cloud-bands. This style characterises the early phase of Iznik ceramics, when the potters were forging their own decorative idiom out of influences including Iranian and Chinese art.
c360d26b-9b7f-5e18-8e84-14c2c3fee2ec.method_for_datation: Stylistic comparison with other wares of the period.
c360d26b-9b7f-5e18-8e84-14c2c3fee2ec.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
c360d26b-9b7f-5e18-8e84-14c2c3fee2ec.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, Istanbul/London, 1989, pp.90–91.
c360d26b-9b7f-5e18-8e84-14c2c3fee2ec.author: Barry Wood

c3763c63-3f3b-50c5-aca7-c1958aac4be6.name: Filter for a water-jar.
c3763c63-3f3b-50c5-aca7-c1958aac4be6.description: A clay water-jar filter perforated with Arabic calligraphic decoration that originates from Fustat, the old capital of Egypt. The filter once sealed the mouth of a small water-jar without a handle; functioning as a lid to protect the contents of the jar from, for example, flies, insects and dust. Neither the jar or its filter are glazed, allowing the water inside the porous body to evaporate a little, thus helping to keep the water in the jar cool. The incised calligraphy that pierces right through the base of the filter is a repetition of the two letters *Alif* (A) and *Lam* (L). They are written here in *kufic* script, a style named after the city of Kufa in Iraq. The *kufic* style is characterised by its geometrical shapes and decoration on the ends of the elongated parts of the words (see the vertical tips of the letters here). Calligraphy was not the only decorative device used to embellish such vessels: animals, geometric patterning and floral designs were also employed. No two vessels appear to be identical, despite the frequent use of animals such as elephants, hares and birds.
c3763c63-3f3b-50c5-aca7-c1958aac4be6.short_description: Arabic calligraphy has been employed to decorate many objects in the Islamic world, from the commonplace, like this Fatimid water-jar filter, to the special, such as that found inlaid on metalwares. Such filters were decorated individually, whereby no two identical ones have been found.
c3763c63-3f3b-50c5-aca7-c1958aac4be6.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
c3763c63-3f3b-50c5-aca7-c1958aac4be6.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: many examples of this type of water-filter have been found during archaeological excavations at Fustat.

c37f1ba0-6080-5fe6-a4db-d79005a48b01.name: Tile panel
c37f1ba0-6080-5fe6-a4db-d79005a48b01.short_description: Each tile of this large stair-shaped panel is ornamented with moulded octagons and partial hexagrams such that one corner is cut out to fit a separate spherical knob. This group of tiles is similar to a well-known group of tiles that once ornamented the exterior of Takht-i Sulaiman (c. 1270), which was the summer palace of the Ilkhanid ruler Abaqa (r. 1265–82). When Doris Duke purchased the tiles in Iran in 1938, they were said to have been excavated from a site called Sanek.

c38b81ca-60f1-57d2-b720-57e2601984a6.name: Tile panel in the form of a tomb cover
c38b81ca-60f1-57d2-b720-57e2601984a6.short_description: This tomb cover consists of three large luster tiles, all of which are covered in cobalt calligraphy in relief. It is presumed that this tripartite panel constituted the upper surface of a sarcophagus marking the burial place of Imam Ja‘far’s daughter. As a descendent of an imam, her tomb would have been known as an *imamzada* (Persian: imam born). During the Ilkhanid period of rule in Greater Iran (1256–1353), Shi‘ite imamzadas preserved some of the finest Persian tilework ever made.

c4678676-f14a-5a4f-a93f-f7811ffd6c6e.name: Tile
c4678676-f14a-5a4f-a93f-f7811ffd6c6e.short_description: Depictions of al-Masjid al-Haram come in a variety of forms. Among the popular depiction is a two-dimensional image found on *hajj* certificates, textiles, manuscripts and tiles. Each unit in these drawings is usually labelled in Arabic script, highlighting the key places shown in the illustration. This Iznik tile depicts the plan of al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah with seven minarets and identifying inscriptions in *naskhi*.
c4678676-f14a-5a4f-a93f-f7811ffd6c6e.obtention: E. Imbert Collection, Milan EU private collection since before 1940
c4678676-f14a-5a4f-a93f-f7811ffd6c6e.bibliography: Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, *Dala’il al-Khayrat: Prayer Manuscripts from the 16th – 19th centuries*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2016: 129.

c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.name: Dish.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.description:
A dish with the shield belonging to the Tondi family of Siena, Italy, in the centre surrounded by radiating chains of 'bryony' flowers (those with blue petals and lustre-painted centres) alternating with chains of blue 'parsley'-shaped leafs (those that are made up of ragged trefoil shapes), and both interwoven with lustre-coloured spindly 'fern' leaves. This style of dish belongs to a distinctive range that was much sought after in Spain and in other parts of Europe where it was exported in large quantities. This explains the presence of the Italian family's shield, for this type of lustre-ware was extremely popular in Italy.  
  
Manises was one of the main pottery-making towns in Valencia, and played a leading role in the manufacture of lustre-wares for export to Europe, principally to France and Italy. Manises's pottery left for export from the Valencian port of Grao where many Manises potters owned pottery warehouses and shops. These potters were a mixture of Christians and Moors (Muslims), the latter of which were not permitted to take their skills to work outside the town, testifying to the value of their special skills to the economy of Manises. By the mid-16th century (AH 956), Manises had a major monopoly on the production of lustre-wares in Valencia.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.short_description: The old name for this type of Mudéjar-style Spanish lustre ceramics is ‘Hispano-Moresque’, a term indicating that the potters who made it were a mixture of Christians and Moors (Muslims), the latter of which were restricted to practising their much-praised skill outside the town of Manises in Valencia.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis and identification of the shield belonging to the Tondi family of Siena, Italy.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.bibliography: Ray, A., *Spanish Pottery 1248–1898*, the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 2000.
c4a199cd-9f33-5a29-aa87-3eb7131bf868.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: Commerce; Hispano-Moresque; coat of arms; floral decoration

c4ac31eb-6f1b-5165-aa8c-6ca2a725eb94.name: Elements of a shutter.
c4ac31eb-6f1b-5165-aa8c-6ca2a725eb94.description:
Four elements of a shutter, each in the shape of a cross and pierced by a circular hole at its centre. They are covered in green enamel, some of which has disappeared from certain parts.  
Golvin (se Bibliography) mentions that the elements that compose this type of ceramic partitioning are usually assembled together with metal studs, and that, in contrast to plaster ones, those of this type do not include any fragments of coloured glass.
c4ac31eb-6f1b-5165-aa8c-6ca2a725eb94.short_description: These four parts of a screen wall are cross-shaped with a circular hole in their centre. They are covered with a green enamel that has disappeared in places. These parts were usually joined together using metal dowels.

c4ac31eb-6f1b-5165-aa8c-6ca2a725eb94.method_for_datation: Elements found in the Qal'at Bani Hammad (5th–6th / 11th–12th centuries).

c4af05d4-9269-5543-8456-f8734f0e243b.name: Conical cup
c4af05d4-9269-5543-8456-f8734f0e243b.description:
Stoneware, celadons, and porcelain from China fascinated the Arab, Iranian, and Turkish worlds. The chronicles of the reigns of the Abbasid caliphs bear witness to this, as do the collections of the Ottoman sultans.  
In the absence of kaolin, and to replace porcelain, ceramists opt for a new clay mixture, obtained from pulverised quartz pebbles, white clay, and frit (pulverised mixture of quartz pebbles and soda from vegetable ash). These are the available materials. The mixture is soft; this piece mimics the translucency of porcelain. This technique was not known in the West until the 18th century, evidence of the technical progress made by Eastern ceramists.

c4af05d4-9269-5543-8456-f8734f0e243b.obtention: Purchased at the Art Musulman gallery in 1993.

c4ea2f24-36c4-5686-ab6e-70e5af5815a2.name: Horse and rider
c4ea2f24-36c4-5686-ab6e-70e5af5815a2.short_description: The small statue in full relief represents a rider on horseback and it was a vase or a bottle.
materials: Frit body; black and cobalt blue decoration under turquoise glaze

c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.name: Tile Bowl
c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.description:
The bowl has a round and flaring rim. Its round body narrows towards the ring base. It is decorated with dark blue, green, red and yellow gilding on a white glazed ground. On the external part of the bowl, there are Surahs of al-Falaq and al-Ikhlas in medallions.  
Produced in China for the Ottoman market.
c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.owner: The Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism

c629077b-adfc-5181-840f-1bdf08974970.name: Bowl with Inscription
c629077b-adfc-5181-840f-1bdf08974970.short_description:
This bowl with white engobe (slip) is decorated with epigraphic inscriptions along its rim and in its centre. The word *ahmad* is written in the centre, and along the rim it reads, “May he do that which is praiseworthy.” The writing is delicate, this style also appears on several other vessels from Nishapur as well as on 11th-century vessels from Lashkari-Bazaar in Afghanistan.  
Epigraphic Nishapur vessels are usually decorated with moral messages or the word *baraka* (blessing). Inscriptions also often contain a name, most likely the name of the owner.
c629077b-adfc-5181-840f-1bdf08974970.method_for_datation: Dated through similar objects, e.g. Metropolitan Museum, 1975.168.

c6878c38-2ab4-59f1-9248-38d2398e71c3.name: Table
c6878c38-2ab4-59f1-9248-38d2398e71c3.short_description: With the introduction of fritware, which is more cohesive than earthenware in its working state, twelfth-century Syrian potters branched out into producing ceramic furniture, such as this turquoise-glazed table. Six-sided tables of this type are believed to be based on wooden versions that have not survived. Perhaps in reference to the spaces in which they were used, the tables feature architectural motifs, such as the miniature pillars (balusters) on the sides and the pierced tabletop that resembles a *mashrabiya*, a type of window screen with openwork geometric design.
c6878c38-2ab4-59f1-9248-38d2398e71c3.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
c6878c38-2ab4-59f1-9248-38d2398e71c3.dates: Hegira late 6th century-early 7th century / AD late 12th-early 13th century
c6878c38-2ab4-59f1-9248-38d2398e71c3.method_for_datation: The table relates to others of its kind and, via glaze and body composition, to ceramic vessels all of which are attributed to the Ayyubid-era.
c6878c38-2ab4-59f1-9248-38d2398e71c3.method_for_provenance: This table belongs to a larger group of such tables believed to have come from Raqqa or the surrounding area. This attribution derives from the discovery of a ceramic table fragment of this type in the Great Mosque at Raqqa (restored in the twelfth century) and its relation in glaze and body composition to other Ayyubid-era ceramics.

c7057540-3049-55c4-895f-145533aab6a6.short_description: This square tile is decorated with a checkerboard pattern in yellow, black, green and white and was reportedly used to create a star-shaped frame. The Victoria and Albert Museum holds identical tiles which were made in Toledo.

c74b04a7-bc79-53ff-971f-1725e4e20a41.name: Deep bowl.
c74b04a7-bc79-53ff-971f-1725e4e20a41.description: A deep dish decorated in green, red, blue and white with black outlines. Two harpies opposite one another are perched on bushes filled with scales, and flanked by boughs of plum-tree flowers which form the decoration of the central field inscribed inside a medallion. On this dish the harpies have a crowned female head and the body of a winged dragon. The depiction of harpies, mythical creatures, is related to various animal fables and takes different forms. Running around the flattened edge of the piece is a frieze of hunting dogs chasing birds, a cat, hares and a pair of owls facing one another. There are two holes in the border and on the foot-ring for hanging the bowl.
c74b04a7-bc79-53ff-971f-1725e4e20a41.short_description: Deep dish with a depiction of two facing harpies perched on bushes filled out with scales and flanked by bunches of plum blossom. The brim is decorated with a lively scene showing hunting dogs chasing birds, a cat and hares.
c74b04a7-bc79-53ff-971f-1725e4e20a41.method_for_datation: From the Jeuniette collection. It was purchased through M. Stora & Co. on 10 April 1919.
c74b04a7-bc79-53ff-971f-1725e4e20a41.method_for_provenance: By expert examination, stylistic and comparative analysis and the exhibition catalogues written by international specialists, mentioned in the bibliography.

c9872ac2-6252-5a1f-a28c-b708fd12ec03.name: Dish with bust of a young man in a turban
c9872ac2-6252-5a1f-a28c-b708fd12ec03.short_description: Artists of Iran’s Safavid period (1501–1722) revelled in portraiture, whether rendered on paper or in other media. The painted panels in royal pavilions displayed small groups of beautiful people engaged in various leisure activities, and the tiled walls of bath-houses showed busts of individual men and women sporting fanciful headgear and coiffures. The dominant figural style of this period originated with renowned painter Reza-i ‘Abbasi (ca. 1565–1635), who worked at the court of Shah Abbas at Isfahan. Many of the features that characterized his figures appear in the works of his followers at Isfahan well into the second half of the 17th century, when this portrait dish was produced. Here, the face is shown in three-quarter view, the neck thrust forward and the chin drooping over the chest, as was fashionable in Reza’s portraits. The chin is full, and the mouth, by contrast, is tiny. The pose is languid (“sway-back”), suggesting an air of ennui.
c9872ac2-6252-5a1f-a28c-b708fd12ec03.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Dish; iran; isfahan portrait; figure; male-figure; pottery; safavid; safavid-pottery; kubachi
materials: Stonepaste body, underglaze-painted with black, turquoise, and slips tinted tan and red

c9ebf772-81c8-5910-9ee0-c3321b952c9e.name: Ewer (*ibrik*)
c9ebf772-81c8-5910-9ee0-c3321b952c9e.short_description: Made mostly from metal or ceramic, ewers are used to hold and pour water. The body of this ewer is decorated on both sides with floral motifs surrounding an epigraphic medallion. The Arabic mirror-image inscription – ‘*Ya habibi, unzur bi hali!*’ (‘O my dear, see what has become of me!’) – suggests the union and complementarity to which all lovers aspire, ideals equally shared by the mystic aspiring to become one with God. The scrolls, flowers, and leaves painted in blue, green, red, and yellow recall the underglaze decoration of Iznik ware, whose famous floral style was continued in Kütahya following the decline of Iznik potteries. The present ewer is a late-nineteenth-century Kütahya revival piece.
c9ebf772-81c8-5910-9ee0-c3321b952c9e.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania

ca90aa20-6045-5b3e-a90f-eb2fa90c0be6.description: The rim is shaped like a rooster's head. In form, it has a thin long neck, vertical round handle, bulging wide body and ring bottom. The white paste is covered with blue glaze. The entire exterior surface is decorated with curly and wave motifs in dark brown paint on blue glaze.

cb759986-93f3-578a-a7c7-9068cd703d02.name: Jar.
cb759986-93f3-578a-a7c7-9068cd703d02.description:
A jar with tiered decoration consisting of four bands: two with a chain of leafs, one with a row of five running hares and another with a row of calligraphy. The calligraphy consists of a repetition of the word *Baraka*, meaning blessings or bounty. The use of words or phrases that blessed the owner or user on the one hand, while acknowledging God's bounty in being able to posses such items and their contents on the other, was common on Islamic ceramics of the time. The row of running hares shows two of the five looking backwards, while the other three run facing forwards. All the hares wear a studded collar-band.  
  
Towards the end of the AH 4th century / AD 10th century the Egyptian potters began to use lustre-painted decoration on their pots. They seem to have learned the technique from Iraqi potters who had migrated to Egypt; they in turn had first learned to paint-in-lustre from the glassmakers of Syria and Egypt during the AH 3rd century / AD 9th century.
cb759986-93f3-578a-a7c7-9068cd703d02.short_description: The expensive lustre-painted decorative technique on this Fatimid Egyptian ceramic jar came from Iraqi with potters migrating to Fustat. Its typical Fatimid decoration and calligraphic band of script also find their origin in the decorative style developed originally in the Abbasid city of Samarra in Iraq.
cb759986-93f3-578a-a7c7-9068cd703d02.dates: Hegira late 4th–early 5th century / AD late 10th–early 11th century.
cb759986-93f3-578a-a7c7-9068cd703d02.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: the style of the hares and the band of *kufic* script resemble those on other ceramic objects and fragments found in Fustat that have been attributed to the Fatimid period in Egypt.
cb759986-93f3-578a-a7c7-9068cd703d02.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

cb759986-93f3-578a-a7c7-9068cd703d02.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: Crafts; calligraphy; zoomorphic imagery; animal decoration

cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.name: Tile.
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.description: The square-edge tile is decorated with a repetitive design painted in cobalt-blue, bright green, manganese purple and turquoise with deep black outlines under a transparent, colourless glaze on a white background. The blue and turquoise colours run and the glaze is crackled. Bands of alternating coloured trefoils between turquoise stripes frame the slightly damaged tile on the vertical sides. The design is symmetrically composed of two opposite arabesques linked with their points to half-trefoil motifs, both filled with arabesques. The area in between is filled with two sprays of carnations at the bottom, three lilies in the middle and two sprays of other flowers above. Two of the three lilies at the centre form an S-shaped tendril with stems growing out of the lower lilies and continue above with stems of flowers emerging from their blossoms. On the back, the tile is cut, showing that it was used in wall decoration.
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.short_description: Square tile with underglaze painted decoration in blue, bright green and manganese. The symmetrically composed design shows arabesques forming an area filled with sprays of carnations, lilies and other flowers. The motif is framed with alternating coloured trefoils.
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.dates: Hegira mid-10th century / AD mid-16th century.
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.dimensions: Height 27 cm, width 27 cm, depth 1.8 cm.
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.method_for_datation: The tile was dated from its colour scheme. In the 940s / 1540s Iznik underglaze painted tile work expanded its palette to include green and purple. Purple was replaced by red when it was introduced as an underglaze colour for tile work in the 950s / 1550s.
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.method_for_provenance: Attribution of pottery tiles showing this colour scheme is difficult since it was used by potters in both Iznik and Damascus. However, this tile seems to be a product of Iznik because of its fine paste and its intricate but delicate composition.
cb75e86e-de6a-5a10-87b0-77f7d01615a4.obtention: There is no information about acquisition.

cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.name: Lustre bowl.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.description: The inner surface of the bowl is decorated with two patterns: symmetrical arabesques and bands of intertwining *kufic* calligraphy. Both motifs are framed within eight separate boxes, and the two patterns alternate with each other. Both are painted in golden brown lustre over a white glaze. The surrounding space is covered in dots or small entwining scrolls. The outer surface is decorated with hastily painted flutings and a braided band, over a light blue glaze. The bowl is one of the most important examples of Nasrid ceramics given its display of painstaking paintwork and the fact that the place where it was made is noted on its ring-base.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.short_description: The technique of lustre-ware pottery was introduced to al-Andalus from Egypt and outstanding quality was soon attained. This bowl with a design of geometrical and vegetal panels has an inscription on the foot stating that it was made in the Spanish city of Malaga.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.dates: Hegira mid-8th century / AD mid-14th century.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.method_for_datation: The production of lustre-ware in Andalusia began in the 6th / 12th century. In 750 / 1350, the Arab chronicler Ibn Battuta noted the production of ceramics in his writings on Malaga. This bowl is the only intact item by which the source may be verified. Overall the decoration also corresponds to other branches of the arts and crafts of that period, an example being the decorative patterns used in textiles.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.method_for_provenance: There is an inscription in cursive Arabic script on the bowl’s base stating that it was made in Malaqa (Málaga). Thus the bowl acts as an important marker for the identification and dating of the entire collection of Spanish lustre-ware from the same period.
cc2e6597-5498-5c64-94ac-0ecb6099dcdd.obtention: A gift donated by Friedrich Sarre. The bowl was bought in 1901 in Italy by W. v. Bode and was given to Sarre as a gift, which he later donated to the museum.

cd2f0486-91f0-5d6c-834e-06e9ae177ed0.name: Bowl.
cd2f0486-91f0-5d6c-834e-06e9ae177ed0.description:
This little bowl is an example of fine Syrian lustre-ware pottery of the Atabeg period. It has a conical body with a carinated base and a columnar foot. The inner part of the vessel is decorated with a drawing of a bird that resembles a spotted dove. A stylised branch carefully fills the space surrounding the bird. The rim of the bowl is lavishly decorated with a repeating pattern of curling leaves with lobed edges. Meanwhile, the outside of the bowl is inscribed with an Arabic text in *naskhi* script that may be translated as follows: “Money, happiness, peace, honour, prosperity, and sovereignty.” All the decoration is executed in a honey-yellow metallic lustre on a pale ivory-coloured base. The fluidity of the vegetal scrolls around the rim, the realism of the bird portrait in the centre and the careful attention to artistic detail indicate the high-level workmanship of this piece.  
Islamic ceramics with metallic lustre were considered the most luxurious. The technique was probably invented in AH 3rd- / AD 9th-century Iraq during the Abbasid period. The technique was popular initially in Abbasid Samarra, but it flourished most expressively in Fatimid Egypt, and continued to spread throughout the Mediterranean and eastern Islamic region. In Syria, Tel Minis and Raqqa were important centres of production, while Kashan in Iran was also a renowned producer of lustre-ware. Valued for its capacity to cloak pottery with a precious metallic sheen, the technique continued to spread as a luxury commodity. By the time of the Nasrid period in the AH 8th / AD 14th century, the technique had developed in Spain and Italy to play an influential role in the artistic expression of painted ceramics on the eve of the European Renaissance.
cd2f0486-91f0-5d6c-834e-06e9ae177ed0.short_description: Lustre-painted pottery was a highly valued luxury product. This bowl decorated with a central bird portrait and a sequence of elaborately curling leaves along the rim is painted with careful attention to detail and harmony. Blessings to the owner are inscribed on the bowl's exterior.
cd2f0486-91f0-5d6c-834e-06e9ae177ed0.method_for_datation: Many similar pieces of lustre-ware have been attributed to the 5th / 11th and 6th / 12th centuries.
cd2f0486-91f0-5d6c-834e-06e9ae177ed0.method_for_provenance: While lustre-painted pottery of this quality has also been found in Fatimid Egypt, the carinated shape of this bowl and the use of cursive *naskhi* script supports the attribution to the Eastern lands of Atabeg-ruled Raqqa and Jazira. There were other contemporaneous production centres in Syria and elsewhere, thus it is not possible to establish the provenance definitively.
cd2f0486-91f0-5d6c-834e-06e9ae177ed0.provenance: Probably Syria; Jazira or Raqqa region.
