cd55af48-0b6d-5d4f-8dcd-ba7574d7bc56.name: Dish with small bull.
cd55af48-0b6d-5d4f-8dcd-ba7574d7bc56.description:
Dish with curved sides and a foot-ring painted in intense red lustre on a white-cream background. At the centre of the decoration there is a silhouette of a small bull or bullock painted in lustre with the detailing obtained by leaving some parts uncoloured, from which emerge four long symmetrical stalks with stylised flowers, probably derived from an adaptation of the plant shoots that occur on other examples of this type of object.  
The four sections into which the dish is divided are each decorated with a large bush with feathered leaves set diagonally, which predate a motif extremely common in later pieces (AH 12th / AD 18th century).  
Each bush bears two pieces of a sort of triangular fruit decorated with a fish-scale pattern obtained by leaving parts uncoloured.
cd55af48-0b6d-5d4f-8dcd-ba7574d7bc56.short_description: The decoration on this plate presages motifs that would become common in objects produced later in Valencia.
cd55af48-0b6d-5d4f-8dcd-ba7574d7bc56.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
cd55af48-0b6d-5d4f-8dcd-ba7574d7bc56.method_for_provenance: The decoration on the base of the dish, filled with groups of dots, other smaller, flowering bushes and tiny cruciform and star motifs, recurs in later Valencian production in then 12th / 18th century. Along the edge of the plate, accentuated by a broad band of solid lustre, there is a frame made up of a series of semi-circles containing small lustre disks, which predates a motif belonging to a later age, and which was probably inspired by the ‘fingernail’ motif that was commonly used on the edges of plates in the first third of the 11th / 17th century.

cd6b2c88-0a74-5d2f-8cba-5b3ea7174b9c.name: Tympanum made of 16 tiles from the palace of the grand vizier Piale Pasha (c. 1515-1578)
cd6b2c88-0a74-5d2f-8cba-5b3ea7174b9c.description: These tiles decorated the palace of the Ottoman Grand Vizier Piale Pasha, or possibly the mosque the Vizier commissioned. Both buildings were completed in 1573 and richly decorated with tile panels. The palace and the mosque were restored after an earthquake in 1890, and the tile panels were sold all over the world. At least nine identical tympanums are now in American and European museums.
cd6b2c88-0a74-5d2f-8cba-5b3ea7174b9c.holder: MAK – Austrian Museum of Applied Arts / Contemporary Art

cdef497c-1efa-5c25-b7ef-048f71a83d64.name: Blue glazed jar
cdef497c-1efa-5c25-b7ef-048f71a83d64.description:
This jar, with two small handles, a narrow neck and a globular body is covered externally with a turquoise-blue glaze, while the interior is covered with a white glaze. The lip of the neck is protruding, which may have allowed for the placement of a small ceramic or wooden lid held by a textile.  
  
This functional object used for the storage and transportation of liquids, such as oil, water, wine or syrup. t was discovered at the Murwab archaeological site in northwest Qatar. The production of this type of jar appears to have ceased in the middle of the 9th century, according to the stratified archaeological findings of Susa (Iran), Samarra and Basra (Iraq). The most important workshop for this production was the centre of Basra.
cdef497c-1efa-5c25-b7ef-048f71a83d64.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

ce05bc9c-4579-5b05-b81e-5aae5c270b67.name: Pottery jar
ce05bc9c-4579-5b05-b81e-5aae5c270b67.description: Although blue and white porcelains were described as vulgar by Chao Zaho (Chao Mingzhong) in his 1388 book about art and antiquities (the first book for connoisseurs) entitled *Gego yaolun* (The Essential Criteria of Antiques), these porcelains became more beloved and fashionable from their earliest appearance in Chinese and European markets. The first use of these two colours: blue (evoking the infinity of sea and sky) and white can be traced back to the Near and Middle East. They had a large impact on Chinese ceramics. Blue is also said to be effective against bad intentions. The pigments used for underglaze blue in Persia were lapis lazuli (*lajavard*) and cobalt, which was cheaper. The inside of the bowl is decorated with dynamic, loose floral motifs applied with sparse brushstrokes under the greyish-white glaze of the bowl on a small base. The rim is lined with blue.

ce44f778-9091-5698-8d43-0e6b3026e21a.name: Jar.
ce44f778-9091-5698-8d43-0e6b3026e21a.description:
A globular jar on a near-symmetrical foot, with a short neck which curls out at the lip. The body of the jar is decorated with three bands of blue and white underglaze painting. The central and largest band contains prominent arabesques in white on blue, while the narrower bands above and below feature Chinese-inspired floral ornament in blue on white. The neck and foot are decorated with narrower bands which include interlocking strap-work and small circular motifs. There are two blank torus mouldings around the neck.  
  
This jar is a fascinating example of the many artistic influences at work in early Iznik pottery. Its body copies a Chinese shape, and the aesthetic of blue-on-white, also of Chinese inspiration, was in vogue in the Middle East during the AH 9th / AD 15th century. The peony motifs on the body, too, are of Chinese origin. On the other hand, the influence of Ottoman metalwork, particularly silver, is also palpable; it can be seen in details such as the torus mouldings and the arabesques crowding the central register. The use of this sort of arabesque design has its roots in a style of decoration originating at the Ottoman royal scriptorium, possibly from the hand of a single artist whom the sources refer to as 'Baba Naqqash.' Designs on paper associated with Baba Naqqash show traditional Islamic arabesques combined with Chinese elements to form a new and distinctively Ottoman idiom. Since their decoration reflects this development quite closely, this jar and other early Iznik ceramics like it – once called 'Abraham of Kütahya wares' after an unusual ewer in the British Museum – have been dubbed 'Baba Naqqash' ware by scholars.
ce44f778-9091-5698-8d43-0e6b3026e21a.short_description: A globular jar on a near-symmetrical foot, with three bands of blue-and-white decoration. The decoration shows the emergence of a truly Ottoman style out of a mixture of influences including Chinese art and contemporary metalwork. It can be traced to developments in the Ottoman imperial scriptorium.
ce44f778-9091-5698-8d43-0e6b3026e21a.method_for_datation: Comparison with the Ottoman decorative style prevalent during the last years of the reign of Sultan Mehmed II (r. twice, 1444-46 and 1451–81).
ce44f778-9091-5698-8d43-0e6b3026e21a.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production during this period.

ce637fbb-3666-5ca2-b5a7-515016f46a6d.name: Star tile with seated figure
ce637fbb-3666-5ca2-b5a7-515016f46a6d.short_description: In Iran, during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, star-shaped luster tiles were made in great numbers for the walls of religious and secular buildings. Figurative and non-figurative imagery was painted in the centre, while verses from the Qur'an or selections from Persian poetry were written around the edges. The halo surrounding the head of the seated figure indicates that this person was an important individual, such as royalty.

cf1afb8b-9458-59a3-ba8d-167823382d2f.name: Table top
cf1afb8b-9458-59a3-ba8d-167823382d2f.short_description: Large circular tiles, surrounded by a border of smaller tiles, were used as table tops. They were mostly decorated with banquet scenes, a recurrent theme in Persian art. Here the composition illustrates an episode from Ferdowsi's epic *Shahnameh* (The Book of Kings), namely the punishment of Zahhak: having chased away the Iranian king Jamshid, Zahhak rules like a tyrant for one thousand years, but is overthrown by Fereydun, following a popular uprising led by the blacksmith Kaveh. His life is spared, but he will be imprisoned in a cave on Mount Damawand, where he will remain until the end of the world. The scene shows the procession with Zahhak being led to the place of his imprisonment. The tyrant riding a camel is depicted in the upper left corner; two snakes feeding on human brains are growing out of his shoulders. On his left, Kaveh in a green robe is carrying a banner made out of his leather apron, inscribed with Arabic numerals. On Kaveh’s left, the young king Fereydun, riding a bull, is carrying his bull-head mace, the weapon with which he defeated Zahhak. The magnificent procession is minutely depicted in a complex scene: hierarchical proportion and diagonal composition are used here to give emphasis to the main characters, accompanied by a richly attired retinue riding on elephants.

d06f4d6a-a257-5324-a2d7-ce12318aa95d.name: Dish.
d06f4d6a-a257-5324-a2d7-ce12318aa95d.description: The deep pottery dish has a flat foliated rim and is decorated in underglaze cobalt-blue, bright turquoise, green, relief opaque red and black for the outlines. The centre of the dish shows a symmetrical design of two curving red dotted tulips and two smaller red flowers on stalks clasped together with a pointed, scalloped medallion between them. Small roses and other flowers springing from a leafy tuft fill the area underneath. The shape of the dish, with a foliated rim, and the stylised pattern of waves breaking on rocks on the rim are of Chinese origin. The latter developed into a popular Iznik design with a tendency to stylisation during the AH 10th / AD 16th century. The rocks and waves, originally painted in different colours, are both blue on this dish, a characteristic feature of later Iznik ware. The pointed, scalloped medallion developed in the courtly ateliers, used to decorate textiles or tiles, occurred on pottery from the AH 980s / AD 1580s. Vessels from the second half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century are mostly not imperial commissions, even if they show designs of the courtly ateliers. The potters, producing for the local market, created their own compositions by combining single elements of various styles and sources. On the back the dish is painted with four blue coloured tulips alternating with four rosettes on a white background. The transparent glaze on the back is slightly yellow coloured.
d06f4d6a-a257-5324-a2d7-ce12318aa95d.short_description: Polychrome underglaze painted dish with a foliated rim. In the centre is a symmetrical design of flowers and a medallion. The single elements, originally designed in the courtly workshops, were combined in a pattern by the potters themselves. The wave and rock motif on the rim is of Chinese origin.

d0cd0d4e-b74c-5e32-a326-e726894f5838.name: Bowl
d0cd0d4e-b74c-5e32-a326-e726894f5838.short_description:
The earthen white bowl has a two-coloured decoration on a white background. The bird in the centre is clearly recognisable, with tendril patterns grouped around it. Provenance has been ascribed to Eastern Iran due to the presence of calligraphic elements, particularly evident in the bird’s body, which has been drawn with only two lines traced in one movement. The bird is undoubtedly a peacock, an ancient Persian symbol. The attractive but somewhat hastily executed decoration suggests that the bowl was made in the 11th century.  
  
Slip-painted ware with coloured decoration are typical of Iran and the eastern Iranian world of the 10th and 11th centuries. They are characterised by their often multi-coloured decoration, very thin bodies and the common use of animalistic decorations.
d0cd0d4e-b74c-5e32-a326-e726894f5838.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar dated objects

d1df60cc-7f00-5222-836d-c786e82473ca.name: Water jug filter
d1df60cc-7f00-5222-836d-c786e82473ca.description: The decorative openings on the necks of this type of water jugs (fired clay vessels that cool their contents through a process of gradual evaporation) are evidence of the inventiveness of Cairo potters. They would trace the design onto wet clay with a sharpened reed similar to a calligraphy pen, in a technique similar to *al fresco* painting.

d209c356-064a-548c-bf26-d4da707c6cfc.description: This hexagonal tile, painted in blue and black beneath a turquoise glaze, is decorated with a stork placed in the centre, on a background of shoots covered in leaves and flowers. This piece was intended for architectural use as a wall covering.
d209c356-064a-548c-bf26-d4da707c6cfc.short_description: In the Muslim world, tiles such as this one were generally used in building, in particular as a domestic wall covering. The technique used in its production place it in Syria or Egypt in the AH 9th / AD 15th century.

The rim of the plate features a wave and rock pattern that demonstrates the influence of Chinese art (especially of earlier and contemporary Ming porcelains) on Iznik production.

d26367ea-3684-5799-b481-4efef3e51786.name: Chimneypiece.
d26367ea-3684-5799-b481-4efef3e51786.description:
A large tile ensemble forming a chimneypiece for a fireplace. The hood is formed as a cone with seven faceted sides, each of which continues down to form the arch surmounting the fireplace niche. A repeat of the chintamani motif of three circles and two wavy stripes provides the main decorative scheme for the hood and arch. The hood is set within a tall rectangular frame whose border contains intertwining flowering stems on a blue background. The spandrels on either side of the hood include white arabesques on a turquoise background, dark-blue arabesques showing European influence on a white background, and two large ceramic bosses. At the base of the chimneypiece, two side panels echo the *chintamani* decoration of the hood and arch.  
  
A band of cartouches at the top of the fireplace arch, one on each of its seven facets, contains inscriptions with the names of the 'Companions of the Cave' and their dog. (One cartouche has two names, so as to fit in all eight.) The 'Companions of the Cave' (*ashab al-kahf*), also known as the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, are the subject of an ancient story which was repeated in the Qur'an (*sura* 18, verses 9–26). According to the story, seven Christian youths went into a cave to escape religious persecution and fell asleep, awakening miraculously several hundred years later. In later Islamic times the custom arose of hanging the names of the Seven Sleepers (as well as their dog, Qitmir) in one's house as a way of averting misfortune.  
  
The fireplace was originally made for the palace of the Ottoman official Fuad Pasha, a building which burned down in 1857.
d26367ea-3684-5799-b481-4efef3e51786.short_description: A large tile ensemble forming a chimneypiece for a fireplace. A band of cartouches contains inscriptions with the names of the ‘Seven Sleepers of Ephesus’ and their dog, names which were thought to bring good luck. It was originally installed in the palace of an Ottoman official.
d26367ea-3684-5799-b481-4efef3e51786.dimensions: Height 360 cm, width 233 cm, depth 53.5 cm.
d26367ea-3684-5799-b481-4efef3e51786.method_for_datation: One of the tiles has a short poem on it which reads, 'A man emerged to pray and said at once by way of a chronogram, “Here are Ottoman tiles apparent”'. The chronogram adds up to 1143.
d26367ea-3684-5799-b481-4efef3e51786.method_for_provenance: By the 18th century, the tile industry at Iznik was in a state of complete collapse. When the Ottoman court began to take a renewed interest in decorative tilework under Sultan Ahmed III (r. 1115–43 / 1703–31), it reconstituted the industry in Istanbul.

d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.name: Konch
d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.description:
The Konch is a fishing device made from bamboo and iron spikes, and is specifically designed to catch larger fish. It is similar to the Juti, but employs at least 10 pieces of bamboo splits, which are firmly fixed in a bunch. In order to increase its effectiveness, the tips of the bamboo are topped with sharp and pointed iron caps. To use it, fishermen must wait with great patience until they find a fish, often spending hours on a boat or at the water's edge. Once they eventually find one, they hurl the implement with great force, pinning the fish down and striking it. The species of fish caught with this device include Rui (Labeo rohita), Catla (Catla catla), Shoal (Channa striatus), and Gozar (Channa marulius), amongst others.  
Traditional fishing gear consists of a long bamboo handle (2-4m) with a 60-65cm iron rode at the base, and is fitted with multiple iron hooks at the apex. The iron rode is securely attached to the bamboo handle using coconut thread or iron wire.
d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.bibliography: Siddiq, M., *et al.*, “Fishing Gears of the Meghna River Estuary of Chandpur Region, Bangladesh”, in *Trends in Fisheries Research, 2(1; 2018): https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325120382\_FISHING\_GEARS\_OF\_THE\_MEGHNA\_RIVER\_ESTUARY\_OF\_CHANDPUR\_REGION\_BANGLADESH \[last accessed: 04/10/25\]*
d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.author: ActionAid Bangladesh

d348585a-7bd5-5541-a59b-2dc830deea8e.name: Bowl fragment
d348585a-7bd5-5541-a59b-2dc830deea8e.short_description: The bowl fragment is decorated with an Arabic inscription in *thuluth* calligraphy reading *‘li'l muhamir al-amir’* (‘to the prince’s cupbearer’) and a heraldic cup motif. The letters and the cup are painted in shades of brown or in white, their outlines are incised. Above the inscription, a narrow register with an incised scroll. A recurrent motif in Mamluk art, blazons were displayed on both monuments and a large variety of objects (arms and armour, ceramics, glass, metalwork, and textiles). Around fifty such blazons are currently known; when accompanied by inscriptions identifying the name of the commissioner they could be actually traced back to a historical personality; others were interpreted on a more general, symbolic level. Animal motifs (the lion, the eagle) were sometimes part of a sultan’s blazon, whilst other motifs were associated with offices held by Mamluks in the sultan’s entourage: the cup with the cupbearer (*saqi*), the polo clubs with the polo master (*jukandar*), the sword, the bow or the mace with the arms bearer (*silahdar*), the lozenge (*buqja*) with the master of the robes (*jamdar*).
d348585a-7bd5-5541-a59b-2dc830deea8e.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
d348585a-7bd5-5541-a59b-2dc830deea8e.method_for_datation: Both materials and technique, as well as the heraldic decoration are characteristic of Mamluk art.
d348585a-7bd5-5541-a59b-2dc830deea8e.obtention: In 1932 the Arab Museum in Cairo donated a collection of ceramic sherds to the Toma Stelian Museum in Bucharest, whose holdings were transferred to the National Museum of Art of Romania in 1949.

d3981150-1dad-5bad-9f7e-e4e7cb1fa469.description: This pitcher (*maşrapa*) has a blue interior glaze and light brown exterior. The exterior surface is coated in a milky brown glaze and decorated with stylised vegetal motifs.

d39da914-020c-5c37-a7ff-589980514ce1.name: Mosque-lamp-shaped vessel with Arabic inscriptions
d39da914-020c-5c37-a7ff-589980514ce1.short_description: With its delicate spiralling stem design, this small vessel belongs to a group of ceramics formerly referred to as "Golden Horn" wares. Current scholarship, however, prefers the term *tughrakes*\-, or "*tughra*‑illuminator" style for such decoration, comparing its design to the fine swirling vines adorning *tughra* calligraphies. During this period, pottery shapes often imitated metalwork forms. This piece, however, emulates glass mosque lamps, which often displayed Arabic inscriptions.

d40f4cf7-8833-5a78-ab2e-a55dbf38460f.name: Large jar.
d40f4cf7-8833-5a78-ab2e-a55dbf38460f.description:
A large, unglazed but richly decorated *khubb* jar used for storing water. It has an oval-shaped body without a base. Most of the body's surface is decorated with a repeating pattern resembling a stylised horned animal head. The cylindrical neck and protruding lip are richly decorated with pierced carving and applied pieces of clay that were attached to the body of the jar after its basic shape was made. These include human forms in profile and in a standing posture amidst allegorical creatures and stylised foliage. A band of Arabic writing in *thuluth* script divides the ovoid shape of the jar between body and neck. It is possible to translate the text as follows: “\[May God grant\] power, prosperity, happiness, respect, bliss and advancement.”  
One of the decorative scenes applied on the jar's neck may be described as follows: in the centre is a frontally oriented person who is sitting in the "Eastern" posture of worship (i.e. with his arms bent up at the elbow and palms facing the object of worship). He is framed by an overhead arch with a pair of open-jawed dragons facing each other. Beneath the dragons' claws there is a protruding knob flanked by a pair of lion-like faces whose eyes, nostrils, and ears are accentuated by pierced circles. Similar fantastical imagery continues below the seated figure. His crossed legs rest on top of two human-headed birds with young female faces, coiffed hair and elegantly decorated wings. Beneath these fantastical birds there is a pair of protruding lion heads. All these figures are placed on a background of stylised, perforated vegetal motifs.
d40f4cf7-8833-5a78-ab2e-a55dbf38460f.short_description: This large water-jar with its ovoid shape, pierced carving and moulded figurative attachments is a masterpiece of the pottery industry of Jazira in the AH 5th and 6th / AD 11th and 12th centuries.
d40f4cf7-8833-5a78-ab2e-a55dbf38460f.method_for_datation: The vessel is extremely similar in size, shape, decoration and apparent use to many other pieces produced during the Atabeg and Ayyubid periods (6th / 12th and early 7th / 13th centuries) in the Jazira region.
d40f4cf7-8833-5a78-ab2e-a55dbf38460f.method_for_provenance: Although this jar was found in Damascus, *khubb* jars were typically produced in the Jazira area, especially in the cities of Mosul, Sinjar and Tikrit.
d40f4cf7-8833-5a78-ab2e-a55dbf38460f.provenance: Jazira (the region located between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, hence known as “the island” and currently consisting of northeast modern Syria and northwest Iraq), or Mesopotamia.
d40f4cf7-8833-5a78-ab2e-a55dbf38460f.obtention: The jar was found in Veterinarian Street (Jadat al-Bayatira) in the Aqaba Quarter of Damascus, and was purchased by the Museum in 1927.

d471ccf4-8028-5b73-9f99-00c909de85df.name: Bowl
d471ccf4-8028-5b73-9f99-00c909de85df.short_description:
The large and diverse museum collection of Samanid pottery from old Samarqand (Afrasiab) includes several stylistic types found only in the Transoxiana region. One of the most distinctive of these is presented by a deep hemi-spherical bowl with concave rim and a ring foot, painted with brownish red, olive green and black on white slip. The palette suggests the dating of the bowl to the 10th century.  
The composition of the décor is radial. A round medallion in the centre is filled with olive green grid and encircled with a narrow band of meander. Walls are divided into six large trapezoidal segments painted with alternating patterns of brownish red “open hearts” motif and olive green grid motif. Segments are separated by six radial bands of black “open hearts” ornament. Along the rim above large segments there are narrow lambrequins with stylized floral pattern painted in black. The bowl is very well preserved and makes a stunning impression by its intensive colours and bright glitter of the high quality glaze.
d471ccf4-8028-5b73-9f99-00c909de85df.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by H. Shyshkina (examination, 1977, date and origin).
d471ccf4-8028-5b73-9f99-00c909de85df.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
d471ccf4-8028-5b73-9f99-00c909de85df.obtention: Acquired by the Khanenko Museum in 1925. From the former collection of the Kyiv University Cabinet of Arts.

d4c79927-459a-53a9-ae7c-8f1aee62f08d.name: Alhambra vase.
d4c79927-459a-53a9-ae7c-8f1aee62f08d.description:
The jar, shaped like an amphora, belongs to the group of so-called Alhambra vases characterised by a swelling body, a neck with protruding lip and wide flat handles. One of the handles of this vase was lost and has been replaced by a bronze dragon. Base supports were added later to the vase to hold it upright. The decoration, overglaze painted in a yellowish lustre, emphasises the different components of the vase: perpendicular designs fill the panels of the long, ribbed neck, alternate narrow and wide horizontal bands define the elongated body, and an all-over lattice of rhombs covers the remaining handle. A limited repertoire of designs consisting of inscriptional, ornamental and vegetal elements is repeated in the individual areas of the body and the neck. The decoration of this vase shows some special features not found on other vases. The most remarkable difference is the obligatory *kufic* inscription of the body which is not set in a wide central area. Another feature is the vegetal pattern composed of thin stems that lack a recognisable inner structure.  
The Alhambra vase in Stockholm is one of the few nearly complete vases. When it was described for the first time in the 16th century by pilgrims as a relic in a church in Cyprus, the vase was believed to be one of the jars from the Marriage at Canaan when Christ transformed water into wine. In 1580 the vase came as booty in the possession of the Ottoman sultan. Some time later, a German ambassador at the Sublime Porte succeeded in buying the Christian relic and the vase passed into the treasury of the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolph II (1552–1612). When the Swedish army conquered Prague in 1648, it was taken to Sweden and became part of the treasures of the royal family. In the first half of the 18th century the Swedish architect C. Härleman restored the missing handle by designing a dragon. He also added the bronze wreath, covering much of the bold *naskhi* inscription on the shoulder, which cannot be read.
d4c79927-459a-53a9-ae7c-8f1aee62f08d.short_description: Large, amphora-like jar (so-called Alhambra vase). Horizontal bands contain inscriptions, ornamental and vegetal motifs. One of the characteristic wide flat handles was replaced by a bronze dragon. The base intended to hold the jar upright was also added later.
d4c79927-459a-53a9-ae7c-8f1aee62f08d.dates: Hegira second half of the 8th century / AD second half of the 14th century.
d4c79927-459a-53a9-ae7c-8f1aee62f08d.method_for_datation: Because of its elongated shape and its decoration scheme, the Stockholm vase is a predecessor of the blue painted vases dated to the late 8th–early 9th / late 14th–early 15th centuries. Its comparison with the architectural and textile ornament of the time of the reign of Muhammad V (764–94 / 1362–91) is evidence for an attribution of the vase to the second half of the 8th / 14th century.
d4c79927-459a-53a9-ae7c-8f1aee62f08d.method_for_provenance: Several jars of this type were found in the Alhambra Palace in Granada, which also gives the objects their name. It is not known exactly where the vases were produced. They were probably made in Malaga, southwest of Granada, which was the centre of lustre ceramic production from the 7th to the 9th / 13th to the 15th centuries.
d4c79927-459a-53a9-ae7c-8f1aee62f08d.obtention: The Alhambra vase was part of the royal collections, which were transferred to the Royal Museum, later the National Museum of Fine Arts, opened in the palace in 1794.

d4cb27ef-ed38-5e0e-a7ee-36d39dde3dca.name: Tile panel
d4cb27ef-ed38-5e0e-a7ee-36d39dde3dca.short_description: These tiles, purchased from a gallery in Iran in 1938, are said to have come from Julfa, an Armenian suburb of Isfahan, Iran. Indeed, the lively animals (such as ibexes, ducks, tigers, and gazelles) seen on the tiles are typical of underglaze-painted tiles of Julfa. To achieve the sharp, polychrome designs seen on haft-rangi tile, the colored glazes were separated by a black line that prevented the colours from blending together.

d4d259e7-4328-5707-904a-64246e07850e.name: Tile panel.
d4d259e7-4328-5707-904a-64246e07850e.description: Lunette-panel of 16 tiles. Said to have come from the mosque of the Ottoman Grand Admiral Piyale Pasha, the panel shows the Iznik potters at the height of their powers. A cloud-band of deep-red undulates through a field of blue flowers and green leaves, all carefully organised around spiralling arabesques. The dark-blue of the border is offset by the green and red of the alternating flowers and leaves. While the form of the panel is a common one, as lunettes were a standard feature of Ottoman architectural decoration, the quality of decoration makes this a particularly splendid example.
d4d259e7-4328-5707-904a-64246e07850e.short_description: A panel of 16 tiles shaped to form a lunette-panel. This particular example is said to have come from a mosque founded by the Ottoman Grand Admiral Piyale Pasha. The quality of the tiles, particularly the use of red and green, shows the splendour of the Iznik pottery industry at its zenith.
d4d259e7-4328-5707-904a-64246e07850e.method_for_datation: The panel was taken from above a window in the mosque of Piyale Pasha in Istanbul, built in 981 / 1573-4.
d4d259e7-4328-5707-904a-64246e07850e.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

d4d259e7-4328-5707-904a-64246e07850e.author: Barry Wood

d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.name: Dish.
d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.description: A small, square relief-moulded ceramic dish with nine sections: five circular and four egg-shaped in the corners. The flat surface around these indentations is covered with relief decoration. This was probably used as a condiment tray with a different delicacy held in each compartment. Unusually for this type of ceramic the craftsman has signed his work; Abu Nasr states that he is from Basra but that this dish was made in Egypt. It is possible that Abu Nasr moved from Basra after a period of political unrest there, to settle in Egypt under the relative stability of the Tulunid dynasty. He offers, therefore, an interesting example of the tendency of craftsmen to leave areas of political upheaval and migrate to more politically peaceful locations where patronage would be more abundant.
d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.short_description: This ceramic dish was made by one Abu Nasr; he states that he is from Basra but that he made the dish in Egypt. This is clear evidence that not only artefacts, such as wood-carvings and ceramics, but craftsmen themselves travelled from Abbasid Iraq to Tulunid Egypt in the AH 3rd / AD 9th century.
d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.method_for_datation: Other lead-glazed ceramics with relief decoration have been found at sites in Abbasid Egypt and Iraq, dating to the 3rd / 9th century.
d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.method_for_provenance: The craftsman has inscribed the dish with the words: 'the work of Abu Nasr of Basra in Egypt'. Therefore although he originated in Basra, he made this dish in Egypt.
d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.obtention: Bequeathed by Augustus Wollaston Franks in 1889.
d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.bibliography: Grube. E., et. al., *Cobalt and Lustre: The First Centuries of Islamic Pottery*, London, 1994, pp.10–34.
d506ae4d-e5e8-5946-b5f5-cc9da28f5457.author: Emily Shovelton

d55b9320-ae0b-59f0-aa56-266f6476f76e.name: Bowl
d55b9320-ae0b-59f0-aa56-266f6476f76e.short_description:
This bowl belongs to a group of quartz frit ceramics with luster decoration produced in Kashan at the end of the Hegira 6th century. Thanks to vessels dated between Hegira 575 and 595 (AD 1179 to 1198), the period in which they flourished can be narrowed down fairly precisely. Characteristic are the individual figures in clearly defined fields.  
  
This bowl is fashioned after a metal prototype. In order to obtain the shape, the vessel was not formed on the potter's wheel but with the help of models.
d55b9320-ae0b-59f0-aa56-266f6476f76e.dates: Hegira end of 6th century / AD end of 12th

d55b9320-ae0b-59f0-aa56-266f6476f76e.method_for_provenance: By comparison with stylistically similar works

d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.name: Dish with conical boss.
d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.description: A large plate turned on a wheel, with an elevated central boss (umbonate). It is profusely decorated with copper-chestnut, with sections in blue, on a white background with metallic lustre. The central subject, heraldic in style, occupies the entire base of the piece and consists of a two-headed eagle, with a crown, surrounded by stylised plant motifs – ivy leaves. The same decorative motifs are repeated on the flat part of the rim, interspersed by four large leaves (similar to parsley leaves) accentuated in blue. The reverse of the object is decorated with stylised marks consisting of inward curving lines, reminiscent of initials. It has three equidistant spurs resulting from the mark left by the trivets. This is a luxury but practical object, used as tableware as a substitute for metal objects, which it imitates in its design.
d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.short_description: Bossed dish from Manises in the Valencia region. The town’s ceramics tradition dates back to the Islamic period. This luxury item has a central, heraldic-style motif consisting of a two-headed eagle with a crown surrounded by stylised plant motifs.
d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.initial_owner: João Maria Correia Ayres de Campos, Count of Ameal.
d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.dimensions: Height 7.5 cm, diameter (of rim) 38 cm, diameter (of base) 9 cm.
d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.method_for_datation: Probable dating by stylistic analogy with the class of gilded lustre-ware ceramics from Manises (15th–18th century). The Muslims of Valencia continued its production until the 18th century, introducing more varied profiles and new shapes, as well as variations in its decoration, especially in the use of polychromy. For this reason it is thought that this piece may belong to the early period of production in Manises. In addition, the stylised elements on the reverse of the object are still characteristic of the 15th century.
d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.method_for_provenance: Manises is the source of the metallic painted lustre-ware which developed a large market as luxury objects all over Europe during the 15th century.
d5968214-2acb-5a7f-a152-88470aecce15.obtention: It was obtained in 1921, through donation.

d597f360-10fd-5808-93c6-1f3065c51d77.name: Tile panel, custom-made for Shangri La's courtyard
d597f360-10fd-5808-93c6-1f3065c51d77.short_description: Creating a tile mosaic is an intricate process. Monochrome-glazed tile slabs are first fired and then cut into small pieces of varying shapes. The pieces are fitted together upside-down, and plaster is poured over them to form a solid, secure backing. The design of this massive tile mosaic, which was custom-made for Shangri La in Iran in 1938, derives from a pair of mosaic tile panels on the portal to the Shah's mosque (Masjid-i Shah) in Isfahan, Iran.

d610db47-e679-5566-8a64-70b9efcac53f.name: Tile with green parrots
d610db47-e679-5566-8a64-70b9efcac53f.short_description:
The colour palette of this beautiful tile includes emerald green and bright tomato red that were mastered by potters of Turkish Iznik in the second half of the AD 16th century. The sophisticated composition of two parrots (or peacocks) sitting on either side of the fountain surrounded by a dense foliage of scrolled serrated "*saz*" leaves represent the style introduced into Iznik décor by Şahkulu, the head of the court design atelier from 1526–56. The old-known Middle Eastern motif of two birds flanking a water pool refers to the idea of Paradise and immortality of a human soul.  
In the 16th–17th century the Ottomans widely used painted ceramic tiles for inside decoration of religious or secular buildings. The idea was to strike a visitor of a mosque or palace by a sharp contrast between the austere external walls and the stunning beauty of the interior.
d610db47-e679-5566-8a64-70b9efcac53f.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by Yu. Miller (publication, 1972, date, origin).
d610db47-e679-5566-8a64-70b9efcac53f.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
d610db47-e679-5566-8a64-70b9efcac53f.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalized by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

d6aabbc5-689a-572b-bc5c-97c69c34d4f6.name: Mina'I bowl
d6aabbc5-689a-572b-bc5c-97c69c34d4f6.short_description: A typically round bowl sitting on a short circular foot. The interior is decorated with pairs of seated figures dressed in brightly coloured clothes separated by small pointed cypress trees with a man on horseback in the centre. Below the rim on the inside is a calligraphic band whilst on the exterior is a red and blue decoration.

d71042b5-7752-5d3f-8e19-eda7d0c3baca.name: Large jar with relief decoration.
d71042b5-7752-5d3f-8e19-eda7d0c3baca.description:
The egg-shaped jar, with three small handles, is covered entirely with a heavy dark-green glaze, which is common in Sassanid ceramic production.  
The decoration is based on a series of concentric circles in relief finished off in the middle with a motif of a stylised bunch of grapes, which is related to a widespread tradition of symbolic figures. Below the brim there is a geometric motif in relief made up of small rhombuses, and the lower part of the body is decorated with apex motifs.  
The shape, decoration and technique used in the piece are evidence of the stylistic continuity between the late Sassanid and the early Islamic periods. The jar was probably intended to store foodstuffs.
d71042b5-7752-5d3f-8e19-eda7d0c3baca.short_description: Sassanid influences are clearly recognisable in the shape, decoration and production technique of this jar, which was probably used to store foodstuffs.
d71042b5-7752-5d3f-8e19-eda7d0c3baca.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
d71042b5-7752-5d3f-8e19-eda7d0c3baca.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis. The shape and decoration of the jar, the technique used and the dark green glaze are all typical of Sassanid ceramics.
d71042b5-7752-5d3f-8e19-eda7d0c3baca.method_for_provenance: Similar examples were common in Persia and Iraq, countries in which they were in use until the 3rd / 9th century.

d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.name: Storage jar.
d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.description:
A small, dark-gray storage jar of beautiful form, with a ribbed body and linear geometric pattern, painted with a single and a multiple-headed brush prior to firing, which covers the entire vessel. The extent of decoration on this jar means that it was probably a costly item.  
  
The jar has a triangular rim, two loop handles and a round umbilical base. It was made of two parts joined by pressing the clay together, as there is a flange between the shoulder and the ribbed body. The jar was broken into pieces when recovered and has been subsequently mended.
d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.short_description: A small storage jar from the nymphaeum at Umm Qays with a geometric pattern painted before firing. It was made of two parts, joined at the flange between the shoulder and body. The extent of decoration probably made it a costly item.
d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.dates: Hegira, second half of the 1st century / AD 2nd half of the 7th century.
d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.dimensions: Height 47.5 cm, diameter (of rim) 10 cm; diameter (of base) 22 cm.
d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.method_for_datation: The jar was dated by stratigraphic context and comparison with similar vessels uncovered at other sites.
d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.method_for_provenance: The jar was found at the nymphaeum of Umm-Qays during excavation, but the original place of production is not known.
d73ce677-c4d9-526d-a784-55d5db6b9325.obtention: The jar was uncovered in the course of an archaeological excavation carried out at the nymphaeum (a pleasure garden) at Umm-Qays in 2001.

d7e18569-9eee-57d9-a0c1-5ccdc6d021f5.name: Covered inkstand
d7e18569-9eee-57d9-a0c1-5ccdc6d021f5.short_description: Whether urban or rural, Moroccan ceramics reflect the country’s ethnic diversity. The city of Fez in northern Morocco was the most important centre for the production of 'urban' ceramics. Most of the objects produced are functional and for everyday use, especially kitchenware. Fez is particularly renowned for its cobalt blue and white glazed ceramic ware. The pottery was wheel-made and produced exclusively by male specialists.
d7e18569-9eee-57d9-a0c1-5ccdc6d021f5.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
d7e18569-9eee-57d9-a0c1-5ccdc6d021f5.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.
d7e18569-9eee-57d9-a0c1-5ccdc6d021f5.obtention: Catalog entry: "Donated by the imperial and royal Secretary of Legation Dr. Michael Count Bukuwky [von Bukuwka], 1910."

d8e83cc2-fed3-5eb6-acf4-5914da8fc9a0.name: Ewer.
d8e83cc2-fed3-5eb6-acf4-5914da8fc9a0.description: A ceramic ewer of rectangular shape, with four feet and sloping shoulders. The original spout and handle have broken off and been replaced, probably in the 19th century, with metal mounts of European origin. The ewer is decorated with underglaze painting in white on a blue ground. The wide sides are decorated with white cloud-bands in a spiralling arabesque framework, reflected in a looser form (without the cloud-bands) on the ewer's sloping shoulders, while the narrow sides feature linked flower motifs. The ewer's feet have been left white. This is one of a group of ceramic objects which represent the waning of the so-called 'Baba Naqqash' style. The scrolling arabesques and stylised cloud-bands recall earlier ornament, but the design has become more open and free, looking forward to the classical Iznik style.
d8e83cc2-fed3-5eb6-acf4-5914da8fc9a0.short_description: A ceramic ewer of rectangular shape, with four feet and a sloping shoulder. The decoration in blue and white features both traditional and innovative elements. The original spout and handle have broken off and been replaced, probably in the 19th century, with silver mounts of European origin.
d8e83cc2-fed3-5eb6-acf4-5914da8fc9a0.dimensions: Height 22.3 cm, width 15.5 cm (including spout), depth 11 cm.
d8e83cc2-fed3-5eb6-acf4-5914da8fc9a0.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
d8e83cc2-fed3-5eb6-acf4-5914da8fc9a0.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, Istanbul/London, 1989, p.95 and p.96, fig. 97.
d8e83cc2-fed3-5eb6-acf4-5914da8fc9a0.author: Barry Wood
materials: Painted and glazed ceramic, the mounts silver.

d971e2da-ec43-53d8-9ea9-f48cb8b3eeee.name: Turkish jugs

d9965187-6fce-52dd-9948-49959f6e177c.name: Bowl with stylised bird
d9965187-6fce-52dd-9948-49959f6e177c.short_description: This flat bowl with a ring base shows a bird with stylised plumage on its head. Painted on white engobe (slip), the outline of the bird is painted in black, its body, wings and tail filled with olive green, black, and red. Around the bird, the bowl is decorated with a floral and vine motif and the rim is decorated with black dots. It was presumably produced in either Nishapur or Amol.
d9965187-6fce-52dd-9948-49959f6e177c.dimensions: Height: 7.4cm, Diameter: 22cm; Diameter of the foot: 10.2cm
d9965187-6fce-52dd-9948-49959f6e177c.method_for_datation: The decoration and technique refer to Sari ware.

d9c388f4-ae74-56f2-b3d4-341eda234a0f.name: Panel with a large bouquet
d9c388f4-ae74-56f2-b3d4-341eda234a0f.short_description: This polychromatic panel is decorated with an image of a bowl filled with pears, apples and other fruits, topped by a small vase with flowers such as carnations, tulips, sunflowers and daisies coming out of it, which are interlaced with a rinceau pattern of palmettes, half-palmettes and vine leaves. The main colours are blue, green and brown. The decorative style, colour palette and manufacture all indicate a typical Tunisian ceramic, containing a mix of Andalusian and Ottoman influences.

d9cffa1d-0e9d-59ee-a8f9-0f2a12a3c7dd.name: Dish serving for dried fruits or nuts
d9cffa1d-0e9d-59ee-a8f9-0f2a12a3c7dd.short_description: Sultan Abdülhamid II founded in 1891 the *Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu* (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace in order to revive Turkish tile art and give it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. Many native and foreign artists have worked in the tile factory of Yıldız. One of them, Halid Naci received training in tile painting in Sevres, France after his education at the *Sanayi-i Nefise Mektebi* (School of Fine Arts) and he was assigned to be head painter of the tile factories after his return.

d9d1975c-a93a-56fc-b9e6-09cc24d00116.name: Dish
d9d1975c-a93a-56fc-b9e6-09cc24d00116.short_description: Among the most noteworthy pieces of the museum collection of Iznik pottery is a dish with a “bush” composition in the central field and a ribbon that meanders on the edge. This plate dates to the AD early 17th century and gives a refined example of painting in the so-called “*saz*” style based on a key motif of a large serrated leaf of a specific shape. The dish is distinguished by a masterly drawing on a perfectly white surface, achieved by applying on the body a high quality white engobe. The artist used liquid paints that contained various metal oxides that gave different colours in the firing. To prevent blurring of pigments, the motifs were outlined with a thin black line in “*cuerda seca*” technique. Application of a transparent lead glaze created on the surface of the dish a dense smoothly glittering layer without cracks. In addition to its decorative merits, the dish attracts attention by a peculiar artistic decision of featuring a broken flower stem that subtly balances the asymmetrical design.
d9d1975c-a93a-56fc-b9e6-09cc24d00116.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by Yu. Miller (publication, 1961, date, origin).
d9d1975c-a93a-56fc-b9e6-09cc24d00116.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
d9d1975c-a93a-56fc-b9e6-09cc24d00116.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalized by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

d9ffdbec-54c1-5b8a-83b7-801a93de7321.name: Lid
d9ffdbec-54c1-5b8a-83b7-801a93de7321.short_description: The Bumiller Collection holds a row of jug lids with moulded zoomorphic or figurative motifs on one side. A part of this one is broken off, but the scene and the remaining part of the circular hole for attaching the lid to the handle of a jug is clearly visible. The upper side shows a mounted falconer, holding a falcon on his right hand behind his back. The falconer on horseback is a standardized and popular motif in all groups of materials and can be found on all kinds of metalwork, ceramics, ivory, textiles, glass flasks and beakers, from the 9th century CE on. Originally meant as an emblem of royal power or nobility, it may just fulfil a reminiscent purpose on this rather modest artefact of daily use.
d9ffdbec-54c1-5b8a-83b7-801a93de7321.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
d9ffdbec-54c1-5b8a-83b7-801a93de7321.method_for_datation: Lids were found in archaeological excavations in Iran (Susa) and Uzbekistan. A set was found in a workshop in Pajkent that according to radiocarbon dating was active form the 9th to 12th century. The falconer on horseback is a motif still popular in the 12th century.

d9ffdbec-54c1-5b8a-83b7-801a93de7321.bibliography: Simeon, Pierre, *From Ordinary to Luxury. Islamic Ceramics from Iran, Central Asia and Afghanistan. Studies on the Bumiller Collection I*, edited by Verena Daiber, Wiesbaden: Reichert, 2020: 27-29.

da5156d7-a825-5d2f-bce3-fb298aee2108.name: Blue dish
da5156d7-a825-5d2f-bce3-fb298aee2108.short_description: This unusually large dish reflects the Chinese influence that was found in by far the majority of Persian blue and white ceramics after c. 1400. But there are differences. The nervous peony, whose petals almost look like Chinese cloud ornaments, is of Far Eastern origin, while the rim’s split-leaf ornamentation, in contrast, is purely Islamic.
materials: Fritware, with decoration cut through a blue slip under a transparent glaze

db0e000c-19a2-52b9-a53e-eab344b9164a.name: Bowl
db0e000c-19a2-52b9-a53e-eab344b9164a.short_description: Abbasid ceramic production in Iraq indicates the significant impact of Chinese porcelain, found in numerous fragments throughout Mesopotamia. The plain elegance of this production is embodied in this small bowl, whose surface, entirely coated in white opaque glaze, is decorated simply by the phrase "work of Khalid" traced in elegant *kufic* characters with cobalt blue, painted directly over the glazing.
materials: Earthenware, opaque white glaze, blue decoration

db82ea3b-e453-5b5e-88c6-45d371143686.name: Jar
db82ea3b-e453-5b5e-88c6-45d371143686.short_description: Fritware jar covered with transparent cobalt blue glaze, painted in monochrome luster and decorated with *kufic*\-pseudo incriptions.
db82ea3b-e453-5b5e-88c6-45d371143686.dates: Hegira mid 7th century / AD mid 13th century
keywords: Glaze; Luster; Kufic; vase; pseudo inscriptions

dba3961b-be9c-5aa5-b797-ef6ba17346fe.name: Jug.
dba3961b-be9c-5aa5-b797-ef6ba17346fe.description: A medium-sized filter jug with one handle that is glazed light-green on top of dark-red ware. It has a simple rim, a flaring neck, a high, loop handle and a round body; the jug has a filter in the neck and a disc base. The body is divided into three bands by horizontal lines that begin at the rim, with one on the neck and another mid-way down the body. The decoration contains 'V'-shaped imbrications especially on the neck and the bottom half of the body, while the upper half of the body is decorated by small 'cactus'-stem shapes. The inside of the neck is also decorated by use of vertical lines of light-green glaze.
dba3961b-be9c-5aa5-b797-ef6ba17346fe.short_description: A medium-sized filter jug with one handle that is glazed light-green on top of dark-red ware. The body is divided into three bands by horizontal lines, and the inside of the neck is also decorated by use of vertical lines of light-green glaze.
dba3961b-be9c-5aa5-b797-ef6ba17346fe.dimensions: Height 17 cm, diameter (of rim) 8.5 cm, diameter (of base) 4.5 cm.
dba3961b-be9c-5aa5-b797-ef6ba17346fe.method_for_datation: The jug was dated by stylistic analysis and by comparison with similar vessels.
dba3961b-be9c-5aa5-b797-ef6ba17346fe.obtention: The object was purchased from an antiquities dealer in 1980.

dbe5d877-10e6-5723-8ea6-cd192909e5b0.name: Tile panel in the form of a fireplace surround
dbe5d877-10e6-5723-8ea6-cd192909e5b0.short_description: Islamic art may often operate on two visual levels: surface impressions and detailed study. A quick peruser may find pleasure from a work of art's bold colors and designs, but those who take the time to look more closely will be amply rewarded. In this tile, shaped to surround a small fireplace, dancing and acrobatic female entertainers, kings in repose who drink wine from small glasses, quietly seated aged advisors, thoughtful soldiers, and busy musicians fill the composition.
dbe5d877-10e6-5723-8ea6-cd192909e5b0.type: Islamic, Indian & Southeast Asian works of art; Tilework; ceramic
dbe5d877-10e6-5723-8ea6-cd192909e5b0.holder: Shangri La, Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art
keywords: tile panel; Qajar; Iran; stonepaste; underglaze-painted; fireplace surround; court life; music; musician; architectural decoration; tilework

dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.name: Vat
dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.description:
Globular vat with a conical base, a flaring neck, a flanged rim and winged handles. The paste is whitish and unglazed. Its decoration consists of a stamped, alternating series of lozenges and eulogetic epigraphy arranged in perimeter friezes.  
  
A common feature of Andalusian homes, these large earthenware vats were strategically placed in the courtyards or in interior rooms to preserve goods such as oil, cereals, or water, as well as to store domestic objects. In this case, the porous nature of the unglazed clay suggests that this example functioned specifically as a water vat, as it would have filtered and cooled the water, keeping it clean and fresh.  
  
Beyond their practical function, some vats had also an aesthetic value, as can be seen in the stamped decoration or glazing. Decorations included epigraphic motifs invoked to protect the vats' contents. The production and use of these vats continued after the Castilian conquest.
dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.dimensions: Height: 68cm, maximum diameter: 203cm, mouth diameter: 34cm, base diameter: 18cm
dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.method_for_datation: Archaeological and art-historical studies have established certain formal features that allow us to date the piece to the 7th–8th century Hegira / 13th–14th century AD. The globular body and stamped decoration are particularly present in the Almohad world, evolving towards more stylised forms, with more pronounced winged handles.

dd39d739-7c94-5fca-8bd3-91cc2964d480.name: Dish
dd39d739-7c94-5fca-8bd3-91cc2964d480.short_description: In the late fifteenth century, Iznik potters developed a distinct ceramic tradition known as Iznik ware, in which a stonepaste vessel was coated in a slip (thinned siliceous clay), painted in polychromatic glazes and additional slips, and covered with a transparent glaze. The entire surface of this Iznik vessel is covered in a fish-scale pattern; the rim features a wave and rock pattern inspired by Chinese models. The reverse is plain with a short, white glazed foot.

dd477064-8dcc-5912-86cc-4b16275db787.name: Dish
dd477064-8dcc-5912-86cc-4b16275db787.short_description: The high point of Ottoman ceramics can be distinguished by brilliant polychrome finish and the richness of the floral and plant compositions (carnations, peonies and *saz* leaves).
dd477064-8dcc-5912-86cc-4b16275db787.dates: Hegira second half of the 10th century / AD second half of the 16th century

de834889-8d91-5a45-91c0-917eb5e7de6f.name: Ceramic panel with eight azulejos [tiles] (from the Odescalchi collection)
de834889-8d91-5a45-91c0-917eb5e7de6f.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". The collections of the M.A.I. included large samples of pottery, wooden objects, fabric, bronzes and ivories dating to Roman, Renaissance and Baroque times. The best part of this collection is on display at the National Gallery of Palazzo Barberini in Rome, while other pieces are housed in Castel Sant'Angelo and Palazzo Venezia. Within the series of the Hispanic-Moorish ceramics are some pottery with azulejos, bought by Prince Baldassarre Ladislao Odescalchi in 1880. The panel with eight azulejos dates from 15th and 16th centuries. It shows both geometric and floral decorations.
de834889-8d91-5a45-91c0-917eb5e7de6f.holder: Museo Artistico Industriale, National Gallery of Ancient Art in Palazzo Barberini
de834889-8d91-5a45-91c0-917eb5e7de6f.author: Marina Minozzi
keywords: Applied arts; manufacture; craftsmanship; museums of applied arts; model; reproduction; motifs; collector; Spain; Moorish; Islamic art; Islamic influence; Neo-Mudéjar style; production of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode; Manises

decb15bf-1760-5bb0-a74f-093a8ac27e5f.name: Large plate with floral decoration.
decb15bf-1760-5bb0-a74f-093a8ac27e5f.description:
This large plate with a flat rim is decorated with a variety of colours and black contour lines. Three composite flowers, lilies and hyacinths, grow, almost straight, out of a blossoming plant, on gently swaying stems. The large composite flowers have been creatively interpreted from elements of the blossoms of palms, lotus and marrow, all brought together to form a whole. This has been referred to as ‘botanical art’. This floral-design repertoire is part of the so-called ‘quatre fleurs’ (four flowers) style that is composed of four garden flowers – rose, carnation, tulip and hyacinth – and which, from around AH 945 / AD 1540, represented the main motifs of Turkish ceramics.  
Across the gently inward tilting rim is a Chinese-based rock-and-wave motif, composed of white waves rolling towards rocks drawn as spirals. This motif is derived from 15th-century Chinese porcelain painting. The Ottoman Court collected Chinese porcelain and used it as tableware, and the porcelain remains to this day in the safekeeping of the Topkapı Palace in Istanbul.  
On the outside are depicted three pairs of tulips and, repeated three times, the three-sphere or *chintamani* motif, which was a symbol of luck that originated from Buddhism. This motif consisted of three circles, each with a dot at the centre, placed in a pyramid formation, linked together with tiger stripes.  
The plate is a typical example of the so-called Ottoman Court-style that was developed in the *naqqash-hane* (writing-house). It was here that the designs for book decoration, textile patterns, embroidery, metalwork and ceramics were developed. Many potters from Iznik worked directly alongside the Court artists from the Topkapı Palace. Craftsmen from the art workshops of the Court in Istanbul travelled to Iznik in order to exchange ideas with the ceramic master craftsmen there. Ottoman ceramics were greatly valued in many European countries, from the AH 10th / AD 16th century onwards, proof of which can be found in Turkish and Western sources, which described Iznik ceramics as being as beautiful if not better than the imperial porcelain of China.
decb15bf-1760-5bb0-a74f-093a8ac27e5f.short_description: The potteries in Iznik made numerous flower plates in different styles. This one is from the middle of the 16th century. On a white ground, sprays of composite flowers and hyacinths are symmetrically arranged using a subdued colour scheme of black, celadon-green and shades of blue.

df8f866f-d263-5658-a871-7c8e7f067012.name: Tile fragment
df8f866f-d263-5658-a871-7c8e7f067012.short_description:
The ancient city of Qalhat, known as the Twin of Hormuz, was the main port of northern Oman from the 7th to 9th centuries AH / 13th to 15th centuries AD. The Great Mosque, where this tile fragment was recovered, was its most famous edifice. The mosque was built around 699 AH / 1300 AD by Bibi Maryam, the wife of Bahauddin Ayaz, King of Hormuz and Ruler of Qalhat. The Moroccan geographer Ibn Battuta visited Qalhat during his travels in the 8th century AH / 14th century CE and wrote a vivid description of the Great Mosque shortly after its completion:  
  
"Qalhat has fine bazaars and an exceedingly beautiful mosque, the walls of which are decorated with elaborate tile work."  
  
At Qalhat, stratified fragments of *lajvardina* (lapis lazuli) tiles have been found in the vicinity of the qiblah wall of the mosque.  
In addition to lustre-painted tiles, the potters of Kashan produced tiles covered with a blue glaze known as *‘lajvardina’* (lapis lazuli). *Lajvardina* (lapis lazuli) tiles similar to those shown here were arranged in friezes and moulded inscriptions with red and white over-glaze enamels and gold leaf.
df8f866f-d263-5658-a871-7c8e7f067012.provenance: The Great Mosque, Qalhat (Oman). Origin: Kashan, Persia (Iran)
df8f866f-d263-5658-a871-7c8e7f067012.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
keywords: Lajvardina; Lapis Lazuli; Tiles; Mosque; Qalhat; Hurmuz

e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.name: Bowl.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.description:
A large conical bowl with an upturned rim that is made of tin-glazed earthenware and decorated with lustre. The exterior of the bowl is ornamented with abstract tree-like motifs, while the interior features a spectacular image of a large sailing ship that is complete with multiple masts and riggings, fore and aft decks, flags, and a rudder. Below the ship, four large fish swim back and forth; around it, tightly wound curlicues and other abstract motifs fill the surface of the bowl. The ship’s sail bears a motif which has been interpreted as the arms of Portugal, possibly indicating that the bowl was commissioned by a wealthy Portuguese merchant. This, plus the fact that the most important centre of Spanish lustre production in the 9th / 15th century was Christian Valencia, initially led scholars to believe that this bowl was Valencian ware. However, scientific tests in 1983 showed the presence of mineral deposits in the bowl which come not from Valencia, but from Málaga. This city, one of the most important port cities of the medieval western Mediterranean, had been the premiere centre of lustre production in Spain until it was eclipsed by Valencia in the early 9th / 15th century; production there appears to have ceased a few decades later. This bowl, then, is spectacular proof that the potteries of Málaga continued to create first-class lustre ceramics right up until the end.  
  
The fish beneath the ship, as well as the tree-like motifs on the exterior of the bowl, are strikingly similar to Fatimid work of centuries before, and remind us that the lustre industry in Islamic Spain was born precisely when Fatimid workers brought the technique from Egypt.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.short_description: A large bowl with lustre-painted decoration that includes a representation of a ship at sea. The ship’s sail bears a coat of arms which has been interpreted as that of Portugal; thus this bowl may have been commissioned by a wealthy Portuguese merchant.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.dates: Second quarter of the hegira 9th / AD 15th century.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.method_for_datation: Stylistic grounds; the large tree-like motifs on the exterior of the bowl, in particular, are characteristically Nasrid.
e01c5dee-ecbd-5793-a4c3-93b23100ee13.method_for_provenance: In 1983 scholars established that the bowl was produced in Málaga, once the centre of lustre production in Spain until it was eclipsed by Valencia in the early 9th / 15th century (see description above).

e0d16aa5-ba9f-5a87-9eda-9fb21d5d5304.name: Plate.
e0d16aa5-ba9f-5a87-9eda-9fb21d5d5304.description:
Many types of glazed pottery were produced during the Islamic period, one of which was a glazed ceramic painted in monochrome. This type was created by coating the fired pottery in molten coloured glass, usually dark-blue, burgundy, or green.  
This dark-blue ceramic plate is decorated inside with the word “al-Mulk” (power, sovereignty, or ownership). This word was carved into the bottom of the plate before the glaze was applied, which meant that the cobalt-blue gathered in the grooves, making the low points darker and the high points lighter, intensifying the effect of the decoration. The overall surface of the vessel, however, was uniform and smooth by the end of the glazing process.  
This method of decoration is similar to that used on *laqabi* wares produced in Syria and Iran, although pieces of this type are usually polychrome.  
“al-Mulk” is written in foliated *kufic* script, in which each letter ends with a sprout or bud decoration. The writing is surrounded by an interior band in the form of a group of small rectangles and an outer band decorated with ornamental elements, each of them in the form of a sequence of three circles connected at their tangents.
e0d16aa5-ba9f-5a87-9eda-9fb21d5d5304.short_description: This large monochrome dish glazed in an intense cobalt-blue and boldly decorated with floriate *kufic* calligraphy inscribing the word '*al-Mulk*' (sovereignty) is executed using the *laqabi* technique.
e0d16aa5-ba9f-5a87-9eda-9fb21d5d5304.method_for_datation: This kind of earthenware was regularly produced in Jazira during the Atabeg period (6th / 12th century). Production of ceramics in the region was interrupted by the Mongol invasion in the 7th / 13th centuries (1269).
e0d16aa5-ba9f-5a87-9eda-9fb21d5d5304.method_for_provenance: This piece was found in Raqqa, in the Jazira region. Ceramics with monochrome glazes and decoration cut into the base were known to have been produced in Jazira at this time, and many have emerged during archaeological excavations.
e0d16aa5-ba9f-5a87-9eda-9fb21d5d5304.provenance: Jazira (the region located between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, hence known as “the island” and currently consisting of northeast modern Syria and northwest Iraq), or Mesopotamia.

e1bda161-d9ba-562d-9078-9d5793a2b451.name: Bowl.
e1bda161-d9ba-562d-9078-9d5793a2b451.description: The interior of this bowl is divided by bold black and white stripes into eight panels; four large and four small. Each of the four large panels are filled with a stylised tree placed under a poly-lobed arch; the trunk, adorned with small leaves on each side of a vertical axis, and topped by a bulbous leaf, branches out into scrolled and trilobed leaves. Two of the smaller triangles contain scrolled trilobed leaves, while the other two are filled with a repeated single word, possibly a benediction, rendered in a cursive (*naskhi*) script. This underglaze painted bowl epitomises the rich artistic creativity of the Mamluk period.
e1bda161-d9ba-562d-9078-9d5793a2b451.short_description: An underglaze painted ceramic bowl of Syrian manufacture. The interior is divided by bold black and white stripes into eight panels filled with stylised flora and architecture, as well as a repeated single word in *naskhi* script, possibly a benediction.
e1bda161-d9ba-562d-9078-9d5793a2b451.method_for_datation: The bowl was dated by stylistic analysis and comparison to similar Syrian bowls discovered in Damascus, Raqqa and Hama, and which are now on display at Damascus National Museum and in the British Museum in London.
e1bda161-d9ba-562d-9078-9d5793a2b451.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this bowl is unknown, but according to the dealer from whom it was purchased it is from Rabba, south Jordan.
e1bda161-d9ba-562d-9078-9d5793a2b451.obtention: The bowl was purchased from an antiquities dealer in 1956, who claimed that the bowl originated in Rabba, near Karak.

e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.name: Footed dish or *tazze*.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.description:
A magnificent circular stone-paste (fritware) dish of the *tondino* form that is characterised by a very shallow wide well and a broad and flat horizontal rim. This shape is derived from early 16th-century, Italian *maiolica* (tin-glazed earthenware) dishes a style that was imitated by the Ottoman ceramicists. The plate rests on a wide and very low, circular foot-ring. Both the inside and the underside of the dish are decorated extensively.  
The well has a naturalistically drawn flower arrangement of carnations, tulips, prunus blossoms and stylised roses, rising from a tuft of green grass. The wide rim displays a fluid band of alternating roses and serrated leaves flowing in an anti-clockwise direction. Small floral and vegetal motifs are set in between the main composition. The underside of the dish is enhanced by 14 flower heads with green centres that alternate with pairs of blue tulips. All the motifs are enhanced by black outlines.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.short_description: This magnificent Iznik plate with its small, deep, concave well and a very wide, flat horizontal rim imitates the *tondino,* an Italian shape popular since the early AH 10th / AD 16th century. Its decoration assigns it to the second half of the 10th / 16th century, the peak of naturalism on Iznik wares.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.dates: Hegira late 10th century / AD late 16th century.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.method_for_datation: The decorative style adopted on this plate assigns this plate to the second half of the 10th / 16th century, when the naturalistic rendition of flower sprays reached its height on Iznik wares.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.method_for_provenance: This plate belongs to a group of Iznik dishes fashioned after the *tondino*, a shape popular in Italy from the early 16th century.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.obtention: Purchased from the Irvine Smith Collection in 1910.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, p.227, figs. 397–9.
e1e46fb9-2121-5c71-8ee2-be38a8978bc0.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
materials: Stone-paste (fritware), green, blue, red and black underglaze, over which a clear glaze.

e25630b9-4eae-5a54-82aa-8350634cc2c3.name: Pot.
e25630b9-4eae-5a54-82aa-8350634cc2c3.description:
Globular vessel with a foot-ring at the base and with a semi-circular cross-section and slightly everted rim. The paste is orange and the surfaces are glazed in a honey colour. On the exterior surface is a plant-form decoration in columns around the whole body, bordered with dark brown to black manganese.  
This type of decoration emerged in Silves in items dating from the AH 5th / AD 11th century, although they became more frequent in the AH 6th / AD 12th century.  
They are thought to be everyday ceramics. The shape suggests that they were used as receptacles for holding oil or other domestic liquids such as water. Smaller versions of this pot may have been used for cosmetics or simply as decorative objects.  
The characteristics of the piece are similar to those with a metallic lustre decoration from Egypt and Iran, dating from the AH 3rd and 4th / AD 9th and 10th centuries. The use of decorative motifs with borders in manganese, but enamelled, dates back to the previous period and may have originated in the East. The decoration of this piece, in spite of its stylistic similarities to oriental ceramics, is similar to other pieces found in Silves, so it may have been produced locally in the region of al-Gharb, and even in Silves itself, in imitation of oriental models.  
Ceramic objects of this kind were made in the region of Gharb al-Andalus throughout the Muslim period.
e25630b9-4eae-5a54-82aa-8350634cc2c3.short_description: Locally produced jar probably inspired by Iranian or Egyptian models. The outside is decorated with plant motifs that create columns around the entire body. The configuration of the piece suggests that it was used to store liquids.
e25630b9-4eae-5a54-82aa-8350634cc2c3.dimensions: Height 19.6 cm, diameter 11.2 cm, diameter (of base) 10.5 cm.
e25630b9-4eae-5a54-82aa-8350634cc2c3.method_for_datation: From the archaeological and stratigraphic context in which it was found. A stylistic analysis has found comparisons with similar objects from the same period.
e25630b9-4eae-5a54-82aa-8350634cc2c3.method_for_provenance: An excavation carried out at Rua da Arrochela (the historic centre of Silves) directed by Rosa Varela Gomes. Excavation inventory number: AR Q5/E15/C2-1.
e25630b9-4eae-5a54-82aa-8350634cc2c3.obtention: It has been housed in the museum since the excavations carried out in the 1990s.

e27cfedb-4426-5918-bebf-2002418ec65c.name: Storage vessels and two-part cooking pot
e27cfedb-4426-5918-bebf-2002418ec65c.short_description:
The contrast between the public and private, male and female spheres offer the Berber women "free space" which allows them to express their own view of life. In the seclusion of the home they make the space of everyday life viable, and visibly materialise a particular life design, in that they symbolically reproduce their bodies: in the hand-built up pottery, repeating the image of "body as vessel." In a world controlled by men, the women have developed a cultural model which is based on their corporeal experience.  
In art, the French philosopher Gilles Deleuze maintained, it is never to do with the reproduction of forms, but with the capturing of powers. Therefore, no art is ever just figurative: "Art is the language of emotions (…). Art has no opinion." The women produced their pottery exclusively for personal use. Limits were only placed on their completely free artistic development by the social norms which applied in their environment and which govern the relationships between people.
e27cfedb-4426-5918-bebf-2002418ec65c.method_for_datation: Entry in the TMS digital collection database and archival documents, personal information from the collector.

e2bffa11-ea9f-5947-ac9b-10e5f5a6b071.name: Drinking vessel.
e2bffa11-ea9f-5947-ac9b-10e5f5a6b071.description:
This vessel, in the form of a small jar, is made of fine well-fired clay covered with engobe (slip). It would have been used as a drinking vessel. Its slightly ovoid belly is marked at the base by a lip protruding above a narrow and shallow foot, which gives it some stability. Its vertical neck ending in a large opening is flanked by two small round handles attached to the top of the belly. Traces from its manufacture appear in the form of horizontal rings marking the belly. The neck, handles and base of the belly are covered with brown manganese paint. A frieze of small excised circles, delimited by two lines, decorates the neck. The belly is painted with medallions filled with stylised plant motifs and separated by double horizontal and diagonal lines. They are framed by large rectilinear motifs imitating epigraphic decoration.  
Its original shape and its decoration (painting and excision) make this recipient characteristic of earthenware common in the Almohad period.
e2bffa11-ea9f-5947-ac9b-10e5f5a6b071.short_description: This small jar-shaped recipient would have been used as a drinking vessel. Made of fine, well-fired clay covered with engobe (slip) and decorated with paint and excisions, it is characteristic of ceramics common in the Almohad period for its original shape and decoration.
e2bffa11-ea9f-5947-ac9b-10e5f5a6b071.dimensions: Height 18 cm, base diameter 5.6 cm, max. diameter 14.5 cm, opening diameter 11 cm
e2bffa11-ea9f-5947-ac9b-10e5f5a6b071.method_for_datation: Found in the ruins of a medieval bourgeois house at the archaeological site of Lixus. The date has been confirmed by stylistic study and comparison with other reliably dated objects found in Murcia and Huelva in Spain from the first third of the 7th / 13th century.

e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.name: Large dish with poly-lobed decoration.
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.description:
This dish is elegantly decorated with a large polylobed motif painted in black beneath a turquoise glaze.  
The side of the dish does not have the usual inscription of good omens, but a verse from the *Divan*of the Persian poet Hafez, which tells of the lament of an unhappy lover: "I have washed \[with tears\] the courtyard of the home of my eyes, but why / since this house is not \[even\] worthy of imagining your form?". The date is written at the end of the inscription: "finished in the year 873" (AD 1468).
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.short_description: This dish belongs to a group of ceramics known as *kubachi* after the village in the Caucasus where they were found. They would have been hung on the walls of homes as decoration.
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.owner: Istituto Italiano per l’Africa e l’Oriente (Is.IAO).
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.method_for_provenance: This piece belongs to a specific group of ceramics known as *kubachi* from the name of the village in Daghestan in the Caucasus where they were found hung on walls for decoration. Ceramics of this type are of exceptional interest as they bear witness to the intense commercial exchanges between Persia and Kubachi, a place known for its production of steel weapons that were particularly sought after by the Iranian market and exchanged for a large quantity of Persian ceramics of unknown origin.
