e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.name: Water seller's jar
e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.short_description: The egg-shaped jar has a narrow neck the top of which is covered by a dome-shaped lid. There is a curved handle on each side of the neck base and a long, straight spout. The lower part of the jar is made of unglazed and undecorated earthenware, a common material for water vessels that enables water evaporation thus keeping the water inside cool. The upper part is made of copper alloy, engraved with decorative bands of intertwined floral motifs; knot work patterns; stylised four-legged animals amongst a vegetal design; and two calligraphic bands. The jar sits in a knotted rope net with handle for carriage on the water seller’s back.
e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.author: Hazelle Page
keywords: Water jar; Water seller; Everyday life; Egypt

e6164946-a5d8-552b-9b6b-c87c10d33682.name: Oil lamp.
e6164946-a5d8-552b-9b6b-c87c10d33682.description:
A lamp made of red earthenware, coloured with slip (diluted clays with a variety of mineral contents that produce natural pigments). The lamp is formed of a round base and pedestal that holds a multiple lamp structure of five cups, these cups hold the oil and wicks. The body has a painted geometric decoration of red, white and black-earth pigments, coated with a resin-varnish, which gives the lamp an overall yellowish hue.  
  
This type of pottery is considered to be the only indigenous type of ceramic in Algeria, which has survived since Roman times. The Berber women in the Kabylie area still make such pottery to the present day, and although the shape and decoration have changed over time, the method of production has not changed much since pre-Islamic times. The pigments are made from natural sources such as clay, rocks, and plants. Being the women's speciality, these ceramics reflect the needs and tastes of the women who produce them. The decorative elements are inspired by their surroundings, and some have protective and talismanic symbolisms. The items that are produced surplus to the domestic needs of the family are sold by the women in the local market to supplement the family's income.
e6164946-a5d8-552b-9b6b-c87c10d33682.short_description: This type of handmade earthenware was the speciality of Berber women from the Kabylie region in Algeria. This pottery, still made today, reflects the needs and tastes of its makers, with some of the decorative elements consisting of talismanic symbols. Surplus vessels are sold to supplement the family income.
e6164946-a5d8-552b-9b6b-c87c10d33682.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
e6164946-a5d8-552b-9b6b-c87c10d33682.dimensions: Height 36 cm, width (max) 22 cm, diameter (of base) 17 cm.
e6164946-a5d8-552b-9b6b-c87c10d33682.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: unique to the Kabylie region, this particular oil lamp can be compared to other similar lamps of the 19th century.
e6164946-a5d8-552b-9b6b-c87c10d33682.method_for_provenance: Stylistic analysis: this style of lamp is unique to the Kabylie region in north-east Algeria.

e6457ad1-6126-508a-9c14-e66c394d18f0.name: Lamp and base.
e6457ad1-6126-508a-9c14-e66c394d18f0.description:
An oval-shaped pottery lamp made using two moulds; one for the upper half and another for the lower, the two halves being joined together by a ridge.  
  
The lamp is decorated with multiple motifs such as small circles within half volutes, wavy and straight lines on both sides of the filling hole, as well as birds and palm branches. The sides of the lower part are decorated with alternate circles and palm branches. The handle is tall and curved, terminating in a crude animal head. The base is a pointed oval, decorated with a chalice within which is a sequence of fish. Similar lamps bear Greek and Arabic inscriptions and are sometimes decorated with crosses.
e6457ad1-6126-508a-9c14-e66c394d18f0.short_description: A pottery lamp from Jarash made using two moulds, one for the top and the other for the base, which is decorated with a chalice within which is a sequence of fish. Similar lamps bear Greek and Arabic inscriptions and are at times decorated with crosses.
e6457ad1-6126-508a-9c14-e66c394d18f0.method_for_datation: The lamp was dated according to stratigraphic context and associated Umayyad pottery vessels.
e6457ad1-6126-508a-9c14-e66c394d18f0.method_for_provenance: The lamp was found at Jerash during an archaeological excavation.
e6457ad1-6126-508a-9c14-e66c394d18f0.obtention: The lamp was recovered in 1968 during the course of an excavation carried out at Jarash by the Jordan Department of Antiquities.

e6753434-4415-5658-ba03-7a1cf0ec79f4.name: Ceramic tile panel.
e6753434-4415-5658-ba03-7a1cf0ec79f4.description: A ceramic tile panel composed of square tiles depicting the *Ka'ba* covered by the black *kiswa*. Architectural components in the Ottoman style are also depicted including doors, domed buildings, minarets, and arches with suspended lamps hanging from them. In the bottom right-hand corner of the panel is the date of production AH 1087 (AD 1676). This date is also written in Arabic letters on the panel reading 'bidars Sulayman'. Traditionally one way for writing dates would be in letter-form in a sort of cipher named *hisab al-gummal (Calculation of total numbers)*, each letter being equivalent to a certain numerical figure, for example the Arabic letter ( **ر** ) is equivalent to 200. This tile panel closely resembles another tile piece in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo (reg. no. 860) which bears the signature of the craftsman who made it, Muhammad al-Shami, and the date AH 1139 (AD 1726), it also has similarities to a frontispiece panel of a Qur'an that dates to the Ottoman period and which also bears a depiction of the Holy *Ka'ba* of Mecca.
e6753434-4415-5658-ba03-7a1cf0ec79f4.short_description: Muslim artisans did their best to depict the Ka'ba, the holy Islamic sanctuary, on their products. This panel bears the name of the sultan, the date of production and its maker's signature.
e6753434-4415-5658-ba03-7a1cf0ec79f4.method_for_datation: This piece was dated based on the date recorded on it.
e6753434-4415-5658-ba03-7a1cf0ec79f4.method_for_provenance: It is strongly believed that this tile panel was made in Istanbul where such panels were produced centrally.
e6753434-4415-5658-ba03-7a1cf0ec79f4.obtention: The piece was donated to the Museum in November 1915 by Prince Yusuf Kamal, who was one of the princes of the family of Muhammad 'Ali and a delaer in antiques. He donated a large collection of his acquisitions to the museum especially jewellery, textiles, ceramic and wooden pieces.

e6931138-cb42-5f87-97c8-30bcf8d0bd8a.name: Bottle
e6931138-cb42-5f87-97c8-30bcf8d0bd8a.short_description:
This bottle was formed in two parts, then joined and refinished on the potter’s wheel leaving a clean horizontal band. The lower part includes the base and the upper part is completed with a wheel-thrown neck. The lower part is decorated with a row of epigraphic medallions followed by one medallion showing two quadruped animals on both sides of a central lam-alif ligature. The medallion is stamped three times on top of each other which makes it illegible, but it could be a patron’s name. The row of stylized ibexes, a common motif on moulded pottery from Lashkari Bazar, on the upper part contrasts with the precision of the epigraphic medallions on the lower part of the bottle’s body.  
Bottles of similar grey fabric, size and design – especially the stylized ibex – were found at Merv and date to the 12th to 13th centuries. Apart from that, moulded bottles and jugs were found in nearly all excavated cities in Central Asia, Iran and Afghanistan in levels dating to the 11th to 13th centuries. The most important archaeological trove for moulded jugs is from Lashkari Bazar. The widely distributed production of this type of earthenware in more than 40 workshops within Central Asia so far shows its popularity among the different techniques of ceramic production.

e6931138-cb42-5f87-97c8-30bcf8d0bd8a.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparison with material found in excavations

e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.name: Sphinx
e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.description:
This sphinx was found in Rafiqa, Raqqa’s twin city, in AH 1343 / AD 1924 together with the cock (Isl 57) and the figure of a horseman in Syria’s National Museum. As ceramic sculptures, they are unique not only in Syria, but also in the rest of the Islamic world.  
  
They are fountain figures, and all have pipes to carry water up to the figures’ heads. The North African historian al-Maqqari wrote that the Iberian Umayyad caliph Abd al-Rahman III had a fountain made with 12 figures: a lion with a gazelle, a crocodile, a serpent, an eagle, an elephant, a dove, a falcon, a peacock, a hen, a cock, a hawk and a vulture.
e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.dates: AH 2nd half of the 6th / AD 2nd half of 12th century

e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.name: Dish.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.description: Ceramics with metallic highlights were exceptionally successful in the late Middle Ages, and were sought after by the finest European courts. The coats of arms of royalty and nobility, in particular Italians such as the Tedaldi or Nasi families, are commonly depicted. These ceramics, so colourful and elegant, are reminiscent of Gothic painting. The manufacturing and decorating processes were complex, as the pieces required several firings to obtain the different colours. This dish was turned on a potter's wheel. Its surface is covered with a white or cream tin glaze. The sides are concave and the brim slightly inclined. The topside is decorated in gold and deep blue. The central, golden coat of arms, inscribed in a toothed blue border, shows an eagle with outstretched wings. It is possible that it belonged to the Despujols family, and it is repeated in other pieces. The coat of arms is surrounded by a thin strip of fringes and spirals and tiny fern leaves. Near the edge, there is a wide band with large gilt pinecones in reserve, alternating with large deep-blue flowers. The remaining spaces are filled with arabesque leaves. On the underside there is another eagle in the same position as the first, covering the entire area, and fern leaves in the empty spaces. The heraldic coats of arms, as well as telling us about the tastes of high society, are useful for determining when the pieces were manufactured, as they include data on family history.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.short_description: Dish decorated in a manner typical of AH 9th-/ AD 15th-century Mudéjar ceramics, with Nasrid-style motifs such as the gold and blue motifs on the front combined with the coat-of-arms of the family that commissioned the piece. In this case, an eagle appears on both sides of the dish.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.dimensions: Height 9 cm, diameter 45 cm, diameter of base 14.5 cm.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.method_for_datation: From its style and from comparison with other similar dishes. In this case, the coat of arms that decorates it serves as a historical reference.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.method_for_provenance: From its formal and stylistic characteristics, from the archaeological digs that have been carried out and from the extensive documentation that is available.
e71fe850-fa1a-5797-b0c5-b50e5f9a25ed.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from Vicente Juan y Amat on 27 June 1872.

e78eac4c-6c8e-50e5-a207-fa39bdf93414.name: Small table.
e78eac4c-6c8e-50e5-a207-fa39bdf93414.description:
A small table, rectangular in shape and on four legs, which consists of a tray clad with Delft earthenware tiles that feature floral decoration and are surrounded by an openwork band.  
Four sides of this small table are covered by sculpted, turned and openwork panels featuring floral or vegetal motifs. In the corners, along the extension of the legs with which they form part, vertical cartouches feature inscriptions in cursive lettering; one of these reveals the name of the craftsman and the location of the object's manufacture through the phrase 'made by Ibn Hadj-la-B'lade al-Djazaïri'.  
The item of furniture is painted in a variety of colours, notably green, orange and gold.
e78eac4c-6c8e-50e5-a207-fa39bdf93414.short_description: Rectangular four-legged table consisting of a top covered with Delft earthenware tiles with floral decoration surrounded by an openwork railing. There are carved panels on all four sides, and inscriptions in cursive characters on each of the corners. The piece is painted green and orange, and gilded.

e78eac4c-6c8e-50e5-a207-fa39bdf93414.method_for_datation: From the style of manufacture and the decoration, as well as from the earthenware tiles of Delft, which were imported from Holland during the Ottoman era.

The rim is widely everted and was used to hold a lid. The wall is decorated with a serrated cord. This vessel was made in Saudi Arabia and found at Al Huwaila baking. e80c1234-42a0-5c12-9754-82402e1fca45.name: Umbonate plate
e80c1234-42a0-5c12-9754-82402e1fca45.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". The collections included large samples of pottery, wooden objects, fabric, bronzes and ivories dating to Roman, Renaissance and Baroque times. The best part of this collection is on display at the National Gallery of Palazzo Barberini in Rome, while other pieces are housed in Castel Sant'Angelo and Palazzo Venezia. The series of the Hispanic-Moorish ceramics, bought by Prince Baldassarre Ladislao Odescalchi in 1880, were among the models often reproduced by the training school inside the M.A.I. The umbonate plate (inv.n. 2828) is an aragonese manufacture dating from the first half of 16th century. It shows concentric strips with blue and red tones.
e80c1234-42a0-5c12-9754-82402e1fca45.holder: Museo Artistico Industriale, National Gallery of Ancient Art in Palazzo Barberini
e80c1234-42a0-5c12-9754-82402e1fca45.author: Marina Minozzi
keywords: Applied arts; manufacture; craftsmanship; museums of applied arts; model; reproduction; motifs; collector; Spain; Moorish; Islamic art; Islamic influence; Neo-Mudéjar style; production of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode; Aragon

e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.description:
The use of patterns in 17th-century Portuguese *azulejos* allowed a number of solutions for covering the architectural surfaces of palaces, convents and churches. Because the Portuguese used *azulejos* to cover surfaces in all areas, including vaults and ceilings, it was necessary to create larger modules for patterns otherwise people below would only be able to see smudges of colour instead of the motifs in the patterns.  
This panel of *azulejos* shows how the patterns were used with frames, which emphasise the proximity between them and the carpets that sometimes inspired them. However, in a panel like this one, we can see the advantage of *azulejos* over textiles: the bright reflection of its surface, the eternal shine of its colours that never fade and the clever solutions to adjusting to the architectural surfaces it was covering. The module of this pattern is a 4 x 4, which implies that 16 *azulejos* are required in order to achieve a single motif that can be repeated to infinity. In this case, the decoration is composed of a four-lobe design motif with acanthus leaves at the corners, which allow a connection with the other *azulejos*. The frame of this composition is achieved by two different solutions: a half *azulejos*, in Portuguese known as a *friso* or frieze, with a “saw’s teeth” motif, positioned in the extremities of the frame. The second element is a double *azulejos* element, known in Portuguese as a *barra* or stripe, with the decoration known as “hammers”, which composes the larger area of the frame and gives a dynamic structure to the panel.
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: in 17th-century production of *azulejos* in northern Portugal, the colours tend to be denser, with harsh greyish blues and a less bright yellow with an orange hue.
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.method_for_provenance: The National Tile Museum holds a large number of *azulejos* of unknown origin, many gathered during the period of the destruction of the convents and palaces in the late 19th century, in the aftermath of the abolition of the religious orders in 1834.
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.obtention: Probably salvaged during demolition of an unknown building where they had once been applied

e9100be3-069e-5d04-b867-dbfe67ede897.name: Bowl with calligraphic and splashed decoration
e9100be3-069e-5d04-b867-dbfe67ede897.short_description: This earthenware dish was covered with an opaque white slip before receiving its ornamentation. Three sets of five or – once – four short brush strokes executed in green glaze highlight the edge of the dish. The centre shows an as yet unread manganese inscription and a green glaze dot. The dish was influenced by both Abbasid and Chinese luxury wares.

ea02005f-0faa-53dc-be44-7a3aab60817e.name: Dish with Foliated Rim and Design of Cypress Tree with Flowering Plants
ea02005f-0faa-53dc-be44-7a3aab60817e.short_description: An Iznik dish of glazed white ground ceramic has a scalloped edge and a broad rim with stylized rock and wave pattern decoration; cloud-shaped areas of white glaze alternate with clusters of royal blue glaze circles filled with thin, dark spiral designs. There are also evenly-spaced wing-like decorations in turquoise glaze. The main ground of the bowl is glazed with a "cypress tree" motif. A tall, vertical cypress in gray-green glaze is surrounded by winding leafy stems bearing dark blue blossoms, rust-collared carnations, and long sprays of blue blossoms. The exterior of the dish, also in white glaze, is decorated with alternating pairs of blue tulips and blue rosettes with turquoise centers.
ea02005f-0faa-53dc-be44-7a3aab60817e.dates: Hegira Mid 10th to early 11th century / AD second half 16th century

ea0a795b-de8c-505a-962f-be5084c447db.name: Dish
ea0a795b-de8c-505a-962f-be5084c447db.short_description:
A few types of the AD 17th century Persian ceramic ware, painted in a free expressive style and covered with cracks, were traditionally known as “*Kubachi*” ceramics. This conventional name came from a village in Daghestan, where in the 19th century huge amounts of Iranian Safavid pottery were concentrated. However, the Iranian production centres of "*Kubachi*" wares are still to be defined.  
Ceramic ware painted in black under transparent turquoise glaze belongs to a distinctive and possibly the earliest type of the “*Kubachi*” group. Turquoise has a special benevolent semantics in Persian culture due of the homonymy of Persian words *firuza* – turquoise (gemstone) and *firuzi* - victory, prosperity.  
The decorative idea of the combination of black and turquoise originated in Iranian pottery in the late 12th century. The Timurid black-on-turquoise ware of the 15th century was the development of the tradition. In the 17th century, the style of black painting became noticeably lighter and freer. The very movement of the artist’s hand revealed the experience of a calligrapher.
ea0a795b-de8c-505a-962f-be5084c447db.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by I. Rapoport (examination, 1963, date, origin), H. Rudyk (publication, 2017, origin specified).

ea21ed66-10ce-5ed1-b13b-1adba67cd058.name: Dish depicting two birds among flowering plants
ea21ed66-10ce-5ed1-b13b-1adba67cd058.short_description: This type of underglaze-painted pottery was produced in Iznik, an important centre of Ottoman ceramic production. The Rhodian type constitutes the third and final phase of Iznik ceramics, lasting from c. 1570 to 1700. These objects are characterized by the use of a thickly applied "sealing-wax" red glaze that stands out in relief. This plate features two birds resting on gently swaying plants bearing carnations, tulips, and hyacinths. Although the motif of flowering plants is pervasive in Iznik pottery of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, depictions of birds and animals are rare. A highly conventionalized wave-and-rock pattern circumscribes the broad foliate rim of this plate. Such designs, which were inspired by fifteenth-century Chinese Ming ceramics, enjoyed much popularity in this phase of Iznik production.

ea2bfceb-f646-51a6-bd3b-36884a93128f.name: Water pipe (*qalyan*)
ea2bfceb-f646-51a6-bd3b-36884a93128f.short_description: The ceramic body, with two openings, recalls the shape of the so-called *kendis* (Chinese pouring vessels with a long neck and a spout), exported ever since the beginning of the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), and which were briefly copied by Persian potters. It was probably in the nineteenth century that this *kendi* was fitted with a silver mount and turned into a water pipe (Pers. *qalyan*), thus making its thorough examination impossible. However, the visible areas provide relevant information which allows for a pertinent stylistic assessment and a meaningful comparison with similar examples. The Chinese-style underglaze decoration, painted in two shades of blue and outlined in black, is placed in five compartments, four of which feature animals and birds against a lush vegetal background. The Chinese-type mark painted on the base is reminiscent of other marks used on Persian *kendis*.

eae5c274-7b09-5dc1-a70e-37e8ae1488d8.name: Vase neck
eae5c274-7b09-5dc1-a70e-37e8ae1488d8.description:
Neck belonging to a vase of the type known as ‘Alhambra’. It has the typical flared shape of the necks of these vases, with a polygonal structure that opens upwards. The lip is thick and ends in a series of outward scrolls. The body is divided into alternating vertical bands of blue and light cream, the latter being approximately twice as thick, which have probably lost their original golden sheen. The lower part has two horizontal grooves that run around the entire perimeter of the piece. There is loss of enamel across the entire surface.  
  
Representative of Nasrid luxury, these vases are a very specific type of container, of which few examples remain. They are notable not only for their rich and luxurious decoration, but also for their monumental size, measuring around 130 cm in height and 60–70 cm in diameter. Given these characteristics, it is difficult to imagine that their function was primarily practical, despite the fact that some of these vases feature epigraphic decorations referring to water, as in the case of the Jarrón de Hornos, also in the National Archaeological Museum (Spain). One possibility that has been suggested is that they contained perfumed water or water to be distributed at certain ceremonies.
eae5c274-7b09-5dc1-a70e-37e8ae1488d8.dates: AH Second half of the 8th century / AD second half of 14th century

eb8d46f9-8d3e-500c-a2cd-e6d2491218a5.name: Elephant aquamanile
eb8d46f9-8d3e-500c-a2cd-e6d2491218a5.short_description:
The large aquamanile in the form of an elephant carries a *mahout* seated in front of a finely decorated *howdah* in which are a dancer and two musicians. Round shields cover the elephant’s ears and the bosses on its body are probably meant to indicate defensive cladding. The details are accurately moulded and are often highlighted with coloured glazes.  
The vessel is filled through a hole in the back, while the trunk serves as a spout. *Laqabi* figurines are exceptionally rare, and only three others are known, the most famous of which is the ‘Raqqa rider’, a horseman in mortal combat with a monstrous snake (in the National Museum in Damascus). The horseman is also hollow but is larger, and a socket for a pole in the horse’s stomach suggests it may have been carried as a standard.

ec2c57d8-01b2-5a85-a6b0-e8cf22d03e9a.name: *Albarello*\-shaped *tarro* (jar).
ec2c57d8-01b2-5a85-a6b0-e8cf22d03e9a.description: An albarello-shaped tarro (jar) with cylindrical body, made of earthenware with white glaze, decorated in brown lustre and blue. High and slightly projecting shoulders slope to the neck that has an almost vertical profile. The broader lower section sits on a circular convex foot. The body is painted with a tree-of-life motif, repeated eight times; four springing from the base-line and four inverted trees springing from the neck. The upright trees alternating with inverted trees form a bold symmetrical design. Framing the foliage of the trees are diagonal lines of pseudo-script on a white background painted in gold. The tree trunks are composed of a row of heart-shapes with gold outline and blue body. The upper part of the tree is also outlined in gold. On the sloping shoulder of the jar is an inscription in naskhi script: 'felicity and prosperity', a typical refrain found in Islamic pottery. A narrow frieze, in blue and gold, decorates the neck. This elegant tarro with its well-proportioned shape and design suggests the work of one of the sovereign's potters. Indeed, the tree-of-life motif appears in wooden decoration in the Alhambra Palace. Given this stylistic connection, as well as the fine-quality lustre painting, this tarro may have been amongst the sovereign's own tableware.
ec2c57d8-01b2-5a85-a6b0-e8cf22d03e9a.short_description: An *albarello*, or jar, decorated with a tree-of-life motif. The elegant shape and striking decoration suggest that this jar was made for the Nasrid court. The tree-of-life motif appears on the ceiling of the Alhambra Palace, the Nasrid royal court in Granada.
ec2c57d8-01b2-5a85-a6b0-e8cf22d03e9a.method_for_datation: This albarello-shaped tarro has been connected by both its form and decoration to the end of the reign of Yusuf I or slightly later (r. 753–64 / 1353-63); the tree-of-life motif appears on the ceiling of the Salon de Comares in the Alhambra Palace, Granada.
ec2c57d8-01b2-5a85-a6b0-e8cf22d03e9a.method_for_provenance: The style, shape and technique of this *tarro* indicate that it was produced under the Nasrids in Andalucia, southern Spain. More specifically the decoration recalls the ceiling design in the Salon de Comares in the Alhambra Palace, Granada.
ec2c57d8-01b2-5a85-a6b0-e8cf22d03e9a.obtention: Part of the Godman Bequest to the British Museum in 1983.

ecbdd816-e352-54a9-ad37-0a37230b8df0.name: Tell Minis bowl
ecbdd816-e352-54a9-ad37-0a37230b8df0.short_description:
Like its Fatimid, Egyptian models, Syrian Tell Minis pottery was experimental. It comprised tin-glazed earthenware, fritware with an opaque, white glaze, and fritware under a clear glaze that let the ware’s pale-pink color shine through.  
The frontally positioned Mediterranean figure and splendid palmettes also point the way to Fatimid lusterware.
materials: Fritware, decorated with luster over an opaque, white glaze. Tell Minis type

ecc253f4-eace-5315-af2c-f64f071f89e0.name: Flask
ecc253f4-eace-5315-af2c-f64f071f89e0.description:
Reddish clay vessel, flattened spherical in shape. It has two ribbon handles that extend from the middle of the vessel to its upper part. The two flattened sides are asymmetrical, one inverted truncated cone-shaped and the other convex with an incised decoration of several small concentric circles inserted in turn within a larger circle. The neck is not too high, cylindrical and slightly flared. The entire body is decorated with a schematic red design consisting of thick parallel brushstrokes in groups of three. The entire piece is fractured.  
  
Historically, this type of container was very common not only during the medieval Islamic period, but also in different eras and cultures, even today. Its function, carrying small amounts of water for consumption, is essential for everyday work in rural areas. In addition, the use of unglazed pottery allows the flask to breathe, keeping the water cool. Even today, cork stoppers and ropes tied to the handles are generally used for transport.
ecc253f4-eace-5315-af2c-f64f071f89e0.method_for_datation: Comparative study with other similar pieces.
ecc253f4-eace-5315-af2c-f64f071f89e0.obtention: Acquired in 1973 by the family of Julio Martínez Santa Olalla.

ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.name: Bowl fragment.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.description: A fragment from a stone-paste (fritware) bowl decorated in cobalt-blue and black under a transparent colourless glaze. This fragment, from the centre of the dish, is decorated with a roundel within which is Arabic calligraphy intertwined with organic stems and leaves. A band of black and white decoration surrounds the roundel. The design and technique of this bowl was common in both Syria and Egypt, making identification of the place of production very difficult. The difficulty lies in the fact that the potters of both Mamluk Egypt and Syria migrated in search of work between the cities of the two regions. The fashion for painting in black and blue under a transparent glaze started in Iran during the late AH 7th / AD 13th century, and spread quickly to Syria and Egypt. The main distinguishing features between wares made in Iran, Syria or Egypt are the different shapes and sizes of the pieces.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.short_description: Arabic calligraphy was employed to decorate a wide variety of surfaces. Although not enough of the text survives to be deciphered, proverbs, poetic verses and prayers were frequently used. The strong vertical lines of the *naskhi*\-style script dominate the centre of the cobalt-blue and black bowl.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the material composition, glaze and decoration of this fragment are typical of ceramics made in the potteries of Syria. Several similar examples have been found in Fustat indicating that ceramics from the Middle East were brought to trade in Egypt.
ece5f0c8-d2d1-5924-bc14-94c826dc2171.provenance: Produced in Damascus, Syria; found at Fustat, Egypt.

ecf2b49c-b70f-51b8-8c61-216edf4189e1.name: Plate
ecf2b49c-b70f-51b8-8c61-216edf4189e1.short_description:
This elegant plate was crafted in Guangzhou (formerly Canton) in AH 1309 / AD 1891-1892, exemplifying the refined artistry of Chinese export porcelain during the late Qing Dynasty. The intricate design showcases scenes of daily life, featuring pagoda-style architecture and traditional Chinese elements, capturing the cultural essence of the period.  
  
A particularly intriguing feature of this piece is its inscription. Written in Arabic-Persian script, it bears the phrase هو الباقي (He \[Allah\] is the Everlasting), emphasising divine permanence. Additionally, the inscription includes the word فرمايش (ordered), indicating that the plate was specially commissioned for Mohamed Sadiq Khan, who is most likely Sarwar al-Malak, a renowned musician from the courts of Shah Naser al-Din and Shah Muzaffar al-Din. This suggests that the plate may have been part of the Persian royal court’s cultural or artistic exchanges.  
  
At the lower part of the plate, we can also notice the marking "ص 92". While its exact meaning remains uncertain, it may indicate the production year (1892) or serve as a workshop code or inventory mark.  
  
This plate stands as a remarkable testament to the artistic and cultural exchanges between China and the Persian-speaking world, seamlessly blending Chinese craftsmanship with Persian artistic and literary influences.

ed2b34d8-0b3b-5e62-9f3b-c352b83a9b49.name: Tile Cup
ed2b34d8-0b3b-5e62-9f3b-c352b83a9b49.description: The drinking vessel is composed of a white clay and slip with polychrome decoration beneath a transparent colourless glaze. The composition features a series of tulips and stylised carnation branches of varying sizes rising vertically from separate roots on a white ground. The red, green and blue motifs are outlined in black. Beginning in the second half of the 16th century, it appears that the emerald green glaze, which was used extensively, would run during the firing process. It is posited that the quality of ceramics began to decline in tandem with the deterioration of the economy. Examples from the 16th century demonstrate that the naturalistic floral motifs, which were widely employed in Classical Ottoman style, were still being used during this period.
ed2b34d8-0b3b-5e62-9f3b-c352b83a9b49.dates: Hegira late 10th century / AD late 16th century

eda86be4-4148-5a1b-b8a5-daa18a385ef8.name: Tile panel
eda86be4-4148-5a1b-b8a5-daa18a385ef8.short_description:
Changes were made in the decoration on Iznik ceramics in around 1540. The very dense patterns of the *Baba Nakkas* and *tughrakes* styles were replaced by a style in which plants dominated. The palette was also expanded with moss green and manganese.  
These tiles with hyacinths, tulips, and cherry branches were designed so that at least two are needed for the motif to be complete.
keywords: 16th Century Iznik ceramics; Floral motifs; Baba Nakkas style; Tugrakesh style; hyacinths
materials: Fritware, painted in blue, turquoise, and moss green under a transparent glaze

edab323b-dc63-5faf-a178-579bc04253cd.name: Pitcher
edab323b-dc63-5faf-a178-579bc04253cd.short_description: Kütahya was the second most important ceramic production centre after İznik due to the rich clay deposits in the area. Although there was a decline in ceramic production at the beginning of the 19th century, in the last quarter of that same century production was revived and new designs inspired by İznik ceramics were produced.

ede6db87-1998-5d51-a8e0-97a1ffe99c48.name: Jug
ede6db87-1998-5d51-a8e0-97a1ffe99c48.description: A ceramic jug with one handle, the body is decorated with diamond-shaped panels, in white and turquoise with a single white flower, superimposed on a blue ground.

ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.name: Footed dish or *tazze*.
ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.description: A large circular stone-paste (fritware) dish that has shallow curved walls (*cavetto*), a wide everted rim with a scalloped edge and which rests on a low, circular foot-ring. The centre of the bowl is decorated with a dense, naturalistic flower arrangement rising from a central, five-petalled tuft below. Despite the optical illusion that the flowers – roses, hyacinths, tulips, prunus blossoms and other floral stalks rendered in bole-red, blue, green and black – are growing freely and as nature intended, the composition is in fact characterised by an underlying symmetry with the flowers on the left and those on the right being disposed on either side of an imaginary vertical axis at the centre, with those closest to the centre – carnations and roses – crossing near the top. Apart from the central carnation that bends downwards, its red flower-head skillfully balancing the other red and blue flower-heads, the flower stalks rise from the well, within the *cavetto*, and towards the rim, lending this apparently regular composition vitality and surprise. The rim is enhanced by a debased wave border, a common feature in Iznik wares since the AH 950s / AD 1550s. The outside of the dish is enhanced by individual flower heads with green centres and black outlines, which alternate with groups of three tied tulips rendered in blue with black outlines. There are 12 floral motifs in all.
ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.short_description: Ottoman Iznik was famous for the production of polychrome wares with exuberant, naturalistic flower arrangements. The Ottoman court and upper classes as well as an increasing European market vied for plates like this one as well as jugs and bowls decorated with roses, hyacinths, tulips and carnations.
ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.dates: Hegira late 10th century / AD mid- to late 16th century.
ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.method_for_datation: Stylistically this dish belongs to a group of Iznik wares datable to the late 10th / mid- to late 16th century.
ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.method_for_provenance: This dish belongs to a well-known group of ceramic wares made in Iznik, Turkey between the late 10th / mid- to late 16th century.
ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.obtention: Bought from J. M. Whitehead, London, in 1883.
ee06519d-540a-50a3-b86f-2f9b5d337adf.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, pp.224–8 (for a discussion on related pieces).

eefabf6a-3ca7-5c93-ade3-a4e5bbb13859.name: Glazed bowl.
eefabf6a-3ca7-5c93-ade3-a4e5bbb13859.description: Glazed bowl with bevelled rounded rim, circular mouth, semi-oval body with gentle carination towards the bottom and convex base with a diagonal foot-ring. The exterior of the piece is glazed in honey-coloured monochrome, while the interior is decorated entirely using the *cuerda seca* technique in which the white, green and honey colours of the glaze are separated by lines of manganese. The central ornamental theme, enclosed in a circle, consists of a deer or antelope in a static pose, with its head raised in an alert posture, ready to flee. Indeterminate plant motifs fill the empty spaces, and seem to suggest the landscape around the animal. Around this, on the wall of the bowl, the composition is completed with a frieze of palmettes made by finger impressions. The object has been restored.
eefabf6a-3ca7-5c93-ade3-a4e5bbb13859.short_description: Bowl made entirely using *cuerda seca*. The central motif of the piece, enclosed by a circle, is a deer or antelope in a static pose with its head raised, alert and preparing to flee. The empty space is filled with plant motifs, which represent the landscape around the animal.
eefabf6a-3ca7-5c93-ade3-a4e5bbb13859.dimensions: Height 8 cm, diameter (of mouth) 25.5cm, diameter (of base) 10.6 cm.
eefabf6a-3ca7-5c93-ade3-a4e5bbb13859.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated to the 6th / 12th century on the basis of comparison with objects of similar form and decorative technique from Málaga and Almería.
eefabf6a-3ca7-5c93-ade3-a4e5bbb13859.method_for_provenance: The abundance of this type of ceramic in Málaga and Almería (Spain), where kilns have been found in which they were made, has led researchers to attribute its production to these localities.
eefabf6a-3ca7-5c93-ade3-a4e5bbb13859.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

f02afe0c-f6ec-51aa-8c81-d0230b93ff9f.name: Animal-head ewer
f02afe0c-f6ec-51aa-8c81-d0230b93ff9f.description:
The Kashan turquoise ceramic animal-head ewer is a stunning example of Persian ceramics from the 12th century. This vessel showcases a vibrant turquoise blue glaze with a top in the likeness of a horned animal head, complete with a spout resembling a long open beak. It stands on a short foot, with a globular body transitioning into a slender neck. A partly curved handle, like a rope, extends from the head to the body. At the top, two curved horns and an upward-pointing finial enhance its overall elegance.  
The exquisite craftsmanship of this ewer highlights the skill and creativity of Persian artisans. This ewer originated in Kashan, renowned for its pottery tradition. The turquoise glaze adds to its allure and symbolises prosperity and protection. The animal motif holds various symbolic meanings, representing virtues and beliefs deeply ingrained in Persian customs and rituals. Used in ceremonial contexts, such as feasts or religious rituals, the ewer reflects ancient Persian traditions and cultural practices.  
Highly prized by collectors and enthusiasts alike, this Persian Kashan turquoise ceramic animal-head ewer serves as a timeless reminder of the beauty and sophistication of Persian craftsmanship. Its rich cultural heritage and artistic significance make it a cherished artefact, showcasing the legacy of Persian artisans.  
The ewer is crafted using traditional ceramic techniques prevalent in Kashan during the 12th century. Skilled artisans shaped the vessel by hand. The firing process ensured the durability of the vessel while bringing out the brilliance of the turquoise glaze, resulting in a masterpiece of Persian ceramics.

f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.name: Plate.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.description:
Chinese earthenware ceramics with a dichromatic decorative scheme of white and blue were very popular and widely admired in the Islamic world. Their export to the eastern Mediterranean began as early as the AH 2nd / AD 8th century. This type of vessel with its bright whiteness and extensive blue decoration was the most popular export ware during the Chinese reigns of the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. They exported profusely, both by land and sea, especially during the AH 8th / AD 14th century.  
Artisans in the Islamic world imitated these Chinese ceramics because of its popularity and because they were not always readily available. Thus imitative Chinese ceramics were themselves a valuable commodity.  
This plate is decorated with a bouquet of flowers that incorporates gracefully sweeping stems bound with a ribbon. A decorative band of stylised vegetal motifs surround the bouquet, and a band of stylised geometric motifs articulates the rim of the plate. The decoration is executed in various shades of blue on a white base.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.short_description: This ceramic dish was found in the Citadel of Hama and it clearly indicates the intercultural influence of exported Chinese blue-and-white porcelain on Syrian and Egyptian Mamluk pottery.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.method_for_datation: The Danish excavations revealed objects that have been dated to the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods, primarily from the 7th–8th / 13th–14th centuries. However, since this piece is influenced by Chinese ceramics, especially in the use of blue and white, and since such ceramics were exported to the Islamic world beginning in the 8th / 14th century, it is believed that the object belongs to this later period.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.method_for_provenance: This object was found in Hama, known as a production centre for this kind of ware. However, the underglaze painted wares found in Syria (Hama and Damascus) and Egypt (Fustat and Alexandria) are essentially identical, so it is difficult to assign a definitive provenance.
f03adf8f-d5b8-514b-88b4-1fa35cd992e2.obtention: The plate was found during archaeological excavations that took place in the Citadel of Hama between 1931 and 1938 by a Danish expedition under the direction of Harold Ing Holt. The piece was registered in the Museum in 1934.

f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.name: Large dish.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.description: A large dish with a surface edge that bends outward to a rim embellished by a consecutive series of triangles that resemble the jagged teeth of a saw. The interior of the dish is painted with a portrayal of a seated woman playing a stringed instrument that looks like a guitar. She wears a long garment with a V-shaped collar and wide sleeves, which is decorated with thick stripes and cross shapes. She wears a choker-type necklace, the V-shape of which sits inside the neck of her garment. The designs on her garment, in which the folds around the legs are embellished with decorations, are distinctive to Fatimid apparel. The musician's face is portrayed in profile. A toque, which resembles a turban, crowns her head and two locks of her hair appear from under the headdress on either side of her face along with a small tuft of hair behind her neck. The background around the figure is embellished with irregular surfaces demarcated by thin strokes filled with circles, dots and painted branches from which cone-shaped leaves grow. On the left-hand side of the woman is a delicately designed ewer surrounded by stylised vegetal-leaf designs; from the mouth of the ewer two flowering branches emerge. Below the rim of the dish underneath the painted serrated edge are a series of thick lines.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.short_description: Economic prosperity in the Fatimid period led to the flourishing of the lustre-ware ceramic industry. Such lustre-ware vessels, where the metallic lustre resembles gold, incorporate a variety of decorations including splendid scenes of Fatimid daily and social life.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.method_for_datation: The dish was dated based on the study of its painted female musician, and specifically the design and decoration of the clothing she wears. The figure reflects the distinguishing traits that mark the portrayal of people in Fatimid art, including circular moon-shaped faces and almond-shaped eyes. The turban seen on the heads of men, and the toques on the heads of women, are also indicative of the period. In addition, the decorations that are present on the dish are borrowed from the vegetal and non-vegetal decorative motifs seen most commonly on wood, ivory and metal objects of the Fatimid period. This date is further supported by a comparison between this dish and other similar examples that bear the signatures of potters who are associated with the period.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.method_for_provenance: The place of manufacture was narrowed down to Egypt in view of the fact that ceramic production and metallic lustre-ware products were renowned in Fatimid Egypt. This industry grew and flourished in Fustat where archaeological excavations have uncovered a large number of ceramic pieces similar to this dish.
f182ff55-9430-5024-a039-37fa558855a8.obtention: The dish was bought in 1944 from a dealer of antiquities, Fuqyan Jaan.

f21d4542-13e1-5350-b5fc-fb0fe10ff753.name: Boccia Vase
f21d4542-13e1-5350-b5fc-fb0fe10ff753.short_description: This Boccia vase embodies a crossover of cultures, decorated with floral patterns and Arabic calligraphy in bright colours. Mesmerized by the aesthetic of Arabic calligraphy, Christian artisans attempted to mimic the script to achieve a similar charm. While many ceramic-makers could not read Arabic, only a fragment of the script may be decoded as the Declaration of Islam. The vase is representative of Italy’s proximity to the Islamic world, incorporating elements of Islamic art into the pottery. Manufactured in Tuscany, the artisan drew inspiration from the Ottoman Empire and integrates recognizable characteristics from Hispano-Moresque pottery such as the whimsical shape and star-shaped handles. The picturesque appearance of Arabic calligraphy still enchants global audiences embellishing pottery, garments and jewellery.

f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.name: Lamp.
f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.description:
A spherical object with a distinctive slightly convex base, a handle at the top that is oval in cross-section, a semi-circular front opening and a conical vertical spike inside. It has a decoration of finger impressions, wavy incised lines and traces of white paint on a reddish background.  
This unusual object was used as a lantern for lighting out of doors. Its closed form protected the flame from the wind and its large horizontal handle made it easy to carry. The object has been restored.
f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.short_description: Unusual object similar to a lamp that was used to light open spaces. The semi-circular front opening allowed the light to come out, while the closed shape protected the flame from the wind and the horizontal handle made it easy to carry. This piece of popular art dates to the Almohad era.
f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.dates: Early hegira 7th century / Early AD 13th century.
f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.dimensions: Height 18.2 cm, width 16.2 cm, diameter (of base) 12.7 cm.
f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.method_for_datation: It was dated to the Almohad period on the basis of stratigraphy, since it was found in the abandoned levels of one of the houses of the citadel vacated after the Christian conquest of Mértola in AH 635–6 / AD 1238.
f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.method_for_provenance: The technical and formal characteristics of this piece are typical of items produced in Mértola, although many similar items are to be found in the Valencia region (Spain).
f26b90aa-a82b-52f5-8ce6-f87882cade6c.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

f2c8cba4-0106-5aa6-880a-9d7bcd2e17ae.name: Tile
f2c8cba4-0106-5aa6-880a-9d7bcd2e17ae.short_description: Decorated in the *cuerda seca* technique, this pair of tiles displays three riders on horseback in brilliant colours. *Cuerda seca* literally meaning dry cord, is a technique that used coloured glaze to produce a polychrome tile. During the process, thin outline bands made of greasy substance are applied to avoid a mixture of glaze while firing. This technique, which was popular among the Iranian potters was introduced in Turkey as early as the 14th century.

f3529449-1169-568c-8cd7-715fa25e50d1.name: Wall tile.
f3529449-1169-568c-8cd7-715fa25e50d1.description: A tile which once formed a part of a continuous decorative scheme of cypress trees and vases of flowers. The Cypress tree is rendered with a spiky border and filled-in with a lighter coloured fish-scale pattern; vases with flowers are positioned between the trees. A similar, if not identical scheme of decorative tiles (dating to the AH 10th / AD 16th century), can be seen in the mausoleum of the famous Sufi Saint, Muhyi al-Din ibn Arabi (AH 560–637 / AD 1165–1240), located inside the Sultan Salim I Mosque in Damascus. The use of cypress trees is appropriate for such a monument, since the cypress is said to symbolise potential wholeness for, biologically, the tree holds both the masculine and feminine principles within it. It is known as the 'perfect Muslim' because of its submission 'Islam' to the wind: 'God's will'.
f3529449-1169-568c-8cd7-715fa25e50d1.short_description: This tile once formed part of a continuous decorative scheme of cypresses and flowers. The cypress tree here is rendered with a spiky border and filled in with a lighter-coloured fish-scale pattern. Similar ones still decorate the shrine of the Sufi saint Muhyi al-Din ibn Arabi in Damascus.
f3529449-1169-568c-8cd7-715fa25e50d1.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: several examples of this type of Ottoman tile survive, including those still on the walls of the Ibn Arabi Shrine in Damascus.
f3529449-1169-568c-8cd7-715fa25e50d1.method_for_provenance: Several examples of this type of Ottoman tile survive, including those still on the walls of the Ibn Arabi Shrine in Damascus, Syria.

f42153ad-bbe2-59c3-9421-b699313f7273.name: Lustre vase with figural decoration
f42153ad-bbe2-59c3-9421-b699313f7273.short_description: This tall fritware vase with its facetted body, tapering neck and projecting lip most certainly copies a metal prototype. Its sides are covered by two horizontal registers above and below, with individual seated figures reserved against a solid lustre background. A band of abstract scrolling separates the registers around the middle.

f4606868-6540-5152-bd07-486c73a7f541.name: Jug
f4606868-6540-5152-bd07-486c73a7f541.short_description: Çanakkale was a pottery production centre between the end of 17th century and first quarter of the 20th century where pottery with interesting and original forms was produced. Mostly coarse red clay and occasionally beige-coloured paste was used. This vase has pear-like shape with a long neck. On its neck there are three horn-like projecting forms. On the sides and in the front there are embossed decorations.

f4aca485-b1db-583e-b83d-c9c533f030c1.name: Jug with a monochrome yellow glaze and three handles
f4aca485-b1db-583e-b83d-c9c533f030c1.description:
Discovered in a house during the 1959 excavations in Murwab, northwest Qatar, this partially reconstructed jug must have had a striking and shiny appearance.  
  
It originally had three rounded handles on the shoulder, two of which are preserved, and is entirely covered with a monochrome yellow glaze. The small size of this jug and its decoration make it a delicate piece of tableware. It could have been a 'table vinegar jar' used to hold sweet and sour sauces that were very popular in the 9th century, as shown in ancient
f4aca485-b1db-583e-b83d-c9c533f030c1.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

f4b3d07d-c2d5-525a-b872-a65798f5a227.name: Jug with spout.
f4b3d07d-c2d5-525a-b872-a65798f5a227.description:
Earthenware ceramics with a dark-brown metallic lustre glaze were produced in the city of Raqqa during the AH 6th–first half of the 7th / AD 12th–first half of the 13th centuries. What distinguishes these ceramics from those made in other places and periods are the types of colours used, particularly distinctive is the dark-brown.  
This jug represents a ceramic of this type. It has a columnar base, a globe-shaped body and a long cylindrical neck with an outward flaying lip. It is outfitted with a long tubular spout and a handle that juts out parallel to the lip and which curves perpendicularly downward to attach at the periphery of the body.  
The jug is decorated with dark-brown lustre glaze from the top of the lip, spout, handle, and neck all the way down to the bulk of the globular body, applied in a series of horizontal bands portraying calligraphic, pseudo-calligraphic, stylised vegetal and geometric patterns. Contrasts in colour intensity and band width are also part of the decorative scheme. The transparent, dark-brown metallic lustre is covered with a layer of very light-green glaze.
f4b3d07d-c2d5-525a-b872-a65798f5a227.short_description: The region of Raqqa was a prolific producer of fine-quality underglazed lustre ceramics just before the Mongol invasion. The brown colour of this lustre is typical of Raqqa-ware.
f4b3d07d-c2d5-525a-b872-a65798f5a227.dates: Hegira 6th–first half of the 7th century / AD 12th–first half of the 13th century.
f4b3d07d-c2d5-525a-b872-a65798f5a227.method_for_datation: Lustre ware in this shade of dark-brown is known to have been produced in the 6th–first half of the 7th / 12th–first half of the 13th centuries in Raqqa. Production of ceramics ended after the Mongol invasion and destruction of the city in 656–7 / 1258–9.
f4b3d07d-c2d5-525a-b872-a65798f5a227.method_for_provenance: Wares with decorations of this type are known to have been produced in Raqqa, as evidenced by the studies of many Islamic scholars, including Oliver Watson.
f4b3d07d-c2d5-525a-b872-a65798f5a227.obtention: The piece was exchanged between the Damascus and Aleppo museums in 1931.

f4bcacb1-5ea8-5c29-af93-fd4527263356.name: Spherical component of a mosque lamp
f4bcacb1-5ea8-5c29-af93-fd4527263356.short_description: Spherical component of a mosque lamp decorated with rosettes, cloud scrolls and arabesques. Stylistically, it is related to an inscribed mosque lamp that bears the signature of the artist Musli al-Din and the date 1549. It is quite possible that both items are works of the same artist, created on the occasion of the restoration of the Dome of the Rock at Jerusalem by Süleyman the Magnificent.

f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.name: Glazed bowl.
f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.description:
Glazed bowl with everted rim with small horizontal edge, circular mouth, hemispherical body and convex base with vertical foot-ring. The exterior is coated in an almost transparent whitish glaze. The interior is decorated with a polychrome glaze in white, green, purple and yellow, with an unusual schematic figurative style. The central motif consists of a lively hunting scene in which a hound and a bird (perhaps a hawk or eagle) are simultaneously attacking a gazelle. The bird carries in its mouth a spiral-shaped object which may be a snake or a branch. The rim has a scalloped pattern of black arcs filled with green glaze.  
When it was in use, the object was repaired with clamps. There are also holes in the base which were probably used for hanging the bowl on the wall. The object has been restored.
f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.short_description: Bowl depicting a hunting scene in which a greyhound and a falcon attack a gazelle. There is a spiral-shaped object in the bird’s mouth. This piece, dated to the second half of the AH 5th / AD 11th century, is similar to others from the western Mediterranean and was imported from Kairouan (Tunisia).
f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.dates: Hegira second half of 5th century / AD second half of 11th century.
f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.dimensions: Height 13 cm, maximum diameter 39 cm, diameter (of base) 13.6 cm.
f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated by comparison with objects of similar form from Qal'a Banu Hammad (Algeria), Tunis and Kairouan (Tunisia), Denia and Cartagena (Spain), and Pisa (Italy).
f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.method_for_provenance: The provenance of this type of ceramic is currently disputed. The abundance of objects with this decorative style in Kairouan has led researchers to attribute it to this origin, but analyses of pastes carried out on the objects from Mértola and Pisa contradict this theory and suggest that they may in fact come from the south of the Iberian Peninsula.
f4d8be9c-5207-5d6b-9a80-d65d6b7fa366.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

f511489c-c7b5-5630-aeeb-24e9da8d840d.name: Bowl
f511489c-c7b5-5630-aeeb-24e9da8d840d.short_description:
“He who believes in a reward \[from God\] is generous with gifts,” reads the Arab saying on this bowl.  
It is difficult to read the phrase, which begins with the four dots, because the exceedingly elegant *Kufi* calligraphy is interwoven and knotted and also embellished with a variety of palmettes.
materials: Earthenware, covered with a white slip and painted in a brown and red slip under a transparent glaze

f54ccda0-cd2f-59b9-b97e-ba28a8e6ef05.name: Pedestal bowl or tazza
f54ccda0-cd2f-59b9-b97e-ba28a8e6ef05.description: A deep bowl, decorated in blue and white, with a sloping rim and supported on a pedestal base. The rim has been embellished with a pattern of rocks and waves, whilst the cavetto is decorated with floral sprays with a medallion surrounded by palmettes at the very centre. The base is also decorated with floral sprays.

f56a2d5c-e6e8-5033-bd68-1e28dd46edad.name: Bowl with two facing peacocks
f56a2d5c-e6e8-5033-bd68-1e28dd46edad.short_description: Birds were a popular subject in the Abbasid period, as artists working in many media transformed the creatures’ beaks and wings into increasingly abstracted designs. The symmetrical pattern of two peacocks facing each other finds iconographic precedents in examples dating from the late antique and Byzantine periods, where it often carried paradisiacal connotations. Monochrome lustre examples such as this were characteristic of the second phase of Abbasid lustreware, which developed in centres in Iraq in the tenth century. The word blessing appears in Arabic on the glazed underside of this bowl.
f56a2d5c-e6e8-5033-bd68-1e28dd46edad.dates: Hegira mid-4th century / AD second–third quarter 10th century

f5b2109e-d0d5-5d0d-bfe9-a0c8b044bdd8.name: Fragment of plate.
f5b2109e-d0d5-5d0d-bfe9-a0c8b044bdd8.description:
Fragment of a ceramic plate, ornamented with an animal and epigraphic representation that has been traced out in brown with a paintbrush on a lead glaze. The circular band surrounding the animal decoration features an inscription in *kufic* characters, the contours of which are traced in brown. The space between these characters is also painted brown. The inscription consists of a word repeated twice, '*al-yumn*' (prosperity). The first word is preceded by the last letter of the word itself, and the second is followed by the first letter of this word, suggesting that the word was repeated around the entire circumference of the band. The animal decoration sits at the centre of the plate, surrounded by a circle, and consists of a fragmented lion represented by a head and a section of shoulder. The head is turned to the front, the eyes are wide open, and the mane is dense and wavy. The lower part of the face is missing, but the first photograph of this fragment, published by Golvin (see Bibliography), shows the missing part of the face: the muzzle, the 'moustache' and a part of the falling mane, giving the impression that the lion is in movement. The space between the lion and the circle is ornamented with two trefoil motifs, one complete and the other incomplete, which suggests that this motif was repeated right around the lion. A remaining section of the circular base can be seen at the back of the fragment. Two other fragments of the same plate are kept at the National Museum of Cirta. One of these features the outline that delineates the lion's back and snake-like tail, and the word '*al-yumn'* on the band.  
The use of brown is one of the characteristics of Hammadid ceramics. The thinness of the paste and the presence of painted motifs indicate that it forms part of an expensive piece of crockery in comparison to other shards found in the Qal'at Bani Hammad.
f5b2109e-d0d5-5d0d-bfe9-a0c8b044bdd8.short_description: Fragment of a dish decorated with the representation of a lion in the centre and an inscription brush-painted around the edge in brown, a colour common in Hammadid ceramics, on top of a lead glaze. The inscription in *kufic* characters repeats the word '*al-yumn*' (prosperity).
f5b2109e-d0d5-5d0d-bfe9-a0c8b044bdd8.dimensions: Height 9.50 cm, length 16 cm, diameter of the base 13 cm.
f5b2109e-d0d5-5d0d-bfe9-a0c8b044bdd8.method_for_datation: The fragment was found in the Qal'at Bani Hammad (5th–6th / 11th–12th). In addition, it features the formal characteristics of Hammadid ceramics and pottery.

f655d504-175d-5d78-8a32-37fc546a4cb2.name: Dish
f655d504-175d-5d78-8a32-37fc546a4cb2.short_description: The massive spread of the pottery made in Iznik had a clear influence on the so-called “Kubachi ceramic”, named after a small village in the Caucasus where countless pottery shards have been found. The dish shows a half-length figure with finely drawn face and vividly decorated garment and hat, set against coloured and varied vegetation.

f67cfcaf-ae72-562f-8eff-5a0f72c4615d.description: This complete table bowl was discovered during the Murwab excavation by the Qatari-French Mission in 2009. This bowl has an open wall and was used to present food prepared at the table. It has a horizontal rim with a rounded end (16cm in diameter) and a flat annular base (8cm in diameter). The glaze is quite damaged and the painted decoration can only be seen in a few places with brown touches of lustreware.

f68ad2e3-66ed-57d2-8adb-c0e1504537b3.name: Glazed bowl.
f68ad2e3-66ed-57d2-8adb-c0e1504537b3.description: Glazed bowl with rounded everted rim, circular mouth, semi-oval body and flat base. The object has an exterior finish in honey-coloured monochrome glaze, and a polychrome glaze of white, green and purple in the interior, representing a plant motif consisting of a radial composition of eight lotus flowers topped by another set of eight oval lotus flowers. On the rim is a composition in four parts with alternating semi-circles and phytomorphic motifs. It has a defect at the bottom caused by the glaze coming into contact with another object in the kiln. The object has been restored.
f68ad2e3-66ed-57d2-8adb-c0e1504537b3.short_description: Glazed bowl with a plant motif consisting of a radial composition of eight triangular lotus flowers each topped with an oval lotus flower. This piece is similar to others found in Madinat al-Zahra and probably came from the Córdoba region.
f68ad2e3-66ed-57d2-8adb-c0e1504537b3.dimensions: Height 6 cm, maximum diameter 29 cm, diameter (of base) 17 cm.
f68ad2e3-66ed-57d2-8adb-c0e1504537b3.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated to the second half of the 4th / 10th century, by comparison with objects of identical form found in Madinat al-Zahra (Córdoba, Spain).
f68ad2e3-66ed-57d2-8adb-c0e1504537b3.method_for_provenance: The shape, ornamental theme and type of paste used are very similar to ceramics from the Córdoba area.
f68ad2e3-66ed-57d2-8adb-c0e1504537b3.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

f7a106fc-4854-569f-bbae-0f22ab8f3514.name: Jar.
f7a106fc-4854-569f-bbae-0f22ab8f3514.description:
This two-handled globular jar with a long, narrow neck is marked along its body with numerous parallel furrows, made when it was turned, which come together towards the top. There are button-shaped grips on the top of the handles. It is decorated in white on a dark engobe (slip) with central horizontal lines alternating with pseudo-epigraphic motifs in *kufic* characters and oblique lines below. The double braid of linked hearts is a typical Islamic motif deriving from stylisation of the palm tree.  
The jar was found, together with other pieces, by the archaeologist Antonio Salinas in the space between the intrados of a vault and the floor of a room of the monastery attached to the Martorana Church built around 1193. The crack in the lower part of the amphora, caused by a firing defect, indicates that the piece, a kiln reject no longer usable as a container, was used to fill vaults in large residences in the first half of the 12th century.
f7a106fc-4854-569f-bbae-0f22ab8f3514.short_description: This jar was intended as a container for foodstuffs, but was actually used as a building material to fill a vault because it had a firing defect that made it unsuitable for use as a container.
f7a106fc-4854-569f-bbae-0f22ab8f3514.owner: Sopraintendenza Beni Culturali e Ambientali, Palermo.
f7a106fc-4854-569f-bbae-0f22ab8f3514.method_for_datation: The fact that the amphora was found in the vaults of the monastery of Martorana Church (built around 1193) suggests that it dates from the 12th century.
f7a106fc-4854-569f-bbae-0f22ab8f3514.method_for_provenance: As a kiln reject, the jar must have been produced locally.
f7a106fc-4854-569f-bbae-0f22ab8f3514.provenance: Church of Santa Maria dell’Ammiraglio, known as the Martorana.

f837717d-83cb-539f-a08b-54027e48d0cc.name: Bowl
f837717d-83cb-539f-a08b-54027e48d0cc.short_description: This ceramic dish is decorated with polychrome, a rosette in the middle. Large spiral-shaped blue tendrils surround the rosette.
f837717d-83cb-539f-a08b-54027e48d0cc.method_for_datation: Work of the 19th century, information from arts dealer.

f84583de-c1e4-56f1-9283-97d00c1e16ce.name: Bottle
f84583de-c1e4-56f1-9283-97d00c1e16ce.short_description: Large fritware pear-shaped bottle with a low foot and tapers to a slender elongated neck at the base of which is a molding. The body is incised all over with a motif of rounded half palmettes.
f84583de-c1e4-56f1-9283-97d00c1e16ce.dates: Hegira late 6th–early 7th century / AD late 12th–early 13th century

f8bbc39a-7541-53c4-abb0-e71124f95b62.name: Bowl.
f8bbc39a-7541-53c4-abb0-e71124f95b62.description:
A large, footed bowl, decorated with underglaze painting in blue, white, and a dark cobalt-blue. The exterior features prominent cloud-bands and arabesques executed in white on a blue background. Both are characterised by the use of tight spirals, as for example in the cloud-bands and the floral motifs interspersed between them. The foot is encircled by a chain of floral motifs. The bowl's interior features a central medallion with a pattern of arabesques and floral stems. It sits at the centre of an eight-pointed star-shape formed by lines in dark cobalt on a white background sprinkled with dot-motifs. The points of the star, in turn, have pendants which are framed by a repeat pattern in blue containing arabesque patterns in an idiom similar to those in the bowl's centre. The extraordinary size of this bowl, as well as the skill with which it is decorated, suggests production for the highest levels of the Ottoman hierarchy, although direct evidence for this is lacking. A nearly identical bowl survives in the Louvre (inv. no. 7880–92), suggesting that a common mould and design model (probably a drawing) were used for both objects.  
  
This bowl is one of a group of similar wares which have been attributed to a workshop whose chief designer has been dubbed 'Master of the Knots'. A favourite motif of this workshop is the use of interlacing lines to form elaborate knot-patterns, as seen in the interior of this bowl. Decorative knot-patterns were common not only in Ottoman art of the late AH 9th / AD 15th century, but in the wider Islamic world as well (compare, for example, the patterns on 'Veneto-Saracenic' metalwork).
f8bbc39a-7541-53c4-abb0-e71124f95b62.short_description: A very large footed bowl on a high foot, decorated with prominent cloud-bands and arabesques in white on a blue background. The size and quality of this bowl suggests that it was made for a high-ranking Ottoman official, possibly for washing the feet during ablutions.
f8bbc39a-7541-53c4-abb0-e71124f95b62.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

f95147cd-064e-504e-9da8-bdc09cd25791.name: Bowl
f95147cd-064e-504e-9da8-bdc09cd25791.short_description: A special variant of blue-and-white ceramic seems to have evolved in Kerman: frugal patterns were incised in sgraffito technique into a thickly coated blue glaze. The two medallions filled with Arabesques are the sole ornaments on the bowl, beautifully enhanced through the distinct colour contrast. The few preserved pieces of this ceramic group are remarkable for their precise form of decoration. It is also assumed that the blue background represents the sky.

materials: Ceramic with cobalt blue glaze, decoration in sgraffito technique

f99b0b36-e5fc-56c8-9a6f-400862cc44ab.name: Glazed bowl with cobalt-blue decoration
f99b0b36-e5fc-56c8-9a6f-400862cc44ab.description:
This large, straight-sided bowl has a continuous loop-and-circle design painted in cobalt blue on a white or cream opaque glaze. The shape and colour of the bowl are highly typical of early Abbasid decorated glazed wares and were originally inspired by AH 2nd-3d / AD 7th–8th-century Chinese ceramics.  
  
Muslim, Christian and Jewish merchants from the Gulf region, Iraq and Iran had trading posts in southern China and imported various products, including ceramics. These imported ceramics reached the great port of Basra (Iraq) by the middle of the 8th century. Famous potters' workshops in Susa (Iran) or Samarra (Iraq) produced their own designs for this type of ware. Their products were distributed throughout the Middle East and the Gulf, including Qatar.
f99b0b36-e5fc-56c8-9a6f-400862cc44ab.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

f9bb568b-afa8-55b3-9d37-45f6a17b547a.name: Dish
f9bb568b-afa8-55b3-9d37-45f6a17b547a.short_description: Fez is an important centre for Moroccan pottery and is particularly associated with a distinctive form of blue and white ceramic ware which became popular in the late 19th century. This dish, or *tabsil*, was used to serve foods with a sauce. The dish was donated to the V&A by George Maw, founder of Maw & Co., a British manufacturer of ceramic tiles. The company won many medals and awards at the international exhibitions which were a feature of the late 19th century. This dish was displayed at the 1871 Annual International Exhibition held in London. A label on its base suggests that it was loaned to the exhibition by George Maw.

fa4916ad-b0f5-5f83-898a-6d97cf9229fd.name: Vase with zoomorphic design
fa4916ad-b0f5-5f83-898a-6d97cf9229fd.description: This vase with zoomorphic decoration perpetuates the shape of ritual libation vases of Zoroastrianism, a religion originating in Iran in the first millennium BC. The pouring spout is topped by a bull’s head whose snout is hollow. Its decoration, in relief, is divided into separate concentric registers whose motifs are geometric and floral.

fa7b3b4f-6bf6-5a1a-84fd-8f70a066b1c8.name: Fragment of a panel with ceramic inlay.
fa7b3b4f-6bf6-5a1a-84fd-8f70a066b1c8.description:
Fragment of a panel for wall-facing in ceramic marquetry, consisting of blue-green enamelled eight-cornered stars that have been combined with lustre-painted crosses with a metallic sheen that feature geometric motifs and epigraphy traced out by paintbrush. Some of the crosses are adorned with circles that enclose a motif reminiscent of a fish or of a flower on its stem, created in white against a yellow background. These circles appear in twos along each of the branches of the crosses. Other crosses are embellished with white ova on an olive green background, which appear in groups of four on the four branches of the crosses. The inscription '*al-yumn*' (prosperity), executed in *kufic* characters in white against a yellow background, is repeated on each of branches of the crosses.  
According to G. Marçais, 'this ceramic takes its inspiration from the 'Abbasid Orient, which itself borrowed from older Semitic or Byzantine civilisations'.  
These kinds of ceramic tile were reserved for wall-facing and were fixed onto the wall at a certain height above floor level. They thus covered the entire surrounding wall space within the rooms of the palace. The fact that they include an inscription confirms their purpose as facings for walls rather than for floors, contrary to what might have been supposed.
fa7b3b4f-6bf6-5a1a-84fd-8f70a066b1c8.short_description: Wall panel made of earthenware tiles decorated with eight-pointed stars in a blue glaze and crosses in a white glaze, as well as brush-painted motifs and inscriptions. It came from the Palace of the Sea (Dar al-Bahr) of Qal'at Bani Hammad.
fa7b3b4f-6bf6-5a1a-84fd-8f70a066b1c8.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
fa7b3b4f-6bf6-5a1a-84fd-8f70a066b1c8.dimensions: Length 96 cm, width 30.5 cm, diameter of the stars 21 cm, diameter of the crosses 21 cm.
fa7b3b4f-6bf6-5a1a-84fd-8f70a066b1c8.method_for_datation: Fragment found in the Dar al-Bahr of the Qal'at Bani Hammad, which dates from the 5th–6th /11th–12th centuries, according to Kitab al-Istibsar: 'The Banu Hammad built a number of important constructions in the *qal'a* … including \[the palace\] known as Dar al-Bahr, at the centre of which stood a vast fountain'.
fa7b3b4f-6bf6-5a1a-84fd-8f70a066b1c8.method_for_provenance: From the report of the De Beylié excavation, 1909; furthermore, the piece was discovered in Dar Bahr.

fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.name: Mosque lamp.
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.description:
This large mosque lamp is composed of a relatively stocky, globular body, over which sits an upper part that is shaped like a funnel. Three rounded handles, which are abstract renditions of snake-dragons, are fixed onto the lamp’s shoulder, and are used for the attachment of chains or cords from which to hang the light. These handles are decorated with floral motifs, as figurative decoration within mosques was prohibited. There is a hole in the middle of its arched, low ring-base, from which an ornamental tassel would have been hung.  
Empty white cartouches decorate part of the lamp’s body and neck. Its neck is also decorated with four blue geometric boxes of similar shape that are linked together by plaited knots, and which contain inscriptions denoting the names of Muhammad and Allah. The inscriptions themselves are interwoven with symbols of luck in the form of three spheres. More cartouches can be found on the decorative border along the lamp’s top edge. The ring-base is decorated with a plaited band. The cartouches on the body of the lamp, and the blue design across the transitional, narrowing space between body and neck, are embellished with a contour pattern of blossoms and leaves. Bands of plaited motifs adorn the space below the handles.  
Mosque lamps made in ceramic were produced in the manufacturing place of Iznik during the Ottoman period until the middle of the 16th century. In earlier centuries, mosque lamps were mainly made of glass and were produced in many regions and lands across the Islamic world. They are based on the so-called ‘Light Verse’ of the Qur’an (Sura 24, verse 35), which states: ‘Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth. His Light may be compared to a niche that enshrines a lamp’.  
Iznik Ottoman ceramic was as popular in Europe as it was in the Islamic world; so much so that Italian manufacturers in Padua, from the AD 17th century onwards, started imitating Turkish ceramics, in response to a ban at the time on private individuals buying Iznik ceramics manufactured in state workshops. The Iznik workshops went into decline from the AH mid-10th / AD mid-17th century onwards.
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.short_description: Mosque lamps such as this ceramic one were intended for use in a mausoleum or a mosque. It is decorated with geometric and floral designs and its inscriptions invoke God and Muhammad. The lamp would hang from the ceiling and would hold an additional container for the oil and wick.
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.owner: Museum of Arts and Crafts, Berlin.
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.dates: Hegira beginning of 10th century / AD beginning of 16th century.
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.method_for_datation: The mosque lamp belongs to a group of vessels, classified together because of their painted decoration, which are dated to the beginning of the 10th / 16th century.
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.method_for_provenance: This mosque lamp could only have originated from the Ottoman workshops of the town of Iznik, given the markings on the ceramic and the style of the paint work.
fb026c57-4f54-5328-a2fb-ee50db163e3b.obtention: Acquired in 1900 by the Arts and Crafts Museum, Berlin, and later transferred as a long-term loan to the Museum of Islamic Art.

fb5dd65d-0a8a-5813-b531-d008701b73be.name: Set of ten inscription frieze tiles
fb5dd65d-0a8a-5813-b531-d008701b73be.short_description: Ten luster tiles compose a frieze signed by Yusuf ibn 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Tahir, the son of the potter who made the DDFIA’s Veramin mihrab (48.327). The Abi Tahir family of Kashan, Iran, is famous for the production of exquisite tilework and ceramic vessels during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The inscription on this frieze is from the Qur’an’s well-known "Throne Verse" (2: 255). The final tile (lower left) is signed by Yusuf. Purchased in New York City, 1940.
