fb606a6f-b8ec-56c9-b78e-78a4d174a94c.name: Jar.
fb606a6f-b8ec-56c9-b78e-78a4d174a94c.description: A jar with blue and black underglaze painting of waterweed patterns and scrolling stems which decorate the sides of the jar. Both the colours of the glazes and the decoration recall Iranian designs, although the blue and black underglaze derived from Chinese wares and came via Iran to influence Syrian ceramics. The arrangement of alternating waterweed and scrolling stems are seen in contemporaneous tile panels in Damascus, where the impact of Chinese wares is witnessed still further in the use of such motifs such as willows, peonies and lotus blossoms. Jars of this shape were used for storage; this one perhaps held medicinal herbs.
fb606a6f-b8ec-56c9-b78e-78a4d174a94c.short_description: This glazed ceramic jar would have been used for storage, perhaps of medicinal herbs. The blue and black decoration was inspired by Iranian ceramics, in their turn influenced by Chinese wares.
fb606a6f-b8ec-56c9-b78e-78a4d174a94c.method_for_datation: The designs on this jar resemble a panel of hexagonal tiles in the complex of Ghars al-Din al-Khalil al-Tawrizi in Damascus, Syria, built just before his death in 833 / 1430.
fb606a6f-b8ec-56c9-b78e-78a4d174a94c.method_for_provenance: The designs on this jar resemble a panel of hexagonal tiles in the complex of Ghars al-Din al-Khalil al-Tawrizi in Damascus, Syria.

fbb80300-6593-572b-a139-40b31becb5db.name: *Mina´i* bowl
fbb80300-6593-572b-a139-40b31becb5db.short_description:
*Mina´i* means enamel in Persian, and the term refers to this type of pottery’s colorful decoration, which lies both in and over the glaze, here further enriched with gold. Like lusterware, it had to be fired twice and was consequently costly.  
The figures are the Turkish-Mongol type, found in all the Persian art of the day and reflected the ruling class’s ethnicity.
keywords: Bowl; Iran; Turkish-Mongol type; Fritware; Figural motifs; minai
materials: Fritware, with polychrome decoration and gold leaf in and over an opaque, white glaze. *Mina'i type*

fbcc03c6-bc1c-58ea-b5ef-157f9009dc3c.name: Dish with floral decoration.
fbcc03c6-bc1c-58ea-b5ef-157f9009dc3c.description: Large dish with a foot-ring, curved sides and a narrow slanting brim. The decoration, traced in black lines on a white background beneath a lead glaze with colour haloing, is painted in blue-violet, green and red lake in low relief. There are some remains of decoration in gold applied above the glaze. The dish shows a typical bush with leaves and flowers including tulips, hyacinths and carnations. The brim shows the customary painted and highly stylised ‘wave-and-rock’ motif. There are small floral elements, alternately in green and blue, along the outer side, with noticeable colour haloing.
fbcc03c6-bc1c-58ea-b5ef-157f9009dc3c.short_description: This plate, typically decorated with a leafy bush and various flowers, as well as the equally common ‘wave-and-rock’ motif on its brim, is an example of 17th-century late Iznik production.
fbcc03c6-bc1c-58ea-b5ef-157f9009dc3c.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
fbcc03c6-bc1c-58ea-b5ef-157f9009dc3c.method_for_provenance: The dish is a typical example of late Iznik production (11th / 17th century) for its less precise design and use of colours.

fcf42d5a-d05c-5ebc-88f3-195d584999e1.name: Vase with curved handles
fcf42d5a-d05c-5ebc-88f3-195d584999e1.short_description: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans. The idea was part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Spanish and Arabian motifs became fashionable in the mid-19th century. The Spanish medieval pottery showed a very strong representation of Romantic Orientalism and inspired a beautiful production of "winged vases"(18th to 19th century). The majolica vase with curved handles is painted in blue and red-brown metallic lustre over a white background. It has a long neck, imitating the Hispanic-Moorish tradition, and its decoration shows a stylised floral motif. It can be dated around mid-19th century for its form and decoration technique.
fcf42d5a-d05c-5ebc-88f3-195d584999e1.holder: Museo Artistico Industriale, National Gallery of Ancient Art in Palazzo Barberini

fd011d86-ad03-55b4-93a7-ea2962665bca.name: Fragment from a container.
fd011d86-ad03-55b4-93a7-ea2962665bca.description:
This piece appears to be the bottom of a glazed pottery container, which is decorated on the interior by two polo-sticks, symbolising polo, a sport that the Mamluks were deeply interested in, especially during the period of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who ruled three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1294–5; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40. Amongst the Mamluk officers, the master of the two polo-sticks blazon was called 'al-Jokandar', 'Jokan' meaning in Persian (Farsi) two polo-sticks, and 'dar' meaning bearer or master. This blazon appears on many Islamic objects made from ceramic, inlaid copper, glass or textiles as well as other mediums. The blazon was an emblem symbolising a specific office and had been used by *amirs* and sultans since the AH 6th / AD 12th century on their buildings, possessions and other objects as a means of indicating their ownership of them. The system of office blazons came to an end with the fall of the Mamluk dynasty in AH 923 / AD 1517.  
Glazed pottery is considered to be the most prolific medium used to make objects for the residences of Mamluk *amir*s. This might be the reason for the abundant use of blazons – in addition to inscriptions which bear the titles of *amir*s and vegetal, animal and geometric motifs – in the decoration of such pieces as this.
fd011d86-ad03-55b4-93a7-ea2962665bca.short_description: The blazon is the symbol which sultans and amirs put on their possessions and buildings to indicate their official posts. The blazon on this fragment from the bottom of a clay vessel glazed with a layer of enamel indicates that its owner was the master of the polo game ('al-Jokandar').
fd011d86-ad03-55b4-93a7-ea2962665bca.method_for_datation: The object is dated based on the technique of glazed-pottery production that was used on it, a method that was known in the late Mamluk period after a marked deterioration in the quality of ceramics had taken place. Studying the blazon ornamenting the bottom of the container also sheds light on the date.
fd011d86-ad03-55b4-93a7-ea2962665bca.method_for_provenance: The piece was most probably produced in Egypt as excavations carried out at Fustat revealed that a cheaper kind of pottery was produced during the decline of the Mamluk Dynasty, replacing the high-quality ceramics produced in the early Mamluk period.
fd011d86-ad03-55b4-93a7-ea2962665bca.obtention: The object was discovered during the course of archaeological excavations in Fustat in 1918.

fd693de4-6eae-5786-94f7-4f1e23d9aedd.name: *Zellij* panel.
fd693de4-6eae-5786-94f7-4f1e23d9aedd.description:
Panel of a wall covering from the Badi Palace consisting of a mosaic of glazed ceramic pieces or *zellij*. Its *testir* decoration is entirely geometric. Its design employs star shapes, squares and triangles, and its composition is radial.  
Thin knotwork lines alternating between blue and black spread from a centrepiece consisting of a 16-pointed star surrounded by a black fillet to form a large cross shape delimited by black knotwork, inside which there is a myriad of small white twinkling stars. Other yellow-ochre, blue and black knotwork lines branch out from this figure to make other larger compositions and star motifs that extend to the edges of the panel.  
This small sample of *zellij* facing is testimony to the finesse and magnificence of the famous panels with which the walls of the Badi Palace were covered, which its founder, the Sa'did monarch Mansur al-Dhahabi (the Doric) wanted to be more beautiful and larger than in the Alhambra in Granada. The coverings of its ceilings and walls were praised by both Moroccan chroniclers and foreign visitors who were received in the Badi Palace in its heyday, before it was entirely destroyed and pillaged at the beginning of the 'Alawid era.
fd693de4-6eae-5786-94f7-4f1e23d9aedd.short_description: This *zellij* panel has a radiating composition and is decorated with star, square and triangle shapes. It is evidence of the finesse and magnificence of the wainscoting in the Badi Palace, whose founder wanted panelling more beautiful than that of the Alhambra.
fd693de4-6eae-5786-94f7-4f1e23d9aedd.method_for_datation: The construction of the monument from which it came would have begun in AH 986 / AD 1578 and would have been completed in AH 1002 / AD 1594.
fd693de4-6eae-5786-94f7-4f1e23d9aedd.method_for_provenance: Object found during excavation of the monument.
fd693de4-6eae-5786-94f7-4f1e23d9aedd.obtention: Salvaged by the Historical Monuments Department after the site was excavated.

fd9231ec-9280-5e60-8248-b9d7c9cf8d62.name: Cup with foot.
fd9231ec-9280-5e60-8248-b9d7c9cf8d62.description: A cup with a foot in ivory-white depicting a court scene in the centre. A young prince is seated on a throne with a tall back on which two falcons are perched. The prince is flanked by two courtiers and at his feet are two peacocks, symbols of royalty, facing each other. Around the central motif are painted pairs of sphinxes face to face, separated by small medallions. On the inside edge of the cup is a votive inscription in *kufic* script and on the outside an inscription in pseudo-*kufic* calligraphy between arabesques.
fd9231ec-9280-5e60-8248-b9d7c9cf8d62.short_description: Seljuq bowl with a court scene in the centre and facing sphinxes, separated by small medallions, painted around this central motif. The inner edge bears an inscription in *kufic* script, and there is a pseudo-*kufic* inscription surrounded by arabesques on the outside.
fd9231ec-9280-5e60-8248-b9d7c9cf8d62.dates: Hegira end of 6th or beginning of 7th century / AD end of 12th or beginning of 13th century.
fd9231ec-9280-5e60-8248-b9d7c9cf8d62.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis methods and by comparison with pieces from the Seljuq period.
fd9231ec-9280-5e60-8248-b9d7c9cf8d62.method_for_provenance: By expert examination. In correspondence relating to the sale of the object, L.A. Raffy provides a 'guarantee of the authenticity of the ceramic from Persia'.

feee4da0-04af-5864-b229-a94005de718d.name: Glazed bowl.
feee4da0-04af-5864-b229-a94005de718d.description: Glazed bowl with rounded rim, circular mouth, slightly carinate hemispherical body and convex base with diagonal foot-ring. The exterior is glazed in honey-coloured monochrome and the interior is decorated in the *cuerda seca* technique in which the white, green and honey colours of the glaze are separated by lines of manganese. The decorative theme is a large flower created by a radial geometric composition which occupies all of the decorated space and which may correspond to a lotus flower viewed from above. Examples identical to this object have been found in various parts of the western Mediterranean, in particular in the citadel of Málaga, in Cartagena, Palma de Mallorca (Spain), Pisa (Italy) and Ceuta (Morocco). The object has been restored.
feee4da0-04af-5864-b229-a94005de718d.short_description: Bowl decorated entirely using *cuerda seca* and decorated with a large flower created by a geometric radial pattern that occupies all of the decorative space. The central motif is a lotus flower seen from above. Similar pieces have been found around the western Mediterranean.
feee4da0-04af-5864-b229-a94005de718d.dimensions: Height 8.5 cm, diameter (of mouth) 26 cm, diameter (of base) 10.5 cm.
feee4da0-04af-5864-b229-a94005de718d.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated to the 6th / 12th century by comparison with objects of similar shape and decorative technique from Málaga and Almería.
feee4da0-04af-5864-b229-a94005de718d.method_for_provenance: The abundance of this type of ceramic in Málaga and Almería (Spain), where kilns have been found in which they were made, has led researchers to attribute its production to these towns.
feee4da0-04af-5864-b229-a94005de718d.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

ff2095d9-b276-5a8d-8731-45db9248f0d8.name: Jar.
ff2095d9-b276-5a8d-8731-45db9248f0d8.description:
This two-handled globular jar with a long, narrow neck is marked along its body with numerous parallel furrows, made when it was turned, which come together towards the top. There are button-shaped grips on the top of the handles (one missing). It is decorated in white on a dark engobe (slip) with horizontal lines alternating with pseudo-epigraphic motifs in *kufic* characters.  
The jar was found, together with other pieces, by the archaeologist Antonio Salinas in the space between the intrados of a vault and the floor of a room of the monastery attached to the Martorana Church built around 1193. The crack in the lower part of the amphora, caused by a firing defect, indicates that the piece, a kiln reject no longer usable as a container, was used to fill vaults in the large residences in the first half of the 12th century.
ff2095d9-b276-5a8d-8731-45db9248f0d8.short_description: This jar was intended as a container for foodstuffs, but was actually used as a building material to fill a vault because it had a firing defect that made it unsuitable for use as a container.
ff2095d9-b276-5a8d-8731-45db9248f0d8.owner: Sopraintendenza Beni Culturali e Ambientali, Palermo.
ff2095d9-b276-5a8d-8731-45db9248f0d8.method_for_datation: The fact that the amphora was found in the vaults of the monastery of Martorana Church (built around 1193) suggests that it dates from the 12th century.
ff2095d9-b276-5a8d-8731-45db9248f0d8.method_for_provenance: As a kiln reject, the jar must have been produced locally.
ff2095d9-b276-5a8d-8731-45db9248f0d8.provenance: Church of Santa Maria dell’Ammiraglio, known as Martorana.

ff401773-95b4-5d80-9dca-780e741d09d7.name: Tile panel
ff401773-95b4-5d80-9dca-780e741d09d7.short_description: This panel is composed of 236 rectangular tiles, which are joined in pairs to form one design unit. The majority of the paired tiles feature an octagonal coffer design with a blossom surrounded by rayed circles. Doris Duke purchased this group of tiles from the Hearst collection in 1941. Though their provenance is unknown prior to Hearst's acquisition, similar tiles are known to have come from the church at Santiago, Carmona, in Spain.

ffd585a4-8d7b-569f-b9b6-1671b03cf69b.name: Oil lamps
ffd585a4-8d7b-569f-b9b6-1671b03cf69b.short_description: In North Africa, urban ceramic production is strictly the domain of professional male potters. Their wheel-made and glazed vessels are produced in specialized workshops expressly for sale. In rural areas pottery is almost entirely made by women alongside their domestic work. They produce a wide range of utilitarian unglazed non-wheel-made earthenware, such as storage pots and containers for food and liquids. Village women produce their pottery primarily to fill their own family’s needs, or for local exchange, which permits them to acquire grain or other items of barter from their neighbours. They decorate their products with elaborate and intricate geometric patterns associated with fertility and abundance. Presently, throughout the Maghreb ceramics hand-made by the women are disappearing.

ffff8d3d-ab9b-5733-9ca0-900b6b34002e.name: *Ghotar* concave dish
ffff8d3d-ab9b-5733-9ca0-900b6b34002e.description:
The radiant design is organised around the seal of Solomon, or eight-pointed star, that adorns the centre of the dish. The contour of the star is painted blue, and a flower with eight green petals is inside it. The star is on a white background with small yellow patterns outlined in black. Oval patterns extend from the points of the star. Decorated concentric bands complete the ornamentation of the piece.  
The decoration and form are characteristic of Moroccan ceramics between the 17th and 19th centuries. They are widespread in Morocco and Spain, and even in France. An Andalusian influence can be seen in certain features, such as the use of geometry. The piece reflects the polychrome earthenware made in Fes, but also in Safi, a production centre. In the 19th century, colours were more assertive, shapes heavier, and decorations less spontaneous than before. This piece is of high technical and aesthetic quality.
